# PREFACE

)( 2

<image-desc>An historiated ornamental initial 'M' at the start of the first paragraph. The letter is white with thick bands, set within a square frame featuring a detailed woodcut illustration. Having set aside the pseudonymous writer on <term>square or measured music</term> <note>original: "musica quadrata seu mensurata"; this refers to early notation where the shape of the note defined its duration</note> found among the works of the Venerable Bede (Volume 1, page 372), we rightly place Master FRANCO of Paris at the forefront of this final volume of ancient writers on song and music. He is the true pioneer of our modern music, which we call <term>figured music</term> <note>original: "musica figurata"; music using complex rhythms and distinct note shapes</note>. Whether Johannes Spadarius, in the defense of his teacher Bartolomé Ramos, names this man or another Franco as a German from Cologne, I do not know, as I do not have a copy of his book. Gesner, in his *Library*, makes him English, while Bontempi claims he was Italian. Father Giovanni Battista Martini, in the first volume of his *History of Music* (page 169), judges that our Franco likely wrote in the 11th century. Certainly, John of Salisbury, who flourished toward the end of the 12th century, complains in the sixth chapter of the first book of his *Polycraticus* about the "cutting" of notes and phrases in the music of his time. Such divisions are exactly what we find in the <term>measurable music</term> <note>original: "musica mensurabilis"</note> of Franco. This style might be called a fragment of the most ancient rhythmic music, but one that is greatly varied. That older style confined itself to the skillful division of long and short syllables—a matter well-known and common to everyone. Indeed, as Quintilian testifies in the fourth chapter of the ninth book of his *Institutes*, even schoolboys know that a long syllable lasts two beats and a short one lasts one.

<summary>This preface introduces Franco of Paris as the foundational figure of measured music, discussing his uncertain nationality and dating his work relative to other historical scholars like John of Salisbury.</summary>
<keywords>Franco of Paris, measured music, music history, notation, rhythmic music, John of Salisbury, Giovanni Battista Martini</keywords>

# PREFACE.

FRANCO <note>Franco of Cologne, a 13th-century music theorist</note> is indeed more sparing in his division of musical time, as is MARCHETUS *of Padua*. In addition to Marchetus's *Lucidarium of Plain Music*, we also publish in this volume his *Orchard of Measured Music*, in which he frequently brings our aforementioned FRANCO onto the stage. These follow the *Science of the Art of Music* by ELIAS SALOMON, from which we have reproduced an image at the beginning of this volume—a figure of four voices singing (just as he explains the matter himself on page 59), with the *table of Master Nicholas of Lucca* <note>original: "Nicolai de Luduno"</note> attached. In this table, one may perceive a type of tailed notes <note>notes with stems</note> that goes further than what we noted in the work *On Song and Music* (Volume II, page 124) regarding JOHN *de Muris*. This John is counted among the most learned masters of mathematical science by BULÆUS in the *History of the University of Paris* (Volume IV, page 963), along with JOHN *de Ligneriis*, with whom he is said to have been very intimate. I remember seeing certain manuscript works of this kind by him in the Imperial Library at *Vienna*.

However, the esteemed BULÆUS seems to identify this JOHN as the same person as JULIAN *de Muris*, whom he later notes (in the same place, page 937) was elected Rector of the University in the month of *December*, 1350. We, however, find him consistently called JOHN in his various works or the digests of his works that we are publishing—excepting his *Mirror of Music* <note>Speculum musicae</note>. That work, preserved at *Paris*, must be his most complete and grandest labor; J. J. ROUSSEAU boasts in his *Dictionary of Music* (page 318) that he read almost the whole of it: *I had the courage* <note>original: "J'ais... eu le courage"</note> *to read it almost entirely, in order to verify the invention attributed to this author.* Rousseau is mistaken, however, when he says that the notes of figured music <note>polyphonic notation</note> received their final addition then, around the year 1330, as already...

# PREFACE

we have observed concerning our **JOHN** <note>Johannes de Muris, a prominent 14th-century music theorist</note>. **IMBERT** *of France* follows him precisely in his rules on measurable music <note>original: "menſurabili muſica," referring to rhythmic notation</note>, proceeding no further than what I have already noted in the previously cited passage regarding **JOHN** *de Muris*, of whom **IMBERT** was a scribe and abridger; for this reason, he has been omitted by us here.

Nevertheless, by the **14th** century, music possessed so many and such great vices, which **JOHN XXII** sharply criticized in the famous decree *Learned Ignorance* <note>original: "docta ignorantia," a papal decree from 1324/25 aimed at curbing complex polyphony in church</note> (Book III, Title I, *On the life and integrity of the Clergy*, single chapter). Nor, indeed, was it used indiscriminately in that same **14th** century, even in royal and Imperial chapels. What **VOLCMAR** relates in **OEFELIUS’S** *Writers of Bavarian Affairs* (Vol. II, p. 539) concerning **WENCESLAUS**, King of *Bohemia* and son of **OTTOCAR**,—that he was accustomed to hearing three masses daily, which he commanded to be solemnly sung before him "tonally"—can be understood as referring to choral chant <note>original: "cantu chorali," or plainsong</note>. It is a bit more, however, which is read in **JOHN** *of Winterthur* regarding Emperor **HENRY VII**: that he daily had the mass sung before him musically, or *chorally*, "tonally with notation."

In *van de* **HARDT’S** *Acts of the Council of Constance* (Vol. VI, p. 1160), among the petitions of the English theologian Richard **ULLERSTON** regarding the reformation of the Church Militant, Article **XII** is directed against the prerogative of singers and officials residing in the courts of lords. There, indeed, he does not condemn singing in the church, but wishes it to be cautioned that greater and better things in the church should not be omitted or hindered by these: namely, the preaching of the word of God, the study of Holy Scripture, holy meditation, and devout prayer without noise. In evidence of this matter, he adds, those who [are] more de-

# P R E F A C E.

*...they are more devout, yet by constantly insisting upon singing, they do not experience as much devotion in the loud shouting as they do in moderate silence; thus, they first recite the canonical hours without musical notation. They would not do this if more devotion were regularly increased within them through singing. And below: we have said these things regarding singers for this reason, because we see, as if with the evidence of our own eyes, that the higher prelates and even secular lords seem to have satisfied themselves and others in all respects if each of them possesses a "globe" <note>original: "globum"; likely referring to a rounded group or choir</note> of elite singers who make a noise for the sake of the world: for whom all the benefices they are able to procure are not sufficient.*

---

Next, we publish the *Introduction to Music* by **Johannes KECK**, a monk of *Tegernsee* <note>A famous Benedictine abbey in Bavaria</note> of the Order of Saint Benedict in *Bavaria*, who is also celebrated for his other writings. This work, composed around those very times—namely the middle of the 15th century—was written specifically for plainchant <term>plainchant: a body of chants used in the liturgies of the Western Church, traditionally unaccompanied</term>. In the manuscript, only a drawing of a pneumatic organ <note>An organ powered by air from bellows</note> is provided as a preface; this can already be seen in the work on song and music, where one may marvel at the simplicity of this instrument and its musical scale of pipes, which did not exceed twenty-one even well into the 15th century. At that time, **JOHANNES TINCTORIUS**, in his *Proportions of Music* (cited in Father **MARTINI**, loc. cit. p. 169), says that in his day the faculty of our music had received such an admirable increase that it seems to be a *new art* <note>original: "ars nova"; referring to the development of polyphony and new rhythmic notation</note>. What the state of music was at the end of the 15th century is shown by the *Musical Instruction* of **ADAM** of *Fulda*, which we are publishing, and finally by the *Constitutions of the Pontifical Chapel*, in which figured music <term>figured music: polyphonic music with complex rhythms, as opposed to plainchant</term> certainly has a place, while any musical instruments, and even organs, are banished.

<summary>This preface critiques the vanity of elaborate choral singing over silent devotion and introduces 15th-century musical treatises by Johannes Keck and Adam of Fulda. It highlights the technological simplicity of the organ during this period and the emergence of the "Ars Nova" or new art of music.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Keck, Johannes Tinctorius, Adam of Fulda, pneumatic organ, Ars Nova, Pontifical Chapel, Tegernsee, Bavaria, plainchant, figured music, liturgical devotion</keywords>

# P R E F A C E .

These organs indeed, and any other musical instruments, and furthermore figured music <term>figured music: polyphonic music featuring elaborate, independent melodic parts, as opposed to simple, unison chant</term> itself, have never until now been admitted into the Greek Church. Their art of chanting <note>original: "τέχνη ψαλτικὴ" (technē psaltikē)</note>—that is, the art of psalmody or singing—is published by us here, insofar as it was preserved for us through copper plates from the *St. Blaise* codex <note>Referring to the Benedictine Abbey of St. Blaise in the Black Forest, where a fire in 1768 destroyed many manuscripts</note> from the flames; in that fire of 1768, both the codex itself and quite significant collections made for that purpose perished, especially those made in *Italy*. In that country, I myself was present more than once at their sacred rites and admired the modesty and sweetness of their singing, performed in that constant and uniform manner which is found in their most ancient liturgical books. The very terms pertaining to this matter were explained in an epistle by *Metrophanes Critopulus* <note>A 17th-century Patriarch of Alexandria; the date 1539 in the text likely refers to an earlier source or is a typographical error for a later date</note> from the year 1539 [sic], which was published in 1740 at *Wittenberg* from the original manuscript; to this, *Johann Jeremias Crudelius* added an explanation of the names in a unique dissertation.

On the contrary, among us [in the Western Church], sacred music adapted to profane <note>secular or worldly</note> styles has always, up to this point, declined for the worse. This license <note>referring to lack of restraint or artistic excess</note> was rejected even outside of sacred rites in the theaters themselves by the *Greeks* and *Romans*. Among the Romans, it had indeed been established by the religion of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of Roman law, c. 450 BCE</note>: THEY SHALL MODERATE POPULAR JOY IN SONG, AND WITH STRINGS AND FLUTES, AND THEY SHALL JOIN IT WITH THE HONOR OF THE GODS. *Cicero* notes this regarding an actor in his *Paradoxes*: 

> If he moves even slightly out of rhythm, or if a verse is pronounced just one syllable too long or too short, he is hissed at and driven off.

And in Book III of *On the Orator*, number 98:

> How much softer and more delicate are the inflections and false notes in singing than those that are certain and severe; yet against these, not only the austere but, if they occur too often, even the multitude themselves protest.

# P R E F A C E .

Indeed, is it fitting that we Christians should be less strict in our temples than the pagans <term>gentiles: a term used here for the ancient Romans and Greeks who practiced non-Christian religions</term> were in their theaters? Or can it not often be said of our own sacred rites what *Ovid* says in Book III of the *Fasti* <note>original: "Fastorum"; Ovid's poetic calendar of Roman festivals and mythology</note> regarding the festivals consecrated to *Anna Perenna* <note>An ancient Roman deity of the circle of the year; her festival was famous for its wild, uninhibited revelry</note>?

# ANCIENT WRITERS
## ON
## SONG & MUSIC
## CHIEFLY ECCLESIASTICAL.
### PART III.

---

## THE MUSIC OF FRANCO.

### NOTICE.

*The Art of Measurable Song* <term>Ars cantus mensurabilis: a landmark treatise that introduced a system where the shape of a musical note indicated its specific duration or rhythm</term> *published by Master* **FRANCO** *of Paris, as it is read in the codex of the Ambrosian Library in Milan, is brought to light by us here, having been compared once again with that manuscript; yet we could not achieve a result where it would emerge perfectly corrected. **MARCHETTUS** of Padua* <note>Marchetto da Padova, an influential Italian music theorist of the early 14th century</note> *cites* **FRANCO** *in his dedicatory letter to King* **ROBERT** *of Sicily, who succeeded his father* **CHARLES II** *in the year 1309.*

### HERE BEGINS THE ART OF MEASURABLE SONG
#### PUBLISHED BY MASTER FRANCO OF PARIS.

Since certain philosophers have sufficiently treated plain music <term>plana musica: also known as plainchant or Gregorian chant, which is sung in unison without a fixed rhythmic beat</term>, and have effectively illuminated it for us both theoretically and

<column-break/>

practically; theoretically Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose writings remained the foundation of musical education throughout the Middle Ages</note> especially, and practically Guido the monk <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–after 1033), the inventor of the musical staff and the "do-re-mi" system</note>, and most particularly concerning the modes <note>original: "tropis"; referring to the melodic scales or "tones" used to organize church chants</note>

<summary>This page introduces a primary source by Franco of Paris, a 13th-century theorist who revolutionized music by creating a system for measuring rhythm. It acknowledges earlier masters of "plain" chant, such as Boethius and Guido of Arezzo, before beginning Franco's specific teachings on rhythmic notation.</summary>
<keywords>Franco of Paris, Ars Cantus Mensurabilis, music theory, plainchant, Boethius, Guido of Arezzo, rhythmic notation, medieval music</keywords>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>This page continues Franco of Cologne’s introductory remarks. Having acknowledged the foundations of "plain music" (plainchant) established by earlier authorities, he now transitions into his specific subject: the "measurable music" of the 13th century. This text is foundational for the development of modern rhythmic notation.</meta>

FRANCO’S MUSIC

Blessed Gregory <note>Referencing Pope Gregory the Great, to whom the tradition of Gregorian chant was historically attributed</note>: therefore, concerning **measurable music** <term>musica mensurabilis: music where the duration of each note is determined by its shape, allowing for complex rhythms</term>, which plain music <term>musica plana: chant sung in unison with a flexible, non-metered rhythm</term> itself precedes as a principal subject precedes a subordinate one, we, wishing to treat this at the request of certain great men, and not wishing to pervert the order, assume that plain music has been most perfectly made known by the aforementioned philosophers.

Lest perhaps someone should say that we began this work out of arrogance, or perhaps only for our own convenience, it is truly because of evident necessity and for the easiest understanding of the listeners, as well as the most perfect instruction of all who write this measurable music. Since we have seen many—both modern and ancient—say many good things in their treatises about measurable music, and on the contrary fail and err in many things, especially in the secondary features of this science, we have judged it necessary to come to the aid of their opinion: lest perhaps through the failure and error of the aforementioned, the science itself should suffer harm. We propose, therefore, to explain measurable music concisely; we will not refuse to include the well-said things of others, while also destroying and putting to flight errors; and if anything new is found by us, we shall support and prove it with good reasons.

### CHAPTER I.

->*On the definition of measurable music and its types.*<-

Measurable music is song measured by long and short durations of time <note>original: "temporibus"</note>. For the sake of this definition, it must be seen

<column-break/>

what measure is, and what time is. *Measure* <note>original: "mensura"</note> is the relationship manifesting the quantity, length, and brevity of any measurable song. I say "measurable" because in plain music such measure is not observed. *Time* <note>original: "tempus"</note> is the measure both of the sounding voice and of its contrary—namely, the omitted voice, which is commonly called a **pause**. I say, however, that a pause is measured by time, because otherwise two distinct songs, one with pauses and the other without, could not be proportionally equated to one another.

Measurable music is divided into "simply measurable" and "partially measurable." Simply measurable is **discant** <term>discantus: a type of polyphony where two or more voices move together using the same rhythmic system</term>, because it is measured by time in every part of itself. **Organum** <term>organum: an early form of harmony; specifically "pure" organum where a melody is sustained in very long notes while another voice sings ornaments above it</term> is called "partially measurable" because [it is not] measured in every part of itself <note>In the "pure" organum of this period, the lower voice (tenor) often held notes for indefinite lengths, meaning only the upper voice was strictly rhythmic.</note>. And it should be known that "organum" is used in two ways: namely, *properly* and *commonly*. *Organum properly so-called* is "double organum," which is called *pure organum*; *organum commonly so-called* is any ecclesiastical song measured by time. But because the simple precedes the complex, we must speak first of discant.

### CHAPTER II.

->*On the definition of discant and its division.*<-

**Discant** is a harmony <note>original: "consonantia"</note> of different melodies, in which those different melodies are proportionally equated through long, short, or **semibreve** <note>original: "semibreves": the shortest note value in Franco’s system</note> notes, and in writing through different figures...

->AND MEASURABLE MUSIC.<-

...are designated to have their figures proportioned to one another. Discant <term>discantus: a style of polyphony where two or more voices move at the same speed using different melodies</term> is divided thus: one type of discant is simply performed; another is truncated, which is called a *hocket* <term>ochetus: from the French 'hoquet' (hiccup); a rhythmic technique where voices alternate rapidly, one resting while the other sings</term>; another is joined, which is called a *copula* <term>copula: a transitional style of polyphony between the sustained notes of organum and the strict rhythm of discant</term>. We must speak of these in order. But because any discant proceeds by means of a *mode* <term>modus: a rhythmic pattern or meter used in 13th-century music, similar to poetic feet</term>, we must therefore first treat the modes, and consequently their signs—namely, the figures or notes.

### CHAPTER III.
#### On the modes of any discant.

A mode is the understanding of sound measured by long and short durations of time. Modes, however, are numbered and ordered in different ways by different authors. For some posit six, others seven; but we posit five, because all the others are reduced to these.

The first mode proceeds from all longs <term>longa: the primary "long" note value in this system</term>, as seen here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing three square "longa" notes with descending tails on the right side.</image-desc> And under this one, we include that mode which consists of a long and a short <note>original: "ex longa & brevi"; referring to a trochaic rhythm of a long followed by a brevis</note> for two reasons. First, because these two are united in similar pauses <term>pausatio: a rest or silence of a specific duration</term>. The second reason is to settle the controversy between the ancients and the moderns <note>Franco is reconciling older rhythmic theories with his own new system of notation</note>, as is clear here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing a sequence of square notes and ligatures representing long and short rhythmic values.</image-desc>

The second mode proceeds from a short and a long <note>an iambic rhythm</note>, as here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing three pairs of notes, each consisting of a brevis (square without tail) and a longa (square with tail).</image-desc>

The third mode consists of two short-

<column-break/>

-s and a long, as is clear here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing three groups of three notes: two square breves followed by one longa.</image-desc>

The fourth consists of two shorts, and a long, and two shorts, as is clear here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing a rhythmic pattern of two breves, one longa, and two breves.</image-desc>

The fifth mode consists of two shorts and semibreves <term>semibrevis: the smallest note value in this system, literally a "half-short," shaped like a diamond</term>, as here: <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing two square breves followed by two diamond-shaped semibreves.</image-desc>

Since, moreover, the voices <note>the actual musical sounds</note> are the cause and the beginning of the modes, as well as their notes, it is manifest that we must indeed treat the notes or figures. But since discant itself is regulated both by the sounded voice and its contrary—that is, the omitted voice <note>referring to silence or rests</note>—and since these are distinct, their signs will also be distinct, because distinct things have distinct categories. But since the sounded voice comes before the omitted one—just as presence precedes absence—we must first speak of the signs that signify the sounded voice, then of the pauses <term>pausa: a musical rest</term> that signify the omitted voice.

### CHAPTER IV.
#### On the figures or signs of measurable music.

A figure is the representation of a sound ordered in one of the modes; from this, it is clear that figures ought to signify the modes, and not the other way around, as some have claimed. Of figures, some are simple, others are composite. The composite ones are ligatures <term>ligatura: a group of notes written as a single connected symbol, indicating they are sung to one syllable</term>. There are three species of simple figures: namely, the long, the short, and the semibreve. The first of these is divided into three: the perfect long, the imperfect long,

It is called "perfect" <note>original: "perfecta"</note> because it is measured by three units of time. For the number three is the most perfect among numbers because it takes its name from the supreme Trinity, which is true and supreme perfection. Its shape is square, having a tail descending on the right side, through which it represents its length, as seen here: <image-desc>square note with a descending tail on the right side</image-desc>. The "imperfect" long, however, although it has the same shape as the perfect one, is worth only two units of time. It is called imperfect because it is never found without the help of a preceding or following breve <note>original: "brevis," the "short" note</note>. From this, it is clear that those who call it "correct" <note>original: "rectam"</note> are mistaken, since that which is correct and perfect ought to be able to stand on its own. The "double long" <note>original: "duplex longa"</note> is formed like this, signifying two longs <image-desc>shape of two connected long notes</image-desc>, which are doubled in a single body <image-desc>staff lines with a duplex longa</image-desc> so that the flow of the plainchant melodies used in the tenors <term>tenor: from the Latin 'tenere' (to hold); the voice part that 'held' the original chant melody in long, sustained notes</term> is not broken. The breve, although it may be divided into a standard breve and an "altered" breve, is nonetheless formed as a square without any stroke for either of them, like this: <image-desc>square note without a tail</image-desc>. Of the semibreves, one is called "major" and the other "minor"; any of these is shaped in an irregular way compared to a long <margin>In the copy: "to that segment"</margin> like this: <image-desc>rhomboid note on a staff segment</image-desc>.

## Chapter V.
### *On the arrangement of notes in relation to one another.*
The knowledge of the value of simple notes is revealed by their arrangement—that is, the position they hold in relation to one another. Their arrangement is understood this way: either a long is followed by

<column-break/>

a long, or by a breve. And note that the same rule applies to breves and semibreves. If a long is followed by another long, then the first long is measured as three units of time under a single accent, and it is called a "perfect long," whether it is a written note or a rest; as is clear here:
<image-desc>musical staff with square notes and text: Tu Beth - le hem.</image-desc>
If, however, a long is followed by a breve, this can happen in several ways, as the breve may be alone or there may be several. If there is only one, then the long is worth two units of time and is called "imperfect," as here: <image-desc>staff showing a long note followed by a breve</image-desc>—unless a certain small stroke <term>tractulus: a small vertical line used to separate notes and define rhythmic groupings</term> is placed between those two (namely, the long and the breve). This stroke is called the "sign of perfection," or by another name, the "division of the mode" <term>divisio modi: a marker that resets the rhythmic pattern or prevents a note from being 'imperfected'</term>. In that case, the long is perfect, and the breve makes the *following* long imperfect, as seen here: <image-desc>staff showing a long note, a vertical stroke, and a breve note</image-desc>.

If, however, several breves follow, this also happens in several ways: there may be two, three, four, five, or more than five. If there are only two, as seen here: <image-desc>staff showing a long followed by two breves</image-desc>, then the first long is perfect, unless a single breve precedes it, as seen here: <image-desc>staff showing a breve followed by a long</image-desc>.

Of two breves, the first is called "correct" <note>original: "recta brevis"; worth one beat</note> and the second is called "another" breve <note>original: "altera brevis"; an 'altered' breve worth two beats to complete a triple unit</note>. ### CHAPTER VI.
### On Plicas in Simple Figures.

Furthermore, there are certain other simple figures which signify these same values and use the same names, but with the addition of what is called a **plica** <note>original: "plica", literally a "fold." It indicates a vocal ornament where the singer "folds" the end of a note into a higher or lower pitch</note>. Therefore, we must see what a plica is. A plica is a note indicating the division of a single sound into a low <note>original: "gravem"</note> and a high <note>original: "acutum"</note> pitch. Of plicas, one is **long**, another **short** <note>original: "brevis"</note>, and another **semibreve**; but we intend to say nothing of semibreves at present, since a semibreve plica cannot be found in simple figures. In **ligatures** <note>grouped notes</note> and arrangements of semibreves, however, a plica can be accepted, as will appear later. 

Also, of plicas, one is **ascending**, another **descending**. An ascending plica is a square-shaped figure, bearing only a right-hand stroke <image-desc>symbol of a square note with a single ascending tail on the right</image-desc> [pointing] upward, as here: <image-desc>musical stave with a single square note with an ascending right tail</image-desc> or more properly two [strokes], of which the <image-desc>symbol of a square note with two tails, the right being longer</image-desc> right is longer than the left, as here: <image-desc>musical stave with a single square note with two vertical tails, right longer than left</image-desc>. I say "more properly" because it deserves to have the name of a plica because of those two little strokes. A descending long similarly has two little strokes, but descending, with the right-hand one (as said before) longer than the left, as here:

An ascending **short plica** <note>original: "plica brevis"</note> is one that has two ascending strokes, but with the left one longer, as here. <image-desc>Musical stave with a square note having two ascending tails, the left being longer.</image-desc> And note, these plicas have the same power and the same regular value as the simple notes mentioned above.

### CHAPTER VII.
### On Ligatures and Their Properties.

Having discussed simple figures, we must speak of compound or bound figures—which is the same thing—called **ligatures** <term>ligature: a single symbol representing two or more notes joined together, indicating they should be sung to a single syllable</term>. A ligature is the binding together of simple figures, arranged by the appropriate strokes. Of ligatures, one is **ascending**, another **descending**. An ascending one is that in which the second note is higher than the first, as here: <image-desc>Musical stave with an ascending two-note ligature.</image-desc> A descending one is that in which the second note is lower than the first, as here: <image-desc>Musical stave with a descending two-note ligature.</image-desc>

Furthermore, of ligatures, some are **with property** <note>original: "cum proprietate"</note>, some **without property** <note>original: "sine proprietate"</note>, and some **with opposite property** <note>original: "cum opposita proprietate"</note>; these categories apply to the beginning of the ligature. Regarding the end of the ligature, some are **with perfection** <note>original: "cum perfectione"</note> and some **without perfection** <note>original: "sine perfectione"</note>. 

And note, these differences are essential and specific to the ligatures themselves. Thus, a ligature "with property" differs from one "without" in its very essence, just as a rational being differs from an irrational one <note>Franco uses a classic philosophical analogy here to show that these are distinct categories of being</note>. The same holds for the other differences previously given. A species is likewise established under its genus; however, no specific name has been given to these species themselves, but rather they are defined by the differences mentioned and by their genus [which] sur...

### CHAPTER VIII.
->*Concerning plicas in ligature figures.*<-

Furthermore, it must be known that every **ligature** <term>ligature: from the Latin "ligatura," a symbol representing two or more notes sung to a single syllable, joined by a single line</term>, whether perfect or imperfect, can take a **plica** <term>plica: literally a "fold," a melodic ornament indicated by a stroke or "tail" extending from a note, usually implying a short passing tone</term>, and this occurs at the end. <image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing two ligatures with upward plica strokes.</image-desc>
and descending thus:
<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing two ligatures with downward plica strokes.</image-desc>
Likewise, an imperfect ligature is folded in two ways. And note that an imperfect ligature is always folded in an **oblique shape** <note>original: "figuratione obliqua," where the notes are drawn as a single slanted block rather than separate squares</note>, ascending like this:
<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing an ascending oblique ligature with a plica.</image-desc>
or descending like this:
<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing a descending oblique ligature with a plica.</image-desc>

And in such a case, where an imperfect ligature must have a plica, it is necessary to use an oblique shape when ascending, so that the last note is shortened <note>original: "breviesetur," made into a breve</note>. For if a straight note were folded in a perfect ligature, it would partake in the nature of perfection. However, an oblique imperfection should not be placed ascending without a plica. For the placement of a straight imperfection is sufficient wherever there is no plica, and it is more powerful and more commonly used. Thus the plicas of all ligatures are revealed.

There are also certain **conjunctures** <term>conjunctures: from "coniuncturae," groups of diamond-shaped notes used as a shorthand for specific rhythmic patterns</term> of simple notes and ligatures, which partake partly of ligatures and partly of simple figures; these are called neither ligatures nor simple figures, as is evident here:
<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing complex conjunctures of diamond-shaped and square notes.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

Regarding the value of such conjunctures, no other rules can be given than those previously given for simple and ligated notes. Furthermore, there are certain other arrangements of simple ligatures, filling the lack of certain symbols not yet established, which is recognized only in the rules for simple notes, as is evident here:
<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing various combinations of square and diamond-shaped notes on a staff.</image-desc>

### CHAPTER IX.
->*Concerning pauses, and how the modes are varied from one another by them.*<-

Having spoken of the figures signifying a sounded voice, we must now consider **pauses** <term>pauses: "pausis," what modern musicians call rests</term>, which represent a voice omitted. A pause is the omission of a sounded voice in the proper quantity required by a particular **mode** <term>mode: the rhythmic patterns or "rhythmic modes" that governed 13th-century music</term>. There are six species of pauses: the perfect long, the imperfect long (under which is included the altered breve, because it occupies the same measure), the straight breve, the major semibreve, the minor semibreve, and the "end of points" [final rest]. A perfect pause of a sounded voice includes three **beats** <note>original: "tempora," literally "times," the basic unit of measurement</note> within itself. Similarly, an imperfect pause, likewise for an imperfect note or an altered breve, is measured by two beats.

A breve pause is the omission of a straight breve, including only one beat. A major semibreve pause omits two semibreves of a straight breve. A minor semibreve pause leaves out only a third part [of a breve]. The **end of points** <term>end of points: Latin "finis punctorum," a vertical line across the staff, similar to a modern double bar line</term> is called immeasurable, for it is also found in **plain music** <note>original: "plana musica," or Gregorian chant</note>. However, this indicates that the penultimate note is long in whichever mode it is found, even if that penultimate note would perhaps have been a breve by the logic of the mode in which it exists.

Furthermore, these six rests are designated by six thin strokes <note>original: "tractatibus," here referring to the vertical lines drawn on the staff to indicate silence</note>, which are also called pauses. The first of these, which is called **perfect**, touches four lines and covers three spaces, because it is measured by three units of time. The **imperfect** one, however, reaching three lines, covers two spaces for the same reason. A **breve** covers one space; a **major semibreve** covers two-thirds of one space; but a **minor semibreve** covers only a third. The **final point** <note>original: "finis punctorum," the sign indicating the end of a section or piece</note>, which touches all the lines, covers four spaces. The forms of these are shown in the present example.

<image-desc>A diagram showing six vertical lines (rests) of varying lengths placed upon a four-line musical staff, illustrating the duration of different pauses from a perfect long to a semibreve and the final point.</image-desc>

And note, rests have a marvelous power: for through them, the **modes** <term>modes: the six rhythmic patterns used in 13th-century music, based on combinations of long and short notes</term> are transformed into one another. Thus, the rest of the **first mode** is a straight breve or a perfect long; the rest of the **second mode** is an imperfect long; the rests of the **third and fourth modes** are properly perfect longs, or more accurately, a breve and an "altered" breve. The **fifth mode**, however, properly deserves to have a breve and a semibreve rest. Hence, if the first mode—which proceeds from a long, then a breve, then a long—places an imperfect long rest after a breve, as here:

it is changed into the first. Moreover, the **fifth mode**, when it is used in **polyphony** <term>discantus: a style of medieval polyphony where voices move at the same speed using rhythmic modes</term> where a fifth mode voice is paired with a first mode voice, is regulated into the first by its rests, and it makes the note before the rest a long, as here:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff with text beneath the notes: "O Mary, virgin of the line of David" <note>original: "O Ma ri a vir go Da vi di ca"</note>.</image-desc>

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff with French text beneath the notes: "I replied that she did not have it" <note>original Old French: "Respon di que nel a voit"</note>.</image-desc>

And note, that in a single piece of polyphony all the modes can run together, because through **perfections** <term>perfections: a grouping of three beats, which was the fundamental unit of measurement in this system</term> all modes are reduced to one; nor should one struggle over which mode such a piece is judged to be. It can, however, be named after the mode which is most prevalent or occurs most often. It follows then that the fifth mode can especially be used with all the others. And let these things concerning rests, and also concerning the variation of modes, suffice for the present.

From this it follows that those who, for whatever reason, link three longs together with the tenors <note>the "tenor" was the foundational voice part in medieval polyphony</note> err greatly. Similarly, those who link a long between two others err, since in the placement of "middle" notes—as was seen previously—all middle notes are shortened <note>middle notes in a ligature are usually treated as breves (short notes)</note>. Furthermore, more than two semibreves cannot be linked together, and this occurs at the beginning of a ligature; understand this to apply to a proper ligature. Breves, however, are linkable at the beginning, the middle, and the end. 

From this it is clear that any rhythmic **mode** <term>mode: the specific rhythmic patterns (like long-short or short-long) used in 13th-century music</term> accepted without ligatures is also capable of being linked, except for the mode that proceeds entirely from long notes. ### CHAPTER XI.
*On discant and its species.*

Having laid out the figures <note>the shapes of the notes</note> and pauses <note>the rests</note>, we must now speak of **discant** <term>discant: (Latin: "discantus") the early practice of adding a second, independent melody above a plainchant base</term>, how it is to be made, and its various types. But because any discant is regulated by consonances, we must look at consonances and dissonances occurring at the same time, and at the different modes. A **concord** <note>original: "concordantia"; today we call this a "consonance" or a pleasing harmony</note> is said to exist when two or more voices produced at the same time

<column-break/>

can be heard as compatible with one another. A **discord** <note>original: "discordantia"; a clash or "dissonance"</note>, on the contrary, is said to occur when two voices are joined in such a way that they clash according to the ear.

There are three species of concords: perfect, imperfect, and intermediate <note>original: "media"</note>. A **perfect concord** is so called when several voices are joined so smoothly that one is scarcely perceived to differ from the other because of the harmony. There are two such types: the **unison** <term>unison: (Latin: "unisonus") two voices singing the exact same pitch</term> and the **octave** <term>octave: (Latin: "diapason") the interval where a note sounds like a higher version of the same note</term>, as is evident here:

[Musical notation on two five-line staves showing two notes on the same line (unison) and two notes an octave apart (diapason).]

An **imperfect concord** occurs when two voices are perceived as differing significantly, yet they do not clash to the ear; there are two of these: the **major third** <term>major third: (Latin: "ditonus") literally "two tones"</term> and the **minor third** <term>minor third: (Latin: "semiditonus") literally "a half-and-two-tones"</term>, as seen here:

[Musical notation on two five-line staves showing the intervals of a major third and a minor third.]

**Intermediate concords** are those where two voices are joined having a greater concord than those mentioned before [the thirds], yet not so much as the perfect ones. These are two: the **perfect fifth** <term>perfect fifth: (Latin: "diapente")</term> and the **perfect fourth** <term>perfect fourth: (Latin: "diatessaron")</term>, as is shown here:

[Musical notation on a five-line staff showing the intervals of a perfect fifth and a perfect fourth.]

Why one concord harmonizes more than another is left to the study of plain music <note>original: "planae musicae"; this refers to "Cantus Planus" or Gregorian chant, where the basic mathematical ratios of music were studied</note>.

There are two species of discords: perfect and imperfect. A **perfect discord** is said to be when two voices are so con-

**Discant**, moreover, is performed either with a single text <note>original: "lyra", literally "lyre", but here referring to the poetic text or voice part</note>, or with different texts, or without a text and with a text together. If it is with a text, this happens in two ways: with the same text or with different texts. Discant with the same text occurs in solo songs <note>original: "cantilenis"</note>, roundels <note>original: "rodellis"</note>, and church chant. Discant with different texts occurs in **motets** (a), which have a third part <note>a "triplum"</note> or a tenor, which tenor is equal in value to a specific melody. Discant is made both with and without text in **conductus** (b) and in certain church music which is properly called **organum**. And

<column-break/>

note that in all these forms, the method of composition is the same, except in the **conductus**; for in all the others, a pre-existing melody is first selected, which is called the **tenor** <term>tenor: (from Latin "tenere", to hold) the foundational voice that "holds" the pre-existing chant melody while other voices play around it</term>, because it "holds" the discant and the discant takes its origin from it. In the conductus, however, it is not so; instead, the melody <note>the "cantus"</note> and the discant are created together by the same composer. Therefore, the word "discant" is used in two ways: first, it is called discant because it is a "song of diverse parts" <note>original: "diversorum cantus"</note>; second, it is called discant because it is "taken from a song" <note>original: "de cantu sumtus"</note>.

## CHAPTER XII.
### Concerning the Copula.

The <term>copula</term> <note>a style of rapid polyphony that "links" sections of a composition</note> is a swift discant joined together in turn. Of copulas, one type is bound <note>ligated</note>, and the other is not bound. The bound type occurs when it begins with a single long note, and follows with a two-note <term>ligature</term> <note>a group of notes written as a single symbol</note> possessing "propriety" and "perfection" <note>technical terms indicating the specific rhythmic values of the notes within the symbol</note>, in the likeness of the second mode <note>a rhythmic pattern consisting of a short note followed by a long one</note>. However, it differs from the second mode in its notation in two ways: first, because the second mode does not have a single long note at the start, whereas the copula does, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation showing two staves of mensural music with ligatures and long notes.</image-desc>

But if a <term>division of the mode</term> <note>original: "divisio modi" - a vertical stroke used to separate rhythmic patterns</note> is placed between the first double note and the ligature, then it is not a copula, but is called the second mode, as seen here:

<image-desc>A single staff of musical notation containing a vertical bar (divisio modi) separating the first note from the following ligature.</image-desc>

For in performance, the copula differs from the second mode: because the second mode is performed with a proper [long], a short, and an imperfect long; but this copula is performed swiftly, using semibreves and breves until the end. An unbound copula is made in the likeness of the second mode: yet it differs

<column-break/>

from it in two ways, in notation and in performance. In notation, because the second mode without text <note>original: "sine littera" - melismatic music where one syllable is stretched over many notes</note> is everywhere capable of being bound into ligatures; but this copula is set above text <note>original: "super litteram" - syllabic music where each note has a corresponding syllable</note>, and yet it is not bound, as is clear in the following example.

<image-desc>A single staff of music showing discrete square notes above a horizontal line.</image-desc>

In performance it also differs from the second mode, because while the second mode is performed with regular breves, the copula is joined together by a swifter performance. And let these remarks suffice concerning the copula.

## CHAPTER XIII.
### Concerning Hockets.

A <term>hocket</term> <note>original: "ochetus," meaning a hiccup; a technique where the melody is broken across different voices</note> is a truncation of the song, performed in a truncated manner with sounded and omitted notes. And it should be known that truncation can be done in as many ways as a long note can be divided into breves or semibreves. A long note is divisible in multiple ways: first into a long and a short, and a short and a long; and from this is made a truncation or hocket (which are the same thing), so that in one voice a short note is omitted, while in the other a long note is omitted, as is clear here:

<image-desc>Four fragments of musical staves illustrating different hocket (ochetus) patterns, showing notes alternating with rests.</image-desc>

<note>The left margin of the original manuscript is partially obscured by the binding, making some letters at the start of lines in the first column difficult to read.</note>

Secondly, it can be divided into three <term>breves</term> <note>a "short" note value</note> or two, or even into several <term>semibreves</term> <note>the smallest note value in this system</note>. And in all these, the truncation of the melody <note>original: "cantus truncatio" — the technique of the hocket</note> occurs through notes sounded and omitted, such that when one voice rests, the other does not rest, or vice-versa. A breve is indeed divisible into three semibreves or two, and from this is created the <term>hocket</term> <note>original: "ochetus" — a "hiccup" technique where the melody is split rapidly between different voices</note> by omitting one semibreve in one voice and sounding another in the other voice, as is clear here:

<image-desc>Three musical staves of mensural notation with square and diamond-shaped notes on five-line staves. The notes are grouped in short phrases separated by vertical division lines or pauses.</image-desc>

And note, that from the aforementioned truncations, common hockets are created by the omission of notes and breves, and even of the <term>prolation</term> <note>the rhythmic relationship between note values</note>. And note, that in all these things, <term>equipollence</term> <note>equality of duration</note> in the beats must be observed, and <term>concordance</term> <note>consonant harmony</note> in the sounded voices. Likewise, it must be known that every truncation ought to be formed over a pre-existing melody <note>original: "cantus prius factus" — a "firm song" or foundation melody</note>, whether it be in the vernacular or in Latin. And let this suffice for the present.

### CHAPTER XIV.
### Concerning Organum.

<term>Organum</term> properly so-called is a song that is not measured in every part. It must be known that <term>pure organum</term> <note>a style where a lower foundation voice holds long notes while the upper voice performs florid, unmeasured decorations</note> cannot be had except over a single <term>tenor</term> <note>the foundation voice that "holds" the melody</note> alone, unless there is only a single note in unison; so that when the tenor takes several notes at once, clearly the tenor immediately becomes <term>discant</term> <note>measured polyphony where both voices move rhythmically</note>, as seen here:

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Two musical staves of mensural notation. The first staff contains several square notes and one diamond note. The second staff features a series of descending and ascending notes including ligatures.</image-desc>

The long and short notes of organum itself are known by three rules. The first is: whatever is noted as a simple <term>long</term>, know that it is long; and in a <term>breve</term>, it is short; and in a <term>semibreve</term>, it is a semibreve. The second rule is such: whatever is long requires <term>concordance</term> <note>consonance or "sweet" harmony</note> with respect to the tenor; but if the tenor results in a <term>discordance</term> <note>dissonance</note>, let it be silent, or let it feign a concordance <note>essentially, adjust the pitch or sustain the note until a consonant point is reached</note>, as seen here:

<image-desc>Two musical staves of mensural notation. The notes are arranged in melodic fragments separated by vertical bars.</image-desc>

The third rule is such: whatever is taken immediately before a rest, which is called the end of the phrases <note>original: "punctorum"</note>, is long, because every <term>penultimate</term> <note>the second-to-last note in a phrase</note> is long. Likewise note, that whenever in pure organum several figures occur similarly in unison, only the first ought to be struck <note>vocalized with a fresh attack</note>; all the rest, however, should be held in a <term>flowering</term> <note>original: "floratura" — a decorative, florid vocal ornament or melisma</note>, as seen here:

<image-desc>A single musical staff of mensural notation showing a complex sequence of square and diamond notes, including grouped notes and a custos at the end.</image-desc>

# ELIAS SALOMONIS
## CLERIC OF SAINT ASTIER
### OF THE DIOCESE OF PÉRIGUEUX IN FRANCE
### THE SCIENCE OF THE MUSICAL ART.

->**EDITOR'S PREFACE**<-

*I have decided to publish this somewhat unpolished <note>original: "inficetam" — literally "unsophisticated" or "unrefined"</note> science of the musical art, shared with us by the very kind B. Oltrocchi from the Ambrosian Library, because it contains here and there certain matters not to be despised regarding the instruction of the church song of that era. Elias Salomonis wrote this little book in the year 1274 for Pope Gregory X at the Roman court. To this end, the author indicated next to a figure—among others he painted here and there, where he represents St. Gregory the Great sitting and himself kneeling below his feet—this petition:* "Most Holy Lord Gregory the Tenth! Elias Salomonis, cleric of Saint Astier of the diocese of Périgueux, supplicates Your Holiness that you deign to write to certain discreet men, so that they may diligently examine, correct, and amend the present doctrine of the science or art of music; and if anything good be found, they may recommend him to you, and cause him to be received as a canon and a brother in the church of said place, in which he has served faithfully and devotedly, and whose son he is." *At the bottom of the first leaf of the Ambrosian Library codex marked D. 75, the following approval is read:* "I, the parish priest, recommend and approve the present work of the musical art, and have found enough utility in it." *This author, whom he calls Salomon, is also cited among other musicians below by Johannes de Muris in the preface to his Summa.*

### HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE SCIENCE OR DOCTRINE OF THE MUSICAL ART.

Since the truth and clarity of the divine <note>original: "di..." — likely "divinae"</note> science of the musical art in every part of the world—

<column-break/>

—upon which the foundation of the universal church, as if after the orthodox faith—

<meta>This page continues the prologue of Elias Salomonis’s treatise. He argues for the divine origin of music, citing its presence at the creation of angels and the birth of Christ, while contrasting this celestial ideal with the technical and moral failings of contemporary singers.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>THE SCIENCE OF THE MUSICAL ART.</header>

...it consists, has vanished and almost fallen away, whereas it clearly stands that this very art was created at the same time as the creation of the angels; for it is their proper nature to praise God. And that which had been prophesied before the coming of the Lord by the prophets and other saints:
> Praise him, all his angels. Praise him with the sound of the trumpet. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals. Sing to the Lord a new song. Sing to the Lord, all the earth;

and at the birth of our Savior, all song and the good art of singing was made sacred <note>original: "canonizata" — meaning officially recognized or established as a rule</note> through that which follows:
> Today Christ is born, today our Savior has appeared, today the angels sing on earth, the archangels rejoice: today everyone exults, saying: Glory to God in the highest, alleluia;

which is the praise of God. Similarly, at His birth, all the pious ranks sing to the Lord syllable by syllable, touching upon <term>neumes</term> <note>the basic symbols of medieval musical notation used before modern notes</note> in an organ-like <note>original: "organica" — likely referring to polyphonic or instrument-like singing</note> manner. And concerning the assumption of the blessed and glorious Virgin, mother of God, we have that which follows:
> The angels rejoice, and the archangels exult, and together in the heavens they praise the Son of God.

Likewise, one reads of the blessed Severinus, that he heard a choir of angels carrying the blessed Martin upward while singing psalms.

And nonetheless, it is almost totally ignored by nearly all leaders of churches, except for certain ones in the Gallic <note>French</note> church and a few places in England. And what is more absurd is that they set themselves up not only as students, but even as Scribes and Pharisees. Concerning that which they are ignorant of even the basic foot, and of which they are not worthy to untie the shoelace, they do not fear to lead others—desiring to catch toads in the air at night and flies on the wall by day <note>a medieval metaphor for pursuing pointless or impossible tasks through ignorance</note>.

<column-break/>

They are utterly ignorant of how to grasp, or begin, or pronounce a <term>point</term> <note>original: "punctum" — the standard term for a single musical note in this period</note>, though they see it in the book; not caring for the things that belong to the "point," but rather for their own interests, acting like mimics <note>original: "simii" — literally "apes," referring to those who imitate sounds without understanding the theory</note> through their usurpation. What is more detestable is that they mock <term>plainchant</term> <note>original: "cantum planum" — the traditional, monophonic Gregorian chant</note>, which was well-ordered by the angels, the holy prophets, and Saint Gregory. Instead, they sometimes adopt the style of the <term>science of organizing</term> <note>original: "scientiae organizandi" — the technical art of polyphony or singing in multiple parts</note>, which was invented as a science entirely above that of plainchant. And they even scarcely deign sometimes to keep their place in plainchant—anticipating, rushing, delaying, and poorly joining the points from which the effect of the "science of organizing" is completed; because perhaps they see the points prepared in such a way in the books. This, however, was done for the beauty and dignity of the placement of the points and the notes in the book, not for singing in the way they imagine. Let them know this for certain: they seek neither what is ours (which they see), nor what is God's, nor the debt owed to the musical art, because they are ignorant of it; but speculating, they cry "miau minau" <note>an onomatopoeic mockery of bad singers who sound like cats</note> in the air, so that the guest may see and hear them; and perhaps, what is more damnable, so that offerings may be brought more frequently—perhaps to be converted to illicit uses and locked away in their purses.

I, **Elias Salomonis**, a cleric of Saint Astier of the diocese of Périgueux, intend to set forth the nature of every letter and point, and to pose objections and solve them, and to place the rules of every letter and point and of the whole science of the musical art, as well as the notable things—without the knowledge of which the science is nothing. Even though I have been established like children in their cradles, who long to speak whatever they hear...

# ELIAS SALOMON
<page-num>18</page-num>
<header>ELIAS SALOMON</header>

...I will take care to provide for you exactly how many letters, how many <term>points</term> <note>original: "puncti" — the visual marks or "notes" used in medieval notation</note>, how many <term>keys</term> <note>original: "claves" — the fixed positions or clefs on a musical staff</note>, how many tones <note>original: "toni" — the musical modes or categories of melodies used in chant</note>, and how many species each tone possesses. I will show which tone governs everything commonly sung or read in the church, and how many types and species each individual tone contains. In doing so, I shall reject what is worthy of rejection and approve what is worthy of approval.

### Chapter I.
#### Rubric on the number of letters.

It must be understood that the art of music is contained within the number of seven letters: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. This is according to the likeness and similarity of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, of which this Knowledge <note>original: "Scientia" — referring to the science of music</note> is one.

What is a letter? It is the smallest part of a composed voice <note>original: "vocis compositæ" — a musical sound or phrase</note> which itself cannot be written down; because that which is indivisible cannot be written, it is therefore called the "subject of the point." A letter is not the point itself, but a sign, the foundation and support of the point. Just as it is said that the letter 'H' is not a true letter but a mark of breathing <note>original: "aspirationis nota" — in medieval grammar, H was often viewed as a breath rather than a consonant</note>, so too the letter is the material upon which the point is rooted. I shall write a chapter on the nature of the letter as it will appear in the following sections. Similarly, in a Calendar, a letter is not the day itself, but a sign by which we calculate which day it ought to be. Likewise, the letter 'V' signifies nothing but 'V', yet we place it in a sequence to represent the number five.

One might ask whether there ought to be more than seven letters, or if they could be comprised of a smaller number, regarding this sci-

<column-break/>

-ence? I respond: there cannot and should not be more, unless some dreamer wished to invent as many letters as there are points he could utter, which is absurd to imagine. There could, however, be fewer in number: for C, F, and G share almost the same nature. In each of these three, we can say—according to the nature of the art—the syllables <term>ut</term>, <term>fa</term>, <term>sol</term>, and <term>re</term>. Therefore, these could be reduced to a single letter, except that in G one does not say *fa*, but *re* is used as a compensation. Thus, the number of letters could be restricted to five or six. I believe this to be true, and by the strict rigor of the science, it ought to be so, following the likeness of the six points <note>original: "sex punctorum" — likely referring to the six syllables of the hexachord: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note>.

### Chapter II.
#### Rubric on the nature of letters.

Having seen the number of letters, let us look at their nature. It should be noted that the letter **A** is rigid, in the manner of a good ruler who does not allow himself to be bent by anyone. It requires a rigid point, so that in **A** one always says *re*, *mi*, or *la*. It should not be <term>sol-faed</term> <note>original: "solfari" — to sing using the solmization syllables</note> or pronounced in any other way. 
**Rule:** No **A** allows for *ut*, *fa*, or *sol*; only *re*, *mi*, and *la*.

**B** requires *fa* and *mi*, and nothing else. 
**Rule:** No **B** allows for *re*, *sol*, or *la*; only *mi* and *fa*.

**C** requires by its nature *ut*, *fa*, and *sol*, and nothing else. 
**Rule:** No **C** allows for *re*, *mi*, or *la*; only *ut* and *fa*. (a)

<meta>This page continues Elias Salomon’s technical breakdown of the musical alphabet. Having established that there are seven letters (A through G), he now assigns specific characters and rules to the letters E, F, and G before moving on to the "Gamma" (the Greek G) and the nature of the six musical "points" or syllables.</meta>

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>THE SCIENCE OF THE ART OF MUSIC.</header>
<sig>C 2</sig>

**E.** is of such a nature that it possesses a most masculine and rigid value; it allows only <term>mi</term> and <term>la</term> <note>These are the solfège syllables used in the medieval hexachord system</note>, and nothing else, and it should always be sung with a lamenting quality. **Rule:** No E admits the syllables *ut*, *re*, *fa*, or *sol*; but only *mi* and *la*.

**F.** possesses a womanly agreement and the nature of the feminine sex; nothing can be sung upon it except <term>ut</term> and <term>fa</term>. In whatever way a singer requires F—whether ascending or descending—it is necessary to humble it and make it "soft" <note>original: "mollificare" — this refers to the "soft hexachord" (hexachordum molle) which begins on F and requires a B-flat</note>. **Rule:** No F admits *re*, *mi*, *sol*, or *la*; but only *ut* and *fa*.

**G.** requires *ut*, *sol*, and *re*, and nothing else. **Rule:** No G admits *mi*, *fa*, or *la*. Behold a notable general rule: whoever uses these letters otherwise than has been stated would fall into the vice of <term>false music</term> <note>original: "falsæ musicæ" — notes or syllables that fall outside the standard hand-diagram or "musica recta"</note>.

### CHAPTER III.
->On the nature of Γ (Gamma).<-

<term>Gamma</term> <note>written as the Greek letter Γ</note> in Greek is the same as G in Latin. But why is it placed at the beginning of the <term>palm</term> <note>original: "palma" — referring to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where parts of the hand represent different notes</note>? I answer: it is placed there as a "point," not as a letter; this is to be noted. Likewise, it is placed there because it so pleased the first inventors, our ancestors, and out of necessity, because G has a more tempered sound than any other letter. Furthermore, no other letter could be placed at the beginning without the order of letters being cut off; consequently, the first <term>key</term> <note>original: "clavis"</note> would seem to be A, and in A we could not say *ut*. Thus, the first key would lack the first "point." For these reasons, since G is the last letter, it was necessary for Gamma to be placed at the very beginning.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER IV.
->Rubric on the number and nature of the points and letters.<-

There are six <term>points</term> <note>original: "puncti" — referring here to the solfège syllables ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note>: *ut*, *re*, *mi*, *fa*, *sol*, *la*. You should not understand this to mean that *ut*, *re*, *mi*, *fa*, *sol*, *la* are themselves the points, but rather they are the names of the points established by our predecessors, and well-constituted at that. Just as in grammar, the word "he" is not the article itself, but is held as a sign for the masculine gender.

I ask, why are there not seven points or more, just as there are seven letters? I answer, the solution is that there are no more: was it not said that C, F, and G have nearly the same nature? Thus, there could be even fewer in number, as was said regarding the letters, but by no means could there be more, since we do not have more names for the points; nor is it necessary to have more. Indeed, according to the strictness of the science of the art of music, there ought not be more than five points: namely *re*, *mi*, *fa*, *sol*, *la*; and we use *fa* in place of *ut* or G, just as we do when multiplying the art. Furthermore, I prove that there are only five points starting from A, such as *re*, and so on, according to the order of the palm, which exists as the beginning and the door of this science. Do we not first use the "seconds" in the palm, then the "thirds," then the "fourths," then the "fifths"—*re*, *mi*, *fa*, *sol*, *la*? Thus the palm is woven from a five-fold ascent and descent, and consequently, the whole art ought to be.

In truth, as far as the rigor and well-being of the art is concerned, every ascent as well as descent ought not to transcend the number five without the mediation of some point:

<vocab>music, solfège, ut re mi fa sol la, Gamma, palm, ascent, descent, points</vocab>

<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>ELIAS SALOMONIS</header>

...and he who puts forth a new song and makes an ascent or descent of five steps <note>original: "quinarium"</note> without an intervening <term>point</term> <note>original: "punctus" — the medieval term for a musical note</note>, clearly acts against the nature of the art; it appears that he does this not as a good teacher, but as one who is malicious and ignorant of the art. Likewise, none of the <term>tones</term> <note>original: "tonorum" — referring here to the church modes</note>, when manifesting their nature, make mention of anything except five points; nor does one ascend in a single stroke except across five points, by whose strength the entire art is governed and embraced. Therefore, we ought not to extend further without an intervening note, and whoever does otherwise does not escape the vice of <term>false music</term> <note>original: "falsæ musicæ" — music that uses notes outside the standard medieval system</note>.

But I ask: are there not nineteen points on the <term>palm</term> <note>the Guidonian Hand, used for teaching singers</note>, and do we not use them in singing, and sometimes even more? I answer: it is true that we use them, but by multiplying the letters and points it is permitted to ascend even to a thousand, or to an infinite number, if our instruments were able. However, because of this there are only six points: nor is permission given to ascend or descend through the nature of the tones except by five steps without an intervening note; and the same must be true by the nature of the palm. Just as we see that on the <term>vielle</term> <note>original: "viella" — a medieval bowed string instrument similar to a fiddle</note> there are only five strings, and yet, according to the variety of the strings' touches, the points and sounds of the vielle can be multiplied beyond five points at the will of the player and the song. The music is governed in those instruments whether the players wish it or not: for instruments are governed by this art, and they are entirely subject to this art in whatever can be harmoniously sung. And just as a letter relates to a syl-

<column-break/>

-lable, a syllable to a word, and a word to a sentence, so does a letter or point relate to a <term>clef</term> <note>original: "clavem"</note>, a clef to a tone, and a tone to a song. By these tones—whether they be Psalms, Hymns, the *I believe* <note>original: "credo"</note>, or the *Glory to God in the highest* <note>original: "gloria in excelsis"</note>, the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: "kyrie"</note>, or <term>prose</term> <note>a type of liturgical chant</note>, or even a secular song <note>original: "cantilena secularis"</note>, or whatever is sung or read in any other way—it receives its beginning, strength, end, and foundation.

### Chapter V.

#### On the nature of each individual point.

What is a <term>point</term>? A point is the smallest part of a simple voice, which cannot be written or pronounced except as a whole. Yet a point, by its very nature, has various effects, and according to these it ought to be begun and pronounced. For if the point is on <term>ut</term> <note>the first syllable of the hexachord, modern "Do"</note> at the beginning, you must moderate yourself with the point, and the point with you. If it is on <term>re</term>, you should place it thick and rigid without any lamenting. If it is on **E**, attack it boldly with a lamenting quality, sounding it rigidly and restricting the point, so that it feels no nature of "softening" <note>original: "mollificationis"</note>. If it is on **F**, use a pleasing and alluring voice, sounding and exalting the voice until it is in its full being, and then persevere well in sustaining it. If it is on **G**, you should take and pronounce it temperately without any lamenting or softening; sustain it rigidly in its own nature without making it soft.

Likewise, a syllable or word which is sung ends either in a vowel or a consonant: if in a vowel, there should be no harshness...

<meta>catchword: ...harshness (original: esse)</meta>

<summary>Elias Salomonis explains that melodic leaps should not exceed a fifth without intermediate notes and provides specific vocal instructions for singing the notes ut, re, E, F, and G, assigning each a unique character such as "rigid," "lamenting," or "alluring."</summary>
<keywords>musical points, vielle, hexachord, solmization, vocal technique, church modes, Guidonian hand, medieval music theory</keywords>

--- Page 33 ---
<meta>This page continues Elias Salomonis's technical instructions on the notation and performance of plainchant. Having previously warned against improper melodic leaps, he now focuses on the rhythmic execution of notes (points), the visual grouping of notes in manuscripts, and the definition of musical "keys" or clefs.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>
<header>THE SCIENCE OF THE ART OF MUSIC.</header>

...the pitch is in the point <term>punctus</term> <note>the medieval term for a musical note</note>, hold this firmly as a rule, and do not change it: it is not for us to add or subtract. If a syllable ends in a consonant letter, it can be clipped, somewhat for the beauty of the point, but it is more correct that the letter be fully pronounced. Likewise, if you sing a note, do not be deceived even if only points appear in some places; for so it should be, though abuse of the art has become common. If in some places notes are grouped by twos, threes, fours, or fives; for this is found in plainchant for the beauty and dignity of the note and the book, and for the pleasure of the viewer, so that the note and the book may be considered more precious. And in this, plainchant imitates <note>original: "fimiat", a medieval variant of "imitatur"</note> the nature of polyphonic song <term>organicus cantus</term> <note>literally "organized song," referring to early polyphony like organum</note>. But do not, because of this, you lesser singer, hurry the points or sing "lo-vi-re-li" <note>original: "lovireli", a phonetic mockery of frivolous vocal trills</note> by spitting them out, mocking polyphonic song or the Lombards <note>singers from Northern Italy, often stereotyped in medieval texts for their specific style</note>.

Likewise, the connection of points is a sign and instruction that a pause should be made after a single point, especially if it contains a syllable that completes a word. Sometimes one pauses after two points, sometimes after three, four, or five. And it should be noted that points joined together in a well-notated book should not be divided for the sake of making a pause: but we are certainly able, and indeed bound by duty, to sing them as distinct notes. Let great care be taken: we must not "put our sickle into another’s harvest" <note>a Latin proverb meaning one should not meddle in things that belong to another discipline</note> by assuming the nature of polyphony <note>original: "organizandi"</note>,

<column-break/>

...by hurrying the points: for he who hurries both, by destroying both, performs neither well. This is an infallible rule: all plainchant, in any of its parts, allows no more haste in one place than in another, beyond what is its own nature. For this reason it is called "plain" chant, because it desires to be sung in the plainest manner possible.

### Chapter VI.

->*Rubric on the number of keys and their nature.*<-

The keys <term>claves</term> <note>referring to both clefs and the pitch-names themselves</note>, according to some, are thirty-five: seven of the seconds, fourteen of the thirds, seven of the fourths, and seven of the fifths, making thirty-five in all. According to others, there are only seven: for those which are in the seconds are the same points as those in the thirds, fourths, and fifths; but they increase their range by coupling together, according to what the nature of the thirds, fourths, and fifths requires. I say with certainty that there is only a single key, but it is multiplied seven times (minus one point) through the nineteen points we have in the palm <note>the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool for singers</note>; similarly, it could be multiplied unto infinity.

### Chapter VII.

->*Rubric on the knowledge of the palm. (a)*<-

What is a key in this art? A key is that which opens the science of the art of music artificially through seven letters <note>A, B, C, D, E, F, G</note> and six points <note>the solfège syllables: Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La</note>, discovered by our teachers through divine inspiration.

It remains that we come to the knowledge of the palm <note>original: "ad palmæ notitiam veniamus"</note>, and through it, to the opening of the key of knowledge of the art of music. For the clarity of those things contained in the palm, it must first be noted that just as the five fingers of the palm are joined from nineteen joints or segments <term>unciis</term> <note>literally "inches," here referring to the phalanges or joints of the fingers</note> including the five tips of the fingers;

<column-break/>

so through each joint we imagine there to be a single point <term>punctus</term> <note>meaning a specific musical note or pitch</note>, and we multiply the science of the art of music—or the first key, which is held as the "genus"—by the key which we call the palm, which is named as the "species" or instrument; and with the palm acting as a mediator, that first key performs its work.
