What is the palm in this science? The palm is the key, the figure, or the instrument containing every kind of knowledge of the art of music, or rather, the manifestation of everything that can be rightly sung. Without the knowledge of this palm, there is no science; otherwise, a singer is not esteemed as such, but is instead considered a jester or a juggler <note>original: "ioculator seu iauglator"; in the Middle Ages, this distinguished a "musicus" (who understood theory) from a "cantor" or "ioculator" (who merely performed by ear).</note>.

Why are there so many orders in the palm and in an odd number? I respond: there are as many orders as there are offices <note>meaning functions or roles</note> for any given letter, and let this be held as a rule. And it must be notably noted that no letter nor point <term>punctus</term> <note>a "point" refers to the solmization syllables: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note> ought to be used in any song in the world in any other way than those ways contained in the figure of the palm. And it must be noted that these should be understood as if all the rules of the letters and points that have been set forth were repeated, so that the truth might shine out more clearly, eye to eye, as they are contained in the palm. Likewise, I prove all the orders of the palm. Is it not shown to those first being introduced to this art the Gamma Γ, A, B, C, D, E, F, G? Second, is it not shown that Gamma Γ is *ut*, and A is *re*? Third, how many keys there are? And thus three orders of the palm are proven. The orders that remain proceed from the multiplication of the art, except that the last order governs the order of the palm, and it begins with the palm and is terminated with the palm.

Why do certain people of Provence or Toulouse <note>The author is likely criticizing regional variations in musical notation or pedagogy common in Southern France during the 13th century.</note> use letters for letters, or letters for points in the palm? I respond: that is nothing but abuse and corruption, and whoever adheres to that palm and uses letters in place of points—that is, in place of *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*—has a poor understanding of the science. The letters were arranged by philosophers in a certain and immutable order, both in the

<column-break/>

alphabet and for reading in their own order, not for singing; rather, they are the signs or subjects of the points. Just as we see in a calendar <term>computo</term>, the letters are not the days themselves, but the signs of the days. Likewise, that way of yours proceeds directly from falsehoods when it takes a letter for a point. Likewise, it perverts the order of the science and of the letters. Is not G the seventh letter of the palm, and A the first, with five in the middle, making seven with those two? And when we follow the palm, we do not sometimes make a middle between G and A. And it must be noted that just as in the human body the palm is composed of four things—bones, nerves, flesh, and skin—and of four humors—blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile—and in the palm are the four elements—earth, water, fire, and air—so in this art there are four things as an instrument, by means of which all song and sonority in the Church Militant and Triumphant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to Christians on earth, while the "Church Triumphant" refers to those in heaven.</note>, and even outside of it, are sung. First, it contains seven letters; second, six points; third, one key with the accustomed multiplication; fourth, the tones, from which the whole of song consists and is governed.

Likewise, you of lower rank <note>original: "tu minor"; referring to a student or someone of lower ecclesiastical status</note>, do not wonder if the palm and the other figures of the musical art are produced in the likeness of a wheel or roundness. (a) Do you not see at the beginning of the wheel clearly the foundation, which is begun through *ut*, and proceeds through the whole to the upper summit with six points, *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*; and afterward it makes its descent through the other part of the wheel back to the place where it began, with an equal balance and equal step: *la, sol, fa, mi, re, ut*. Likewise, a song cannot only begin with a point in the bass and

This figure contains the letters, the clefs <note>original: "claves"</note>, and the pitches <term>punctos</term> <note>literally "points," referring to the specific notes or solmization syllables</note>, just as we must use them while ascending and descending in song, as is clear to anyone who looks closely. Through those elements situated outside the wheel, we have the clefs and the specific letter on which each clef must begin. Through the first circumference, we have the letters, their number, and their order. Through the second circumference, we have the number of pitches and their order. Do not be surprised if the first pitch begins in *gamma* <note>the Greek letter Γ, representing the lowest note of the medieval system, "G-ut"</note> or *G*, wherever it may be in the entire figure, and ends in *la* at *A*, since this is proper to whatever letters and pitches belong to *G-ut*. Through the first radius <note>the "spokes" of the wheel diagram</note> of the wheel or figure, we have the first key <note>or instruction</note> of the art of music, which opens and teaches how to sing the pitches from the second to the second—ascending on one side and descending on the other—and for this reason, they are called "seconds." Those cuts <note>original: "scissuræ"</note> which are made after each pitch indicate that the pitches are divided and separated from one another and should be sung with pauses, as it were. Through the second radius, we have the second key or second instruction concerning three pitches to be sung continuously without a pause, almost as if divided, and afterwards joined together without a pause. And because they should be sung separately, there are <term>trictæ</term> <note>see footnote (a)</note> between each pitch, and afterwards they must be joined together as the line directs them: and because they are sung three by three, they are called "thirds."

Through the third radius, we have another way of singing in which they are joined two by two, as is clear by the line that keeps them joined: and because they are sung two by two, there is no <term>tricta</term> between pitch and pitch; nevertheless, they are called "thirds" in a different manner than the first ones. Through the fourth radius, we have the fourth way of singing and joining four by four, as they are joined by lines, and therefore they are called "fourths." <term>Trictæ</term> are placed between each pitch; for although they are joined four by four, they must nevertheless be sung separately at first. Through the fifth radius, we have the fifth way of singing, as is clear from what has already been said, and through the lines and <term>trictæ</term> contained in that same radius.

And why does the fourth radius not have its full foot? I answer: it lacks for no reason other than that custom has abolished it.

I ask: why does the fifth lesson of this art begin with *re*, and not with *ut*? I answer: for it would have a weak beginning on *ut* and a similar ending on *G*. This art proceeds from divine command, from the great humility of praise directed toward God, and from the playfulness <note>original: "lascivia"; in a musical context, this can mean the natural flexibility or ornamentation of the human voice</note> of men: therefore, it seeks to begin humbly and strictly on *re*, to ascend more nobly to *A*, and again to finish moderately on *re* where it began.

I ask: this art does not ascend, as I see, except by five pitches, and yet we can sing five notes higher, as far as our instruments are able to extend themselves. I answer: regarding what you say about being able to sing five notes higher, this proceeds from the complexity of the art, and especially from its very nature. Which I prove: the alphabet does not extend itself—nor should it, nor can it—beyond 24 letters,

### CHAPTER X.

->*The Rubric concerning the figure and order of all the tones in reading.*<-

It remains for us to discuss the present figure of the tone in general. And first, it must be noted that the arrangement of the tones—both in general and in their specific types—is presented according to their due and proper nature, and that each of the tones occupies its rightful seat.

What is a tone <note>original: "tonus"; in this context, it refers to the church modes</note> in general? A tone in general is a figure of seven letters <note>the pitches A, B, C, D, E, F, G</note>, and of one clef, six notes <term>punctorum</term> <note>literally "points," referring to the six syllables of the hexachord: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note>, and eight tones, containing the nature of the whole song, both artificial and natural. But since the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> says that every definition must be interchangeable with the thing it defines, and names must harmonize with the things they describe, let us come to an understanding of the definition and the knowledge of the "tree" <note>a diagrammatic layout common in medieval teaching</note>. And we must note beforehand that the tone in general is divided into eight species of tones. Four are like sons—namely the first, third, fifth, and seventh <note>the "Authentic" modes</note>—and the remaining four are like grandsons—namely the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth <note>the "Plagal" modes</note>. This is to say that the four "sons" are like the source and head of the four remaining "grandsons." Therefore, they are placed on the right side of the tree and touch the tree as a father through an ascending line, and touch themselves as brothers; and they touch the remaining four on the left side of the tree with a descending or nearly equal line, as species, or as their own sons and the grandsons of the said father. And because they are equal in syllable, the first four act as the genus, each for its own share, and the remaining four as species, according to what was said above. For this reason, they occupy equal 

<column-break/>

seats, or occupy their places, established in a general assembly with their highest part, so that within the circuit of each is contained its proper seat, naming, and property.

How many letters and notes does each of the tones obtain by its nature? ℞ <note>Response</note>. The first letter for *re*, the last for the *final* <note>the concluding note of a melody</note>, and the rest as desired for ascending and descending, both below and above itself. And if anyone ignorant of music should presumptuously attribute more notes and letters to any of the tones than has been stated, by its nature those letters and notes are completely superfluous.

To that question which might be asked—concerning the fact that each of the tones, in most cases, exceeds the aforementioned letters and notes in actual song—an answer will be given in the figure or "tree" of the first tone.

Having looked at the tone in general, and the tones in their species, and everything contained within the wheel <note>the circular diagram</note>, it remains for us to look at those things placed in the definition or the circumferences of the wheel.

First, the order of the first seven letters contained in the circle is clear enough. These should be shown and taught to children first, before they come to the knowledge of the tones: for they are held in the place of the subject of the "palm" <note>original: "palma," referring to the Guidonian Hand used to teach the musical scale</note> and of the whole song. And it should be noted that whatever is contained in the palm and in the song should be presented with equal distance, as is established here and in the tree of art by the evidence of the matter. Therefore the notes, because there are only six, and likewise should be arranged with equal distance, cannot nor should they be placed in this figure...

[the] figure, nor is it placed directly above the letters in the figure of the art of music; but regard is had for the equality of the steps <note>intervals or degrees of the scale</note>, not to the number of letters.

The clef <note>original: "clavis"</note> and its multiplication is deservedly placed in the second order of the figure after the letters, because it is founded upon them. Is it not said that such a clef or mutation <note>original: "mutatio"; the process of shifting between hexachords</note> on such a letter makes its beginning? Certainly so.

The notes <term>puncti</term> <note>literally "points," here referring to the six syllables of the hexachord: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la</note> are placed in the third circumference, because they are ordered by the clefs and are produced in a straight arrangement, namely *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la;* and therefore they rightly begin above gamma <note>the lowest note of the medieval system, G</note> or G, which is the same thing, and from then on they proceed by equal steps. In the fourth circle, the tones are deservedly placed below the letters, so that it may be clear on which letter each of the tones makes its own letter; and because they are added last to this figure, it is called the "figure of the order of tones."

And why is "tone" placed in the middle of the tones in such a species, when there are only eight? The answer is clear if one pays close attention: it is placed there as the genus <note>the overarching category</note> and nature that generates the other tones, and from it they are generated and take their origin. In the "tree of marriage" <note>a common medieval diagram used to show family relations and legal restrictions on marriage</note>, is the trunk not placed in the person of a man, not so that he himself is a degree <note>of kinship</note>, nor consists in a degree, but because the others descend from him? Certainly so.

### CHAPTER XI.

->*Concerning the ordering and status of the first tone with the second, in reading and in the figure.*<-

Having set these things forth regarding the ordering of the first tone—as it is the genus with respect to the second, and

<column-break/>

likewise regarding the ordering of the first [tone] with its *seculorum* <note>original: "seculorum"; a mnemonic for the vowels of "Saeculorum, Amen," used to identify the ending formula of a psalm tone</note>, and the five letters which each has under itself—let us proceed. And first, let us see what the first tone is.

->Figure 4.<-

The first tone is a figure of ten *seculorum* formulae, containing five specific letters according to the hand <note>original: "palmam"; referring to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where each joint of the hand represented a specific pitch</note>, and if any others are inserted among them, ruling the whole song, both natural and artificial: which begins on F [on] its rule <note>the line of the musical staff</note>, and ends on D; and it both begins and ends, as it were, with the support of the second tone, which is from its own bosom and is its species, and they both terminate under one root.

The order of the figure is clear enough through the already stated definition and by inspecting it with the five letters from the circumference serving it, even if others are placed between them. It says in the definition "because of G," which is inserted to rule the whole song, which begins in G and ends in D.

On the contrary: do not the responsory *Virgo flagellatur* <note>original Latin: "the virgin is lashed"</note> and the antiphon *Amicus Dei Nicolaus* <note>original Latin: "Nicholas, the friend of God"</note>, and many others, begin in F? Are they not therefore of the first tone? The answer is in the definition, if one pays close attention. It is contained there that it begins on the "rule" <note>staff line</note> of the first tone, not merely designating the letter F; but rather that he who established this art out of obscurity, uncertainty, and near-ruin, [established] that the first tone made its rule on F, and the definition proceeds upon that basis. It does not proceed on the fact that the sixth tone also made its rule on the said F, or that the fifth tone did the same on that F. Therefore, it was added in the definition "and terminates in D." You, the opponent, are committing the fallacy of the "qualified and the absolute" <note>original: "fallaciam secundum quid & simpliciter"; a Scholastic logic term for misapplying a specific case as a general rule</note>.

# ELIAS SALOMONIS

Another point of opposition: is it not true that the Responsory <note>original: "℞."</note> *I saw the Lord* <note>original: "Vidi Dominum"</note> and the antiphon *Go and tell John* <note>original: "Ite dicite Iohanni"</note> belong to the first tone, even though they begin on the note A? Likewise, the Responsory *They delivered up* <note>original: "Tradiderunt"</note> and the antiphon *This Saint* <note>original: "Iste Sanctus"</note>, along with many similar examples, begin above or below the staff line, yet are nonetheless considered part of the first tone? I answer as was stated in the definition: a tone begins on F and ends on D, both "as it were" beginning and "as it were" ending. This "as it were" is to be understood so long as that which is sung conforms more to the first or second tone than to any other. For a chant is judged to belong to the tone whose nature it possesses most strongly, and it is categorized quickly by that nature. For example, if someone is beardless but possesses all other necessary masculine traits, he is judged to be a man. And what I say regarding the first and second tones, I intend to be applied as a rule to all eight tones. Another rule: any chant having a proper sound must belong to some tone. Another: every chant is judged to belong to that tone whose nature it most holds.

It should also be known that the first tone is divided, as many agree, into eleven species of <term>endings of the *seculorum*<note>The Latin "seculorum" refers to the concluding words of the *Gloria Patri* ("...saecula saeculorum. Amen"). In music theory, these represent different melodic endings, or "differentiae," used to transition smoothly back to an antiphon.</note></term>, as is clear in the figure. But why was the fourth *seculorum* cut out? Because it was meant to be rejected, and it was simply taking up space on the parchment; perhaps others should also be rejected, as will appear in the practical application of this same first tone.

Furthermore, let it be that the ten mentioned *seculorum* are divided into four ranks, or four "seats": why are three *seculorum* placed in the first rank or seat? I answer: because they follow the *seculorum* of the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria Patri"</note> and achieve their end on the same letter.

<column-break/>

Why is one *seculorum* placed in the second rank only on the note F? Because no other ending concludes with it on that same letter F. And perhaps—indeed, without a "perhaps"—it is because it is more worthy than all the others and better tempered; it alone would suffice to perfectly govern the entire chant of the first tone if it had pleased our master inventor. Therefore, like a sun and a more worthy thing, it has been given its own seat and assigned to the second rank.

Why are three *seculorum* placed in the third seat? Because they all end on G. I say the same of the other three, because they end on A.

Why does the second tone take its origin in the middle of the first, in the middle of the figure, and among the letters on the left side of the figure? I answer: by necessity. Has it not been said that it is the "species" or "son" of the first tone? Therefore, it begins in the middle of the figure; and because it establishes its rule where the first tone ends, the letters of the second tone begin on the left side because the first tone ends right there.

Why is the second tone content with only two species of *seculorum*? I answer: because no more were assigned to it from its first establishment. Perhaps it would be content with one; indeed, I believe that by the nature of the art, any of the tones ought to be content with a single *seculorum*. This will be evident in the practice of each, because both are designated by a single trunk and the two "feet" of that same trunk. The answer is that although the first and second tones have different notable features, they agree in many things and achieve a single ending.

What is the second tone? The second tone is a figure containing five letters, and if any others are inserted,

Why is the transversal rule <note>a diagonal line in the diagram</note> placed below F and touching D? That split ℞ <note>original: "℞. scissa," the symbol for a Responsory</note> on the circumference of the wheel is placed as a rule for the first and second. ->*Rubric and practice for governing the* **SECULORUM** <note>original: "seculorum," referring to the various melodic endings or "differentiae" of a psalm tone.</note>.*<-

And first concerning the first order, whose *amen* endings I set down here, because the *seculorum* themselves take the strength of their governance from them. ### CHAPTER XIV.

->*Rubric for the explanation of:* **SEEK FIRST**.*<-

Having looked at the "palm" <note>the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool for learning notes</note> and those things which precede and follow it; secondly, the "tree of the art of music" and those things

<column-break/>

from which it is composed and from which it draws its essence; thirdly, the tone in general and how it relates to the eight tones <note>the eight church modes</note> we use; fourthly, the first tone in its capacity as the "genus" <note>the primary form</note> relative to the second, its *seculorum* endings, and the chants governed by it; fifthly, the second tone and how it relates to the first as its "species" <note>the derivative form, specifically the Plagal version of the mode</note>; let us now see how those things established regarding the first tone operate. ...is finished by the neuma <term>neuma: a melodic flourish or sequence of notes sung to a single syllable, often used to help singers memorize the character of a mode</term> at the end, which performs a great function: fourth, because in every part it expresses the specific property of its tone; fifth, it establishes the true order in many ways, as in *Seek ye first* <note>original: "primum quærite"; the standard mnemonic for the first tone, referencing Matthew 6:33</note>. First, it invokes the help of the kingdom of God and the first principle of the things of the first tone. Likewise, the neuma is placed there as a model; for we ought to use a similar neuma at the end of the antiphons of the first tone—those to which we wish to apply a neuma—with nothing added and nothing removed, and let this be held as a rule.

I say the very same regarding the beginning of the second tone and the others: *But the second* <note>original: "secundum autem," mnemonic for Tone 2</note>; *The third day is* <note>original: "Tertia dies est," mnemonic for Tone 3</note>; *The fourth watch* <note>original: "quarta vigilia," mnemonic for Tone 4</note>; *Five were wise* <note>original: "quinque prudentes," mnemonic for Tone 5</note>; *The sixth watch* <note>original: "Sexta vigilia," mnemonic for Tone 6</note>; *There are seven* <note>original: "Septem sunt," mnemonic for Tone 7</note>; *There are eight* <note>original: "Octo sunt," mnemonic for Tone 8</note>. First, they establish the order of their tone; second, they express its property; third, they are governed by the different *seculorum* <note>original: "seculorum," the ending formulas of the psalm tones</note> of whichever tone, as will be clear in their practice; fourth, their neumata serve the same purpose as was said regarding the first tone. And it should be noted that lately, in the neuma for *Seek ye first*, certain cuts or "divisions" <note>original: "scissuræ sive tristæ"</note> have been made intentionally; for they ought to be sung in the manner of pauses. This does not mean one stops entirely, unless the singer wishes, but when it is necessary or pleasing, one may lawfully pause wherever a division is found in the neuma—even after singing one note, or two, three, four, or five notes joined together in the neuma—and indeed in any other chant, provided that a syllable of a word already started does not remain to be expressed. Let this be noted for every other tone and every chant, and let it be held as a rule, so that it is not necessary to repeat this. The **Golden Rule**: that a pause must not be made

<column-break/>

when a syllable of a word already begun must still be expressed in any part of that word, except in organum <term>organum: an early form of polyphony where one voice sings a melody while another holds a sustained note</term> out of necessity. He who makes a pause there sins against the nature of the chant and defiles the song, since the chant is intended to decorate the prayer, not to dishonor it; secondly, he sins against the prayer he utters, because he cuts it apart just like the tearing of the Lord's seamless tunic.

### CHAPTER XV.

->*Rubric on the explanation of the* **GLORY BE TO THE FATHER**.*<-

It remains, secondly, to look at the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note>. It should be noted generally that just as the *Glory be to the Father* begins above, so should all psalms begin or be "intoned" in the Church of God, especially on solemnities, when they are intoned according to the chant of the first tone. And what I say of the first, I say of the second, and so of each one according to the manner of the *Glory be to the Father* of each—of the third and of the fourth. But whoever wishes may remove a single note from the fourth tone on G; and for the fifth and sixth tones, the same as for their *Glory be to the Father*. Or, the psalms of the sixth tone may begin like the first by removing two notes, because modern singers delight in brevity. For the seventh tone, the first four notes may be kept silent, so that the beginning of the psalm does not seem burdensome; and similarly for the eighth tone, let the psalms be begun like the *Glory be to the Father*, with whoever wishes omitting one note on G, just as in the fifth tone; and let this be held as certain.

We have spoken of the beginning of the *Glory be to the Father* and the intonation of the psalms; now I ask if in the middle of the verses of any...

...of the psalm be spoken in this way, as it is sung for "to the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "Spiritui sancto"</note> in the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note>? Likewise, I ask the same concerning the end of the psalm verses: should they be done in the same way as "forever and ever, amen" <note>original: "seculorum amen"</note> is sung in the *Glory be to the Father*? Thirdly, I ask, if it has not been observed as it is in the *Glory be to the Father* in those two places, which is better: the way of the *Glory be to the Father* or the way of the psalms? I respond that the way of the psalms is better, and so it is to be held: and thus all three questions are answered.

Likewise, if it please our master inventor, perhaps the *Glory be to the Father* would be better sung entirely with its aforementioned "forever and ever" <note>original: "seculorum"</note>, as contained in the previous section; then the first tone <term>tonus: one of the eight melodic scales or modes used in medieval chant</term> would not overstep its bounds nor ascend to the note C. For as far as the strict rigor of its nature goes, it does not transcend the note B-flat <note>original: "secundum b"</note>; similarly, perhaps the *Glory be to the Father* ought not to do so either. But perhaps the composer published it after a heavy meal and was feeling playful <note>original: "lascivus," suggesting a lack of discipline or excessive ornamentation</note> when he issued it; or perhaps he did it so that it would appear to differ from the *Glory be to the Father* of the sixth tone. But that was not necessary; for they are quite compatible, in that both follow their rule on the note F, and lament on A, B, and C—and yet in their nature they are entirely diverse. In this same way, a simple man can comfortably eat good bread just like one greater than himself, but they will not be of the same status because of it. 

Likewise, I say that I do not see what purpose that note <term>punctus: literally a "point," referring to a single musical note</term> on C in the "forever and ever" of the *Glory be to the Father* serves, except for playfulness or superfluity. Furthermore, it is well to be noted that the final note of the "forever and ever" of the *Glory be to the Father* is on F. For if it were on E, it would taste of the nature of the fourth tone, and would not taste of the nature of the first.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, from another perspective: that "forever and ever" <note>original: "seculorum"</note> of the *Glory be to the Father* cannot be applied—except improperly—to the beginning of the verses of the Offices, at the end of all of which it is sung with its own musical flourish <term>neuma: a melodic phrase sung to a single syllable</term>, especially on solemn feast days, as it ought to be done. Concerning the manner of intoning the psalms, it has been discussed above.

### CHAPTER XVI.

->Rubric concerning the number of ENDINGS of the first tone.<-

I ask, since eleven "forever and ever" endings <note>original: "seculorum"; these are the E-U-O-U-A-E melodic formulas used to transition from a psalm back to an antiphon</note> were listed above, whether there can or should be more, or if they can be reduced to a smaller number? I respond that there cannot and should not be more; indeed, one has been cut out because the parchment was occupied, for which reason there are ten. Otherwise, there would have to be as many as there are different beginnings of antiphons <term>antiphon: a short sentence or verse sung before and after a psalm</term>, responsories, offices, and any other chants whatever which are governed by the first tone, which is impossible and absurd to imagine. 

It follows that some of the ten mentioned are superfluous; and this is true, except for one alone which ends on F, according to the rule of that same tone, as will appear in what follows. The first three serve only as one, since they make their end on D (leaving aside the fourth, which prevails over all). The fifth, sixth, and seventh end on G, according to the rule of their tone: and of these, likewise, one would suffice. The eighth, ninth, and tenth end on A, according to the rule of their tone. And so we have one from the first three, and leaving aside the fourth, we have two from the remaining six: and thus we have three endings for the first tone, and with the fourth, there are four.

He also analyzes the various "Seculorum" endings (differentia) for the first mode, arguing that most are redundant and can be reduced to four essential formulas.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Salomon's argument regarding the structure of musical modes. He is moving from the specific debate about melodic consistency in the "Glory be to the Father" (Doxology) to a broader rule: that each musical tone should ideally have only one standard ending (the seculorum) to avoid confusing students.</meta>

THE SCIENCE OF THE ART OF MUSIC.

And therefore let us see how many *seculorum* <note>original: "seculorum," referring to the "seculorum. Amen" melodic formula used to link a psalm to an antiphon</note> should exist within each tone according to their individual natures. I say, for the reasons assigned above and to avoid repetition and confusion, that each tone ought to have only one well-tempered *seculorum*, and that it should end on the "rule" (the final note) of the tone it serves; and for the seventh tone, it should end on the note *a*. This ought to be taught to the boys, since the *Gloria Patri* <note>Glory be to the Father</note> must be joined with that same formula. This I prove, so that no tone may have anything but a single *Gloria Patri*; likewise, that it should have only a single ending for antiphons in the "Seek first" <note>original: "primum quærite," a common mnemonic chant used to teach the first tone</note>, and likewise for the other tones. Similarly, for all the *seculorum* formulas of any given tone, only one *Gloria Patri* is provided. Likewise, there is a single *neuma* <term>neuma: a wordless melodic phrase sung on a single syllable, often used to close a chant</term> at the end, where the *seculorum* of the *Gloria Patri* is placed for each tone. Likewise, the second tone is not satisfied unless there is a single *seculorum*. The sixth and fifth tones, I consider as one, since they both end on the same letter [note].

Do all tones have only a single clef? Certainly not. Therefore, all tones should be content with a single *seculorum* each, which is more better tempered. Regarding the first tone, this is clearly established: namely the fourth [ending], which ends on the rule of its first tone; and that must be entirely joined with the *Gloria Patri*, for the reasons assigned above.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->A rubric concerning things to be noted beforehand regarding the nature of the SECULORUM.<-

Before we come to the nature of any *seculorum*, it must be noted beforehand that art imitates nature as much as it

<column-break/>

can: and especially this art [music], which was sung at the creation of the angels, and which by its very nature praises God. And just as we see that a father is bound to nourish his son, and by civil law a guardian is bound to rule the minor he has under his care, and in grammar a noun is appropriately governed by a verb and other parts of speech; so in the present science, the whole chant is governed by tones and by the species <term>species: the specific arrangements of tones and semitones that make up scales</term> contained within them; and specifically, all things that can be sung under a tone are governed by the *seculorum* of that tone which they serve.

And it is notably to be observed that, just as boys are shown that the beginnings of antiphons <term>antiphon: a short chant sung before and after a psalm</term> are governed by the *seculorum*, so in truth the beginnings of the Responsories, Offices, *Alleluia*, Offertories, and Communions <note>These are different categories of liturgical chants used in the Mass and the Divine Office</note>, and the whole chant which is sung in harmony, are governed. But knowledge ought to be handed down to boys first through a simple, easier, and more instructional path, lest despair harm them; and similarly regarding responsories and other chants, they are withheld for two reasons: to avoid multiplying the complexities of the art, and because it is presumed they will be more advanced in knowledge when they come to the teaching of responsories and beyond. Likewise, it is true that the appropriate *seculorum* can be adapted to any chant. For in many books, in place of the *seculorum* at the head of what is to be sung, a numbering is placed—I, II, III, and so on for each—representing the number of the tone. It is both praiseworthy and very useful for this numbering to be added to every chant, or the appropriate...

# THE SCIENCE OF THE ART OF MUSIC

...obligation of the *seculorum* <note>original: "seculorum," the melodic formula for the "world without end" (saeculorum Amen) that links a psalm to an antiphon</note>. But some people claim—and wrongly so—that neither the *seculorum* nor the musical notation should be written down, so that the singer might better commit it to memory; this opinion is worthy of rejection. Instead, some wicked teachers, led by a spark of malice, even erase them from books so that "blood may be drawn from the students' sides" <note>An idiom for causing physical suffering or extreme hardship through harsh discipline</note>. I myself have seen such erasures and have suffered beatings because of them, and I still know of a book where the notation was scraped away.

Also, in every book, the numbering of the pages should be placed in order on every leaf, as I have seen in the books of the Lord Pope's chapel and in all the books of the Lombards <note>Lombards: People from Northern Italy, known in this period for their organized legal and financial record-keeping</note>. For when you find a reference to something you are missing, you will find written on that page which leaf you should look for; then you may turn to it boldly, without suffering the shame of appearing ignorant.

Next, let us see whether the antiphon is governed by the *seculorum* at the first, third, or fourth note of any beginning, and at which note the *seculorum* joins its strength with the antiphon to rule its beginning and act as a sign of which tone it belongs to. It should be noted that sometimes it does not take hold at the second, fourth, or seventh note, until the antiphon is established and makes it clear which tone it intends to be. Only then, by a certain will, the *seculorum* of the antiphon joins and confirms that the antiphon or chant belongs to the tone which the *seculorum* serves. I can prove this. Does not an antiphon of the eighth tone sometimes begin on C, the first note of the hand <note>original: "palma," referring to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where parts of the hand represent musical notes</note>, such as: *We who live* <note>original: "nos qui vivimus"</note>? And at...

<column-break/>

...first glance, does it not look like it belongs to the second or first tone? Likewise, it sometimes starts on E, and so appears to be of the fourth or third tone; or sometimes on F, appearing to be of the sixth tone; and so on with other letters. Thus, the *seculorum* of a particular tone does not join with the antiphon until we have sung enough of it that we can judge by the nature of the tones which one it ought to be. I also prove what was said before: that sometimes even by the first eight notes <term>puncta: literally "points," the individual notes of the melody</term> at the beginning of an antiphon, we who see it in the book cannot judge which tone it should be. Much less should the *seculorum* join with it, for it is a "dead voice" until we can judge the tone. Indeed, with *Your birth, O Virgin Mother of God* <note>original: "Nativitas tua Dei genitrix virgo"</note> or *John rebuked Herod* <note>original: "Arguebat Herodem Iohannes"</note>, we can barely judge what tone they should be.

The rule is that every chant of the first mode <note>original: "primi toni"</note> beginning on the first C is governed—and must be governed—by the *seculorum* ending in D, without exception. But the things put forward in the second treatise concerning the *seculorum amen* should be taken as examples; they suffice for now for the sake of brevity, since one must proceed from like cases to like cases.

But an objection is raised regarding the ninth *seculorum amen*, suggesting that what was recently said ought to be governed by it. I respond that it was already stated that the first two *seculorum* should govern these and similar cases, and no other. This I prove: Who more truly attends the Lord Pope? Is it the one who comes to him and stays by his side, such as a cardinal deacon? Or is it the one who, when he senses him coming, flees and climbs into a tower to watch him approaching from afar? This is exactly what the ninth *seculorum amen* does; when it senses a chant or antiphon beginning on C, it flees from F to A. Surely, the one who actually goes to the person, or stays near him, is the one who governs, just as the fourth *seculorum* does. Likewise, I prove that they cannot be governed by the aforementioned ninth *seculorum amen*. By the rules of law, "no one transfers more right to another than he is established to possess." <note>original: "nullus plus iuris in alium transfert, quam constat ipsum habere." This is a famous maxim of Roman Law.</note> But neither the "hand" <note>The Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool used by medieval singers to find notes on their joints</note>, nor the art of music itself, nor the modes give power to any *seculorum* when it governs beyond

<column-break/>

five notes <note>original: "quinque punctos," referring to the intervals or notes in the musical scale</note>, nor is such a thing found expressed in writing. Therefore, it is impossible for the ninth *seculorum amen* to govern any chant that begins more than five notes away.

### Concerning the governance of the third *seculorum*.

-> [Musical notation for "Se-cu-lo-rum A-men" on a four-line staff with an F-clef.] <-

I will speak briefly of this: I see no reason why it should even be placed in the books. No other chant is attributed to it, because it is more truly governed by the fourth *seculorum amen*, or the first two. The whole melody is different in itself, almost sounding like the sixth mode; and it may rightly be said of it: *foul is the part which does not harmonize with its whole.* <note>original: "turpis est pars, quæ suo non congruit universo." A common philosophical and legal maxim regarding consistency.</note> But let us restore to it those things that were first attributed to it and its like: the antiphon *Virgin of Christ* <note>original: "Christi virgo"</note>, and the antiphon *From which it was made* <note>original: "Ex quo facta est"</note>. Also *John rebuked Herod* <note>original: "Arguebat Herodem Iohannes"</note> and the antiphon *If I* <note>original: "Si ego"</note>. And because it extends to nothing else, I do not assign a rule for it, except the one it follows: that it ought not govern any chant except those beginning on F (like *Virgin of Christ*) or on D (like *From which it was made* and *If I*).

### Next follows the "split" *seculorum*.

-> [Musical notation for "Se-cu-lo-rum A-men" on a four-line staff with an F-clef.] <-

This *seculorum* is entirely superfluous. Is it not totally identical to the second one, except in the last note, where it kicks back like a fool throwing pebbles? And yet, regarding its antiquity, it has nothing to do with the rule; nor did it govern except when I asked...

->On the governance of the fourth *seculorum*.<-

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff in F-clef. Square neumes are arranged above the text "Se cu lo rum A men."</image-desc>

Concerning the fourth *seculorum* <note>The "seculorum" refers to the "differentia," a melodic ending of the Doxology (Gloria Patri) used to transition smoothly back into an antiphon. Salomon numbers these specific melodic formulas.</note>, would that it governed the whole chant of the first mode <note>original: "primi toni"</note>, which it could and should do most fittingly. Why should it not govern a chant beginning on the first C, which is only four notes <note>original: "punctos"</note> away, since the ninth *seculorum*—which does not even end on the regular pitch of the first mode—governs a chant that begins five notes below itself? Likewise, why should it not govern every chant ending on F, which is the rule of that same mode, and consequently every chant that begins between A and D? Certainly, it would govern them well, and it ought to do so. However, custom dictates that it only governs chants beginning on D by one note, such as the antiphon *Angelus Domini* [The Angel of the Lord], or by two notes, such as the antiphon *Ecce nomen* [Behold the name]; or by three or four notes without a slur <note>original: "copula," a musical term for notes joined together in a single breath or syllable</note>; and it would immediately descend to C by one note, or ascend to F, as is clear in the antiphon *In tympano* [On the drum], and proceeding from similar cases to similar cases.

Rule: that the *seculorum* of the first mode ending on F governs every chant of the same mode beginning on D by one, two, or three notes without a slur, descending to C or ascending directly to F, as is clear from the examples already mentioned. And it would also suitably govern every chant of the same

<column-break/>

mode in the manner of the *Gloria patri* [Glory be to the Father], of which there is only one.

->Behold the fifth species of *seculorum*.<-

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff in F-clef. Square neumes are arranged above the text "Se cu lo rum A men."</image-desc>

Rule: that the *seculorum* of the first mode ending on G governs all beginnings of chants of the same mode starting on D and ascending directly to G, such as the antiphon *A bimatu* [From two years old], and similar ones; it adds nothing of its own nature. But a strong objection is raised regarding the antiphon *Tecum principium* [With thee is the principality], which begins on E, suggesting that this species should govern it. I respond that it may govern it out of custom <note>original: "ex usu"</note> or even misuse <note>original: "ex abusu"</note>, but it ought not to do so. Rather, it is governed directly by the first two *seculorum* (which I consider to be the same), or it is governed by the ninth *seculorum amen*; this I prove by necessity. *Tecum* begins on E, but in starting on E, it seems to belong to the third or fourth mode, because the third mode ends on E, and the fourth establishes its rule and ends there as well. The second note of *Tecum* directly possesses the nature of the first *seculorum*, as does the third note and the rest of the antiphon. It is true that by ancient custom, the third note of *Tecum* and the rest of the antiphon follow the nature of the ninth *seculorum amen*; yet it is more truly of the fourth *seculorum*. As for *Tecum*, I leave it to common usage whether it be of the first, fourth, or ninth *seculorum*, as it may be found in the books.

### CHAPTER XIX.

->*Rubric on the practice and governance of responsories, and of other chants.*<-

It remains to consider the beginning of the Responsory *Tradiderunt* [They delivered up], which is positioned for the same reason as the *Gloria Patri* and the *seculorum*—namely, to designate that the verses of responsories and similar chants belong to the first mode. On the contrary, it could be argued from this that responsory verses which are sung differently than the ones mentioned above are not of the first mode, which would be an inconvenient thing to say. Here is the response: this is true for those that belong to the second, third, or fourth modes, and so on for the others. However, all those chants whose rule can be fitted to the F first placed on the palm <note>The "palm" refers to the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where parts of the hand represent specific musical pitches</note> and which end on D, will belong to the first mode; and this is the first rule. The second rule: every chant that establishes its rule on F and its end on D or on the first C—wherever it may begin from the second B of the palm down to Gamma—it will be

...will be of the first mode. The third rule: every chant, no matter how high it ascends in the **hand** <term>palma: the "Guidonian Hand," a visual map of the musical scale used by medieval singers to find their notes</term>, even if it should transcend the hand and descend as far as **Gamma** <term>Gamma-ut: the very lowest note of the medieval musical system</term>, it will be of the first mode, provided the rules of the first mode are observed or nearly observed. Whether it is a long antiphon, a long responsory, a Kyrie, a sequence <note>original: "prosa," a type of chant sung before the Gospel</note>, or whatever kind of chant it might be, it will be of the first mode. And this rule extends to all modes, if it is understood soundly. By this rule, the opinion of the ancients is rejected—those who used to say that every chant was "irregular" if it did not begin on the regular note of that mode whose nature the chant most closely followed, or if it did not end where that mode usually ends.

**Rule**: Every chant is judged to belong to that mode whose nature it most assumes. 

**Rule**: No chant sung in harmony <note>original: "concorditer," likely referring to organum or polyphony</note> can be irregular, even if it were to ascend so high that for the greater part it transcends the hand, the nature of its ascent, and the usual course of the modes in the hand. An example is the sequence by Lord Clement, *In Praise of Mary* <note>original: "Mariæ præconio"</note>; and yet it is directly in the seventh mode if it begins on the high G; or, if it began on the first G of the hand, it will be of the eighth mode. If this [transgression of the range] made a chant irregular, then any chant that transcended the usual course of the modes in the hand would be irregular, and it would never be sung in four voices; for in the greater part of what is sung in four voices, the range transcends the course of the entire hand. Nevertheless, the chants of the fourth, third, and second voices belong to the same mode as the first voice. Thus, it is necessary to fix the second voice,

<column-break/>

the third, and the fourth, on those same letters and points in the hand through which the first voice runs. Furthermore, I prove that this must necessarily be understood in such a way: Does not the antiphon *Kind Mother of the Redeemer* <note>original: "Alma redemptoris"</note> ascend to the final G of the hand, along with the responsories *Behold the Lamb of God* <note>original: "Ecce agnus Dei"</note> and *Beholding from Afar* <note>original: "Aspiciens"</note>, and many others? And yet we approve by ancient usage that they are of the seventh mode; and thus it is true.

Likewise, just as I see in Grammar that there are certain parts of speech that govern and are not governed, some that both govern and are governed, and some that do not govern but are governed; so it is in the science of the art of music. The first, third, fifth, and seventh modes <note>These are the "authentic" modes</note> govern the other four modes <note>the "plagal" modes</note>, and all eight (for in this they are equal) govern the entire art of singing, each according to its own proportion throughout the whole hand. Furthermore, the **seculorum** <term>seculorum: the melodic endings used for the Doxology to transition back to a chant</term> of any mode are governed by the modes themselves, and they in turn govern the entire chant. A chant that does not begin on the true rule of a mode, nor ends as such for the greater part of its length, departs from the nature of the modes—such as the phrase *Grant, Lord, a blessing* <note>original: "Iube domine benedicere," the opening of a liturgical lesson</note>, and the greater part of the monks' readings which they read while singing at Matins, such as the lessons, and sometimes in other hours and similar things. Even good and well-ordered chants are not always governed by the modes (or they are governed by them poorly), because of how tastelessly and inappropriately they are sometimes performed.

The *Holy* <note>original: "Sanctus"</note> and the *Lamb of God* <note>original: "Agnus"</note> which begin on **a** and end on **G**; the Epistles and Gospels, and hymns in schools, and things similar to these which begin on **a** and end on **G** or on **a**—how can they be of the first mode? I answer: in the same way they can and should be...

<meta>This page continues Elias Salomonis's defense of the supremacy of the musical modes over other elements like the hexachord syllables (solmization) and the Guidonian Hand. He specifically targets the "French" style of teaching, which he views as overly complex and theoretically flawed.</meta>

# THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE ART OF MUSIC

...to be of the first mode <note>original: "primi toni"</note>, just as the verse *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note> of the same mode, and the verse of *They have washed their robes* <note>original: "Laverunt stolas suas"</note>, because they are sung in G and in a, just like the *Glory be to the Father* and *They have washed*. You who ask such questions, you seem to be ignorant of music!

There follows the **neuma** <term>neuma: a melodic flourish or melisma sung on a single syllable, often at the end of a phrase</term> of the end of the verse for the responsories *They delivered* <note>original: "Tradiderunt"</note> and the verse *They have washed*. And it should be known that this is presented for the sake of instruction, to apply a similar melodic ending <note>original: "finem neumatis"</note> in all verses regularly belonging to the first mode. And it is well worth noting that the **neuma** should generally be started on the fifth-to-last syllable of the responsory verses.

**On the contrary**, it is argued that the modes <note>original: "toni"</note> do not rule every chant. For in the teaching of the French concerning this art, it is held that a certain part of some antiphon, responsory, or other chant is ruled in some way by "nature" <note>original: "per naturam"</note> through several notes <note>original: "punctis"</note>—that is to say, through *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*. But they have not explained this well. A certain part of the same chant is ruled by **B-natural** <term>B-quadratum: the "square B," indicating a natural B</term>, another part is ruled by **B-flat** <term>B-molle: the "soft B," indicating a flattened B</term>, and many similar phantasms, which they speak against this system of letters, chants, and notes of the **hand** <note>original: "palma"</note>, about which they are poorly taught—and at more than double the fair price! <note>Elias uses a legal term for fraud—"ultra dimidium iusti pretii"—suggesting students are being cheated by these teachers.</note> If any of these objections are worthy of a response, no better one can be given than a summary of what was said before the objection and throughout this whole art. Was it not said that there are seven letters—A, B, C, D, E, F, G—and the locations of the first subject or instrument are found in this art? Also, that there are six notes—*ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la*—rooted upon the aforementioned

<column-break/>

letters in the place of the subject or second instrument in this art? Also, the third instrument or subject in this art is the **hand** <term>palma: the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where each joint of the hand represents a note</term>. Also, the seven **keys** <term>claves: the clefs or fundamental pitches that define the scale</term> rooted upon the nature of the letters and notes are held in the place of the fourth subject. These four, with everything contained under them, serve the entire art as the lowlier instruments of the art; and even the "lordly modes" <note>original: "domini toni"</note> hardly deign to call these four their "instruments." Nor do they call these four their "species," but only their "instruments." Certainly, it is so: neither the aforementioned four, nor any letter, note, hand, or key, possesses any rule or any power, but only the duty of serving in the whole chant; nor should they be named by anyone except for the purpose of serving, not ruling.

Furthermore, it was said that there are four principal modes—the first, third, fifth, and seventh—which are not ruled, but rule everything that is or can be of chant. Therefore, they are not ruled by their servants—by B-natural, B-flat, and other phantastics, etc. Nor is the chant sung under them ruled by anything in any part of itself, nor by these [servants]. A lesser student does not rule the master, nor a servant the lord. How could one rule others who has not learned to rule himself, and has not taken on the form of a student? To be brief, neither letter nor note, hand nor key, nor both together, extend themselves to any rule or anything else; nor by their nature do they desire anything else, but only that they be brought forth in the correct way, as was said, without injury, and that their due be rendered to them. Would that the lord clerics would do so, when...

He dismisses French musical theories regarding B-natural and B-flat as "phantasms" that distract from the true nature of the modes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Elias Salomonis’s technical argument regarding the relationship between the eight musical modes. # THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE ART OF MUSIC
### BY ELIAS SALOMONIS

no one should be excused from knowledge of them, much less than one is excused from ignorance of the law. It is true that the four tones <note>original: "quatuor toni"; Elias uses "tone" and "mode" interchangeably</note>—the second, fourth, sixth, and eighth—are "species" or subtypes, as has been said, of the other four tones. The **seculorum** <term>seculorum: the melodic endings of the 'Gloria Patri,' used to transition back to an antiphon</term> are subtypes of all eight modes. Antiphons, the Offices of the Mass, Responsories, the Alleluia, Offertories, Communions, and all other chants, whatever they may be and without exception, are the expressions of the modes—which cannot be otherwise—and they are rightly called the "flowers and fruits" of the modes. But for anyone who feels differently throughout regarding the governance of this art and the nature of any of the aforementioned things, as was stated above, one should neither oppose nor respond to him, as he is ignorant of the principles; rather, let him fall into the pit like a blind man.

Regarding the error contained in certain books, and the delusional belief of some who say that the fourth mode <note>original: "quartus tonus"</note> follows its rule on the note **F**, as these are erroneous claims, it is not necessary to respond. However, if they did require a response, it could be said that as far as the East is from the West, so far is the nature of **F** from being held as the rule for the fourth mode. For this mode desires, for the most part and especially at the beginning and the end, to always be "plaintive" <note>original: "plangi"; Elias refers to the mournful or somber quality traditionally attributed to the fourth mode</note>, whereas **F** is never so; indeed, **F** is totally removed from a plaintive nature, both as a letter and as a musical note. Likewise, through what has been said, the second mode begins and ends where the first does; the sixth begins and ends where the fifth does; the eighth where the seventh does: consequently,

<column-break/>

and by necessity, the fourth begins and ends where the third ends, and thus the fourth mode follows its rule. Otherwise, it would be considered something monstrous that does not fit into its own universe. Therefore, one should not believe such a person as an individual, nor those who knowingly affirm such things.

### CHAPTER XX.

->**On the practice of the keys, and how they ought to be used in solfying. (a)**<-
<note>(a) Otherwise known as solmization <note>original: "solfizare"</note>, that is, singing musical notes, derived from the syllables *sol* and *fa*.</note>

Concerning the coincidence and the **mutation** <term>mutation: the process of changing from one hexachord (set of six notes) to another while singing</term> of keys <note>original: "clavium"; in this context, the clefs or the specific pitches on the Hand</note> at the same point in the sequence of the **Palm** <term>Palma: the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool where each part of the hand represents a specific note</term>, no better teaching can be given than that which is placed upon the Palm itself. For as it is contained in the Palm, it is necessary that singers use the points and letters in various ways according to the diversity of the chants and keys, as appears through inspection of the Hand, with nothing added and nothing removed. Let this be held as certain, for whoever uses it otherwise would fall into the vice of **false music** <term>musica falsa: the use of notes outside the standard medieval gamut, such as accidentals</term>. However, it should be noted for the instruction of younger students who are **solfying** <note>original: "solfiant"; practicing their scales using syllables</note> that they should be careful as to which key their chant begins in, and follow it boldly up to the syllable *la* in the same way the chant proceeds. Then, when they reach *la*, if the chant should ascend higher, they must "mutate" and resume with the key nearest to that key which it was necessary to leave behind, and similarly ascend through that one up to *la*. The same applies to each step when ascending, and when descending, when one reaches *ut*: likewise, if one wishes to descend further, they should resume the key most suitable for it. No better teaching can be given through any other way than the figure of the Palm.

# THE KNOWLEDGE OF THE ART OF MUSIC.

And it should be noted that anyone who moves from one clef into another without doubling the notes <note>original: "sine duplicatione punctorum"; referring to a specific technique in solmization to ensure pitch accuracy when the hexachord shifts</note> could be called a "false musician" lowing falsely <note>original: "falsa mugiens"; Salomonis is making a derogatory pun on the word "musician" (musicus) and the lowing of a cow (mugire)</note>, a thief of song, and he would fall into the vice of "false music" <term>false music: *musica falsa*, the use of notes outside the standard medieval hand/scale, often requiring accidentals</term> without any fear of contradiction.

Since the practical application of the first mode <term>mode: the medieval system of melodic scales, also called "tones"</term> generally ought to extend to all the modes insofar as it touches them—for "it is your business when your neighbor’s wall is on fire" <note>A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, implying that a mistake in one part of the system affects the whole</note>—let us therefore look at the practice of all eight modes regarding their reading. We shall focus on the first mode most especially, because it must be made manifest to children before they arrive at a full knowledge of singing.

The **first mode** establishes its rule <note>original: "regula"; likely referring to the starting position or the reciting tone</note> on **F**. It sounds <note>original: "plangit"; literally "laments," used here technically to describe how the melody moves or resonates</note> at the third above it on **a**, at the fourth above it on **b**, and it sounds at the second below it on **E**, and makes its end at the third [below the rule] on **D**.

The **second mode** establishes its rule on **D**. It sounds at the second above it on **E**, and at the fifth above it on **a**, and sounds at the third below it on **B**, and makes its end on that same **D**.

The **third mode** establishes its rule on **G**. It sounds above it on **a**, and at the third on **b**, and at the third below it on **E**, and finishes on that same **E**.

<column-break/>

The **fourth mode** establishes its rule on **G**. It sounds on **E**, and sounds at the fourth above it on **a**, and at the fifth above it on **b**, and finishes on that same **E**.

The **fifth mode** establishes its rule on **a**. It sounds at the second above it on **b**, and at the fifth above it on **e**, and sounds at the fourth below it on **E**, and finishes at the third below it on **F**.

The **sixth mode** establishes its rule on **F**. It sounds at the third above it on **a**, and at the fourth above it on **b**, and sounds at the second below it on **E**, and finishes on that same rule on **F**.

The **seventh mode** establishes its rule on **b**. It sounds on **b**, and sounds at the fourth above it on **e**, and sounds at the second below it on **a**, and makes its end at the third below it on **G**.

The **eighth mode** establishes its rule on **G**. It sounds at the second above it on **a**, and at the third above it on **b**, and sounds at the third below it on **E**, and makes its end on that same rule on **G**.

### The manner of singing psalms.

It should be known that according to the *world without end* <note>original: "seculorum"; refers to the *Euouae*, the vowels of the last words of the Gloria Patri (*saeculorum. Amen*), used to indicate the melodic ending of a psalm tone</note>, which ought to be attached to the *Glory be to the Father*, the body of the *world without end* in the *Glory be to the Father* is totally assimilated to the *world without end* of the *Glory be to the Father* of the **sixth mode**. The *Amen* of the first *world without end* ends on **D**. Thus the first and second versions are considered the same regarding their rule, though the second is more appropriate than the first, and the second alone would suffice for both. That *world without end* does not have its own rule, but rather it governs every song of the **second mode**. I wish that in all the modes it had been so ordained from of old; thus many people's errors would have been provided for—those who perhaps believe they see well into the art, yet do not yet see in the book the value of a single note <note>original: "puncti"; literally "point," the standard term for a musical note in this period</note>.

Dearest student <note>original: "Karissime tu minor"; likely addressing a junior cleric or choirboy</note>, do not be deceived in the pronunciation of that little verse *The Lord has risen* <note>original: "Resurrexit Dominus"</note>; for in the word *Lord* <note>original: "dominus"</note>, only the last syllable should fall on **D**, just as in the first *Francis* <note>original: "Francisce"</note>. For just as the word *Lord* has a long accent on the first syllable *Do*, and the remaining two syllables have a short accent: so the first note <note>original: "punctus"</note> shall be drawn out, and the remaining two are shortened in a dignified manner without any smearing <note>original: "expingamento"; likely referring to vocal slides or sloppy ornamentation</note>, and it will be sufficient

<column-break/>

for both syllables and notes; otherwise, by singing differently, the notes and syllables would be harmed. Likewise, it should be notably noted—if you do not wish to mock God, men, and yourself—that in the same manner, in the same voice, and through the same notes that you sing the verses of the psalms under the rule of any mode, the response must match the singing of each little verse. Does not he who cries out wine <note>i.e., a wine merchant advertising his wares in the street</note> use an equal and fitting voice? If he emitted sounds in different pitches, would he not be mocked by the people and considered insane? Certainly so. Likewise, I prove that *Lord* and similar words ought to be pronounced as is contained above.

For if a melody <term>neuma: a group of notes sung to a single syllable</term> should fall upon a syllable that is meant to be shortened, whichever one it might be, it would be proper to follow and pursue it; and so we hold in many places. The reason we do this is that the text <note>original: "littera"</note> is there in the place of the subject, and it serves the song in that the song predominates and decorates the word. Therefore, in the said song, a syllable that should be shortened sometimes has a long accent, and conversely, one that should be lengthened sometimes has a short accent, especially in the **science of organum** <term>science of organizing: *scientia organizandi*, an early form of polyphony where one or more voices are added to a plainchant melody</term>. From these
<meta>catchword: things then (igi-)</meta>

and under the pretext of piety, he falls into impiety, damaging both: the syllables and the notes <note>original: "punctos"; literally "points," the term for musical notes in medieval notation</note>, by casting them down from their proper place on the third line, **F**, into **D**.

Rule. Every chant of the third mode beginning on **G** that makes a stepwise ascent to **c** or similar, is governed by the *seculorum* of the same mode ending on **G**.

Rule. Here, by a fiction of the art <note>original: "fictione artis"; refers to a theoretical adjustment or transposition to make a melody fit the rules of the mode</note>, we imagine a chant that began higher to actually start on **G**. With the phrase *with the Holy Spirit* <note>original: "sancto spiritu"</note>, we imagine it to begin on the first **E**. Or, if it were to begin on **b**, it would end on **b** in one way, and in another way on **G**. And if anyone were to object that it was ridiculous for it to end on **G** or **b**, the reply would be: it is shameful for a teacher when his own fault refutes him; for the *seculorum* of the third mode, which governs other chants, ends in **b**, and therefore the objection is invalid.

Rule. Regarding these five *seculorum* endings, we must know that the third *seculorum* is the most significant in its melody <note>original: "praevalet punctum"; suggesting it is the standard or most important ending</note>, and it can most excellently and appropriately govern all chants of the third mode; no other *seculorum* of the same mode is considered as suitable for doing this. I am not proceeding with any further discussion on this matter for the present. However, these points and others that could be noted regarding the nature of what has been said about the third tone <note>The third mode, or Phrygian mode</note> can be sufficiently gathered from what was stated in the first mode. I am not providing a diagram for the third and fourth tones here; but you, young student, if it pleases you, may have them drawn up following the pattern of the diagrams for the first and second modes. Likewise, the definitions of the third and fourth tones can be obtained through the definitions of the first and second, provided you observe the letters in which they begin and end. Regarding the first *seculorum* <note>The "seculorum" refers to the concluding cadence of the "Gloria Patri," which must match the beginning of the following antiphon</note> of the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note>, I did not bother to give a specific rule of governance; for in its concluding melody <note>original: "neumate"</note>, it governs entirely the same as the second *seculorum*, which ends on **E**. Or, without any melodic flourish, it governs in its entirety the same as the third *seculorum*. And note, young student <note>original: "tu minor"; likely referring to a junior cleric or student at whose request Elias wrote the treatise</note>, at whose request I am arranging these modes, that if you were to provide me with the books used

<column-break/>

in the bishopric of your diocese, I would gladly collect the beginnings of the chants from them and place them into the tones as examples. In this way, through the practice of the chants provided in the examples, you might learn the music more easily over time and commit it more effectively to memory. Do not wonder why I do not double or multiply the examples; for such multiplication would lead only to confusion and the slowing down of scholarly instruction. Indeed, the multiplication of examples that many others perform seems to proceed from the blindness of ignorance of the art. Note also that within the examples I provide, I intend to include examples of all chants that can be sung in harmony by anyone and restricted under the rules of the *seculorum*.

->The method of intoning the psalms according to the fourth tone.<-

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff with square neumes. Lyrics: The Lord is my light,</image-desc>

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff with square neumes. Lyrics: and my salvation; whom shall I fear?</image-desc>

Rule: Every chant of the fourth tone beginning on **E** and ascending from **E** to **G** with a middle-

<column-break/>

ending, or beginning on **F** and descending to **D** (such as the introit *The salvation of the people*), <note>original: "salus populi"</note> or beginning on **a** and above, is governed by the *seculorum* of the same tone ending on **a** without any fear of doubt. Those other two *seculorum* endings are entirely useless, and for that reason, they have been cut out. For do they not sing them exactly like the second *seculorum*, except for the very last note? Regarding that note, or those notes, they cannot be said to do any more good than a fifth wheel on a wagon. <note>original: "quinta rota in plaustro"; a medieval idiom for something completely redundant or useless.</note> The second *seculorum* is superior, and it is sufficient all by itself. The *seculorum* of the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note> governs nothing other than the second *seculorum*, and therefore no other governance is assigned to it. Here we ought to understand the daily practice as if it began on **E**. For the person who discovered this melodic ascent did so only for the greater exaltation of the glory and praise of God, as if he were lifting himself higher in the second voice; this is especially true because the lamentation <term>planctus<gloss>a mournful or expressive musical style</gloss></term> on that same **a** produces this same effect. Furthermore, the chant and the prayer are essentially the same as the first ones, except that they are sung higher.

The monks’ manner of reading: first they begin on *e*; second, they descend a third to *a*; and they ascend a second to *b*, and they soften <term>soften<span>In medieval music theory, "softening" (<i>mollificando</i>) refers to the use of a "soft" B (B-flat) instead of a "hard" B (B-natural).</span></term> it against all reason; and afterwards they descend a fourth to *F*.

A second manner of reading is the opposite: first they descend a fourth from *c* to *G*; and afterwards they ascend to *a* or to *b*, softening both, and afterwards they descend to *F*. And this is according to their own bad will, among whom no order reigns. The readings will be in the fifth tone; but while they should be well-proportioned, they conduct themselves poorly while glorifying

<column-break/>

God with the art of singing; by softening *a* and *b*, they fall into the vice of <term>false music<span>Originally <i>musica falsa</i> or <i>musica ficta</i>. This refers to the introduction of accidentals (sharps or flats) that are not part of the standard hexachord system, which Elias views here as a technical error.</span></term>. Concerning the knowledge of this art, they do not care because of the deficiency of their superior; and perhaps God cares no more for them than for the one to whom He said: *you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you may not serve me as a priest* <note>Hosea 4:6. Elias uses this biblical condemnation to emphasize that musical errors in the liturgy are a serious spiritual failing.</note>; for it is better that a donkey's millstone be hung around your neck, and you be drowned in the deep <note>Matthew 18:6.</note>.

### On the governance of the second *seculorum*.

<image-desc>Full-width musical notation on two four-line staves with square notes. Wisely, they are intoned at the end of the tone with this verse: *Let every spirit praise the Lord* <note>original: "Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum"</note>, for the end of the work begun in song. In truth, since the present little work was begun for the honor of our creator and savior Jesus Christ—to whom belongs honor, power, and empire without end—and of the glorious virgin, his most blessed Mother, and has been perfected by their support, as is evident; now that the book is finished, let there be praise and glory to Christ.

The <term>seculorum</term> has been cut out above because it adds nothing to the third <term>seculorum</term> except for a single <term>punctum<note>A single square-shaped musical note.</note></term>, which produces nothing but folly and perversion. The <term>seculorum</term> of the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note> is entirely the same in all its governance as the third <term>seculorum</term>.

No rule has been assigned to the second or fourth <term>seculorum</term>, nor are there many examples, because it is entirely dissonant with the

<column-break/>

Behold the way of beginning psalms according to the eighth tone and imposing the ending in the manner of its own <term>seculorum</term>, by which it is governed.

Rule. Every <term>seculorum</term> of the eighth tone ending on *c* governs every chant of the same tone beginning on *c* and above, without exception, and it ought to govern no other chant.

nature of the other <term>seculorum</term>. Likewise, it should be noted that this <term>seculorum</term> does not belong to the eighth tone, nor to any of the tones, except by mockery and abuse; it tastes more of the nature of the first tone than of any other. And even if it had been assigned to the first tone from its first imposition, it would still be judged useless, irrelevant, and superfluous, since its entire governance would be more truly managed by the second <term>seculorum</term> of the first tone than by itself. Likewise, if it were left with the eighth tone, it would be more usefully governed by the third <term>seculorum</term> of the eighth tone than by the second, as would all those chants attributed to it for governance. And I wish that no memory were held of this second or fourth <term>seculorum</term> of the eighth tone, since it mocks all other <term>seculorum</term>, and even itself.
