<header>THE ELUCIDATION OF PLAINCHANT.</header>

<image-desc>Three lines of musical notation in square neumes on four-line staves. The first example shows a melody that stays primarily on and above the staff. The second example includes a flat symbol (b-rotundum). The third example descends below the main staff lines using ledger lines.</image-desc>

The chant in the first example is <term>authentic: a "master" mode that covers a higher range (original: "authenticus")</term>, because it ascends one tone beyond what a <term>plagal: a "subordinate" mode that covers a lower range (original: "plagalis")</term> can reach, and it does not descend more than a semitone beyond what an authentic mode is allowed. Likewise, the chant in the second example is authentic; although it descends a semitone twice (a depth an authentic mode usually cannot reach), those two semitones together do not equal the size of a full tone, which is the limit for a plagal mode. This is because these semitones are smaller, being <term>enharmonic: a specific tiny interval in medieval theory (original: "enarmonica")</term>. Thus, we say that whatever ascends above the first high B <note>original: "b primum acutum"</note> belongs to the substance of the first mode and not the second; for as stated above, the second mode must always and necessarily be sung using <term>B-flat: indicated by a "round B" symbol (original: "b rotundum")</term>. The chant in the third example is plagal, because the three semitones to which it descends exceed a full tone by one <term>diesis: the smallest interval in this system, often a fifth of a tone (original: "diesi")</term>; for three enharmonic semitones contain six dieses in total, while a single tone contains only five. In this way, the aforementioned rules must be observed in all chants. *The twelfth treatise ends.*

## HERE BEGINS THE THIRTEENTH TREATISE.

### *Concerning pauses, and how they should be shaped in plainchant.*

It follows that we should look at pauses—specifically, how they ought to be shaped in plainchant. For there are some who, according to their own whim and without any regard for the law of musical logic or the nature of melodic 

<column-break/>

structures, draw these pauses in the chant, failing to realize that just as there are different modes or tones, so too are there different beginnings, sections, structures, <term>neumas: melodic figures or groups of notes (original: "neumæ")</term>, and endings. We judge the modes by their structures, and we must recognize the structures through their sections. Indeed, the signs that serve to distinguish one structure from another are the vertical lines drawn down through the spaces and lines [of the staff], which are called pauses. For wherever a pause occurs, it indicates that we are to stop singing. These pauses ought to distinguish the musical structures and differentiate them according to how they are arranged in the chants of the various modes. Those figures which are distinct in each of the modes are called "neumas"; these are placed near the beginning, the middle, and even the end. However, because they always conclude on the <term>final: the "home" note of a mode (original: "finali")</term> where the chant itself must end, the modes can also be identified through these figures by ear. For according to <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential scholar whose work was standard for medieval music theory.</note> Isidore, a neuma is a joining of small notes in any of the modes, which forms, distinguishes, connects, and concludes the chant. But because the structures and neumas mentioned above are composed of different note-names, it is necessary to look at the signs through which we recognize the names of the notes shaped in the chants; these signs are universally called <term>clefs: symbols like C or F that "unlock" the pitch of the lines (original: "claves")</term>. *The thirteenth treatise ends.*

### THE FOURTEENTH TREATISE BEGINS.
->*On the clef: what it is, and how many there are.*<-

A <term>clef: from the Latin word for 'key' (original: "clavis")</term> is the unlocking of the notes marked in any given song. Just as a door is unlocked by a key to preserve the things within the house, so in a song, the song itself is unlocked by the clef; the names of the notes are preserved, and we recognize them as distinct from one another. Universally, two such clefs are in use: low F <note>the F-clef or bass clef</note> and high c <note>the C-clef or tenor/alto/soprano clef</note>. Through their distinct placement upon the lines of the staff, every song, regardless of its <term>mode: the melodic category of the piece (original: "tonus")</term>, can be rationally arranged. These two clefs are a <term>fifth: a musical interval spanning five notes (original: "diapente")</term> apart, for F is established among the low notes and c among the high.

But someone may ask: what is a "low," "high," or "very high" voice? We say that a voice is called "low" <note>original: "gravis"</note> when, in any human voice, it is closest to silence. This is formed in the "voice of the chest" <note>original: "voce pectoris"</note>, which is the lower resonance and closer to the windpipe of the lungs, from which the voice proceeds; it is called low because it is primarily formed in that lower place. In the structure of the <term>Hand: the Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool for singers (original: "manus")</term>, there are seven such notes: A, B, C, D, E, F, and G. "High" voices <note>original: "acutae"</note> are so called because they produce a sharper sound compared to the aforementioned low ones; they are formed in a higher place, namely the "voice of the throat" <note>original: "voce gutturis"</note>, and therefore yield a sound above the others. There are seven such notes, which do not differ in name from the first group. "Very high" voices <note>original: "superacutae"</note> are so called because they produce a sound above the aforementioned high ones. The reason is that they are formed in the highest place,

<column-break/>

namely the "voice of the head" <note>original: "voce capitis"</note>. There are four such notes: a<gloss>b</gloss> b<gloss>b</gloss><gloss>c</gloss> c<gloss>d</gloss> and d<gloss>d</gloss>. There is also another added note, g-la, so that we may complete the perfection of the sequence that begins on high c. It should be noted that in every human voice—however much it can ascend or descend, or however much it may suffer from a lack of range—these low, high, and very high registers are necessarily distinguished.

->*The fourteenth treatise ends here.*<-

<header>THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC.</header>

# THE SIXTEENTH TREATISE BEGINS.
### *On the Musician and the Singer.*

According to the testimony of <term>Boethius: an influential 6th-century philosopher whose "Fundamentals of Music" shaped all medieval music theory</term>, a musician is one who possesses the faculty of judging modes, rhythms, and genres of songs according to the <term>speculation: theoretical contemplation (original: "speculationem")</term> and reason of the science of music itself. For every art or discipline naturally possesses a more honorable status through reason than through the mere <term>craftsmanship: the physical act of making (original: "artificium")</term> which is practiced by the hand and labor of the artisan. The musician understands the power and the logic of musical proportions and judges based on this, rather than by sound alone. The singer, however, is like a certain instrument belonging to the musician, on which in-

<column-break/>

strument the artisan or musician works, putting into practice those things he has already understood through reason. Therefore, the musician stands in relation to the singer as a judge to a <term>herald: a public messenger (original: "præconem")</term>; for the judge ordains, and commands the proclamation to be made through the herald; so it is with the musician and the singer. For the musician knows, feels, discerns, chooses, orders, and disposes all things that pertain to the science itself; and through the singer, as through his messenger, he commands them to be practiced.

->And let these words concerning <term>plainchant: unmeasured, monophonic church music (original: "musica plana")</term> suffice for you. 1274.<-

*The "Lucidarium" of Marchetto of Padua on the art of plainchant ends, begun in Cesena and completed in Verona. Thanks be to God.*

# THE ORCHARD IN THE ART OF MEASURED MUSIC
# BY THE SAME MARCHETTO OF PADUA.
### From the Vatican Manuscript.

<margin>Analysis of the work, just as it is placed before the text in the said manuscript.</margin>
There are four causes <note>this follows the Aristotelian framework of the "Four Causes" used to analyze the existence of any object or work</note>, namely the material, formal, efficient, and final: the material cause is <term>measured music: music with specific rhythmic durations, or polyphony (original: "musica mensurata")</term> itself; the formal cause is the method of treating it within this work; the efficient cause is the author himself; the final cause is so that measured music may be understood and sung rationally, and not merely according to the whim of one's will, as it seems to be for some.

*The title of the book is as follows:* **The prologue begins etc.**

This book is first divided into two parts, namely the prologue and the treatise. The se-

<column-break/>

cond part begins there: *Since, as the philosopher <note>original: "philosopho" — referring to Aristotle</note> says.* The first part remains undivided; the second is divided into three: for 1) it treats of matters pertaining to measured music by way of perfection. 2) By way of imperfection. 3) By both ways. The second part is at the beginning of the second book, and the third is at the beginning of the third book. The first part is divided into two, because it first treats the <term>accidents: non-essential properties (original: "accidentibus")</term> of measured music; in the second, its essentials. The second part, in its beginning, treats of <term>perfect time: a rhythmic system based on triple meter (original: "tempore perfecto")</term>, namely: *Having shown above etc.*

The first is divided into four according to the four accidents of which it treats within it...

Regarding the first point, it should be known that everything except the notes themselves—in which alone the essential nature of music consists, as shall be shown, God willing—are accidents or accidental features occurring in measured music, for reasons to be stated below. These include tails <note>original: "caudæ"; these are the vertical lines we now call "stems."</note>, properties <note>original: "proprietates"; a technical term referring to the specific shape of the opening notes in a group or "ligature."</note>, rests, dots, and a certain sign which is commonly called false music <note>original: "falsa musica"; now more commonly known as *musica ficta*, this refers to the use of sharps or flats to alter notes outside the standard medieval scale.</note>.

So that we may proceed in this present work in a scientific manner, imitating the philosophical method, we must first deal with these accidents or accidental features. And because the tail is an accident more closely joined to the note itself than other accidents—being the first thing attached to the notes and incorporated with them—we must therefore deal with the tails of the notes before the other accidents. In the treatise on these, we shall proceed in this order: First, the errors of those who say erroneous things about these tails—things that should not be said at all—will be refuted; consequently, it will be seen what these tails do not do (in a negative sense) in measured music.

### *Concerning tails and properties, and when they do not function in measured music.*

Regarding the first point, it should be known that certain lines are found in measured music that are entirely distinct 

<column-break/>

and separate from the notes; these are properly called rests <note>original: "pausæ"</note>, about which more will be said below. Others are joined to the notes themselves and drawn downward on the right or left side; these are properly called tails. The reason for this is that it is in the nature of a "tail" to begin from its upper principle and be drawn downward below it. Since these lines have the notes themselves as their principles—both in terms of position, because the notes are above them, and in terms of meaning, for they would mean nothing without the notes except to rest and cease from singing—it is therefore right that such lines drawn downward should be called "tails" by their proper names. In this way, tails are distinguished from rests: tails are lines joined to notes, while rests are not. Similarly, these tails are distinguished from "properties"; although properties are also features <note>Marchetto uses "proprietates" both as a general term for characteristics and as a specific technical term for the beginning of a ligature.</note> like lines added to notes and drawn upward, they differ in this: tails must be lines drawn downward below the notes for the reason already mentioned and for reasons shown below.

In treating these tails so that we may see when they do not function in measured music, we shall proceed in this order: First, we shall set forth the common saying of others; second, we shall bring forward an old objection of certain "ancients" that has been rejected by the practice of singing; third, we shall refute that objection through logic. Regarding the first point, everyone says that a tail is always a sign of length in notes, provided it is drawn downward from the right side of simple square notes or tied notes <note>original: "ligatæ"; ligatures are groups of notes written as a single connected symbol.</note>, as is evident here:

And they assign a reason for this: because a line which is called a rest, when drawn through one space, possesses one time-unit in itself, and the note itself possesses another time-unit. Therefore, if such a line is added to such a note, then the note will have two time-units, and so on.

Regarding the third point, we first refute the aforementioned method and its reasoning using their own words. For it is manifest that extending time and not extending it are contrary opposites. The proof is this: to rest <note>original: "pausare"</note> means not to sing, or not to allow the voice; but to extend the time-unit or units means to sing and to allow the voice. Therefore, just as singing and not singing are related, so are extending the time and resting. of its own property: therefore, according to their reasoning, it is impossible that any line added to a note could add any duration <term>tempus: The basic unit of time in medieval music, often compared to a modern beat.</term> of singing to it, no matter how far it is drawn through the spaces; rather, it would produce various durations of silence <note>original: "tempora pausandi"</note>, if their reasoning held at all; but this clearly suggests a contradiction, as has been shown.

But they might say: “Brother! <note>A common scholastic form of address between monks or scholars.</note> You previously distinguished tails <note>original: "caudas"; refers to the stems of notes.</note> from rests; but we do not say that the rests do not add to the notes (for then your reasoning would be valid), but rather that other lines, which are called tails, produce the aforementioned effect in the notes themselves.”

**The Solution.** We then argue as follows: It is impossible for an essential characteristic <term>propria proprietas: In scholastic logic, a quality that belongs only to one specific species.</term> of one thing to belong to anything other than itself; just as it is impossible for the ability to laugh <note>A classic Aristotelian example: only humans are "risible" or capable of laughter.</note> to belong to anything other than a human. But the essential characteristic of rests is that they are drawn through various spaces. If, therefore, according to them, a line added to a note and drawn through various spaces produces various lengths of time, it follows that such a line possesses the essential characteristic of rests. But it is impossible for an essential characteristic to belong to anything other than itself, as has been said. Therefore, such a line added to a note either will not have such a characteristic—which goes against their movement—or it will be the same thing as a rest, and then the absurdity demonstrated above would follow.

But they might still argue: the essential characteristic of rests is that lines drawn through various spaces produce a variety of durations in *resting*; but as for the tails that we join to notes, we say that when they are drawn through various spaces, they produce a variety of durations in *singing*; and

<column-break/>

thus we do not attribute the property of rests to the tails themselves, as you were saying... Then we argue again as follows: the tails that are joined to notes are certain lines, and this is evident to the senses; therefore, does drawing them through various spaces so that they introduce a variety of durations belong to them insofar as they are lines alone, which are distinct from the notes, or insofar as they are joined to the notes? If in the first way—namely, that this belongs to them insofar as they are lines alone distinct from the notes—then it follows that they are rests; for no line distinct from a note performs any function in music except for the rest alone. 

If, however, it belongs to them insofar as such lines are joined to notes, then we argue thus: if any effect is to be produced by two things together, it must taste of the nature of those things from which it proceeds; otherwise, it would not be their effect. For it is necessary that an effect resembles its cause, just as paleness is caused by blackness and whiteness together, and therefore it tastes of the nature of both. If, therefore, a variety of duration is caused by the joining of such a line with a note, it must exist in a different way of drawing it out, because the cause of such a drawing out and such a variety of durations occurs either in the nature of the note itself or in the nature of the line itself. 

But this is not in the nature of the note itself, because without the line it has only one duration; nor will this be in the nature of the note [as modified], nor in the nature of the line itself considered in the note, because such a line is a rest: therefore, from the joining of both together—namely, the line with the note—such an effect cannot follow, since it would be outside the nature of its causes.

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

But then they might say: "How, then, does a tail added to a note make it long?" We reply that it does not change the substance <note>In scholastic philosophy, the "substance" is what a thing is in its essence, while a "property" is an accidental quality.</note> of the note, but is only a certain property indicating the substance of that note; it is called a "tail" <note>original: "cauda"</note> for the reason demonstrated above. 

**The Demonstration:** Contrary to the manner and reason of their claims, we shall then lead them to another absurdity in the art of measured music <term>musica mensurata: Music where the duration of each note is precisely defined by its shape, rather than just by the text.</term>. And the first is this: they say that such a line drawn from the right side across various spaces produces a prolongation in the note to which it is added. But it is certain that a tail added to a note on the left side brings about brevity, according to them and to everyone. Therefore, if such a tail were drawn from the left side, it would be shortened by as many durations <term>tempora: The basic units of time in this system.</term> as the number of spaces through which they draw it; for just as a proposition follows from a proposition, so does an opposite follow from an opposite. 

For if whiteness is a color that disperses the vision, its opposite, namely blackness, must be that which gathers the vision. But "right" and "left" are opposites; therefore, if the aforementioned tail placed on the right side of a note prolongs it for various durations, the same thing placed on the opposite left side will shorten it for various durations. But this is impossible, because it would then follow that if we drew a tail through three spaces, the note would lose three units of time, and then it would be a note without any time at all, which could not be sung. Therefore, since the consequence is impossible, the premise must also be impossible: namely, that any tail drawn on the right side through various spaces indicates a diversity of durations.

<column-break/>

Likewise, another absurdity follows, because sometimes a note descends below all the lines and spaces of the staff; in such a case, it would be impossible to draw "various durations" for it, because the tail could not be drawn through various spaces. Furthermore, if such a tail were multiplied beneath all the lines and spaces, it would be included within one of the letters <note>original: "litterarum"; referring to the text of the lyrics written below the music.</note> existing in the song, or it would be blocked from being drawn by that letter; and thus it would be impossible for a musician to recognize the length of such a tail.

### *Regarding tails and properties, and what they do in measured music.*

Having shown what the tails and properties <term>proprietas: In notation, this refers to the strokes or "tails" added to notes to indicate their rhythm.</term> of notes do *not* do (by way of negative proof), we wish to proceed by the way of science to see what they and other properties added to notes actually do when they establish a position in the measurement of a song. And this must be treated rationally, considering these and other properties added to notes together. For tails, compared to other properties, only add the reason for "prolongability" <note>original: "producibilitatis"</note> within the notes themselves, and not above them like other properties; but as has been said, they too are called properties. Let us speak, therefore, concerning all these properties added to notes.

Regarding this, it should be known that Master Franco <note>Franco of Cologne (mid-13th century), the most influential theorist of rhythmic notation before Marchetto.</note> and the other doctors of measured music differentiate these properties in this way. For they say that a property added to the right side of a note indicates a long note, whether it is a single note <note>original: "simplex"</note> or joined in a ligature <note>original: "ligata"; a group of notes written as a single symbol.</note>, but it must always be drawn downwards, as seen here:

But although those teachers said such things, they are not found to have proved their statements in any books. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that such great and eminent teachers proceeded reasonably: for we, according to our small capacity, demonstrate all the above things in this way, and we assign ourselves two principles. The first is that a diversity of notes was necessary through different lines and spaces so that the song could be sung high and low by the singers. For if all notes were on one line or in one space, the sounding of such notes would not result in singing, but rather in **howling** <note>original: "ullulare." And from this principle we proceed thus: Just as it was necessary to situate notes through different lines and spaces so that singing might arise from them in **plainchant** <term>cantus planus: Unmeasured monophonic music, such as Gregorian chant.</term>, so it was necessary to add certain signs or certain properties to the notes themselves for the sake of measurement in **measured music** <term>cantus mensuratus: Music where every note has a specific, proportional duration.</term>. Thus, it is clear that it is necessary to add properties to the notes themselves so that they may be measured in song.

<column-break/>

But why it was necessary to join them to the notes in this way, as has been said, we demonstrate thus, and then we assume the second principle: **art imitates nature** as much as it can <note>original: "ars imitatur naturam." A central tenet of Aristotelian philosophy used here to justify musical rules through natural laws.</note>. Proof by example: For he who paints a lily or a horse strives to paint it as much as he can in the likeness of a natural horse or lily. Since, therefore, these written notes belong to the art of music—although music itself is an accepted science—it was necessary that the properties added to these written notes (required by the method of teaching) be added to them according to the perfections found in man himself, who instituted this art. 

In man, first and primarily, **right** and **left** are found. Proof: because neither in a column nor in any non-living thing is there said to be a right and left side, except in relation to a man; for one and the same column is "right" if it is on the right side of a man, and "left" if it is on the left. Therefore, these properties added to the written notes are rightly added to them through "right" and "left," and this is in relation to man. 

But in man, it is the case that the **right side is more perfect** than the left. For that side which contains that by which the whole body is nourished and perfected is more perfect than the side which does not contain it. But the right side in man contains that which nourishes and perfects the whole body, namely the blood; for the **liver** <term>hepar: The liver. In medieval medicine, the liver was believed to be the organ responsible for creating blood and the source of the body's nutrition.</term> contains the blood and is on the right side. Therefore, the right side in man is more perfect than the left. This is the reason why Christ on the cross...

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

...He willed to be struck on the right side, so that He might pour out all His blood for the human race. And we say this according to the physicians; but according to the philosophers, we say that the heart is the beginning of the generation of blood, and the beginning of all movement is on the left side, and yet the left side is more imperfect and less powerful than the right. The reason for this is that the "point" <note>the apex</note> of the heart tends toward the left, but the "mouth" of the heart tends toward the right, sending heat and nourishment into it first. This is apparent from the arrangement of the right-hand limbs, which are indeed more powerful and more capable of work than the left as the "moving part," while the left are less powerful as the "moved part." Having established these things, we form the following reasoning: the right side is more perfect than the left, as has been proven; but a **property** <term>proprietas: In medieval music, this refers to the specific shape or "tail" added to a note or group of notes (ligature) that determines its rhythm.</term> added to a note is added to it via the right or left, as is obvious to the senses; therefore, a property added to a note on the right side perfects it, while one on the left side "imperfects" it. To "perfect" a note is to lengthen it, while to "imperfect" it is to shorten it.

Therefore, the aforementioned teachers spoke well when they said that a property added to a note on the lower right side perfects it <note>making it a "Long" note</note>, but on the upper right side it affects the way it is performed; whereas on the lower left side it "imperfects" it, making it a **breve** <term>breve: A "short" note, usually half or a third the length of a "Long."</term>, and on the upper left side it makes it a **semibreve** <term>semibreve: The shortest standard note value in this system, literally "half-short."</term>. Indeed, a property drawn upward always "imperfects" a note. The reason for this is that the whole substance of the song is in the note itself; for a property without a note does not cause one to sing, but a note without a property certainly does, just as in a

<column-break/>

man, the whole substance of nourishment is the liver <note>original: "hepar"</note>, in which there is no blood <note>Marchetto follows an ancient medical theory that the liver produces the "humors" of nutrition.</note>. Just as it is not natural for the liver to be pulled upward but rather downward, so it is not natural for a note to be pulled upward but rather downward. For the "perfection" of a note is likened to the perfection of the man who instituted it; but to pull something contrary to its own nature is to make it imperfect. Thus, to pull a note by a tail upward is to "imperfect" it, since it happens contrary to the nature of the note itself, as has been shown.

But a property that is on the left side and pointing upward "imperfects" a note even more than one placed on the right side; for it shows two "imperfections" in that note: one because it is on the left side, and another because it points upward. Therefore, it does not merely make the note a **breve**, as does the property on the lower left, but it makes it even a **semibreve**, because it adds the "upward" imperfection on top of it. 

However, a property that is on the upper right side indicates only one imperfection, and it is joined with the "perfection" associated with the right and the downward direction. Therefore, it only gives a certain kind of imperfection to the note—namely, that we perform it in a diminished way and by means of a **plica** <term>plica: An ornament where a note is "folded," involving a secondary, unwritten passing tone.</term>. Concerning these *plicas*—whether long, short, or even semibreve, whether simple or joined in ligatures—it will be shown below in their own chapter.

# MARCHETTO OF PADUA

...shine forth more clearly, just as whiteness does next to blackness. But it is the case that through **properties** <term>proprietas: the structural features of a note, like a "tail" or stem, that indicate its rhythmic value.</term> and **tails** <note>the stems attached to notes</note> we are instructed on what we should do regarding the notes themselves while singing; through rests, however, we are instructed on how we should conduct ourselves regarding the notes while resting. Since singing and resting are opposites, it is fitting that after discussing the tails and properties that instruct us in singing, we must treat the rests that instruct us in resting. In treating them, we shall proceed in this order: first, we will say what written rests are in song; second, how they ought to be written and marked according to the ancients; and third, confirming the sayings of the ancients, we will show—by adding to them—how they ought to be written and marked in the singing of the moderns.

### *What Rests Are in Song.*

Regarding the first point, we say that a rest is nothing other than a cessation of the voice or sound for a certain **time** <term>tempus: the fundamental unit of measurement in medieval rhythm.</term>, or a certain part of a time, from singing. This is the definition of an unperformed rest; for a written rest neither rests nor sings, but rather indicates the manner in which we ought to rest. The definition of such a written rest is as follows: a written rest is a certain line drawn through parts of a space or through entire spaces <note>the gaps between the lines of a musical staff</note>, in no way attached to any note, joined together but totally separated from the notes, indicating that we must cease and rest from singing for a time or for a part of a time. And such rests are necessary in song; for just as the diverse stretching of the voice or sound, high or low, creates consonance in song,

<column-break/>

so too a diverse manner of resting allows one to find better consonance in song.

These written rests differ in two ways from tails and properties according to the definition given: one is that they are not joined to notes as properties and tails are; the other is that by their nature they follow the spaces and parts of spaces, causing one to rest more or less (as will be clear below and immediately following), whereas tails and properties do not have this quality, as was demonstrated above in the treatises concerning them.

### *How Rests Ought to Be Written and Marked According to the Ancients.*

Regarding the second point, we say with the ancients that a rest drawn through one space indicates resting for one time; through two, two; through three, three; of which these are the examples. (a) <note>original note: "Examples are missing."</note> And so the time measuring both the rests and the notes must be (b) <note>original note: "Something is missing here."</note> without those same elements of musical nature; as will be defined below, God willing. If, however, there is any rest drawn through all the spaces or the lines of four spaces, we say that such a rest is not measurable in song, but is called (and rightly so) by Master **Franco** <note>Franco of Cologne, a 13th-century theorist who pioneered the system of measured rhythm.</note> the "end of points" <term>finis punctorum: a vertical line across the entire staff used to mark the end of a section or melody rather than a specific rhythmic silence.</term>. # THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

Again, it should be known that any rest can sometimes be drawn across one entire **space** <note>the gap between the horizontal lines of a musical staff</note>, and in such cases, we call this the omission of one **time** <term>tempus: the primary unit of measurement in medieval rhythm, similar to a "beat" or a full measure depending on the context.</term>. Since the "time" itself is divided into three in its primary division—as will be shown below—the rest must be proportioned to it and divided into three parts of the space. Therefore, a rest drawn through a third of a space indicates the omission of one part of a time; through two parts, the omission of two; and through three, which is the whole space, it indicates the omission of three parts. Because the ancient musicians did not care to provide any further division of time beyond three **semibreves** <note>the smallest standard note value of that era</note>, it was not necessary for them to divide these rests into more than three parts of a space. As for why they did not care to do so, nor wrote about it—and we say this with all the respect we owe to such teachers—it must be said that they refrained from doing so because of the **coarseness of their listeners** <note>original Latin: "grossitudine audientium"; Marchetto suggests the audiences of the past were not yet refined enough to appreciate more complex rhythms</note>, and not because of any ignorance on the part of those teaching the aforementioned music.

### *How the confirmation and sayings of the Ancients should be written and marked in the singing of the Moderns.*

Regarding the third point: the Moderns have divided those three parts of a time into even smaller, ultimate parts, forming six, nine, and twelve semibreves, or whatever could be formed from the divi-

<column-break/>

-sion of such parts of time. We must see, then, which rests and what style of writing correspond to such newly discovered divisions of the parts of time. We say that because it would be difficult to measure these quickly in a third of a space—as is fitting and necessary in song—the singer should not be forced to act without readiness and deliberation. This is supported by **the Philosopher** <note>Aristotle; a standard medieval way of referring to him</note>, who says that a good **lyre-player** <term>citharœdus: an ancient term for a skilled musician, used here to mean any professional performer.</term> does not hesitate or deliberate while playing. Therefore, because one cannot divide a third of a space into further parts without some delay—which is unsuitable for singing—and because it would be impossible for the eye to perceive this (since every bodily sense, and sight especially, can be deceived; for the eye could easily fail to grasp the exact portion of such tiny parts), the Moderns have found it necessary to create a certain new way of drawing rests that correspond to these many semibreves. We give this general rule for them: they should be drawn similarly to a **tailed semibreve** <note>a semibreve with a stem or "tail"</note>, without considering the staff space at all, whether they precede or follow those semibreves. They take the form of the shortest possible little stroke, always ending with a **little dot** <term>punctello: a small mark used in notation to indicate specific rhythmic groupings or divisions.</term>, which is also found in measured music and will be discussed below. The forms of these little strokes are as follows:

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

### *What was the necessity for such a small dot to be measured in written music.*

Concerning the first point, it should be known that, speaking metaphorically as well as naturally, land is said to be divided when it is separated by a flow of water; in such a case, a person cannot cross from one land to another except by boat or by bridge. And if one asks: which way is easier? We say by a bridge, because then many things necessary for steering a boat are omitted. Now, just as a boundary is found in land (or a part of the land) through which we are said to use a bridge, so it is in song: when a finished **proportion** <term>proportio: the relationship of rhythmic values to one another</term> is reached, if we wish to cross over to another proportion, we must use a certain sign in music so measured. This sign is called a **dot** <note>original: "punctellus"; a small mark used to organize rhythm</note>, speaking by way of analogy. For just as we escape from one finished part of land to another by a bridge, so by the dot we are signaled to transfer ourselves from one finished proportion of time to another proportion. And because such a dot separates one proportion from another, it is called by the masters and teachers of music the "divider of the **mode**" <term>modus: the rhythmic framework governing the relationship between long and short notes</term>.

<column-break/>

How the mode is divided will be discussed immediately below. For now, it is enough for us to know the reason why such a sign—namely, the dot—was introduced into measured music. This concludes the first point.

### *How it should be treated after properties and rests.*

As for the second point, it should be known that the dot is rightly treated in order after the rests. The reason is this: because a rest, as has been said, causes one to stop singing, it is necessary to explain immediately after those rests what the dot itself does in measured music to resolve this. This concludes the second point.

### *What the dot itself does in measured music.*

Regarding the third point, we say that the dot itself is called the "division of the mode" for the reason given immediately above. Let us see how it divides things from one another. Here it should be known that sometimes it divides modes by distances, such as when it is placed between two or three **breves** <term>brevis: a "short" note, though it serves as a primary unit of time</term> situated between two **longas** <term>longa: a "long" note, typically worth two or three breves</term>. By its addition, it makes the aforementioned notes belong to a different mode of **discant** <term>discantus: a style of polyphonic singing where parts move at similar speeds</term> than they would have without it, as seen here:

<meta>This page continues the transition from Marchetto's discussion on the "dot" (punctellum) to the introduction of "colored music" (musica colorata), specifically the use of accidentals to refine the beauty of musical intervals.</meta>

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

...it was necessary to introduce this sign into measured music <term>musica mensurata: music in which each note has a specific, defined rhythmic duration</term> for identifying dissonances that occur in measured songs. We have already demonstrated what these dissonances are and how they relate to consonances in a certain work of ours on plain music <term>musica plana: unmeasured chant, such as Gregorian chant</term>. Indeed, we could in no way identify these dissonances through the other two signs—namely, the square ♮ <note>original: "♮ quadratum"; the ancestor of the natural and sharp signs</note> and the round ♭ <note>original: "b rotundum"; the ancestor of the flat sign</note>—which are, or can be, present in any song, whether measured or plain. The reason for this is that those two signs always divide the whole tone into enharmonic and diatonic semitones <note>In Marchetto's system, a whole tone is divided into five parts called "dieses." A "diatonic" semitone is four parts, an "enharmonic" is three, a "chromatic" is two, and a "diesis" is one</note>, or vice versa; however, this [new] sign always divides by the chromatic semitone and the diesis. For it is necessary that these dissonances correspond to one another so that they are separated from the consonances toward which they tend by the smallest possible distance. But this could not happen except through the division of the tone into the chromatic and the diesis, or vice-versa. Why, how, and where these divisions occur will be more clearly shown in the aforementioned work on plain music. And this concludes the first point.

->*How such a sign should be properly named.*<-

Regarding the second point, we say that a name ought to follow the nature of the thing itself. Since this sign was discovered in music for the purpose of finding and creating more beautiful consonances, and since "falsehood" <note>original: "falsum"</note> as such is always taken in a negative rather than a positive sense (for that which is false is never good), we say—saving the respect due to others—that it should more properly be called **colored music** <term>musica colorata: the practice of adding accidentals to "color" or inflect the standard notes of the scale</term> rather than "false music" <term>musica falsa: a common medieval term for accidentals, which Marchetto argues is misleading</term>, as the latter name attributes a sense of falsity to it. And this concludes the second point.

<column-break/>

->*How this sign should be treated after the dot and the properties.*<-

Regarding the third point, we say that "accidents" <term>accidentia: non-essential properties that are added to a subject; here, sharps and flats added to the "natural" notes</term> pertaining to music are treated after the rhythmic properties and the dot. And just as rhetorical colors are used in grammar for the beauty of sentences, so too in music, "colors" are occasionally created for the beauty of consonances. Therefore, colored music should be treated immediately after properties and the dot. And this concludes the third point.

->*How the sign itself should be marked in music.*<-

Regarding the fourth point, we say that it was the opinion of some that because we ascend by the square ♮ above the soft or round ♭ in the same space or on the same line by three parts of the divisible tone (which are the diatonic and enharmonic semitones), and since by this new sign we only ascend by one part of that tone (which is the diesis) above the square ♮ in the same space or line, we are dividing the enharmonic semitone to be used for the "coloring" of consonances. Therefore, these people say—since there is such an effect in the stated sign that it adds one part of the enharmonic semitone (called a diesis) above the square ♮—and wishing to relate this to geometry, they say it ought to be marked as half of a square ♮, like this: **b**. Their reasoning is that the square ♮ always immediately signifies the elevation of an enharmonic semitone above itself. And since this figure divides that enharmonic semitone by its ascent, they conclude that it should be shaped like a triangle—representing half of the square ♮, which is a four-sided figure.

<meta>This page continues Marchetto's argument regarding the visual representation of musical accidentals. He is specifically refuting critics who argue that because a new accidental sign (the sharp/chromatic sign) represents a smaller division than the square B (♮), it should be visually "smaller" or "half" of the square. Marchetto uses geometric and natural philosophy to argue the opposite: that more complexity in sound requires more complexity in the written sign.</meta>

# MARCHETTO OF PADUA’S *POMERIUM*

But these critics conclude correctly neither in regards to music nor geometry; and we shall demonstrate this solely through their own words, showing that their own speech supports our proposal and opposes theirs. First, they speak geometrically: it is certain that a pentagon <term>pentagonus: a five-sided polygon</term> adds one angle beyond a square <term>quadragonum: a four-sided polygon</term>; therefore, this is a valid conclusion: a pentagon does not add as many angles as the square has, but only one angle. Therefore, they argue, it should be drawn as half of a square. It is certain that this deduction is false; rather, it must be said that a pentagon must be drawn with one more angle than a square has. Rightly, then, they reach their own conclusion in music by speaking geometrically, saying: the square B <note>original: "♮ quadrum"; the ancestor of the natural and sharp signs, used to indicate a "hard" or higher pitch</note> makes one ascend by a tone divisible into three parts—which are first the diatonic semitone <note>In Marchetto's system, a whole tone is divided into five equal parts called 'dieses.' A diatonic semitone consists of four of these parts, while an enharmonic semitone consists of three</note>—and after these, two parts, which are the enharmonic semitone. This [new] sign, however, beyond this, makes one ascend by one additional part of that same tone more than the square B does, by dividing that enharmonic semitone in half. Therefore, they say, it should be drawn as half of a square B; whereas they ought rather to say: it should be drawn with a further "perfection" <term>perfectione: in medieval logic, a state of being more complete or highly developed</term> than the square B, because it adds both a higher ascent and a further division beyond it. Therefore, speaking and concluding according to their own words, let us say that for the

<column-break/>

aforementioned reason, such a sign ought to be drawn like the first square B but with further perfection, because it adds ascent and division beyond it. But such perfection is hinted at through the multiplication of angles—for instance, by making a pentagon or a hexagon—even though angles themselves belong not to music, but to Geometry.

<margin>(a) This ♮ sign should be drawn out further at the top, though this is not possible here because of the printing type <note>original: "typum"; the translator/editor is noting a limitation of the movable type used to print this edition</note>.</margin>
But because it was said regarding the "properties" <term>proprietatibus: specific characteristics or categories of melodic hexachords</term> that the perfection of times <note>original: "perfection temporum"; referring to rhythmic or melodic completeness</note> indicates a perfection according to "more" or "less," therefore such a sign should be made with a certain characteristic beyond the square B, as seen here: ♮; (a) for it suffices to make further extensions in it than in the square B. And most especially, the extension in such a sign ought to be made in an upward direction and on the right side, where "perfection" is signified, as was shown in the treatise on properties. It is drawn upward because that is the "formal" <term>formalis: relating to the 'form' or soul of a thing, which was considered superior to its 'matter'</term> direction; for superior things are more formal than inferior ones, and through this, they are more influential. For water is more formal than earth, air more than water, and fire more than air, which are higher in their placement. For it is the nature of a "form," just as it is the nature of a "place," to contain what is within it. In which places such a sign ought to be placed is shown more fully in our work on plain music <term>musica plana: unmeasured chant</term>, where the division of pitch-space is treated. And this concludes the discussion of "colored music" <term>musica colorata: music using accidentals or chromaticism to 'color' the intervals</term>.

# HERE BEGINS THE SECOND PART OF THE FIRST BOOK ON THE ESSENTIALS OF MEASURED MUSIC.

## TREATISE I.
### *Concerning Time.*

Having shown above the "accidents" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an 'accident' is a property that can change without changing the essence of the thing, such as a note's pitch being altered by a sharp sign.</note> operating extrinsically to the measurement of music and song, we must now look at those things which are intrinsic and essential to the substance of the song itself. And this is done reasonably; for science is not concerned with accidents, but rather a cognition of the essentials and those things belonging intrinsically to each science is required. The substantial elements of the song itself, or of music, are the notes, in which the science of music essentially consists; therefore, we must look at the notes. And because in the present work we intend to treat the measurement of song—for we have treated plainchant <term>cantus planus: unmeasured, monophonic church music, like Gregorian chant</term> elsewhere—therefore, in this present little work, so that we do not leap from one category to another, we do not need to look at these notes simply and absolutely, but only insofar as we can sing something in a measured way through them. For all measurement consists in a certain quantity and time; for time is the measurement of motion, according to the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophum"; referring to Aristotle</note> in the third book of the *Physics*. Therefore, we must look at time itself: first, specifically how it is understood in music, and how it is applied to the notes themselves, so that consequently we may see in measured song <term>musica mensurata: music where each note has a specific rhythmic duration</term> how these notes are understood and how they are measured. To examine time as it is understood in music, let us proceed in this order. First, we shall set forth the truth of what musical time

<column-break/>

actually is. Second, we shall distinguish it in the way it is divisible in music. Third, we shall refute the opinion of certain people regarding both its definition and its division.

### *What Musical Time Is.*

Regarding the first point, we say following Master Franco <note>Franco of Cologne, a highly influential 13th-century theorist who established the foundations of rhythmic notation</note> that, speaking musically, "time" is that which is the minimum in the fullness of a voice, and we prove this definition thus. Everything is perfected by the smallest of its kind, according to the Philosopher in the book *Meteorologica*; and this is clear. For unity, which is the minimum and the principle of number, perfects the whole number itself; for to say 10 is to say ten units, and to say 20 is to say twenty units, and so on for all things: that which is first and smallest in each kind is the perfection and first measure of all things in that kind. Since, therefore, the measurement of the song or notes consists in time itself, as has been said, it is concluded that the minimum time to be found in music is the cause and perfection of measuring. But because time, insofar as it is time abstracted from all matter, would be divisible to infinity—just as a separate line would be divisible to infinity—therefore, since our consideration is not of such abstract time (because in that case there would be no "first" time), but is of time as it is understood in music, we say that not every minimum time is the perfection and first measure...

measure of song, but musical time. Therefore, that which is the minimum musical time is the first measure and the rule for measuring the entire song itself. This is that minimum time in which the "fullness of voice" can be formed. For this reason, Master Franco <note>Franco of Cologne (c. 1250), whose work *Ars Cantus Mensurabilis* defined the system of note shapes used for centuries.</note>, after stating that musical time is a minimum, immediately adds: not just any minimum time, but that which is the minimum in the fullness of voice; because that minimum time in which the fullness of voice can be formed is the very first unit of time and the rule for measuring everything contained in music.

But someone might say: "Explain this to me." Then we say: it has been stated elsewhere in the study of plainchant <note>original: "musica plana"</note> how many instruments are necessary to form the voice. Therefore, when these aforementioned instruments work together fully and properly—neither too much nor too little—to form the voice, then the "fullness of voice" is achieved. This happens when the windpipe <note>original: "canna pulmonis"</note>, having been steadily and properly filled with breath, and with a proper expansion of the belly to express it, sends out the breath and strikes the hearing in such a way that the person performing perceives this produced sound or voice fully—whether resonating in their own chest, the chest of another, or like the ringing of a small bell. Therefore, that minimum time in which the fullness of voice can be formed in the manner declared above is the "first time," by which all music is measured according to Master Franco. So much for the first point.

### *How time itself is distinguishable in music.*

As for the second point, we say that the aforementioned definition is for "perfect time" in

<column-break/>

music. For, as was said above, every single thing that is measured first is the perfection of its own kind, just as we see in the example of numbers. But the musical time defined above is the first and the minimum, and it is "perfect" because it exists in the fullness of voice. Therefore, the aforementioned definition is of perfect time in music, and not of imperfect time, since such a time becomes the measure of all others. Now, anything that differs from the perfect by even the smallest degree is necessarily "imperfect." Therefore, every unit of time—whatever it may be—that is not the minimum in the fullness of voice, but is *more* than the minimum, is not perfect but "more-than-perfect" <note>original: "plusquamperfectum"</note>. And that which is the minimum but *not* in the fullness of voice is not perfect, but lacks the perfection of the fullness of voice, and is thus "imperfect." The division of musical time is therefore clear: one is more-than-perfect, another is perfect, and another is imperfect. Whether a middle ground exists between these will be made clear below. So much for the second point.

### *The opinion of certain people is refuted, both concerning the definition of time and its distinction.*

As for the third point, certain people speak against the aforementioned definition of musical time in many ways. First, they say: "You say that musical time is that which is the minimum in the fullness of voice, which you say should be formed by the 'instruments' [of the body], and you say this time is the measure of song. Having rejected that opinion regarding the definition of musical time, we now reject the opinion of those regarding the distinction of time itself who say that a middle ground can be granted between perfect and imperfect musical time. We respond that this is impossible: it is certain that music is composed of notes, and these

<column-break/>

notes are composed of numbers. Therefore, time as applied to these notes follows the same rules as numbers. In numbers, there is no "middle ground" to be found between the number three <note>original: "ternarium"</note> and the number four <note>original: "quaternarium"</note>, as they differ by "more" or "less" and according to their essential perfection. Likewise, there is no middle ground between three and two for the same reason. Just as the number four exceeds three because it possesses one perfection more, and the number two falls short of three because it possesses one perfection less—and there is no middle ground between them—so too does everything that exceeds perfect time possess one more perfection, and thus it is imperfect <note>In this context, Marchetto is arguing that anything deviating from the "perfect" number three is technically "imperfect"</note>; there is no middle ground between them. Furthermore, "perfect" and "imperfect" are contradictory opposites according to the **Philosopher** in his *Metaphysics*, because it is impossible for the same thing to be both perfect and imperfect at the same time and in the same respect. Between contradictories, there is never a middle ground according to philosophy. Therefore, there is no middle ground between perfect and imperfect time when speaking essentially, intrinsically, and regarding the very nature of perfect and imperfect time.

...as stated previously, the "time" defined above is that by which measured song is measured. We must, therefore, apply this "time" to the notes themselves—not simply and absolutely, as is done in **plainchant** <note>original: "musica plana"; the traditional, unmeasured liturgical chant of the Church</note>, but according to the logic of measurement. We apply it to the notes in such a way that the entire **measured song** <note>original: "cantus mensurabilis"; music where the duration of notes is strictly determined by their shape and relationship</note> is measured by it. Here it must be understood that these notes, as said above, are distinguished according to numbers. 

Therefore, the "time" that must be applied to these notes must be applied according to both numerical proportion and the proper proportion of singing, from which various kinds of **harmony** arise. According to numerical proportion, time is applied to notes in this way: for in the world of numbers, every number is perfected first through "one," and secondly through the first two numbers—namely, "two" and "three"—and no others. 

For the number four is nothing other than two pairs; five is nothing other than a two and a three; six consists of two threes or three twos; and seven is nothing other than two twos and one three. Therefore, the whole of number is encompassed by "two" and "three," and these are still measured primarily by "one." For two and three are themselves measured by one, which is the measure of all others. Among numbers, "one" is more perfect than "two," and we say "three" is more perfect than "two," for two cannot measure three, but two can certainly be measured through three <note>Marchetto is arguing from a Pythagorean perspective that the number 3, representing the Trinity and the first "complete" number with a beginning, middle, and end, is the standard of perfection</note>. One, then, is the first in measurement, but three is the most perfect measure that can be found in numbers. Following this method by which

<column-break/>

notes in music must be measured, it is necessary to apply this logic to the notes themselves, so that we may say: just as "one" is the primary logic for measuring notes, and just as "two" and "three" measure all other numbers in the manner declared above (since all other numbers are reduced to them), so **two times** and **three times** are the measure of all durations that can be measured in music. 

And just as "two" in numbers cannot measure "three," but "three" can well measure "two," so two musical times cannot measure three, but three can well measure two. Since "three" is the most perfect number that can be found in the measurement of numbers, so "three" in music is the most perfect logic of measuring that can be found in music. 

Because one must always begin with the more perfect things, the note of **three times** <note>In the notation of this period, this refers to a "Perfect Long," which lasts for three beats</note> holds the first rank among notes as a complete measure, containing within itself the durations of all other notes; after it comes the note of **two times** <note>An "Imperfect Long"</note>, and in the third place, the note of **one time** <note>A "Breve"</note>. This is the method of applying musical time to these notes according to numerical proportion.

But someone might say against this: "You told me before that one musical time is both the first and the perfect logic for measuring all other times contained in music, since the first in any category is the logic for measuring everything that comes after it." We respond that we still say the same thing; but we add that if it is asked: "What is the first time that measures other times in music?" we say absolutely that it is **one time**. And if it is then asked, how many times...

Therefore, the final **perfection** <note>original: "perfectio"; in medieval music, "perfection" refers to the completeness of the number three, symbolizing the Holy Trinity and defining triple meter</note>, although it can measure one **unit of time** <note>original: "tempus"; the basic unit of measurement in mensural music</note> itself, is the **trinity of time** <note>original: "trinitas temporis"; a duration of three beats</note>, as it contains within itself all other perfections. It was, therefore, well said earlier that although one unit of time measures the trinity of time by repeating it three times, because one cannot go any further, it must be measured by other times—which is not the case for notes smaller than itself. Therefore, the note of three times holds the first rank, the note of two times the second, and the note of one time the third. The reason for this is that the mode of measuring three units of time is the more perfect mode, to which all other modes of measuring must necessarily be reduced. For beyond the mode of three units of time, or beyond <unclear>hiatus</unclear>, all other modes are reduced to it or to what is contained within it, just as all numbers above the **ternary** <note>original: "ternarium"; the number three</note> are reduced to it, or to the parts contained within it.

### Concerning the doubt of some regarding the note of two times, which is called the altered breve.

And because, according to some, the note of

<column-break/>

two units of time—which is called the **altered breve** <note>original: "altera brevis"; a note that normally lasts one beat but is doubled to two beats in specific rhythmic patterns to complete a "perfection" of three</note>—is denied as being necessary in song, on the grounds that it contains two times essentially and by itself, and not by accident (such as by subtraction). Or at the very least, they argue that there is no note of two times in the manner stated above. They say that if such a note existed, it would be written with some unique **property** <note>original: "proprietas"; a visual characteristic of a note's shape, like a stem or "tail"</note>, just like the note of three times. For example, it might have a **tail** <note>original: "cauda"; a vertical stem attached to the note head</note> smaller than that of the note of three times; yet this note is written exactly like a **breve** <note>original: "brevis"</note>, which lasts only one unit of time. 

Therefore, these people say, either there is no note which is essentially and primarily of two times, but only becomes so by subtraction—for instance, when one unit of time is subtracted from a note of three times by a breve preceding or following it, as shown here:

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC <note>original: "Pomerium Musicae Mensuratae"; Marchetto's influential 1318 treatise on rhythmic notation</note>

First, we shall demonstrate that it is necessary in **mensural music** <note>original: "cantu mensurato"; music where the shape of the note defines its specific rhythmic duration</note> to establish one note which is essentially and by its very nature worth two **units of time** <note>original: "temporum"; the *tempus* was the basic building block of medieval rhythm</note>, and not merely by accident or by the subtraction of some third unit of time from it. Second, we shall show in what position or place such a note ought to be written. Third, we shall demonstrate that it is written with a certain unique, perceptible, and well-known characteristic by which it differs—and can be perceived by the senses to differ—both from a note of one unit of time and a note of three. Fourth, from the things said above, we shall conclude why such a characteristic is its own, and not that of another note.

For we demonstrate the first point thus: In every movement, it is necessary to pass from one extreme to the other through some middle point; and by necessity, that middle point differs essentially and by itself from the extremes, as is clear in local movement <note>physical movement from place to place</note>. For he who goes from one place to another must necessarily pass through a middle, and through such a middle that is not one of the extremes. But it is certain that singing is a kind of **motion of the voice** <note>original: "motus vocis"; a medieval concept viewing melody as a physical movement through the "space" of different pitches</note>, which is measured by time, just as all local motion is also measured by time. Therefore, just as in local motion there is a first time in which that which is moved is at the starting point, and another in which it is in the middle (which differs from the first), and a third in which it is at the final goal—and thus all these three times are naturally distinguished from one another—so it is in mensural music itself. It runs through movements by measuring from one note to another until it reaches the **perfection** <note>original: "perfectionem"; a grouping of three beats, symbolizing completeness</note> of a three-time measure, as has been proven.

<column-break/>

First, one must provide a note measured by one unit of time, another by two, and another by three. Thus, just as "one" is the first and essential principle in numbers, "two" is the second essential principle in them, and "three" is the third—all of which differ essentially—so it must also be in music. Since music is founded upon numbers, there must be one note that is essentially and by itself worth one unit of time (not by accident), and another worth three. It is clear, therefore, that in mensural music it is necessary to provide a note that is worth two units of time primarily, by itself, and essentially—and not by accident or subtraction, as sometimes happens with a note of three units of time, which is made into a note of two by a **breve** <note>original: "notam brevem"; a "short" note</note> or its value preceding or following it, as seen here:

<image-desc>A fragment of mensural music notation on a five-line staff. It displays a sequence of square and diamond-shaped notes (breves, longas, and semibreves) used to illustrate rhythmic proportions in perfect and imperfect time.</image-desc>

->*In which position and place notes should be written which are measured by different units of time.*<-

Let us see, therefore, in what place and position the note called the **altered breve** <note>original: "altera brevis"; in triple meter, if two breves appeared between two long notes, the second breve was "altered" to double its length (2 beats) to complete the "perfection" of 3</note> must necessarily be written. We say that it must necessarily be in the last place; and by "last place," we mean the position of the note in which the three units of time are completed. Thus, if we wish to proceed further in singing, a **longa** <note>original: "longa"; a long note, usually worth three breves in this system</note> necessarily follows. We derive the reason for this from the proportion of the notes to one another and the joining together that must occur among the notes so that the music is sung in a measured way. The reason is this: it was proven above that the measure of three units of time is the more perfect measure, which...

<meta>catchword: which</meta>

<summary>Marchetto argues that music, like physical motion, requires a middle point (the number two) between its beginning (one) and its perfection (three). He establishes the theoretical necessity of the "altered breve," a note that essentially represents two units of time to complete a triple-meter grouping.</summary>
<keywords>mensural music, altered breve, perfection, unit of time, motion of the voice, musical proportion, rhythmic theory</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Marchetto continues his discussion on rhythmic proportions, specifically focusing on the "perfection" of the number three and how the "altered breve" (a note worth two beats) functions within a triple-time measurement system.</meta>

# MARCHETTO OF PADUA <note>original: "MARCHETI DE PADUA"</note>

which can be found in song, because it is the container of all measures. Since, therefore, in song—whether in a single note or in several—there are three measured **units of time** <term>tempora; the basic units of rhythmic measurement in medieval music</term>, we must repeatedly return, either through one note or a combination of several, to measure another three units of time. If, therefore, after a note of three units <note>a "perfect" long</note> another **breve** <term>a "short" note, typically worth one unit</term> is given, five units of time would be created between that first one and this second one. In this case, you would either have to subtract from the note of three units and give it to this other breve; and it would then follow that the note of three units would become two, and the **perfect ratio of measuring** <note>the ideal triple division (3:1)</note> would not be found within it. It follows, then, that from the joining of these two notes together, the perfect ratio of measuring three units of time cannot be found in either of them, which is against the logic of measurement. But if you were to say, "after the second breve I add another breve," from which two notes the ratio of measuring is completed; then it is against the first principle in music, which is that music is the application of number.

Just as in the case of numbers, no living person could conceive of "two" unless he had first conceived of "one"—for two is nothing other than two units—and just as in music no one could conceive of two notes unless he had first conceived of one: so too, no one could conceive of two units of time unless he had first conceived of one. In the order of nature, therefore, one unit of time precedes two, and a note of one unit of time precedes a note of two. Thus, the breve note, as has been shown, naturally precedes the **altered breve** <term>altera brevis; a breve whose value is doubled to two units to fill out a triple measure</term>, just as one precedes two.

<column-break/>

It is necessary, therefore, that the note of two units of time be situated in the "last place"—which we call the final position—in which the three units of time are completed, for it is in these three that the perfect ratio of measuring consists. For it cannot be written after a **long** <term>longa; a note of greater duration</term>, nor can a breve be written after it, for the reasons mentioned above. Therefore, it holds the last place in the measurement of the song, as has been declared; and this is uniquely characteristic of the **altered breve** <note>original: "alterae (alterius) brevis"</note>. And since this note is the "perfection" of its own breve <note>meaning it completes the group of three with the preceding breve</note>, with which it makes three units of time, it is necessary that if we wish to sing further, we begin again from another note in which the perfect ratio of measuring consists—that is, three units—unless perhaps it is made **imperfect** <term>imperficiatur; the process where a note's value is reduced by a neighboring note</term> by what follows it, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff showing square notes, including longas and breves, illustrating the musical concept of imperfection described in the text.</image-desc>

For by that altered breve, the first three units of time are completed: and this is the reason why a long must necessarily follow after an altered breve. And by this, the error of certain people is refuted; they claim that by a **point** <term>punctus; a dot used in notation to change a note's value or divide measures</term> or some other added property to the altered breve itself, it becomes an altered breve, and then they add a breve after it again. They are wrong because they do not begin the subsequent melody from a perfect ratio of measuring. And we say the same if they add a point to several breves, claiming they become altered breves, then adding more breves after them again, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a four-line staff with several square notes, used to illustrate a theoretical musical error involving the addition of points to notes.</image-desc>

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC <note>original: "POMERIUM MUSICÆ MENSURATÆ"</note>

## With what property the altered breve should be shaped.

We shall demonstrate, therefore, that the **altered breve** <term>altera brevis; a breve note that is doubled in value to two beats to complete a triple measure</term> has a singular, clearly recognizable property through which it is shaped and distinguished from both the **breve** <term>brevis; the basic short note</term> and the **long** <term>longa; a longer note value</term>. For this is evident from what was said above; a long can be shaped or situated both before and after a breve, and at the beginning of a **perfection** <term>perfectio; a completed unit of three beats</term> as well as after it. A breve can also be situated both before and after a long, as is evident here:

<image-desc>A five-line musical staff displaying mensural notation. The notes include square brevis and rectangular longas, some with stems (caudae) extending downwards.</image-desc>

But a breve cannot be situated after an altered breve; furthermore, an altered breve cannot be situated in a song except in the last place of a perfection of the measure. What, therefore, is the specific characteristic—or property—of the altered breve itself, by which it can be recognized as distinct from both the long and the breve? We say it is the **placement** <note>original: "situs"</note> which it holds in the last place of a perfection of the measure. Others <note>referring to longs and standard breves</note> can be situated at the beginning or in the middle, which is not the case for the altered breve; for by necessity, it is situated in the last place of the perfection and nowhere else, as has been demonstrated. Such a placement, therefore, is specifically the property that clearly distinguishes it from both the long and the breve, just as the long and breve are distinguished by having a **stem** <term>cauda; literally "tail," the vertical stroke attached to a note</term> or lacking one. By this, the error of those who say that the altered breve and the standard breve are not distinguished by any property of their shapes is refuted, for they themselves drew stems to distinguish those notes from one another. From this it follows that such a property belongs to the altered breve itself and not to another note; and from

->SCRIPTORES VET. DE MUSICA. P. III.<- <note>Ancient Writers on Music, Part 3</note>

<column-break/>

the aforementioned things, a **syllogism** <term>a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</term> is formed: that which belongs "only and always" to something is its specific property—just as being **visible** <note>This is likely a transcription error for "risibile" (capable of laughter), the standard medieval logical example of a property unique to humans</note> belongs to man "only and always." But to be always situated and located in the last place of the perfection and measure of the song, and nowhere else, belongs to the altered breve and only to the altered breve, and always to the altered breve, as shown above. Therefore, such a situation and location is the specific property of the altered breve itself, through which it can be clearly recognized as distinct from the long and the breve. And thus it is clear how **musical time** <term>tempus musicum; the unit of duration</term> is applied to the notes themselves in the measure of the song: for one unit of time is the duration of the breve note, a double unit of time belongs to the altered breve, and a triple unit of time belongs to the perfect long.

And because time itself is applied directly to the notes according to "natural perfection" <note>triple meter</note> as a whole unit and not according to division, therefore such notes ought to be drawn as plain squares in the manner of a rectangle, featuring no cut at the corner, nor division, nor addition, with their properties mentioned above and not without them, so that through these marks their essential property may be recognized in this way.

## Concerning time, and how it is applicable to the notes according to its division into its parts.
