<meta>catchword: or</meta>

...time itself with these notes according to the proper mode of its division, through which it is divided into various parts, so that by this we may show the nature of certain **imperfect notes** and the different way of shaping them according to their various properties. Regarding this, we shall proceed in this order: first, we will show how **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a unit of three beats</term> itself is divided into its primary divisions; second, we will show the essences of the notes which are shaped from such divisions; third, we will show how such notes relate to division regarding the first mode of measuring time; fourth, from what has been said, we will conclude the way of shaping them along with their properties; fifth, we will say how **semibreves** <term>semibreves; notes smaller than a breve</term> are named with their own names; sixth, we will show how semibreves relate to one another regarding the second mode of measuring time.

## How time itself is divided into its primary divisions.

As to the first point, it must be known that the primary division and perfection of perfect time is the **binary** and **ternary** division—that is, to divide time itself into two or three parts, and no more. The reason for this is that those divisions of time are more perfect which are the root and origin of all other divisions; but such are the binary or ternary divisions; therefore [they are the primary ones]. The proof of the minor premise: for if we divide time into more than three—say, into four—we are simply repeating "two"; for to say four is to say twice two, and to say five is to say two and three,

<column-break/>

and so it goes for the rest. Therefore, the divisions of time into two or three parts are the most perfect divisions that can be found in time itself, and the division into three is even more perfect than the division into two. The proof: that division is more perfect which contains another as a part of itself, and not vice versa; but three parts contain two, just as the whole contains its parts. Therefore, just as three is more perfect than two, so the division of time into three parts is more perfect than its division into two. And this concludes the first point.

## Demonstration of the essences of the notes which are shaped from such divisions.

As to the second point, we shall show the essences of certain notes which arise from such divisions of time and are shaped in song. And we say that such notes are **imperfect**: for that which contains only parts and not the whole is imperfect; but these notes contain only a part of the time and not the whole; therefore they ought to be called imperfect. And because **perfect time** <note>original: "tempus perfectum"</note> is that which contains or measures a whole perfect breve, measuring these imperfect notes as its parts: it follows that such imperfect notes are called **semibreves** <term>semibreves; literally "half-shorts," though they could be a third of a breve in triple time</term> as if they were parts measuring the time of a breve. And because they represent a part and not the whole, it follows that they should be simply shaped with an oblique acute angle at the top and bottom, and filled in <note>original: "obscuro," referring to the black ink of the notation</note> on the right and left, as seen here:

<image-desc>A musical staff with five horizontal lines containing four solid black rhomboid (diamond-shaped) notes.</image-desc>

...or into a **ligature** <term>ligatura; two or more notes joined together</term> with a tail on the left side pointing upward, which makes that tied note—whether it is square or oblique, ascending or descending—likewise a **semibreve** <term>semibrevis; a note value shorter than a breve</term>. The reason why the said tail does this has already been stated above in the treatise on tails. And this concludes the second point.

### *How such notes relate to one another, concerning the single semibreve alone.*

Regarding the third point, we must see how notes are taken in relation to each other in song. First, we say that a single **semibreve** cannot be found on its own in **measured music** <term>cantus mensurabilis; music with a defined, regular pulse</term>. The reason for this is that, just as it is necessary that the perfect logic of measuring **perfect notes** <term>notae perfectae; notes equal to three beats</term> consists in the "primary perfection" (which is three beats), so it is necessary that the perfect logic of measuring the very **time** <term>tempus; the duration of a breve</term> of a **breve** note through semibreves must contain three parts of that time. Through these three parts, the measurement runs and is measured through the entire nature of **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; triple meter</term> itself. But if we were to place a single semibreve alone, it could not contain three parts of time, because then it would not be a semibreve, but a breve. If, however, it were to contain one or two parts of time, the perfect time could not be measured by such parts, because the time would then exceed the note by a third part. It remains, therefore, that if semibreves are to be placed, there must necessarily be two, so that a single one cannot in any way be found alone in a song.

But you may ask: if there are two, how do they relate to each other? We say that if

<column-break/>

they are shaped in exactly the same way in every respect, the last one holds two parts of time and the first holds one. The reason for this is that when parts measure a whole, that which is last in the "way of nature" always completes and perfects that nature. For the end (as an "end") is always the final perfection; indeed, all things act for the sake of an end, and when a thing reaches its end, it has its perfection. For the "end" is the cause of causes, and the most noble among all causes, according to the **Philosopher** <note>Marchetto refers here to Aristotle, a standard authority for medieval writers.</note> in the second book of the *Physics*. Therefore, if it is necessary for us to measure three parts of time using two notes, we ought to measure the time itself as one part with the first note (which is the beginning), and with the second note (which is the end, the perfection, and the measure), we must measure the two remaining parts of time. This is the reason why, of two semibreves shaped identically in every way in a song, the first contains one part of time and the second contains two.

But you might ask: if I add a tail to the first one, it is made to consist of two parts, and the third part of the time to be measured remains in the last note. What is the reason for this? We say that for the sake of clarity, it must be known that it is one thing to arrive from the parts to the whole <note>original: "a partibus ad totum"</note>—which is done by the path of composition—but it is another thing to arrive from the whole to the parts <note>original: "de toto vero ad partes"</note>, which is done by the path of division. <note>The text here has a slight gap. A later scholar noted: "The gap is perhaps filled thus: 'and it is another thing to arrive from the whole to the parts; for one goes from the parts to the whole etc.'"</note> Now, however, whether one arrives from the whole to the parts or from the parts to the whole, it must be so that one does not exceed the other, nor one fall short of the other—for instance, that the whole does not exceed the parts, nor the parts the whole.

Here, Marchetto explores the mathematical and "artistic" logic of how two or more semibreves combine to fill that unit.</meta>

-># MARCHETTO OF PADUA<-

...[the whole] and the whole should not fall short of its parts, nor the part from the whole. Then we say that none of the parts has a reason within itself why it should contain more of the whole than another, especially if they are equal... Let a **breve** note be given; this is a certain whole. Let this whole, which is **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a unit of measurement consisting of three beats</term>, be divided by its primary division into three parts; the aforementioned note will be divided into three equal **semibreves**. Therefore, the breve note relates to these semibreves just as the semibreves relate to the breve, because such parts do not exceed the whole in measuring, nor does the breve note (which is the whole) exceed its semibreves (which are its parts), nor does it fall short of them. In the same way and uniformly, the breve relates to the semibreves and vice versa; for this reason, they must be marked equally and with equal properties. 

But if the whole exceeds the parts—for instance, when a breve is divided into only two semibreves—since these two cannot equal the whole, it is necessary that one of them claims two parts of the time to achieve the required **perfection of measurement** <note>In triple meter, if you only have two notes, one must be twice as long as the other to fill the three-beat "perfect" unit.</note>. And then we say this will be applied to the notes either by the way of nature or by the way of art. If by the way of nature, the last note, which is the end, will claim two parts of that time; the reason is stated above: because the end is always more perfect than the beginning. But if by art, then it suffices that in two or more semibreves joined together, a perfection of measurement arises so that the whole can be measured and equaled by the parts. And because there is no inherent reason why one part should take priority over another,

<column-break/>

therefore, by applying some **accident** <term>accidens; a visual modification like a stem or a dot</term> to a semibreve note through art—perhaps for some specific cause—we can apply the whole to the parts, not by a whim of the will, but according to a rational method. In this way, the whole applied to the parts is perfectly measured by them, and the parts perfectly measure the whole. This is the reason why we can add a tail to the first semibreve, and it will be made "major" <term>maior; literally "greater," meaning the note value is doubled</term>, because this will be by art and from the nature of the notes, yet above nature. 

If it is said: "Art imitates nature as much as it can"; we say this is true regarding the foundation, and yet natural things are combined in art in such a way that they are not found that way in nature. For a goat and a stag are natural things, but art joins them together to make a **goat-stag** <note>original: "hirco-cervum"; a legendary creature used in medieval philosophy to illustrate how the mind can combine real elements into a new, imaginary whole</note>; yet such things do not exist together in the nature of things, even though art had them both as its foundation. Thus, although such a thing is not from nature but from art, art nonetheless received it from natural things. 

We say, therefore, that a musician can diversify and add conditions to these notes which indicate that they have properties beyond their nature; and he does this by composing the different natures of notes together in various ways. Hence, although he does this through art, he takes his foundation from natural things—namely, from the parts of time and from the notes themselves—by composing them from different parts of time. To add something through such composition is above the nature of such notes, but not against their nature. And so that these things may be made clearer in examples, let us apply this to breves.

### Concerning the three semibreves in the primary division of time.

In the primary perfect division, the unit is divided equally into three, which are represented by identical shapes; this is because they relate equally to the whole, and the whole relates equally to them. However, if the unit is divided into only two notes, as shown here:

<image-desc>A short musical staff with three rhombus-shaped semibreve notes.</image-desc>

then, by the **way of nature** <note>Marchetto argues that music follows natural logic: a concluding note naturally carries more weight and duration than a starting note.</note>, the last note—because it is the conclusion—claims two parts of the time for itself, and the first note claims only one. And because this arrangement is "accidental" <note>In medieval philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential; here, it means a variation chosen by the composer.</note>, it is necessary to add a **tail** <term>cauda; a vertical stroke or stem attached to a note to change its value</term>, as shown here:

<image-desc>A short musical staff with three rhombus-shaped semibreve notes; the first two notes have thin vertical tails descending from their right sides.</image-desc>

which makes the first note hold two parts of the time. While a note can sometimes carry this value without a tail, the tail indicates the "will" of the person measuring the breve; it signals that through these two semibreves, the first contains two parts of the time.

### Concerning the second division into six semibreves.

In this division, each note contains a sixth part of the time by the "way of nature," though in practice the "way of art" allows for different methods of harmonizing, as will be shown below. Sometimes it is found that the **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a three-beat rhythmic unit</term> is divided into only four semibreves through a secondary division; this is achieved by using "twice three" parts, as shown here:

<image-desc>A musical staff with four rhombus-shaped semibreve notes.</image-desc>

It is necessary, therefore, that these parts still measure their whole, so that they are joined

<column-break/>

to one another in such a way that they are encompassed by those six parts of time. This is not contrary to reason; for it is enough for musicians, acting as musicians, to be able to measure the breve with these two semibreves, so that a perfect harmony and the proper proportion of measurement arises from such a count. 

Indeed, the breve cannot be divided into the last three semibreves by a "primary division" because, as has been said, the primary division of perfect time is into three equal parts. If we must divide the time into more than three parts, we must resort to the "secondary perfect division," which will consist of twice three parts (six), and not just three, for reasons to be stated below. It is in these "twice three" parts—and not in three—that the secondary division of perfect time must consist. From these are formed another "twice three" notes, which are called **minor semibreves**, as shown here:

<image-desc>A full-width musical staff containing three groups of three rhombus-shaped semibreve notes each, separated by thin vertical bar lines.</image-desc>

These parts are adapted to each other so that they are contained within the six parts of time. Then, by the way of nature, the first part is divided first because it is closer to the whole; for it is in the nature of a "whole" to be divided into its primary parts. If we must divide those primary parts further, we must begin again from the first, then the second, and thirdly from the third. Therefore, of the four semibreves mentioned, the first two become "minor"—that is, containing two of the six parts—and thus those two complete the first part of the primary division of time (which is divided into three). However, if semibreves are sometimes noted for the time, as here:

The first two notes will be **minor** <term>minor semibrevis; a note value representing one-third of a full beat</term> for the reason stated, because it is the nature of the first part to be divided first; and the second two will also be minor, because it is the nature of the second part to be divided second. If, however, there are six, as seen here:

<image-desc>A musical staff with five horizontal lines and six diamond-shaped notes. The first note has a downward-pointing stem; the others are stemless.</image-desc>

Then all will be minor, because the first, second, and third principal parts (which were originally three) will be divided into twice-three <note>original: "bis tres"—meaning 2 times 3 equals 6</note>. All of them together will equally measure the primary parts of **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a rhythmic unit traditionally divided into three equal beats</term>. And because this follows the **way of nature** <note>Marchetto argues that musical logic reflects natural order; here, "nature" refers to the default equal division of the beat</note>, all the notes written above are naturally drawn with the same shape. Although we also intend to show, by the way of nature, that they possess certain **properties** <term>proprietas; the visual features of a note, like stems, that indicate its rhythmic value</term> by which they can be recognized by their upward stems, distinguishing them from one another in their rhythmic notation. We show this in the treatise on their properties and shapes.

And because, as stated, the musician strives for a unified way of creating harmony rationally, it follows that the musician—considering the divided way of applying the parts of perfect time to create a different harmony than would arise from the previously mentioned method—arranges them differently, assigning to the first semibreve

<column-break/>

note of a pair two parts of perfect time, and to the second only one, as previously mentioned. This is signaled by the addition of a **tail** <term>cauda; a vertical stem attached to a note to change its duration</term> to that note, as seen here:

<image-desc>A musical staff with five lines and five diamond-shaped notes. The first note features a prominently long downward-pointing stem (cauda).</image-desc>

But if the first semibreve of a group of three is given a downward tail, we must move to the second division of time, which is divided into six. The reason for this is that a tail added to a semibreve must either add something to its value or nothing at all. If it adds nothing, then it was added in vain; but it does add value. Let us see, then, how much it adds: it does not add a full third of the time, for then it—along with the others joined to it (namely, the two that remain undivided)—would exceed the measure of the time unit. Therefore, it is necessary that either both accompanying semibreves or one of them be divided, so that the portion divided from them (or one of them) is necessarily included within the note with the tail. Here we say that only one should be divided, specifically into two parts of the **six-fold division** <term>senaria; a meter where the beat is divided into six units</term>. We add one of these parts to the stemmed semibreve, which then contains three out of the six parts of the time, while the other semibreve remains undivided in the three-fold division.

But you might argue against the above as follows: the two following semibreves will become "minor," each containing a third part of the time, while the one with the tail contains two, and thus you have your harmony. We respond: just as we add one part of that division (namely, the three-fold division) to the first of two semibreves with a downward tail to give it two parts, so to this semi-

# POMERIUM OF MEASURED MUSIC

To the **tailed semibreve** <term>semibrevis caudata; a diamond-shaped note with a vertical stem, indicating a specific rhythmic value</term> we must add one part of that division which we must necessarily enter—namely, the **six-fold** <term>senaria; a rhythmic division where the basic unit of time, the breve, is divided into six equal parts</term>. We provide an example as follows:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff consisting of nine mensural notes: two groups of a longa followed by two breves, then a group consisting of a semibrevis caudata and two semibreves.</image-desc>

These are nine notes, of which the first is a **long** <term>longa; a major note value in medieval theory</term> and the two following are **breves** <term>brevis; literally "short," the standard unit of time</term>. These first three notes contain six **breve-times** <note>original: "tempora brevia"</note>; specifically, the first note is **perfect** <term>perfect; in medieval music, "perfect" refers to a value divided into three parts</term> containing three times, the first breve contains one, and the second contains two, thus totaling six. The others that precede them are formed in the same way. Indeed, this rule applies correctly to semibreves. Let us therefore place three semibreves, the first of which is tailed downward, as seen here:

<image-desc>Musical notation showing three diamond-shaped semibreves on a staff; the first semibreve has a downward tail.</image-desc>

These three necessarily contain six **semibreve-times**, based on the reasoning given for the long: out of the two breves, the first **tailed semibreve** contains three parts of the second division (which is the division into six), the first following semibreve contains one, and the second contains two. Thus, six parts of the time of the second division are included in such semibreves. An example of the long and the breves themselves is clear here:

<image-desc>Musical notation showing a sequence of six notes on a staff: a longa, two breves, another longa, and two more breves.</image-desc>

But if a tail is added to the middle note, then that tailed note has three parts for the reason mentioned above; the first has one, and the last has two, because it is the end. If, however, the last note is tailed, as seen here:

<column-break/>

<image-desc>Musical notation showing three semibreves on a staff, where the third one has a downward tail.</image-desc>

then the tailed note itself has three parts of the six-fold division for the aforementioned reason; the first has one, and the middle has two, because it more closely approaches the end.

### *Whether two out of three notes can be tailed.*

Someone might say: can I never tail two out of the three, so that all six parts of the time may be measured through them? We answer that this is not possible. The proof: a tail added to two such notes either signifies something beyond its nature, or nothing at all. If nothing, then it results in nothing, for it would be there in vain <note>original: "frustra"</note>; but nothing is in vain, neither in nature nor in art. If it signifies something, then it would add at least one of the six parts of time to both such tailed notes beyond what they had by their nature. By their nature, each has two parts of the six; therefore, if another part is added to such tailed notes, they would each have three parts individually, and thus they alone would encompass the six parts of the time. In that case, the third note would be superfluous, or the tail on one of the tailed notes would be in vain. Therefore, only one of three semibreves can be tailed in the manner demonstrated above; however, out of four semibreves, two can be tailed. But first, let us see how one out of those four can be tailed. Let us then place four semibreves, one of which is tailed, as here:

<image-desc>Musical notation showing four diamond-shaped semibreves on a staff, with the second note having a downward tail.</image-desc>

<meta>This page continues Marchetto of Padua’s discussion on the "senaria" (the division of the unit of time into six parts) and how "tails" or stems added to semibreves by the "musician’s art" alter their duration relative to "nature."</meta>

Of these, the first is **tailed** <term>caudata; a semibreve with a stem</term>, and because through such notes we can perfectly measure the secondary division of time into six, without dividing that time any further. Then we shall say that, by the institution of the musical author through **art** <note>original: "per artem"; referring to the deliberate rules of musical composition</note>, for the reason stated above, the first has two of the six parts, while the others each have one. And you might object as follows: granted that the first, which is tailed, will only have two of the six parts of time, while the two immediately following it have two, and the third has two, because it is the end—granted that the "end" always signifies **perfection** <term>perfectio; in medieval theory, the completion of a rhythmic unit</term>; yet this perfection must always be achieved in the most suitable way possible. But the "way of nature" is more suitable than the "way of art" in natural things, while the "way of art" is more suitable in artificial things than the way of nature. Because, therefore, such a tailing is created by art more than by nature—for according to nature no **semibreve** <term>semibrevis; a diamond-shaped note</term> contains more than one part of time—it follows that according to the division of the part of time through the way of nature, we would have to multiply the notes. For if the time of the primary division is divided into three parts, we must draw three notes corresponding to those parts; and if time is divided into six by the secondary division according to the way of nature, six notes will be drawn corresponding to those six parts. But the musician, through art, wishes to measure the six parts of time using four, five, or three notes, as has been said; therefore, he can, through art, apply those parts that exceed the others to whichever note he wishes, so that by applying them through the way of art, he exceeds the way of nature. It is therefore not

<column-break/>

necessary to consider the "way of nature" in any note when the musician wishes to apply such parts through the "way of art." If, therefore, it is brought about through art that one of four notes contains three parts of time, since the others must remain in the way of nature (because no change is made to them by art), it must be said that the three following notes are three parts of time containing their value naturally. And if it is asked: "Can I tail the last note?" we say yes; and in this case, that note will contain three of the six parts of time through art, and the three preceding notes will naturally contain one part of the six parts of time individually. We say the same for any of those four notes that is tailed, because it always takes three of the six parts of time, with the remaining notes individually containing one of the six.

### *Whether two out of four can be tailed.*

But someone might say: "I can tail two out of the four, specifically the first and the last," as shown here:

<image-desc>A musical staff with three separate examples of four diamond-shaped semibreves. In each example, the first and the fourth (last) semibreve have downward-pointing stems (caudæ), while the middle two are stemless.</image-desc>

We reply that art does not contradict itself. If you wish to measure six parts of time with four semibreves and no more through art, then if each of the tailed notes contained three parts of time, the two [middle] notes would necessarily be in vain <note>original: "frustra"; meaning they would have no time-value left over within the six-part unit</note>. Therefore, to find the proper proportion of measurement in such cases through art, it is necessary that each of those two tailed notes should contain only two of the six parts of time, while the two remaining non-tailed notes will naturally contain the other two parts. And so it is said—

### *Whether three out of four can be tailed.*

For someone might ask: can three out of four never be tailed? We respond that they cannot; the reason for this is that such a tail either indicates something added to these three through **art** <note>original: "per artem"; referring to the deliberate rules of musical notation created by humans rather than the "natural" inherent value of the note</note>, or it indicates nothing. If it indicates nothing, then it is useless. If it indicates something, then it will add at least one part of time through art to each of the tailed notes. Thus, the three tailed notes alone would measure all six parts of the time, and the fourth untailed note would be there in vain <note>In medieval logic, nature and art do nothing in vain; every note must have a mathematical purpose.</note>, which is impossible and inappropriate. Therefore, it is impossible for three out of four to be tailed, no matter how they are tailed by art.

### *Regarding five semibreves: which and how many can be tailed?*

But let us see, regarding five **semibreves** <term>semibrevis; a diamond-shaped musical note</term>, which and how many can be tailed: first, we say that the first can be, as here:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing three groups of five semibreves. In each group, only the first note has a downward stem.</image-desc>

And then that tailed note, through art, will contain two out of the six parts of time, while the four following notes will remain in their natural parts. The reason for this is that we cannot have a note that does not contain at least one part of time in its natural degree; otherwise, one would be providing a note that is not singable.

<column-break/>

Therefore, four notes out of five will necessarily contain four out of the six parts of time naturally; the tailed note, however, will contain two parts out of six, and it cannot contain more than two parts of six, because then the parts would exceed their whole <note>Since the total measure is 6, and 4 notes take up 4 parts, the remaining note cannot be more than 2.</note>. And this will be the case whenever one of five is tailed through art, whether it is the first or one of the middle notes, as shown here:

<image-desc>Musical notation on a five-line staff showing three groups of five semibreves. In each group, a single note in a medial position (second, third, or fourth) has a downward stem.</image-desc>

The last note, however, cannot be tailed. The proof: does such a tail indicate something added to it through art beyond its nature, or nothing? Not "something," because that would be adding one part of time out of six to it; but it already possesses this by nature and in its own meaning without a tail, because it is the **end** <note>original: "finis"; the final note of a group often carried more duration in medieval theory to complete the "perfection" of the measure.</note>. Nor can art add a third part of the six to it, since the four preceding notes already contain four of the six parts; such a tailed note, combined with them, would create seven parts, and thus exceed **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a unit of musical time divided into three or multiples of three (here, six)</term>, which is divided into only six parts.

...with three **tailed** <term>caudatis; notes with an added vertical stem</term> and three untailed, seven parts of time would arise. For it is impossible that out of five notes, more than one alone can be tailed in the **secondary division** <note>The secondary division of the "Breve" into six equal parts, known as "senaria."</note>, which is into six; that one tailed note, together with the remaining four, will measure six parts of time.

But it must be noted that regarding all the aforementioned tailed musical notes, through the way of **art** <note>original: "per viam artis"; refers to the rules established by musicians to modify the "natural" or standard value of a note</note>, the musician always adds less of a tail to a note that is at the end of a group than to one at the beginning. The reason for this is because the end possesses more of **natural perfection** <term>perfectio; in medieval music, this refers to a state of completion or a full count of three or six</term> in measurement, for the reason stated above; therefore, it requires less assistance from the artist to measure the time. 

The argument is as follows: that which possesses more true perfection in measuring requires less assistance from the artist to complete the measure than that which possesses less. This is true to the senses: for in measuring six **ells** <note>original: "ulnas"; a traditional unit of length used for measuring cloth</note>, a line of five ells possesses more of the perfection of nature than a line of three. Since any note at the end of a group possesses more perfection for measuring time by the way of nature—because it contains two out of the six parts of time—whereas one at the beginning only contains one part, therefore the artist, in adding a tail to the note at the end, only adds one part of time out of six; but in adding a tail to the one at the beginning, he adds two. And we say these are the parts in groups of four and five. For

<column-break/>

if none of the four are tailed, those which are at the end always contain more perfection (because they have two out of the six parts of time each) than those at the beginning, which only contain the other two parts together. Therefore, by adding a tail to the last note, we only add one part of time out of six; but by adding a tail to one of the first notes, we add two. The same applies to a group of five. And this is naturally true, because in adding a tail to any of those at the end, we always add less than when adding a tail to those at the beginning.

But it must be noted that what has been said regarding the tail to be added to a **semibreve** <term>semibrevis; a diamond-shaped note</term> up to this point is to be understood as a tail drawn **downward** <note>original: "in deorsum"</note>. The reason is this: whenever something is added to another thing, that thing is always "perfected" (completed) by what is added; for since it is added, the thing did not have it before, and thus it has more than it had previously. When a musician, through art, adds a part of time to a note which it did not have by the way of nature, it is certain that he perfects it beyond its own nature. 

Therefore, such a sign must be added to it that indicates such **perfection** and not imperfection. But it was shown above in the treatise on tails that a downward tail indicates perfection, and one drawn **upward** <note>original: "in sursum"</note> indicates imperfection. Therefore, since it has been shown here that the musician always perfects these semibreves through art—which perfection the tail indicates—it must be understood that such notes tailed by a musician ought to be tailed downward. ...[semibre]ves, they will contain six parts of time, and this will be by the **way of nature** <note>original: "via naturæ"; Marchetto distinguishes between the inherent mathematical properties of notes (nature) and the rules created by musicians (art).</note>, and then the whole will equal the parts, and the parts the whole, and this will be the natural measure.

We respond that by the way of nature (or "naturally"), every note is shaped to measure exactly one part of time and no more, unless it is at the end; for then, by necessity, the end always contains more, as was shown above. Now, does a note naturally indicate something about the time—either just one part, or several, or the whole? Not the whole, because then we would only need one note for measurement, which has already been rejected. If it indicates more than one part, then give me a note that essentially contains the first part of time out of three; you will not be able to give it, because according to your logic, the very nature of any note is to contain multiple parts of time. Thus, three parts of time could never be measured by three notes, nor by two; for if measured by two, one of them would have to hold two parts, while the other note would necessarily

<column-break/>

contain one part essentially and naturally. This contradicts your position: first, because you claim a single note cannot contain anything except multiple parts of time, yet you then provide one note out of two that contains only a single part of time. Furthermore, you say that the note containing two parts requires the **help of the artist** <note>original: "adiutorio artificis"; meaning the note requires a special sign or rule ("art") to change its value from the natural default.</note>—that is, an **artificial sign**—which implies that it does not possess this value from nature. Therefore, since we cannot measure three parts of time through three notes of the same shape, nor through two or one of them, if it were the nature of a note to contain multiple parts of time: it follows by the opposite argument that it is the nature of every note to naturally contain only one part of time, but **artificially** to contain more. We say, therefore, that naturally, six notes cannot measure twelve parts of time, but only six; "artificially," however, they can. Thus the question just asked is answered.

But let us see how this is done artificially. It must be understood that if the time is divided into twelve parts by the **third division**, it is necessary that we can and must reasonably represent those twelve parts of time in writing through twelve notes. Therefore, it is necessary that in music, twelve notes are provided corresponding to the aforementioned twelve parts of time, so that it may be known when the time is to be measured as if divided into twelve parts, or into six, or into three. And it must be known that **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a unit of music divided into three or multiples of three, considered "perfect" or complete in the medieval period</term>, by which the whole is measured, by whatever notes...

<meta>This page continues Marchetto's logical demonstration of how "perfect time" (a full musical measure) can be subdivided. <meta>catchword: tis</meta>

...is measured according to every one of its parts. The logic is formed as follows: that which measures something perfectly must necessarily measure it according to every single part of itself; otherwise, it does not measure it perfectly. Now, **perfect time** <note>original: "tempus perfectum"; in medieval music, this refers to a basic unit of time or "measure" that is divided into three equal parts.</note> is measured by three notes as a whole, or by six, or by twelve—briefly, by any number of notes that contain every part of that unit of time. 

Therefore, whether three, six, twelve, or more or fewer notes are written—following the logic cited above—to measure that unit of perfect time, it is necessary that the time be measured according to every one of its parts. However, the difference is this: whatever a larger number of notes measures **explicitly** <note>clearly and individually shown</note>, a smaller number of notes measures **implicitly** <note>contained within the value of the notes without being seen</note>. 

For it is in the nature of a "divisible whole" that fewer parts contain as much *implicitly* as more parts contain *explicitly*. Just as the three parts of a line into which a whole line is divided contain as much *implicitly* as twelve parts would contain *explicitly* if you were to divide it into twelve: so too, three or six notes measure as much of the parts of perfect time *implicitly* as twelve notes do *explicitly*.

But someone might ask: how can it be known whether three or four or more notes are measuring the time according to a **twelve-fold** <term>duodenaria; a division of the beat into 12 parts</term> or a **six-fold** <term>senaria; a division of the beat into 6 parts</term> division? Can this be known simply through the different shapes of the notes without adding any other characteristic? 

We say: no. The reason is that the nature of a **semibreve** <note>a diamond-shaped note</note> note, as a semibreve, implies nothing other than a single part (whatever that may be) or multiple parts (whatever those may be), and it is not understood to measure the whole unit of time;

<column-break/>

for if a note falls short of the measurement of the time in any way it wishes, it is a semibreve note. Therefore, if there are only three semibreves or two, they cannot be written in a simple way (for the reason stated above) unless those three parts of time were to measure the whole time by containing it entirely. 

From three up to six notes, the time itself cannot be measured except through the **six-fold division** <note>senaria</note>, as was shown above. The number of notes alone is sufficient when the time is measured by a **three-fold** <note>ternaria</note> or six-fold division; thus, for notes numbering between three and six, there is no need to change their shapes to know when they are measuring time by three or six parts; we say these notes are shaped **uniformly**. 

But to recognize when the time is being measured by notes according to twelve distinct parts, the mere number of notes is not enough—unless there were actually twelve notes present to indicate the twelve parts of time. And because any grouping that uses fewer than twelve notes to measure those twelve parts would have to do so **implicitly** and not **explicitly** (which is the nature of notes measuring three or six parts of time), a problem arises. For as we said, notes that measure three or six parts *explicitly* also measure twelve or more *implicitly*. 

Therefore, in the notation of such shapes, to show how and which notes contain certain parts of the twelve "explicit" parts, and which do so "implicitly," a certain **sign** indicating that these notes have distinct identities must necessarily be 
->added<- <note>original: "appositum" or "apponendum"; the catchword "appo-" indicates the text continues with the addition of a stem or "tail" to the note to change its value.</note>

<summary>Marchetto explains that while different numbers of notes (3, 6, or 12) can fill the same amount of musical time, the smaller groups "implicitly" contain the values of the larger groups. He concludes that simple note shapes aren't enough to distinguish these complex rhythms, requiring the addition of special signs like tails.</summary>

And such a sign in these [semibreves] we apply, saying that a **semibreve** <term>semibrevis; in this period, the diamond-shaped note that was the primary unit for subdivision</term> note—whether it is one of four, or of five, or of many—which has an **upward stem** <note>original: "cauda in sursum"</note> positioned directly upon it, contains only the twelfth part of the time **explicitly** <note>original: "expressive"; the note represents exactly one unit of the twelve-fold division</note>, as seen here:

-> 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 𝄔 <-
<note>The original manuscript contains a musical staff with eleven or twelve diamond-shaped semibreves, each with a thin vertical line (stem) pointing upwards.</note>

And when placed with other notes that remain in their natural form, since such notes pertain to the **six-fold division** <term>senaria divisio; a division of the beat into six equal units</term> regarding their meaning (though perhaps not regarding their number), we therefore say that a note with the aforementioned upward stem represents a twelfth part of the time. The remaining notes without that stem will represent the other parts in the manner to be declared below, **implicitly** <note>original: "inclusive"; the note's value contains or "includes" several of the smaller twelve-fold units</note> rather than explicitly. 

And because this was done by notes not pertaining to the **three-fold** <note>original: "ternariam"</note> or six-fold division, it is not necessary—even if there are more than three or six notes joined to some figures with an upward stem—for them to be shaped differently than notes measuring a third or sixth part of the time implicitly; unless, through **art** <note>meaning musical artifice or technique</note>, you wish one to exceed another in value against the order of nature. In that case, the sign of "art" must be placed on the exceeding note, which is a **downward stem** <note>original: "cauda in deorsum"</note>, as demonstrated above.

But someone might say: "Is it merely according to your fantasies and your own whims that you say, for some reason, that a note which must measure only a twelfth part of the time must have an upward stem? Could it not

<column-break/>

also have the stem on its side, or in some other way, just as you might have wished?" 

We say: No. We say and propose this only because we are compelled by **reason** <note>original: "ratio"; Marchetto emphasizes that music theory is a logical science, not a matter of personal taste</note> itself, and as those who use only reason in such a science; otherwise, we would be handing down no science at all. And our reason is this: just as it was determined above in the treatise on stems, an upward stem always suggests **imperfection** <note>original: "imperfectionem"; in medieval theory, "perfect" things were whole or divided by three, while "imperfect" things were lesser or subdivided</note> in a note. 

Now, it is more "imperfect" to measure only one out of twelve parts of time **individually** <note>original: "exclusive"; meaning the note stands alone as a single tiny unit</note> than to measure several parts **combined** <note>original: "inclusive"</note>. Therefore, a sign ought reasonably to be added to notes measuring so imperfectly, so they might be known as distinct in essence from the others which measure several parts of time combined. And such a sign reasonably had to be an upward stem, because that sign alone signifies imperfection.

Now, therefore, it remains to see how, and with which notes, and in what quantity a note having an upward stem (indicating it contains only the twelfth part) may be joined to other semibreve notes—whether many or few—and first, why this is so.

Therefore, do we say that such a stem pointing upward will contain the twelfth part of the time, while the remaining note—because it is at the end—contains the other eleven parts of time inclusive? We answer: no. Because a **semibreve** <term>semibrevis; the primary unit of subdivision</term> note cannot contain more parts of the time, inclusive, than it does in a **three-fold division** <note>original: "ternaria divisione"; the basic grouping of notes into threes</note>, whether it be the last note by way of nature, or the first note by way of art. For by no reasoning can a note—whether by nature or by art—contain more than two parts of the time itself in a three-fold division, which equals **eight parts** in a twelve-fold division of time **exclusive** <note>meaning the note itself cannot represent more than 8/12 of the total beat</note>. We cannot, therefore, attribute eleven, ten, or nine parts of time to another note inclusive, because this would exceed both art and nature; we can only attribute eight at most. Thus, the question is answered.

Secondly, it is asked: can one note measuring a twelfth part of time, when added to two natural notes through art or nature, measure a twelfth part of time; as here by nature:

We say that it can. For two natural notes fall under the three-fold division of time, each of which will contain one principal part of the three parts of time; and if this note becomes the final one among natural notes, it will contain double, because it is the end. If, however, a natural note is at the beginning, it will contain double through art. This is to say it contains four of the parts of time naturally, and eight if it is the end or the beginning through art. And understand this: that the note at the beginning is the one stemmed downwards. For none of the middle notes can be stemmed downwards, neither by the way of art nor the **way of nature** <term>via naturæ; the inherent, logical properties of the notes</term>; because, on account of the note preceding or following it, it would lose at least one part of time from its nature in the proportion, which we cannot supply even by way of art.

Wherefore, for the clarity of what precedes and follows, it must be noted that it cannot be brought about through art that any note contains more parts of time than the **end note** itself does. This is because art would then exceed nature, which is impossible; rather, art imitates nature as much as it can, as has been said. Nor can art make any note contain more or fewer parts of time than are required to create the **perfection of the proportion** <note>The mathematical balance required for a complete musical measure</note>, along with the notes joined to it, because art exists solely to find the methods of making proportion measurable—for this purpose was art established. And because in the present treatise on these **semibreves** <note>The primary unit of time being discussed</note> we proceed by a more perfect division, which begins from

three and proceeds to six, and finally to **twelve parts of time** to be measured: from this it follows, as concluded, that every note that is in no way stemmed holds four or eight parts if it is the end (in regard to **three-fold division** <note>original: "divisionem ternariam"</note>), or two or four parts if it is the end (in regard to **six-fold division** <note>original: "divisionem senariam"</note>). It can contain neither more nor fewer than twelve parts of time inclusively. 

Hence, no note joined with **upward stems** <note>original: "caudis in sursum"; these are minims</note> can be made, neither by art nor by nature, to contain five or six parts beyond eight parts of time. This is because such numbers, primarily and principally, do not fall into either three-fold or two-fold division, neither directly nor indirectly. Instead, they are composed of even and odd numbers, falling only indirectly and in a mixed fashion into the divisions; we say this regarding the numbers five, six, ten, and eleven. 

As for the number **nine**, even if it falls into a three-fold division (in the manner described below), no semibreve—neither by the way of art nor nature—can be said to contain nine parts of time. Such a note would not fit in the three-fold division because it would exceed it, nor in the two-fold division because it would fall short of it. It is necessary, therefore, that every unstemmed note joined to upward-stemmed notes be made, by way of art or nature, to consist of two, three, four, or eight parts of time. If this cannot be achieved by increasing or diminishing the value, such a note must be joined with others for the reason stated above.

### *How the aforementioned semibreves are to be named with their proper names.*

Now, however, we must see how the **semibreves** belonging to the said division are named with their own proper names. It must be known that certain semibreves ought to be called **major** <term>maiores; "greater" notes</term>, some **minor** <term>minores; "lesser" notes</term>, and some **minimal** <term>minimæ; the smallest possible subdivisions</term>. Furthermore, the major notes must be distinguished, because some are called major by the **way of art** <term>via artis; rhythmic value determined by musical rules and context</term>, and others by the **way of nature** <term>via naturæ; rhythmic value determined by the inherent perfection of the number three</term>.

By the way of nature, notes cannot be called major unless they contain one of the three parts of a unit of time. The reason for this is that a note should be called "major" when it naturally contains more of the time than it could ever naturally contain otherwise. But since a unit of time is divided by its first, principal, and more perfect division into three main parts, there must be three notes that naturally correspond to those three parts. Therefore, no single note belonging to this division can ever contain more than one of those three parts of time. Thus, a semibreve should be called "major" by the way of nature when it contains one of those three parts.

On the other hand, a semibreve is called "major" by the **way of art** when it contains two out of the three parts of a unit of time. Indeed, it could never contain two-thirds of the time unless it were through the way of art. Art accomplishes this in two ways: either by reason of its position or location—as when we take a note which naturally contains one-third of the time and place it at the end of another; because it is the end, and by reason of its location and the art of the one placing it at the end...

at the end another part is attributed to it, and thus through the technique of art such a note is made a **major semibreve**; just as by adding a downward **stem** <term>caudando; the act of adding a vertical stroke or "tail" to a note</term> to the note preceding it, it is then said to contain two parts out of three of the beat through the technique of art.

Therefore, notes with downward stems and final notes that contain two out of three parts of the beat—since this occurs only through the nature of the art—should be called **major semibreves** <term>maior semibrevis; a longer semibreve, typically worth two-thirds of a "perfection" or full beat</term>, and it is reasonable for them to be named this way both by way of art and by way of nature. And although **Master Franco** <note>Franco of Cologne, a highly influential 13th-century music theorist whose work Marchetto is refining</note> considered these things naturally in the treatise he wrote, many things that can be done in music cannot be fully captured in writing by way of natural logic alone. For this reason, he calls such semibreves "artificial," a point with which we agree, saying they are "major" only by way of art. He calls the others "minor," which we say is true if they are compared in value to the artificial ones. However, if we proceed by the way of nature, we then call those "major" because they contain more of the time being measured than they could ever naturally contain—namely, one out of the three parts of the measured time.

Those notes that belong to the **sixfold division** <term>senaria; a division of the beat into six equal parts</term> should be called "minor," because they contain less time in value—specifically, only one of the six parts of the measured time. These are further distinguished because sometimes they should be called "imperfect minor," for instance when one contains only one of the six parts of time; but when it is joined to another, such as one with an upward

<column-break/>

**stem**, then it expresses one and a half of the six parts of time in value. This is called a "perfect minor" because it contains more "perfection" <note>In medieval theory, "perfection" refers to the completeness of the ternary (three-fold) structure</note> than before. It can also, and perhaps better, be said that the note containing only one of the six parts is "naturally minor," while the one that contains one and a half parts when joined to another is called "minor by art." For this does not happen except through art—for instance, if the note joined to it is given an upward stem—so that there is a proportion in this: just as notes that are "major by art" contain more than those "major by nature," for art always adds something above nature. The remaining notes belonging to the **twelvefold division** <term>duodenaria; the division of the beat into twelve parts</term> are called **minims** <term>minimae; the "smallest" note values</term>.

<meta>This page continues Marchetto of Padua's exploration of "perfect time"—the fundamental unit of musical rhythm in the 14th century. # THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

-> Concerning the first point, it is first asked why it seems that in the proposed work we do not proceed in a uniform manner. <-

For if **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a primary unit of musical measurement divided into three equal parts, often associated with the Holy Trinity</term>, as was proven above, is divided by its primary and principal division and perfection into three parts, it would seem that those first three parts, by a primary and more perfect division, should be divided into another three, and not into two first, as we have divided them. See the immediately preceding chapter. Either [the ternary division] should have been placed before the others, or it should have necessarily belonged to the binary division; and from this, it seems that the order here was pre-established and not necessarily changed. As has been said, perfect time itself is divided into three parts by a primary and more perfect division for the reason alleged at the beginning of the preceding chapter. We ought to treat this division in the manner in which those three parts are themselves divisible, beginning from the first and lower mode and proceeding to the last, just as we begin to count from one and proceed to the final number. 

And just as when we wish to see in what ways unity itself is multipliable, we must first, in the process of knowing, say "two," and afterward "three"; so too, wishing to multiply any of these parts of time, we must first say "two," and afterward "three." Therefore, the first chapter ought to have been placed first, in which those first three parts are divided into two, and those two into another two; and afterward, this chapter should follow, in which those first three parts are divided into three, and those three into others. To the argument to the contrary, we say that when time is divided into three parts, and those [three] parts are afterward divided into two, one proceeds from the perfect to the

<column-break/>

imperfect. For this reason, it is said there that this **binary division** <term>divisio binaria; dividing a note or time unit into two equal parts</term> belongs to **imperfect time** <term>tempus imperfectum; a measurement of time based on the number two, considered less "complete" than three</term>. However, when those three parts are divided into another three, then one proceeds from the imperfect to the perfect—namely, so that all the modes may be seen by which those first parts are divisible. Hence, it is necessary for us first to divide into two, and secondly into three; and thus the proposition is clear.

Secondly, it is asked if those first three parts of perfect time are divisible into four, or into five, or into more? We say they are not; but just as all numbers, both even and odd, are reduced to two and three <note>original: "ad duo & tria"</note>, so all divisions made from them are reduced to the binary and **ternary division** <term>divisio ternaria; dividing a note or time unit into three equal parts</term> of the parts themselves. For if we divide them into four, then we divide them into twice two; if into five, into three and two, and so on for the rest.

Then it is asked if anything that pertains to all the divisions of the three parts of perfect time, or to any one of them, can be a "middle ground" between the ternary division and the binary division of perfect time itself? Or, what is more, can there be a middle ground between perfect and imperfect time? We say no; and the reason is as follows: that which falls inclusively under one of two opposites can never be a middle ground between those opposites. For example: **corporeal** <term>corporeum; having a physical body</term> and **incorporeal** <term>incorporeum; lacking a physical body, like a spirit or mathematical concept</term> are opposites. Therefore, everything included in the incorporeal is necessarily opposed to the corporeal, and can never be a middle ground between the two. 

Therefore, let a figure be given.

It is therefore clear that however those three parts of **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum; a rhythmic unit divided into three equal parts</term> are divided, no division of those parts or of the perfect time itself can ever be a "middle" between perfect and imperfect time, since all such divisions are included under perfect time. For this reason, the error of those who say that eight or six—or briefly, any number taken in a **semibreve** <term>the diamond-shaped note that was the basic unit of division in 14th-century music</term>—becomes a middle measure between perfect and imperfect time is obvious. For every measure and every number is necessarily included under one of these opposites: namely, under perfect time or imperfect time. Because they err in understanding the nature of perfect and imperfect time and the division of their parts, they also err by placing a "middle" between them.

Regarding the second point, it must be known that by a secondary division, imperfect time—already divided into three parts—is divided a second time into another three, and those three into another three, and so on; and this division is necessary. For three signifies more than two, nor is it included

<column-break/>

within them. Therefore, once the parts of perfect time have been divided into two, and those into another two <note>this refers to the binary or "imperfect" division</note>, in order to know perfectly in what principal ways they are divisible, it was necessary to establish their division into three parts, which make nine <note>3 x 3 = 9, known as the *novenaria* division</note>, and so forth. We must see, then, how perfect time is measured by them.

### *Concerning four semibreves in the novenary division.*

If, therefore, four semibreves are placed, how will the nine parts of the time be measured by them, as seen here?

We say that the first, or one of them (except the last), will contain one part out of the nine units of time. Because the first is then more "imperfect" than the others in value, it must be drawn with a sign of imperfection—namely, with a **tail pointing upwards** <term>cauda in sursum; an upward stem used in Italian notation to indicate the smallest note value, the "minima"</term>. Then, the note immediately joined to it, either before or after, will contain two of the nine parts of time, while the remaining two stay in their "natural" state—that is, each containing three parts of the nine in value <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 9</note>.

Likewise, it is asked: what if there are five? We say that two will have upward tails, not immediately next to each other, but it is necessary for some of the others to come between them. ### *Regarding the names of these semibreves.*

Next, it is asked: what are they called? We say that the first three notes that are divided <note>the three primary parts of a perfect beat</note> are named as before. For it is these that are divided into nine. These nine are called "minor by nature" <term>minores per naturam</term> if they contain one part out of nine. If, however, they contain two parts out of nine, they are called "minor by art" <term>minores per artem</term>; for "art" <note>referring to the skill or system of musical notation</note>, by proportioning them to one another, makes them contain exactly two parts of the nine-fold beat.

The reason for this is that logic is its very foundation. Therefore, this nine-fold division is reducible to that twelve-fold one, and this most clearly demonstrates the nature of singing nine semibreves <term>semibreves; the shortest standard note value in this system</term> at once. But afterward, it is asked: can nine, eleven, or more or fewer notes be fixed <term>taxari; to set a formal limit or tax</term> as a "perfect whole" fully measuring the time? We say no, although we can provide so few notes that it is self-evident more could be made, and we can provide so many that it is obvious they cannot be uttered. But to fix a number either below or above which semibreves measuring the whole nature of "perfect time" <term>tempus perfectum; a primary unit of musical time, traditionally divided into three parts to symbolize the Trinity</term> cannot be determined, is entirely impossible, since this depends upon the agility of the voice. The argument can be formed thus: that which is in itself entirely formal and probable is not distinguished by anything material, because it would then not be simply separated from matter. But music is a certain science and a consideration of the measure of the perfect time belonging to it; it exists in the intellect, and the intellect is separated from matter, as is consequently the science and whatever parts belong to it. If,

<column-break/>

therefore, a chest—due to the stiffness of the vocal organ <term>organi; referring here to the physical physiological apparatus of the voice (throat and lungs)</term>—can only form three semibreves, they ought not to be limited to that number, because a "Martin" might be able to form nine, and a "John" eleven <note>original: "Martinus... Ioannes"; standard placeholder names used in medieval logical examples, similar to "John Doe."</note>. Thus, one person forms fewer and another perhaps more, so that it is entirely impossible to fix a limit for men. Only God and the Angels, who know the nature of human organs, could say who possesses an organ more suited for such semibreves, and how many semibreves they could produce corresponding to the measure of perfect time. It is ridiculous and entirely vain to say that "exactly this many" semibreves can be made together to measure a perfect time; rather, it should be said that as many semibreves can be made for a perfect time as the human voice is able to produce, provided the proper measure of that perfect time is observed.

> *Here ends the first book on the accidents and essentials of measured music. Here begins the second book, concerning imperfect time.*

Since the study of opposites is one and the same <note>A common medieval scholarly maxim derived from Aristotle: to understand one thing, you must understand its opposite.</note>, having seen our treatment of "perfect time" in measured music, we must likewise look at "imperfect time." In looking at this, we shall proceed in this order: first, we will treat it by itself and absolutely, to perceive its essence; second, we will treat it through its application to notes according to its total multiplication; and third, we will treat it by applying it to notes according to its partiality and division.

<meta>This page continues Marchetto of Padua's treatise on musical time. Having previously established the nature of "perfect" (triple) time, he now moves to define "imperfect" (duple) time by contrasting it with the completeness of the perfect beat.</meta>

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

Measured musical **imperfect time** <term>tempus imperfectum; a musical meter based on groupings of two, considered "imperfect" because it lacks the "trinity" of triple time</term> is that which is the minimum **not** in the fullness of the voice, but in its semi-fullness; and we prove this definition as follows. For it is certain that just as the "perfect" is that which lacks nothing, so the "imperfect" is that which lacks something. But it is certain, by the definition of perfect time proved above, that perfect time is that which is the minimum in the integral fullness of the voice, in the manner declared there. It follows, therefore, that since imperfect time falls short of the perfect, it must not exist in that integral fullness of the voice.

But someone might say: you ought not to take the deficiency of imperfect time relative to the perfect from the "fullness of the voice," but rather from the "minority of time" <note>original: "minoritate temporis"; meaning that imperfect time is simply shorter in duration than perfect time</note>. Therefore, you should say that both times—the perfect as well as the imperfect—exist in the fullness of the voice, but that very fullness of the voice occurs in a shorter span of time when it happens in imperfect time than when it happens in perfect time. Thus, according to those people, that "minimum" which occurs in the fullness of the voice is imperfect time, not perfect. But to this we respond: to be in the fullness of the voice and to be the "minimum" <note>Marchetto uses "minimum" to mean the fundamental, indivisible unit of measurement</note> is, of necessity, musical perfect time. This is because musical perfect time is the primary measure of all things; for this reason, the measure of imperfect time is taken in relation to the perfect by subtracting a part from it, as will be said shortly. Since, therefore, the minimum in every genus is the measure of the others (as was said above), it is concluded that the minimum time is always perfect of itself, provided it occurs in the fullness of the voice. We immediately subtract from the quantity

<column-break/>

of perfect time and thereby constitute the imperfect. Thus, it is clear that defining time by the fullness of the voice is the same as defining it by its essential "majority" or "minority" <note>the relative "greater" or "lesser" quality of the sound's duration</note>. Therefore, the aforesaid definition stands: namely, that imperfect time is that which is the minimum **not** in the fullness of the voice, but in its incompleteness. And this concludes the first point.

->*How are perfect and imperfect time essentially opposed?*<-

Furthermore, perfect and imperfect time are essentially opposed in themselves and absolutely, even without respect to any division or multiplication of them, as is quite clear from the definition declared above. But we also prove this same thing. For it is certain that the "perfect" and the "imperfect" are not totally the same; because if they were totally the same, then by essence imperfect time could be called perfect, and vice versa, and therefore they would (not) differ by essence. To differ by essence is to say, in reality, that one thing does not become another. But then they are not opposed "privatively" <note>a philosophical term meaning one is simply the absence of the other, like darkness is the absence of light</note>, because in reality one has something that the other does not have. And then it also follows that they are not "contradictories," because both cannot be verified of the same thing at one and the same time; for no time can exist that could essentially be both perfect and imperfect in reality at once. And if it is said that there will be some given time that can be perfect and imperfect for different reasons, we say: either some real things correspond to these reasons, or nothing does. If nothing, then it is nothing to you; if something, then it is one thing...

<meta>catchword: will be (erit)</meta>

<summary>Marchetto defines imperfect (duple) time as a deficiency or subtraction from the "fullness" of perfect (triple) time. He argues that the two are essentially different and mutually exclusive categories of musical measurement.</summary>

MARCHETTO OF PADUA

...would be two things, which is impossible. It is therefore impossible that any musical time could be both perfect and imperfect in reality and essence, as some imagine, for this would involve a manifest contradiction; it would be like saying that someone was a human and not a human. And this concludes the second point.

### By how much does imperfect time fall short of the perfect?

Imperfect time falls short of the perfect by at least a third of its value, which we prove as follows. It is certain that imperfect time would not be as great in quantity as the perfect, for then it would not be "imperfect." Therefore, it must fall short of it by some quantity. Furthermore, it cannot fall short by less than one part; for if you say it falls short by "half," that half will itself be one part, even if it cannot be half of another part. Since the primary and principal parts of perfect time are three—for as established above, it is divided by a triple division as its first and principal state—it follows that if imperfect time falls short of the perfect, it cannot do so by less than the aforementioned third part of that time. It remains, therefore, that imperfect time, of itself and essentially, contains only two parts of the quantity of perfect time.

### On the application of imperfect time to notes, namely its totality and multiplication.

Imperfect time, according to its own nature and according to its totality and its multiplication, is applied to notes in every way just as the 

<column-break/>

perfect is. In the same manner, notes of three beats, two beats, and one beat are found when speaking of imperfect time just as with the perfect, and they are shaped in the same way. All "accidents" <term>accidentia; in medieval music theory, these are the properties or features of a note, such as its shape, stems, or surrounding dots</term> regarding rests, tails <term>caudae; the vertical stems attached to note heads</term>, dots, and all other accidental features are treated in a song of imperfect time just as they are in perfect time. 

The reason for this is that there can never be a material science <term>scientia materialis; knowledge based on the physical properties of things</term>, nor even sensory perception, of imperfect things except by comparison to the perfect. We can never know through the intellect or the senses that something is imperfect unless we first know what it would be if it were perfect. Thus, science—insofar as it concerns things that fall under the intellect or the senses—is always about perfect things. 

Music, therefore, regarding both its notes and its accidents, is always about perfect time first and principally. Music becomes a science of imperfect time only through a subtraction made by the intellect of a part—specifically, a part of perfect time. If imperfect time were to have its own unique notes and its own unique accidents that differed from the notes and accidents of perfect time, it would follow that there could be a science of imperfect things, and principally a sensory knowledge of them, without any reference to the perfect. This is impossible according to both the intellect and the senses, as was stated above.

And if it is said: "Very well, I shall have respect for the perfect by comparing the notes and accidents of imperfect time to the notes and accidents of perfect time," we say that this would be in vain, since...

<summary>Marchetto argues that imperfect (duple) time is essentially perfect (triple) time with one-third removed. He explains that music uses the same notation for both because "perfection" is the only standard by which the mind can measure anything.</summary>

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

...through such a comparison, it could satisfy only in the notes and properties <note>original: "accidentibus," referring here to the attributes or characteristics of the notes rather than modern accidentals like sharps or flats</note> of perfect time—namely, by subtracting fullness and consequently quantity from it. Thus, you would be making the notes and properties of imperfect time in vain.

But you will say: how shall anyone know when a song should be in perfect time, and when in imperfect, since according to you there is a complete uniformity in both the notes and their properties? We say that this is to be left solely to the judgment <note>original: "arbitrio"</note> of the author who perfectly understands the science of music. But so that it may be known when the author's will is that it be sung in imperfect time and when in perfect, we say that this sign <note>Marchetto is referring to early time signatures, which were just beginning to be standardized in the 14th century</note> must be added at the beginning of the song for both imperfect and perfect time when they are joined together, so that through it, the will of the author establishing such diverse songs may be known. For on the part of the figured song and the notes, no natural difference can be found. It is proven that every notated song can

<column-break/>

be noted in both perfect and imperfect time: for such a difference in singing is established only by the author, namely by reason of the harmony <note>original: "harmoniæ," referring to the vertical alignment of voices and the overall musical effect</note>, and not from the nature of the song itself. Therefore, the sign indicating such a difference should be placed solely according to the author's will, nor can a specific reason be found why this sign should be placed rather than that. 

For some use "I" and "II" to indicate perfect and imperfect; others use "3" and "2" to indicate the triple division of time and the double; and others use various signs according to their own pleasure. This is because every song, of itself and naturally, regards perfect time more than imperfect, since the latter implies imperfection and the former perfection. Therefore, a song by its nature is not determined toward imperfect time, but rather toward the perfect by the will of the composer. It happens that for the sake of harmonizing <gloss>original: "monizandi" (to harmonize)</gloss>, time may regard imperfect time, having set aside the perfect: and therefore it is necessary to note that the composer himself places a sign, indicating his intent within his song regarding perfect time.
