### On the secondary division of imperfect time.

The two main parts of <term>imperfect time</term> <note>Time based on a grouping of two beats (binary), as opposed to "perfect time" which is based on three (ternary).</note> are each divided into three, thus creating six notes. These six can further be divided by two, giving us twelve; or they can be divided by three, giving us eighteen. In their method of notation, proportion, and all other properties and names, these notes behave exactly like those of perfect time. From what was just said, a significant error has arisen in <term>measured music</term> <note>Latin: *musica mensurata*. Music where the duration of each note is specifically defined by its shape.</note>. For some have said: "You say I can divide the two parts of imperfect time into three each, resulting in six; but we also arrive at six by dividing the three parts of perfect time into two." Therefore, they concluded that the <term>senaria</term> <note>Latin: *senaria*. A division into six parts.</note> division can be a middle ground between perfect and imperfect time. 

But we say that while any number used in the division of two things can always be found in both, no part of one thing can ever be a "middle" between itself and another thing. It is like two lines: if both are divided into two, three, or four parts, these divisions can be found in each line, yet a part of the first line can never be a middle ground between that line and the second line. Therefore, no matter how many times you divide imperfect time into various parts, even if you happen upon the same number of parts as when you divide perfect time, no part of imperfect time can ever be a middle ground between it and perfect time. Neither can they be combined, since the nature of 

<column-break/>

imperfect time is, by itself and essentially, distinct from the nature of perfect time. This is most evident in the way one sings in perfect and imperfect time. And if it is asked, "Do you say that only the imperfect falls short of the perfect?" we reply that this is true regarding the proportion of perfect to imperfect. In their essences, they are two distinct times, separate and opposite, as is clear from their opposing definitions: one exists with <term>fullness of voice</term> <note>Latin: *plenitudo vocis*. This refers to the rhythmic completeness or "perfection" inherent in triple meter.</note>, while the other exists with <term>semi-fullness of voice</term>.

### On the distance and difference in singing imperfect time between the French and the Italians, and who sings more reasonably.

It must be understood that there is a great difference between the Italians and the French in the way they proportion notes and in their manner of singing in imperfect time. For the Italians always attribute "perfection" to the beginning; thus, the Italians say that the final note contains more perfection because it is the end. But the French say the opposite: namely, that while this may be true of perfect time, in imperfect time the final note is always "more imperfect" because it is the end. Who, then, sings more reasonably? We answer: the French. 

The reason for this is that just as in a perfect thing, its ultimate completion is said to be at its end (for a thing is "perfect" when nothing is missing, not only at the beginning but also at the end); so too in an imperfect thing, its imperfection and deficiency are taken from its end. For a thing is called "imperfect" precisely because something is missing from its end.

<meta>catchword: Therefore (Latin: igitur)</meta>

<summary>Marchetto argues that despite sharing certain numerical subdivisions, perfect and imperfect time are essentially different. He concludes by siding with the French school of notation, arguing that in a duple system, the "imperfection" is logically located at the end of the measure.</summary>

Therefore, if we wish to sing or proportion the voices in the style of <term>imperfect time</term> <note>Binary meter, which Marchetto views as a "lesser" or incomplete version of the three-beat "perfect" time.</note>, we must logically always attribute "imperfection" to the final note, just as we attribute "perfection" to it when singing in <term>perfect time</term>. From this, it is concluded that the French sing better and more rationally in this style than the Italians. However, the Italian method can be defended by saying that they imitate perfection as much as they can, which is reasonable enough—namely, to always lead the imperfect back toward the perfect. Since a proportion of imperfect time can be reduced to the perfection of perfect time (which is the act of bringing the imperfect to the perfect), the Italian way of singing in imperfect time can be reasonably supported. Nonetheless, it must be said that in such a mode, the French sing more correctly and better for the reason stated above.

Since measured music is principally concerned with song that is measured, and having shown, determined, and demonstrated the "accidents" <note>In medieval philosophy, "accidents" are the properties or characteristics of a thing (like the shape of a note) rather than its essential substance.</note> of measured music regarding the simple method of their notation, considering them simply and absolutely: it now remains to see how these notes, with their properties, are connected to one another, so that from them may arise that diverse and rational harmony which is properly called <term>discant</term> <note>A style of polyphony where one or more voices are added to a pre-existing melody.</note>. ## ON THE METHOD OF BINDING NOTES TOGETHER, OR ON LIGATURES, FROM WHICH DISCANT ITSELF ARISES.

### Chapter I.

*On the definition of a ligature, and its distinction.*

A <term>ligature</term> <note>original: *ligatura*; in medieval notation, a single symbol that represents two or more notes "bound" together, indicating they should be sung to a single syllable.</note> is the transformation of simple note-shapes arranged through proper strokes. Some ligatures are ascending and others are descending, as will be shown, and this is according to Master Franco. By this, it is clear that by its essential nature, a ligature exists through ascent and descent; by this word and others, we intend to reject the error of those who bind several notes together on the same space or on the same line.

### *On plicas and ligatures.*

To see in <term>ligatures</term> <note>original: *ligaturis*; notes joined together into a single symbol.</note> which note should be plied and how, we must look at the plicas themselves. It should be known that the plica was invented in song so that through it, similar notes might be uttered more sweetly, which was for the purpose of establishing a more perfect harmony. To recognize it, it was necessary to add some "property" to it, which would express its nature in writing just as in the voice; and therefore it was necessary that such a property be joined to it. And because a stretching out is indicated by <term>tails</term> <note>original: *caudas*; the vertical stems attached to note heads.</note>, naturally one tail was applied more often; and by comparison to it, on the right or left, upward or downward, such a long plica signifies an ascending or descending <term>short</term> <note>original: *brevis*; a note shorter than a long.</note> by giving tails or properties, which signify long or short notes through their upward and downward, right and left directions. For a long plica is shaped upward and downward; and likewise in the shape of plicas, and conversely in ligatures, the short is like this:

while the long is like this:

### *On the error regarding ligatures, and first in general.*

It should be known, however, that several notes on the same line or in the same space

<column-break/>

are bound together <note>original: *colligantur*; referring to the use of ligatures, where multiple notes are joined into a single symbol.</note> by some, both perfectly and imperfectly. We reject this error in this way: It is certain that a <term>ligature</term> <note>original: *ligatura*; a group of notes written as a single connected figure.</note> has "ascent" and "descent" as its essential difference, both in <term>plainchant</term> <note>original: *plana musica*; unmeasured liturgical chant.</note> and in <term>measured music</term> <note>original: *mensurata*; music where every note has a precise rhythmic duration.</note>, which we prove thus. A ligature is the combining of simple shapes; this, moreover, is done solely for the purpose of singing. But there is never "singing" in notes on only one line or in one space. This is proven by the fact that all singing consists of a <term>tone</term> <note>original: *tono*; a whole step or melodic interval.</note> or a part of one; and a tone and its part always consist in the distance of two sounds from each other through <term>arsis</term> and <term>thesis</term> <note>original: *arsim & thesim*; Greek terms used in music theory to describe the "raising" and "lowering" of the voice or the beat.</note> according to all authors of music. A tone, however, cannot exist in ligatures of the same space or the same line, and consequently neither can singing. Therefore, such ligatures would not be made for singing, but rather for howling <note>original: *ululandum*; Marchetto famously mocks those who write repeated notes as ligatures, suggesting they sound like animals wailing rather than humans singing.</note>.

### THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC

->THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC<-

We specifically reject this error against measured music <term>musica mensurata</term> <note>original: *musica mensurata*; music in which every note has a defined, measured duration, as opposed to "plainchant" where durations are more flexible.</note> in the following way. For in the conversion of such notes and in the comparison of them to one another, they <note>meaning Marchetto’s opponents or those using the "erroneous" notation</note> either intend for such figures to be a single geometric body, or several distinct ones. If they are several, then they imply a plurality of the voice with distinction; thus the distinction is figured and separated by lines: for then there will be diverse and distinct notes; and then they ought to be performed with a distinction or "repercussion" <term>repercussio</term> <note>original: *repercussio*; in medieval music, the distinct re-articulation or re-striking of a note on the same pitch, rather than holding one long continuous sound.</note>. If, however, they say that they are a single body, and because it signifies more, it therefore should not be drawn out further? And if they say, specifically, that the voice is drawn out for three times <term>tria tempora</term> <note>original: *tria tempora*; "time" (tempus) was the basic unit of measurement. In "perfect" time, three units made up a complete cycle.</note> for a note that is simply shaped, yet you must draw out the voice further, without repercussion, as much as the value of the note incorporated into it. To this we respond: first, do they wish to create a note with a value beyond three times, or do they stop at a note of three times?

But they assign a value beyond three times to a note, which is impossible, since it is against what was stated in the first book: that a note of three times in measured music is inclusive of everything; for all other values are contained within it, nor can a single note be created that encompasses more which is not already contained within a note of three times. For if a note were made of four times, it would become twice two times, and two is a part of three; and if it were made of five, it would become a three and a two, and the long note <term>longa</term> <note>original: *longa*; one of the primary long-duration notes in medieval notation.</note> will always measure and encompass under itself every note compared with it. Therefore, there cannot be a note incorporated within itself that is not understood as distinct from it, since it is of a different nature than the other.

<column-break/>

And further we argue as follows: it is impossible for the essence of diverse notes to be shown and declared through a single sign or through a single thing, just as we could never demonstrate a horse and a man at the same time through one thing or one sign. Therefore, since in measured music, in the real and scientific concept, any notes are really distinct and diverse and separate in species by their numbers and essences—just as the <term>longa</term>, the <term>brevis</term>, and the <term>semibrevis</term> <note>The three main levels of note duration: the Long, the Breve (short), and the Semibreve (half-short).</note> are distinct by their numbers; and likewise the longas are distinct from each other, as are the breves and semibreves—it is therefore impossible that any one figure, existing as a single and solitary thing, could signify and demonstrate the essences of such notes through one and the same concept.

If, however, it is argued that different concepts will arise because of the different lines used for different notes compared to one another: then they shall be refuted. For they were saying that such a figure was a single body, but now they distinguish that very body through different lines; consequently, there ought to be different bodies there: for bodies and geometric figures are not distinguished except by different lines. If, therefore, they were distinct bodies, a "repercussion" <note>re-striking the note</note> will be necessary. For this reason, they calculate there the addition of space which the incorporated notes make; and by this they say that a longer drawing out of the voice ought to occur; and then we say that by the same reasoning a shorter drawing out should occur, because in that figuration none of those will be a note taken on its own or as only one. Thus, by such geometric logic, a single space enclosed by the same lines cannot reasonably be contained in different bodies at the same time, for every...

<meta>catchword: enim (for)</meta>

<summary>Marchetto argues that musical notes must be visually distinct to represent distinct sounds, using geometric logic to claim that a single shape cannot represent multiple rhythmic values without being physically divided by lines.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Marchetto's argument from page 183, where he critiqued the practice of merging multiple notes into a single physical shape. He maintains that notes must remain distinct to represent distinct durations and articulations, using geometric and philosophical analogies to support his case.</meta>

# MARCHETTO OF PADUA

<columns>2</columns>

For a body has its own proper space enclosed by its own lines. Therefore, the space which you take away from notes by joining them to one another either leaves the specific note not in the form of a note—due to the subtraction made by the line of the second note being included within it—or, if the said space remained in the first note, the second note would then possess the form of a note, and so on for the others. Therefore, to join such things together into one body is not to "form notes," but is rather to add certain angles to a square to create pentagons and hexagons, which have nothing to do with music. If, however, one follows these concepts to which the physical reality does not correspond, they must be considered impossible. For, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in his teaching, the intellect is vain when it seeks the impossible. 

He allows, however, a "double long" <term>duplex longa</term> <note>original: *duplex longa*; a single note shape representing the duration of two long notes.</note> in song, and yet it is called "double," which is to say nothing else than it is conceived as double, but not triple or more. The reason for this is that parts can certainly equal the whole, but they cannot exceed it. Therefore, a double long note is equal in each of its parts; but if it were triple or quadruple, an excess would be created, which is not the case in a double long. Furthermore, two breves <term>breves</term> <note>original: *breves*; literally "shorts," the standard unit of time in this system.</note>, or a breve with another breve, cannot be incorporated into one body; for to place them in one body is to create a single "long," whether imperfect or perfect, which is indicated only by the addition of stems <term>caudae</term> <note>original: *caudae*; the vertical lines or "tails" attached to the square body of a note to indicate its value.</note>, as was shown above. And similarly, comparing semibreves to one another, it would be like establishing one "major semibreve" out of minor ones, which is also done

<column-break/>

by the addition of a stem, as was said above—namely, by way of the art <note>original: *via artis*; according to the formal rules and techniques of musical notation.</note>. If, however, for the sake of a more beautiful harmony, it is not necessary to strike <note>original: *percutere*; to articulate or re-attack a note.</note> multiple notes, we say: if they can be included in one body by way of the art, as has been said, let them be included; but if they should flee even closer together until they touch, they should do so in such a way that the separation of one takes nothing away from the other, for the reason alleged above.

->centered text<-
*Concerning the Modes, and what they are.*

Since every measured song <term>cantus mensuratus</term> consists in some "mode" of singing, let us see what such a mode is, and for what purpose it was invented. Now, "Mode," according to Master Franco <note>Franco of Cologne, a 13th-century theorist who pioneered the system where the shape of a note specifically indicates its rhythm.</note>, is the knowledge of the long <note>original: *semilongis* (likely a scribal error for *longis*)</note> measured by short times. <gloss>(a) This should perhaps be corrected thus: the knowledge of measuring time by means of longs and shorts.</gloss> This is to say nothing else than that Mode is the knowledge of the proportion that arises from short and long notes by measuring time itself through a system of measurement. Furthermore, the modes of descanting <term>discantandi</term> <note>original: *discantandi*; the art of composing or singing a melody (discant) against a fixed plainchant.</note> were invented and diversified solely for this purpose: namely, for multi-faceted harmony in measured music.

->centered text<-
*Concerning the distinction of the modes.*

Mode is distinguished by a primary distinction: namely, the "perfect" and the "imperfect." For wherever perfection is given, imperfection is also designated by subtraction. Likewise, modes are distinguished between those that are "first and principal" and those that are "reducible" to them. For just as all numbers are reduced to two and three, or to even and odd—and these are the principal numbers, while others are reduced—so also the modes of descanting, which are various, are first and principal, both perfect...

<summary>Marchetto argues that note shapes must remain distinct to be musically meaningful, using geometric principles to reject irregular note-groupings. He then introduces the concept of rhythmic "Modes," defining them through the proportions of long and short notes as established by Franco of Cologne.</summary>

# THE ORCHARD OF MEASURED MUSIC
<note>original: "Pomerium Musicæ Mensuratæ"</note>

...as are imperfect, and others are fundamentally reduced to them. Therefore, it is our intention to show the nature of modes <term>modes</term> <note>The rhythmic patterns used in medieval polyphony, roughly equivalent to modern meters but based on specific repeating sequences of long and short notes.</note> both perfect and imperfect, focusing only on the principal ones and leaving aside those that can be reduced to them.

### Why the mode was invented.

A "mode," as said above, is simply the knowledge by which we recognize when a "perfect proportion of time" <term>proportio temporis</term> has been found through the joining or separation of the notes that make up such a proportion. And because time is not multiplied unless it is tripled—for many reasons cited earlier in the first book <note>Medieval theorists associated the number three with the Holy Trinity and thus considered triple time "perfect."</note>—therefore, that single note, or those notes distinct from one another that give three "times" <term>tempora</term> for each of them, are the first and principal ones, as they contain the perfection of the "times." For this reason, discant <term>discantus</term> <note>A style of polyphonic singing where parts move at similar speeds against each other.</note> having such notes as its foundation must be the first.

The first and more perfect mode of discant, therefore, is that which consists of all longs <term>longas</term>, as seen here:
[A musical staff showing six rectangular "long" notes]
And the sole reason for this is that it contains the full perfection of three "times" in every part of itself; it is called "first" in an absolute sense. And because proportion is also found in another way, for instance by placing a breve <term>brevis</term> <note>A "short" note, which in this system is a fraction of the long note.</note> after a long, as here:
[A musical staff showing three pairs of a long note followed by a square short note]
so that the more "perfect" note is at the beginning and the less "perfect" at the end: therefore even still

<column-break/>

this mode is said to be "first" in a secondary sense <note>original: "secundum quid"</note>; for it is the first way of finding a proportion of three "times" using a long and a breve.

In the second mode, however, the less perfect note is placed before and the more perfect after—that is, a breve before and a long after, as here:
[A musical staff showing three pairs of a short note followed by a long note]
And this is the second way of finding the proportion of three "times" between notes; and discant having such notes as its foundation is said to be the "second mode."

The third mode of finding the proportion of three "times" is to place a long first, which signifies three "times," then a breve which is one "time," and another breve which is two "times," as is clear here:
[A musical staff showing two sets consisting of one long note followed by two short notes]

The fourth mode is to place a perfect long after a breve and another breve, as is clear here:
[A musical staff showing two sets consisting of two short notes followed by one long note]

The fifth mode is (a) <margin>Perhaps it should read: "by the omission of the long to find the proportion."</margin> the omission of the long, to find the proportion of triple time <term>ternarii temporis</term> only with breves and semibreves <term>semibreves</term> <note>The "half-short" note, even smaller than a breve.</note>, as is clear here:
[A musical staff showing three sets of one short note followed by two diamond-shaped semibreve notes]

And because the modes for finding such a proportion cannot be further diversified,

...which are not reduced to these; therefore, it must be said that the perfect modes <term>modi</term> <note>In this context, "modes" refer to the rhythmic patterns used in medieval polyphony, similar to modern time signatures but based on specific sequences of long and short notes.</note> of singing discant are only the five primary and principal ones. And let it be known that all of them can be sung in both perfect and imperfect time.

### On the subtraction of the perfect modes, by which the imperfect modes are established.

Since all imperfection arises whenever something is subtracted from perfection, the imperfect modes are subtracted from the first perfect modes (in which the triple perfection of the mode is found). In these imperfect modes, one finds only a binary division; and such a subtraction is made from the perfect modes that while five remain [perfect], only four remain as imperfect.

The first imperfect mode consists of a subtraction from the perfect; for just as that one consists of all perfect longs <term>longae</term> <note>The "Long" was one of the primary note shapes of the period, normally representing a longer duration.</note>, so this one consists of all imperfect longs. The second consists of an imperfect long and two equal breves <term>breves</term> <note>The "Breve" (short) was the basic unit of time.</note>. The third is the opposite. The fourth consists only of breves and semibreves <term>semibreves</term> <note>The "Semibreve" was the smallest division of the breve.</note> measuring a binary proportion. And note that the imperfect modes can be sung in both perfect and imperfect time <term>tempus</term> <note>Tempus refers to the relationship between the breve and the semibreve.</note>. To know which mode should be sung as an imperfect mode, we say that at the beginning of that imperfect mode's song—if there is a long note there, or wherever that long note occurs at the beginning—an upward tail must be added on the left side; and it can be demonstrated thus: as was said above regarding properties, a tail going up-

<column-break/>

-ward on the left side indicates imperfection. Therefore, if such a tail is added to the long note itself, it cannot signify the imperfection of the *time* (because it is a long note); it will therefore signal the imperfection of the *mode*. And this we say finally: take the + as the final sign and the proper way to recognize a song in the imperfect mode. If, however, a song is mixed—for example, consisting of both perfect and imperfect mode—we say the aforementioned sign should be added to every long note of the imperfect mode. This is most proper, because such songs are marked with different colors <note>Medieval scribes often used red ink (coloration) to signal a change from triple to duple rhythm.</note>, as is shown here:

According to these rules, any song can be diversified as it pleases the Musician, thereby suggesting a different harmony. And let these remarks suffice concerning measured music.

I ask all singers: *sing praises to our God, sing praises, for God is King of all the earth, sing praises wisely.* <note>Psalm 47:7. Marchetto emphasizes "sapienter" (wisely/with knowledge) as the foundation for professional singing.</note> The illustrious herald of Christ, David—the most excellent prophet among prophets—commands a conformity between the Church Triumphant (which diligently sings praises and hymns through the triple hierarchy of Angels to our God)

<column-break/>

and the Church Militant <note>The "Church Triumphant" refers to the saints and angels in heaven, while the "Church Militant" refers to Christians living on earth.</note> (which speaks praises to Him seven times a day). In the words proposed, he mandates two things: namely, to sing praises to God, and to do so *wisely*. He implies, therefore, that one must sing with the mind and spirit according to Apostolic teaching, and in a third way, one must sing with reasons and figures <note>Marchetto argues that music is not just "feeling" but is governed by logic (reasons) and specific notation (figures).</note>; he implies this second point when he adds with one voice: *sing praises wisely.*

Therefore, wishing to follow the prophetic path as one of Christ’s singers, I, Marchetto of Padua, after the book I established on the wisdom of <term>plain music</term> <note>referring to his earlier work, the "Lucidarium," which dealt with Gregorian chant or plainsong.</note>, have added the composition of this book of <term>measured music</term> <note>original: "musicæ mensuratæ"; music with a defined rhythmic beat, the ancestor of modern notation.</note>: specifically, what and how things ought to be sung, and how they should be reasonably shaped and written in every part.

In this, I was assisted by that truly religious man, Brother Siphante of Ferrara of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans.</note>; I reported to him *what it is*, and he, through his reasoning, demonstrated *why it is*. Thus, measured music is not written and sung according to whatever one's whim desires, but is accounted as a science among the sciences, with its own proper principles, means, and conclusions. By this, errors are removed, truth is set forward, and everyone desiring to sing to the Lord wisely may be instructed.

Furthermore, we wish for this volume to be called the **Pomerium** <note>The word "Pomerium" means an "Orchard" or "Garden."</note>, because the flowers and fruits of all beautiful music are planted within it to the praise and glory of the Creator: to whom is honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

<meta>This page concludes the technical classification of "Time" (tempus) in Marchetto of Padua’s *Pomerium*. # MARCHETTO OF PADUA’S POMERIUM.

<columns>

Since these do not have species differing beneath them—not in number—which are the <term>diesis</term> <note>original: "diesis"; in Marchetto’s system, a diesis is the smallest melodic interval, specifically one-fifth of a whole tone</note>, just as the "species of man," although it is the most specific, is categorized by its various parts from its genus, as is cited in Divine Scripture. Thus, in music, these most specific categories are predicated as if they were <term>genera</term> <note>The author is using Aristotelian logic to explain that the smallest units of music are the building blocks for the broader categories of rhythm.</note>.

**Standard Perfect Time** <note>original: "Tempus perfectum recte"; perfect time refers to a triple meter, considered "perfect" because of its association with the Holy Trinity</note> is that in which twelve <term>minims</term> <note>original: "minimae"; the smallest note value in this period</note> are written for one "time." If, however, it is sung more slowly, and if more than twelve were placed there, it would be called **more-than-perfect** <note>original: "plusquamperfectum"</note>. In this division, six notes are called "minor semibreves," while three are called "natural majors." Thus, one of two notes can hold two parts of the time, and is called an "artificial major." This method of singing is the **Italian style**, and it is considered more powerful than the French.

Likewise, the same time exists in a quantity where three notes are placed for the time and are called "majors" (as said above), but they are divided into nine minims rather than twelve. This method of singing is the **French style** <note>original: "modus Gallicus"; Marchetto is one of the first theorists to codify the differences between Italian and French rhythmic notation</note>, rather than the Italian. These can be diversified through the art in many other ways, as is evident elsewhere.

Regarding its division, **Perfect Time** can be divided into three, and then into six, and no further, according to the will of the singing style. However, regarding its quantity, it represents half of the superior perfect time that was divided into twelve, and this is called **Minor Perfect Time**. If that time were sung such that seven or eight semibreves could be placed within a single time without completing the twelfth, it would be said to be "greater than the major perfect," just as was said above regarding the "more-than-perfect."

<column-break/>

This **Perfect Time** is so-called regarding its division because it is divided into three and no further, due to its speed. But regarding its own quantity, it represents the third part of the superior perfect time (the one divided into nine) and follows that style of singing; this is called **Minimum Perfect Time**. Furthermore, that time is half of the <term>imperfect time</term> <note>original: "tempus imperfectum"; binary or duple meter, considered "imperfect" compared to triple meter</note> divided into six, which is called the **French Senary** <note>original: "senarius Gallicus"; a grouping of six beats</note> and belongs to the French style in quantity. If this time were sung more slowly, it would be called "greater than the minimum perfect." The three semibreves of this time are called minims; if one of two is "tailed" <note>given a vertical stroke or "cauda" in notation</note>, it holds two parts of the aforementioned time and is called a "minor."

This time is called **Imperfect** because it is divided into two equal parts. This time lacks a third part compared to the superior perfect time divided into twelve. In this time, eight minims are written; four are called "minors," and two are called "natural majors." These can be diversified through the art in many other ways, as is evident elsewhere.

This time, called **Standard Imperfect Time**, can also be sung more quickly, and then it is called **Minor Imperfect Time**; if sung more slowly, it is called **Greater than Standard Imperfect**. This imperfect time lacks a third part compared to the perfect time divided into nine. It is first divided into two equal semibreves, which we call "natural majors," and those two are later divided into six semibreves, which are called minims.

*Here end the brief rubrics of Master Marchetto of Padua, Musician. Thanks be to God.*

# JOHANNES DE MURIS’S TREATISE ON MUSIC.

## EDITORIAL PREFACE.

*In this section, we present various musical short works of this most celebrated author, gathered from different manuscripts. The first is the* **Compendium of Master Johannes de Muris**, *composed in both prose and verse* <note>original: "soluta & ligata oratione"; literally "unbound and bound speech," a standard way to describe prose and poetry</note> *from a* **Parisian Manuscript**, *recently sent to us from* **Paris**. *To this is subjoined in that same source* **On the numbers which contain musical consonances, according to Ptolemy of Paris**, *and another anonymous treatise on proportions, apparently written after the death of* **Johannes**.

*Following this from the same manuscript is his* **Theoretical Music**, *which we also found in two manuscripts from the* **Imperial Library of Vienna**, *specifically Philosophy 294 and 113. It is also found in a* **Bern** *manuscript, where it is titled* **The Speculative Music of Johannes de Muris**, *organized and corrected with great labor and diligence by* **Conrad of Nuremberg** <note>original: "Conrado Norico"</note>, *a Master of the Liberal Arts at the Academy of* **Leipzig**; *it had been obscured for a long time. In the first of the* **Vienna** *manuscripts, the following is noted at the end of this musical work:*

> The end of the music, corroborated and confirmed by Conrad of Nuremberg, Master of the Academy of the Liberal Arts of Leipzig: praise be to Him who can lead us back to the Holy of Holies. In the year of grace 1503, with the sun entering the 20th degree of Aquarius, read by the same in the aforementioned school.

*There is another version, noted in Codex 113 (Philosophy) of the Vienna Library as* **The Music of Johannes de Muris**, *which is called* **"the music of the Parisian peasants who do not know how to sing and are silent in the churches of God"** <note>original: "musica rusticorum Parisiensium cantum nescientium in ecclesiis Dei silentium"; this likely refers to a simplified or basic primer on music theory</note>. *In the* **Parisian** *manuscript, only these words are noted at the end of the "Theoretical Music" which we are publishing:*

> Here ends the speculative music according to Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the fundamental textbook for medieval music theory</note>, abbreviated by Master Johannes de Muris. In Paris, at the Sorbonne, in the year of the Lord 1323.

*Where nothing is mentioned of* **Conrad of Nuremberg**, *who lived nearly two centuries later; and yet the* **Parisian** *manuscript agrees almost word for word with the* **Bernese** *one. However, both differ in wording here and there from the* **Vienna** *manuscripts, which do not even always agree with each other. This discrepancy perhaps arose because the music of* **Johannes** *was explained by* **Conrad** *either in writing several times or only orally, and the explanation itself was recorded on paper in different ways by the listeners.*

*Other manuscripts from* **Vienna**, *and also from* **Melk** *in* **Austria**, *exhibit this same music of* **Johannes de Muris** *much shorter than the others, and as if in a summary. From this we conjecture that that version is the genuine and original* **Speculative Music of Johannes de Muris**, *while the more expanded version in the other manuscripts was interpolated and more broadly explained by* **Conrad of Nuremberg**. *Whatever the case, we have decided to place both here: first the shorter version from* **Melk**, *then the longer one from* **Paris**, *with the more notable differences from the other manuscripts noted at the bottom of the pages.*

# THE COMPENDIUM OF MASTER JOHANNES DE MURIS.
## From the Parisian Manuscript, now at St. Blaise.

The just and honorable request of friends is considered a form of compulsion; thus, with this urging me, I have intended to compose, write, and teach a doctrine of music. I do this because in any notable church, some people are easily found who are competently skilled in this art; and if I should presume to say anything trifling about music, it might perhaps be ascribed by them either to my arrogance or to my accustomed rashness. They might ask, whether I am present or absent, how such a thing could be—a question sometimes proposed to the foolish and ambitious: namely, whether they require <term>better bread than wheat</term> <note>A proverbial expression meaning to seek something better than the best possible thing, or to be impossibly fastidious</note> and better drink than wine.

But since I frequently noticed that very many of my associates and students wander gravely from the path—that is, in those things which are the principles of music, namely in the knowledge of <term>intervals</term> <note>The distance in pitch between two sounds</note> which are sung from the equality of sounds, or according to <term>rise and fall</term> <note>original: "arsin & thesin," terms derived from Greek referring to the upward and downward motion of a melody or beat</note>—I felt I must come to the aid

<column-break/>

of their confessed ignorance. I felt it most important to consider how they might sing by knowing "regular" <note>meaning "according to the rules" or "canonical"</note> song, so that through singing they might attain honor among the unskilled, as those who are more advanced.

However, concerning whether music is a <term>liberal art</term> <note>The seven subjects of classical education, divided into the Trivium and Quadrivium; music was part of the mathematical Quadrivium</note> or not, and what it has as its subject, and what the specific <term>property</term> <note>original: "passio"; in logic, a characteristic that necessarily belongs to a subject</note> of that same subject is, and how intervals ought to be founded and established according to the <term>proportions of numbers</term> <note>The mathematical ratios that define musical harmony</note>, and the consistency regarding them, I shall refrain from speaking. For this business is beyond the strength of boys and is in need of greater inquiry. But I will attempt to write how both certain moderns and certain ancients—and especially among these **Odo**, **Guido**, **Solomon**, and **Hermann** <note>Refers to the great medieval authorities: Odo of Cluny, Guido of Arezzo, Elias Salomon, and Hermannus Contractus</note>—have more probably treated these matters and the propositions, while abstaining from the higher questions. Aiming moderately at simpler things, I will nevertheless omit many...

<meta>The catchword "tam" (nevertheless) at the bottom indicates the transition to the next page of the manuscript.</meta>

### *Verse by the Same Author.*

When a friend makes a just request, it is rightly spoken;
Then he asks and urges what an unfair man might show himself to be.
Thus the clamor of wickedness makes my heart cold,
But the love of virtue drives away whatever troubles me.
Perhaps God Himself will help and make me bold.
I speak small things to small people, and this labor will not weigh me down.
What subject music has, toward which its movement <note>original: "passio" — in medieval logic, an attribute or property being studied</note> is carried,
And how it is related to mathematics <note>original: "mathesim" — referring to the Quadrivium: the four mathematical arts of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music</note> as the fourth part.

This is not easy to describe; for it is too high,
Beyond the strength of boys; it would cause a leap <note>A jump in logic or difficulty that is too great for a beginner</note>.
Let us allow those things that are not of our purpose to sleep;
Let us let those fruits that are too high hang where they are;
Nevertheless, let us relate in due interval those things which follow,
And those which precede, and how these things arise.
But when practice <note>original: "practica"</note> accompanies the candle of theory <note>original: "theoricae"</note>,
Without which theory wanders in darkness,
From here it will also be shown why individual things are said to be known,
So that it may happen to go further with voices as with notes.
Be present then, O God, lead my sails to the harbor,
And reveal quickly to me those things of which I may speak well.
Let the pipe of fame not be my reward as I write:
No other earthly thing is demanded by me.
May You be my reward, without whom nothing is proven to exist
Anywhere, that is known to have the appearance of goodness.
Nothing is past to me, and nothing can be future;
In every wave, O God, I choose You as my pilot <note>original: "palinurum" — a reference to Palinurus, the famous navigator from Virgil's Aeneid</note>.

<header>JOHN DE MURIS</header>

### Preface to the Chapters.

Since among all the arts music, more than the others, requires many distinctions so that a reader may more easily find the specific subject they intend to study—for to many, a part is sufficient for the whole—and since those things which will be said later are divided into chapters, it seems expedient that the titles of the chapters be presented now, observing the same order that the chapters

<column-break/>

themselves will be seen to have in their proper places. That music requires many distinctions and signs beyond the other arts, by which error may be turned away, is manifest from this: the more clearly a fault is perceived, the worse it is proven to be. Now, chant, among the other arts, is performed with a great sound <note>original: "clamore magno" — literally a great shout or loud noise; emphasizing that musical mistakes are audible to everyone</note>, and thus a mistake in it is perceived further and faster, and brings greater disgrace.

---

### Chapters or titles of the Chapters.

I. What music is, and by whom it was discovered.
II. For what purpose music is useful.
III. Who first used music in the church, and why.
IV. On the division of music into natural and instrumental, <term>mundane</term> <note>The "music of the spheres," or the mathematical harmony of the universe</note> and human.
V. On human music <note>The internal harmony of the human body and soul</note>.
VI. On the notes of common chant, what they are, and for what they were invented.
VII. On the six voices of the notes <note>The solmization syllables: Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La</note>, and their sufficiency.
VIII. On the palm or the <term>musical hand</term> <note>The Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic device used by medieval singers to find pitches</note>, and its lines and spaces.
IX. Why the hand is the instrument of music rather than another limb.
X. On intervals and their species.
XI. Why there are no more than nine intervals, and why no more than nineteen joints <note>Referring to the nineteen specific pitch locations on the joints of the hand</note>.
XII. On the signs of the intervals as arranged in different ways by different people.
XIII. On the precautions by which a new and unrefined singer may learn chant.
XIV. On the discovery of the <term>tones</term> <note>The musical modes or scales</note> and their number according to the ancients and the moderns.
XV. Which are the final keys and <term>sub-final keys</term> <note>The pitches that end a melody or support the final note</note> of the tones.
XVI. Which are the initial keys of the tones, and how one should ascend and descend, and by how much.
XVII. How <term>plagal</term> chant is distinguished from <term>authentic</term> by distinctive keys <note>Authentic modes have a higher range, while Plagal modes sit lower around the same final note</note>.
XVIII. On the <term>trope</term>, the <term>tenor</term>, and the <term>cauda</term> <note>The "tail" or concluding melisma</note> that are observed in chant.
XIX. How and where the *Gloria* of the tones is begun, and concerning semitones, etc.
XX. How and in how many ways error may occur in chant.
XXI. How a new chant is to be made and diversified.
XXII. Which vices are to be avoided in a new chant.
XXIII. On <term>Polyphony</term> <note>Music with two or more simultaneous melodic lines</note>, and its division.

# CHAPTER I.
## What Music is, and for what purpose it was invented.

Music, according to its intended purpose, is the art of modulating sounds discretely <note>original: "discrete" — meaning sounds that are distinct and measured rather than a continuous, unstructured noise</note>. Regarding this, we must first see where the name comes from and by whom it was invented; afterwards, we must discuss its utility; and then how music is divided, and what comes before and after it. Thus, in honor of the <term>ternary</term> <note>The number three, which medieval scholars viewed as a symbol of perfection and the Holy Trinity</note>, this treatise consists of three principal areas of investigation. The ternary is the first odd number that cannot be divided into two equal parts; it is the first number that has a middle point in which unity exists, which is why it is consecrated by philosophers to the "Upper Beings" <note>original: "Superis" — referring to the gods or the divine realm</note>.

Leaving that mention aside, it should be known that different people currently hold different views regarding this music. Some say that music is named as if it were *moysica*, from *moys*, which is the word for water <note>The author is citing a common medieval etymology connecting music to the sound of water, similar to the naming of Moses</note>, because rainwater—or any other water—while falling upon various materials, now upon roofs, now upon stones, now upon the earth, now upon water, now upon empty vessels, now upon the leaves of trees, is seen to give back diverse sounds. By comparing these to one another, the ancients are said to have discovered music. Others say that music is named after the *musa* <note>The "musa" here refers to a type of bagpipe or simple pipe</note>, an instrument they call the most excellent and perfect among all musical instruments, and that music is named after it through <term>antonomasia</term> <note>A rhetorical device where a title or the name of a famous example is used instead of a general name</note>, as if from the more worthy thing. Others say it comes from the poetic Muses, because of the different modes of writing which they were said to provide to the poets; but music was invented before the era of the poets.

<column-break/>

Because of this, let it be said—and more correctly—that music is named after the *musa*, a very simple instrument which was first invented by the shepherds of flocks near the beginning of the world. This was made from a marsh reed or from the stalk of grain; and the shepherds, in this *musa*, perceived the diversity of tones by means of its different sizes, lengths, and the placement of holes. Etymologically, however, it is well said that music is named as if it were "fortifying the singer by use" <note>original: "muniens usu canentem" — a medieval folk etymology that links the Latin words for "music" and "fortifying"</note>. Concerning this invention of the pipe by shepherds, the poet says (*) > *so that pastoral labor may rejoice from that point.*
And because this was the first musical instrument, music is deservedly named after it.

Moses ascribes the invention of this pipe to Jubal himself, of whom it is said that he was the father of those who sing to the cithara <note>A reference to Genesis 4:21; the cithara is an ancient lyre-like stringed instrument</note>. Others give the first invention of music and ascribe it to Methuselah, while he was digging wells of water; when he heard the many-layered sounds of hammers there, he turned them into the practice of singing. Boethius ascribes it to Pythagoras, who was walking near a blacksmith's shop and heard the multiple sounds of hammers; he noted that they differed in sound, and he set up several hammers unequal in size and different in weight; and thus, having multiplied the differences of sounds, he turned them into the practice of song. Some also ascribe the invention of singing to Amphion of Thebes, and some to Orpheus of Crete. To all of these, it can be appropriately said, along with Aristotle, that the principles and instruments of all arts are found over the course of time.

...these rudiments <note>original: "rudia" — referring back to the rough beginnings of music mentioned on the previous page</note> were few and crude, to which each succeeding author added something new. In this way, just as a river carrying ships is formed from a tiny stream of a mountain spring through the gathering of waters, so it could be that Jubal was the first—as Moses says—from whom both *jubilus* <note>a joyful shout or song</note> and *jubilare* <note>to rejoice</note> are named, and that the other aforementioned 
<column-break/>
subsequent ones added something new. And so it continues to this day, for just as it is said that it is permitted to coin names for new things as they arise, so it can be said of the "new way of singing" <note>original: "novo modo canendi" — likely referring to the *Ars Nova* movement of the 14th century</note> that something is added by the moderns which was not discovered by the ancients; wherefore, as Priscillian testifies, the more recent the thinkers, the more insightful they are.

### *A Poem by the Same Author.*

Let music be called the art that modulates correctly,
And discretely orders sounds; by this name it is rightly called.
The pipe <note>original: "fistula"</note> was once the *musa* <note>a simple rustic flute or bagpipe</note> suited to shepherds,
By its sound, the ear and the mind were both captured.
Let them clearly learn the long, the short, the greater, and the lesser notes <note>These terms refer to specific rhythmic durations in medieval notation: *longa*, *brevis*, *maior*, and *minor*</note>,
The first shepherds heard this gladly,
And frequently joined these concordant sounds together;
Although they may seem discordant, they are fittingly arranged.
Others say this art takes its name from the Muses,
Accustomed to teaching many things to the hearts of poets.
Or perhaps *moys*, which signifies water, is held as its source,
From whose multi-sounding splashing the first new things are taught.
Jubal, Methuselah, and Pythagoras were the teachers,
Orpheus and Amphion were also among the first.
One was the very first; they were not all first at the same time,
But by increasing the original discoveries, they could all be joined.
Thus many today live having performed this service,
Thus the "new letter of the point" <note>original: "nova... littera puncti" — referring to the development of musical notation</note> is drawn out from its origin.
For those singing by practice, because music fortifies its name,
It possesses this; and gives a favorable omen from those who chant.
The name and the authors are made clearly manifest by these sayings,
After which its utility follows respectably.
For the purpose of the art warns the lazy, excites, and approves
The series of the whole of such a small part of the service.
The third part follows, which divides and teaches how to use it,
And who those people are whom the unwise are accustomed to abuse.
Thus the ternary <note>the number three</note> holds this and occupies the whole volume,
Marking the happy divine power with a happy omen.
This first number leaves behind the infamous <note>Even numbers were often considered "infamous" or imperfect in medieval numerology compared to odd numbers</note> numbers before it,
Nor is it devoid of a middle point signifying virtue.

### CHAPTER II.
->*What music is useful for.*<-

Those investigating the utility of music should consider what Horace says concerning a good poet; indeed, commending him, he says:

> He has gained every point, who has mixed the useful with the sweet. <note>original: "Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci" — a famous line from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* suggesting that the best art provides both pleasure and instruction.</note>

Indeed, both are found in music. It is **sweet**, because among all the arts, none delights so quickly or so much. It is **useful**, because its practitioner—who is the musician—is the inventor of new and regular song, its judge, and the corrector of that which is irregular.

From what has already been said, the difference between a musician and a singer is clear to the diligent observer: for every musician is a singer, but not the other way around. For a singer who is a musician is both a theorist <note>original: "theoricus"</note> and a practitioner <note>original: "practicus"</note> in this art. However, a singer who is not a musician should not even be called a practitioner, except by a misuse of the name; for practice is supposed to proceed according to the logic of the preceding theory, as is contained in the introductory primers <note>original: "isagogis" — likely referring to standard introductory textbooks like those of Porphyry or Boethius</note>. To what, therefore, can we compare a singer who is unskilled in the art, if not to a drunk person running toward a destination, or to a blind man wanting to strike a dog? But since we have perceived and known many such singers, we see happening to them what Boethius says of the less advanced in his book *The Consolation of Philosophy*: that they tear the cloak of 

<column-break/>

philosophy, and when they have snatched a small scrap of it for themselves, they boast that the whole garment has yielded to them and that they possess it in its entirety. But returning to our purpose, let us briefly touch upon the utility of music.

Music, therefore, is medicinal and works wonders. Through music, diseases are cured, especially those generated by melancholy and sadness; through music, one is prevented from falling into the ruin of despair and grief. Music comforts travelers, and it disheartens and puts to flight thieves and robbers. Through music, the fearful are emboldened in war, the scattered are recalled, and the conquered are encouraged. We read of Pythagoras that he restored a certain lustful man to self-control through music. For there is a certain kind of song by which lust is driven away, and another by which it is provoked; just as there is also a certain kind that puts those who are awake to sleep, and another that rouses those who are sleeping. Music soothes the angry, makes the sad joyful, and dissipates and dissolves various troubling thoughts. Music also—which is a greater thing—terrifies and puts to flight evil spirits, just as we read in the Book of Kings concerning David the harpist, who drove away the demon from King Saul when he was possessed. And it is no wonder that man, being a rational animal, delights in music, since even herds of four-legged animals, certain birds, and even certain fish seem to be soothed by the delight of music.

### *Metrical Verses on the Same Topic.*

If you seek to know the harvest of this present art,
recognize the truth in the words of Flaccus <note>original: "Flaccum" — referring to the Roman poet Horace (Quintus Horatius Flaccus).</note>:
He who mixes the useful with the sweet shall enjoy praise. <note>original: "Utile qui miscet cum dulci" — a reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*.</note>
The present art of music holds this truth; it is rightly bound to be praised.
It soothes the ears, charms the mind, and its
use is beneficial, for it effectively removes what is worse.
The musician is the judge and inventor of song, and the 
corrector of those ways in the art which have been distorted.
A musician is a singer, but you must not flip this logic 
simply because you take whatever signs are offered to you. <note>A warning against the logical fallacy that all singers are musicians; the true "musician" is the one who understands the underlying theory.</note>
A singer who lacks art <term>Ars</term><note>In this context, "art" refers to the formal, theoretical knowledge of musical principles.</note> should not be praised;
he is deceived, believing he sees the whole when he sees only a part.
The singer is like a drunkard wandering through the village streets,
but the musician knows well what he sings through a thousand instances.
Call the singer who lacks art similar to a blind man;
fortune alone guides both the one and the other as they walk.
He who wishes to know well how much music is worth and its power
can find what he seeks through synecdoche. <note>original: "per synodochen" — a rhetorical figure where a part represents the whole; perhaps suggesting that music's specific effects point to its universal governance.</note>
Music heals the sick and strengthens the healthy;
it cheers the child, the youth, and even the short-lived gray-haired man.
It especially eases and alleviates diseases of the brain
and terrors of the mind; it puts them to flight and makes them lessen.
In this way, Pythagoras cured a debauched man,
when he, through song, caused him to leave behind his alluring and dark vices. <note>Refers to a famous legend where Pythagoras used a specific musical mode to calm a drunk youth who was trying to burn down a house.</note>
There is one kind of song through which lust increases,
and there is another which, by restraining it, knows not how to play.
Music comforts the sad and consoles the traveler;
it makes him climb the mountain, forgetful of the way’s difficulty.
It terrifies thieves and forces robbers to depart;
it dispels cares and sometimes makes them perish entirely.
It aids the timid in war and recalls those who flee;
it pushes forward the brave who seek the palm of victory in battle.
Furthermore, even Bucephalus <note>The famous horse of Alexander the Great.</note> leaps against the enemy at the sound of song;
he prostrates them as if they were unmoving posts.
Even an unclean spirit flees through the mediation of music,
signaling that it is discordant now, just as it was before.
Thus David soothed the demon’s wrath in Saul,
showing the wondrous power of the lyre <term>cithara</term> through song.

### CHAPTER III.

->*Who first used music in the church, and why.*<-

Since so many and such great—indeed, countless—praises of music are to be found, Ignatius <note>Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD), an early Christian martyr who is traditionally credited with introducing antiphonal singing (alternating choirs) to the church.</note> first, and after him the blessed Ambrose, Archbishop of Milan, established that God should be served in the church through song for His greater reverence and honor. Thus, organizing what and how much, and when and in what manner things were to be sung in the church, they commanded that singing in the divine office before the Lord in the holy church should not be done by joking, laughing, or dancing, but humbly and with devotion. This same Ambrose created a specific and specially assigned chant for every single day of the whole year, and he instituted it to be solemnly observed throughout all the churches under his jurisdiction.

Thereafter, Saint Gregory, the Bishop of the Roman See—above whose shoulder Peter the Deacon saw a dove sitting while the same Gregory was writing with foresight for the benefit of the church <note>This refers to the legend that the Holy Spirit, in the form of a dove, dictated the Gregorian chants into the Pope's ear.</note>—composed a chant to be promulgated throughout the whole Roman Church, and first transmitted it to the cathedral churches. However, he did not make it as long-winded <note>original: "prolixum"</note> as Saint Ambrose is said to have made his chant. Some claim this was on account of the exhaustion of his illnesses, for he was always suffering from quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every four days.</note>, and was further afflicted by fainting spells <note>original: "syncopis"</note> and gout. Others say, and perhaps more correctly, that whatever Gregory wrote, both in song and in prose,

<column-break/>

he received its matter, quantity, and quality from the Holy Spirit.

The authority for singing in the church for the sake of devotion is drawn from the singing of the religious ancients in both the New and Old Testaments. We read in Daniel of the three youths singing praise to God in the furnace. We also read in Exodus that after the Hebrews had crossed the sea and seen the Egyptians overwhelmed and submerged in the waters, Miriam, the sister of Moses, along with her brother, sang praises to God in her song, narrating through chant the great works of salvation. Likewise, King David sang with the harp <note>original: "citharando"</note> before the Ark and before the Lord, and he urged others to sing with various musical instruments, saying: *Sing to the Lord a new song* and so forth; and again: *Sing, and exult, and play the psaltery*; and again: *To the Lord with the timbrel and choir, with the psaltery and harp, with well-sounding cymbals, with strings and the organ, with trumpets of metal and the sound of the horn-trumpet.* <note>These are paraphrases of the Psalms, particularly Psalm 98 and Psalm 150.</note> In the New Testament also, after a single angel had announced the birth of Christ to the shepherds, lest the authority of one seem too little, a multitude of angels sang together with him, *Glory to God in the highest* etc. Furthermore, one finds the song of Zechariah, namely the *Benedictus* <note>original: "Benedictus" — "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel."</note>; the song of Mary, the *Magnificat* <note>original: "Magnificat" — "My soul magnifies the Lord."</note>; and the song of Simeon, the *Nunc dimittis* <note>original: "Nunc dimittis" — "Now let your servant depart in peace."</note>, which are called "songs" <note>original: "cantica" — canticles.</note> not without cause. Thus, the manner of singing both reveals the devotion of the singer himself and, if the listener is of good will, stirs up a feeling of devotion within them; for this reason, it is rightly practiced in the church with humility and devotion.

### Verse on the Same Subject.

The great fruit of singing is weighed constantly;
Observing this, both Ignatius and Ambrose
Decreed that God should be celebrated in the church
With song, which should accompany a devoted mind.
Ambrose provided a special office for the day,
With extensive material in song for everyone.
Thereafter, Gregory the Roman Pope followed,
Whom this manner pleased so that man should not stand as if mute,
For it is fitting that the Savior of the world, three and one,
Should receive the threefold gift of our service.
Let the heart desire, let the mouth sound, and let the whole mechanism
Of the body labor toward the Lord, so that he may pray more devotedly.
He who prays by working well with mind, sound, and deeds,
Is deservedly called a musician <note>original: "citharista," literally a harp-player, but used here to mean a true practitioner of sacred music</note> in the temple of the Lord.
The Pope distinguished a new chant, composed in order;
The Holy Spirit taught him this, as it was performed.
For Peter <note>Peter the Deacon, Gregory’s secretary, who claimed to see the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove whispering to the Pope.</note> saw that a beautiful dove sat there,
Which, touching the ears of the Pope, advised him from time to time.
Some attribute the brevity of the chant to illnesses,
Some set down the goodness of the Lord as the cause.
For although it is short, some seem not to know it,
Yet they boast that they are great singers.
It is better that much confusion does not run wild;
I judge that this brevity was hidden by the piety of the Lord.
Fainting <note>original: "syncopis"</note>, gout, and quartan fever commanded silence,
And sometimes did not allow him to sing, even briefly.
It is asked from the past <note>original: "a tergo," literally "from behind" or "from the back"</note> what he had sung before,
By which it is fitting to fill the vacuum that cannot be held.
He took as an example the three singing in the furnace, <note>A reference to Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in the Book of Daniel, who sang a hymn of praise while inside a fiery furnace.</note>
And Moses, when the pursuers perished beneath the waters. <note>The Song of Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea.</note>
King David taught how to serve with every kind of song
Before God; and holding the lyre, he struck it,
Commanding many times to sing; the psalmist repeated
The word of singing, signifying what he called for from then on.
And also, when Christ was born during the time of night,
By the angelic citizens learned in this melody,
The *Gloria* <note>original: "Gloria," the hymn "Glory to God in the highest"</note> was sung and recited to the shepherds,
And through them, it was spoken, written, and delivered to us.

> Song in the church, if it be devout and honorable,
> Both pleases, and the profit from it is immediately great.

### CHAPTER IV.

<margin>**On the division of music into natural, instrumental, worldly, and human.**</margin>

Music is partly <term>natural</term><note>Natural music refers to sounds produced by nature or the cosmos, rather than by human-made tools.</note>, and partly <term>instrumental</term>; natural music is divided into <term>human</term> and <term>worldly</term> <note>original: "mundana," often referred to as the "Music of the Spheres."</note>. Worldly music is created through the variety and concord of sounds caused by the movements of the super-celestial bodies. For as the philosophers testify, it was not possible for such great bodies to move so swiftly and so continuously without sound. Since, therefore, the firmament and the planets have special and different motions, they generate from themselves special and different songs and a certain harmony, which is called <term>worldly music</term>.

Artificial musical instruments are many, and they are divided into three types: for some are said to be <term>stringed</term> <note>original: "chordalia"</note>, some <term>wind</term> <note>original: "foraminalia," literally "having holes."</note>, 

<column-break/>

and some <term>vessel-like</term> <note>original: "vasalia," referring to percussion or instruments made of hollow bodies.</note>. Stringed instruments are those seen to be played by means of metal, gut, or silk strings; such as citterns, vielles and fiddles, psalteries, <term>chori</term> <note>A medieval instrument, possibly a type of stringed crwth or a small bagpipe, though here grouped with strings.</note>, the monochord, the <term>symphonia</term> or <term>organistrum</term> <note>A hurdy-gurdy, a mechanical string instrument turned with a crank.</note>, and others like them. Wind instruments are those whose diversity in sound is created by a diversity of holes; such as the muses <note>A type of bagpipe.</note>, panpipes, the flute, pipes, horns, whistles, trumpets, and the like. Vessel-like instruments are those which lack both holes and strings and are formed in the manner of hollow vessels; such as cymbals, basins, bells, pots, and the like, which emit different sounds according to the diversity of their material and shape. But among all other musical instruments, the instrument of the human voice is the most noble, because it brings forth both sound and words, whereas the others serve sound alone, not the voice, and it is universal.

### CHAPTER V.
### *On Human Music.*

Having spoken of instrumental music, let a return be made to human music, which is the primary focus of this discussion. Since, therefore, music is the <term>discrete modulation of sounds</term><note>original: "modulatio ſonorum diſcreta." Here, "discrete" implies sounds that are distinct, rational, and articulated.</note>, this word "discrete" must be taken in its strict sense. For if it were taken broadly—so that "discrete" meant the same as "distinct," that is, sounds made with a mere distinction between them—then music would also apply to irrational creatures, such as certain birds that distinguish various sounds well enough in their song. 

But if it is taken strictly, "discrete" is the same as "made with discernment" <note>original: "cum diſcretione facta"</note>, and music understood in this way applies only to humans; for among all the animals, the human alone sings with discernment and exercises other actions in the same way. The nightingale, the parrot, the lark, blackbirds, the crane, the swallow, the 

<column-break/>

rooster, and similar creatures are said to "sing," but these express their song only by the impulse or compulsion of nature. The human, however, sings with discernment, joining words to his song in a perfect sequence.

"Song" <note>original: "Cantus," which the author etymologically links to a "sonorous act."</note> is so named as if it were a sonorous act; while "melody" <note>original: "canor"</note> is named as if it were "labor with breath" <note>original: "cum anhelitu labor"</note>. Therefore, the inventors of song and the first teachers observed that the <term>windpipe</term><note>original: "trocheam arteriam," an archaic term for the trachea.</note>, which is the organ of the human voice, could produce a threefold song according to a threefold physical arrangement. For sometimes it is greatly dilated, and emits a low sound; sometimes it is greatly constricted, and returns a very high sound; and sometimes it holds the middle way, and returns a medium sound. And they called this threefold song <term>diatonic</term>, as if referring to the natural property of the tones. They also placed after these a song that is lower than the lowest, because of its softness...

### CHAPTER VI.
*On the little notes of common song: what they are,
and for what purpose they were invented.*

Ancient singers did not only take care to delight greatly in song, but they diligently studied how to teach others to sing. Therefore, they devised certain figures which, assigned to each syllable of the words, would denote the individual impulses of the voices like proper signs; hence they are called **notes** or **little notes** <note>original: "notæ vel notulæ"</note>. And because song proceeds in many forms—now

<column-break/>

evenly, now ascending, now indeed descending—for this reason the aforementioned notes are formed in different shapes and receive various names. For a certain little note is called a <term>punctus</term> <note>A "point" or dot, the simplest form of musical notation.</note>, another a <term>virga</term> <note>Literally a "rod" or "branch," representing a higher note.</note>, another a **greater or lesser clivis** <note>A descending neume.</note>, another a **greater or lesser plica** <note>A "fold" or "pleat," indicating a decorative or passing tone.</note>, another a **greater or lesser pes or pedatus** <note>Literally a "foot," an ascending neume.</note>, another a **greater or lesser quilisma** <note>A "wavering" or "rolling" note, often shown as a jagged line.</note>, and another a **greater or lesser pressus** <note>A "pressure" note, usually indicating a sustained or stressed pitch.</note>. And the *punctus* is formed in the manner of a dot, and it is sometimes joined to a *virga*, sometimes to a *plica*, and sometimes to a *pedatus*.

given, sometimes as a single mark, and sometimes several together, especially when the melody descends. A **Rod** <note>original: "Virga"</note> is a simple note, long in the manner of a rod. The **Clivis** <note>original: "Clivis," a descending neume</note> is named from *cleo*, which means a melody <note>original: "melum"</note>; it is composed of a note and a semi-note, and signifies that the voice must be bent downward. The **Plica** <note>original: "Plica," meaning a fold</note> is named from "folding," and it contains two notes, one higher and the other lower. The **Pressus** <note>original: "Pressus," meaning a pressed note</note> is named from "pressing"; the smaller version contains two notes, while the larger has three, and it must always be performed evenly and quickly. But even through these signs, song is understood imperfectly; no one can learn it by himself through these alone. Instead, it is necessary that the song be heard from another and learned through long practice; and because of this, this kind of singing has taken the name **Usage** <note>original: "usus," referring to practical singing as opposed to theoretical music</note>.

### A Poem on the Same Subject.

Once, singers were so pleased with song,
That they wished to teach their knowledge to their heirs.
It happened, then, that they devised these new figures,
So they could represent the various durations of the voices:
These they called "notes" of the song, from which is named
The "course of singing," which is joined to the vocal part;
**Clives**, **plicas**, the **rod**, **quilismas**, **points**, and **podati**,
Are the names of these; let the **pressi** be joined with them.
The "Foot" <note>referring to the Podatus</note> wishes to rise upward with two notes;
Yet that note which the sharp "liquid" <note>original: "liquescens," a type of note where the sound fades or glides</note> signifies is diminished.
The **clivis** always wishes to descend with two notes,
And its final note marks a shadowed sound.
It precedes a pause, or stands in the mouth of one pausing,
As if it performs the honor of a complete note.
If you take away the **rod**, it is held in the plural number,
For the rest, it is often seen as smaller or larger.
Yet from these, the eyes cannot fully grasp the song,
Unless the ear is present along with the voices of those leading the melody.
And because it grows in this way through such habit,
It is held as **Usage**, not the **Music** <note>the science of music</note> which knows it not.

...the inventors <note>Continuing from the previous page: "the inventors [of music]"</note> studied most diligently with much investigation to obtain this: so that he who does not know music and desires to learn it, proceeding technically according to the rules of music, may learn musical song—that is, the writing of music—without a teacher, and may examine, judge, confirm what is rational, and correct what is incorrect.

Therefore, the first musical teachers invented six syllables: ***ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la***, which are the names of the six notes <note>These six syllables form a "hexachord," the building block of medieval music theory</note>, if they are considered without alternation and mutation. If they are alternated above and below all notes as far as infinity by compelling necessity, they signify and are the names of those notes. By these names, as has been said, the notes are called by the French, English, Germans, Hungarians, Slavs, and Danes, and other Cisalpines <note>original: "Cisalpinis," referring to those living on "this side" of the Alps, usually meaning Northern/Central Europe from the author's perspective</note>. The Italians, however, are said to have other notes and names; whoever wishes to know them should ask the Italians themselves.

The six aforesaid names of the notes are sufficient, not only because of the dignity of the number six <note>original: "senarii"</note>, but also so that excess in the art may be avoided. The dignity of the number six is that it is the first **perfect number** <note>In medieval mathematics, a "perfect number" is one that equals the sum of its divisors (1+2+3=6)</note>, as the mathematicians say; and this is proven, for Moses says in Genesis that God created the heaven and the earth—that is, the four elements—in the space of the first day, and during the five days continuously following He adorned them, and on the seventh day He rested from all the work He had performed. And Moses says: *Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, etc.* <note>original: "igitur perfecti sunt cæli & terra &c."</note> For after it pleased God to perfect the work of the world not in one day, but in several over the span of six days, this happened rightly, since the number six is and is called perfect, so that from this

<column-break/>

He might show His work to be perfect. And because of this, it is rightly added: *and He rested*.

Necessity or opportunity also turns away a plurality of notes, since excess in an art is considered a vice. This is proven thus: since by beginning from ***ut*** one arrives in music—of which more will be said later—as far as ***la***, if one were to ascend further, a **semitone** <term>semitone: the smallest interval used in this musical system, essentially a half-step</term> would be placed, of which more will be said later. But the semitone was already held previously; thus, the same thing would be placed twice uselessly, and that is considered a vice in the art. But perhaps someone will ask: why is the semitone thus located in the middle of the six aforesaid notes, and not at the beginning or the end? To this it must be answered along with the Philosopher <note>A standard medieval reference to Aristotle</note> that **art imitates nature**. In natural things, it is so that soft members are located in the middle and enclosed within, such as the brain in the skull, the intestines and lungs <note>original: "sputalia"</note> in the cavity of the ribs, and marrow in the bone. And since the semitone has a "soft" sound compared to the other notes, it is located in their middle rather than at the extremity.

It may also be asked why those syllables rather than others are the names of the six aforesaid notes—that is, why these letters are placed in the syllables? To this it should be said, according to some, that this happened by chance without reason; I do not consider this to be true. For Persius <note>A Roman satirical poet</note> says that some people, seeking a comfort for their own ignorance, think the positions of the parts of speech are accidental and that the order of the rest cannot be investigated; but to say this is foolish, and po-
