<meta>This page continues the technical justification for the six-syllable hexachord system (ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la), moving from the mathematical perfection of the number six to the phonetic and musical logic behind the specific sounds chosen for the notes.</meta>

# JOHN DE MURIS

<columns>

...can be proven. It should be known, therefore, that since the aforementioned syllables are signs of the voices, and since vowels possess much of the quality of the "voice"—from which they take their name, being called **vowels** <note>original: "vocales"</note>—it is right that all of them are sometimes placed within these syllables. There are six syllables, however, whence it is necessary that the first of the vowels is repeated in the last syllable. These vowels are not arranged in these syllables in the same way as in spelling; for there they are arranged according to the position of the vocal organ <note>Referring to the physical placement of the tongue and mouth in articulation</note>, but here they are arranged according to whether they have more or less sonority, so that a progression is made from a less open sound to a more open one. As has been said, the music is first low (grave), then high (acute), and finally very high (peracute). And so it is clear

<column-break/>

to the inquirer that one vowel is repeated with the sixth syllable rather than any of the others because it has more sonority.
Regarding the consonants, it must be said that "mutes" <note>A category of consonants in classical grammar that cannot form a syllable without a vowel</note> are placed there according to how two of them have more sonority in the syllables, namely **c.** and **s.** <note>The author is likely analyzing the phonetic building blocks of the syllables *sol* and potentially an alternate spelling or specific phonetic theory of the time</note>. They also contain four semivowels, and thus all types of letters are used to signify that the signs are taken generally for all differences of the note in song; thus the number and sufficiency of the said notes are clear. The reason that neighboring vowels are not placed continuously but mixed together is so that the proximity of sounds—which are sung in a nearly similar way—does not introduce a "bad-sounding gap" <note>original: "hiatus cacophaton"; a Greek-derived term for an ugly or unharmonious sound</note> or boredom.

->*Verse on the Same Subject.*<-

The teachers of the art, which is named Music,
Praised the song that is taught with reason:
They rejected mere habit, as if it were often too burdensome,
Saying, *"Because it is so,"* but proving nothing by "therefore."
Immediately a rule removed such error,
And gave a certain and special course for singing.
A four-line staff <note>original: "quadrupla... regula," referring to the standard four-line musical staff of the period</note> was made with fixed spaces,
With certain notes filled with certain reason:
***Ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la***, the six names of the notes,
These notes suffice, through which music is made full.
Nor is it a wonder; the same perfect number is held,
By which the "machine of the world" <note>A common medieval metaphor for the structure and operating principles of the universe</note> is taught to have been made.
That six are sufficient, you can prove by this reason,
If you attempt to continue the note after the last, ***la***.
For as you ascend further, you will repeat what was already placed,
Or you will place that which is smallest, which abounds in the art.
Since a half-step <note><term>semitonus</term>: the smallest interval in the medieval scale, occurring between *mi* and *fa*</note> preceded, and this would follow,
It is therefore better that the preceding sequence be repeated.
The six notes, which placed a half-step in the middle,
If we look closely, were used with good reason;

->That which opens the mouth more, sounds more, and is thus placed:<-

->And the fifth vowel is placed in the fourth seat,<-

### CHAPTER VIII.
**Concerning the palm, and its lines and spaces.**

We have spoken of the six notes, which suffice for the notation of any chant, and how they must be placed upon lines and spaces. However, what and how many the names of these lines and spaces are has not yet been touched upon or expressed. I say "interposed" because below the line which is the lowest of all, and above the highest, no notable space is held. To make this evident, we must first consider that the ancient teachers studied to instruct those who came after them with skillful observation; for they considered that any craftsman can more easily achieve his goal through a well-arranged instrument. Therefore, they devised that the principles of music should be placed upon the inner part of the

<column-break/>

hand, and more skillfully on the left hand than the right—provided that nature, in its shaping, did not err in the hand itself; that is, if the hand does not suffer from a surplus or a lack of fingers. Since there are 19 joints <note>original: "articuli"</note> of the fingers—counting their tips or summits as the same thing—the aforementioned teachers located 19 "seats" of numbers upon them. They assigned one specific seat to each joint, composed of a letter (which is the name of the clef) and a note, or the names of the note or notes which that clef indicates. They designated the first joint as a line, the second as a space, and so on until the end; however, the lines and spaces on the back of a page differ more than those on the hand.

Thus, in the fleshy part or the tip of the thumb, they located a notable seat, that is, the note—

# JOHN OF MURIS

...fitting, they called it *Gamma ut*, or *G ut* <note>The first note of the medieval scale</note>, which is said to be composed of the Greek letter <note>original: "C"; likely referring to the Greek letter Gamma (Γ), which looks like an inverted L or a stylized C in some scripts</note> that is called G among the Latins—which is the key for that joint—and from the name of a certain note called *ut*, which is domestic to that key; it has no other notes. Further along, in the middle <note>original: "gremio"; literally 'the lap' or center-joint</note> of the thumb, they placed *A re*; *A* is the name of the key, and *re* is the note assigned to it, and this key has no other notes. Likewise, at the root of the thumb is placed *B mi*. *B* is the name of the key, and *mi* is the note assigned to it; this seat, or this joint, has no other notes.

Likewise, at the root of the index finger, they placed *C fa, ut*. *C* is the name of the key; *fa* and *ut* are the names of the two notes assigned to that key; *fa* is used in relation to the lower keys, while *ut* is compared to the higher ones. Likewise, at the root of the middle finger, *D sol, re* is located; *D* is the shape and name of the key; *sol* and *re* are the notes assigned to it; *sol* is compared to the lower notes, and *re* to the higher ones. Likewise, at the root of the ring finger <note>original: "medici"; literally 'the medical finger,' so named because it was believed a vein ran directly from this finger to the heart</note> they placed *E la, mi*; *E* is the name of the key, and *la* and *mi* are the notes assigned to it; *la* is compared to the lower notes, and *mi* to the higher ones. Likewise, at the root of the pinky finger—the little finger, which is the same thing—is located *F fa, ut*; *F* is the name of the key, and *fa* and *ut* are the notes assigned to it; *fa* is assigned to the lower, and *ut* to the higher.

Likewise, in the middle joint of the pinky is situated *G sol, re, ut*. *G* is the name of the key; *sol, re*, and *ut* are the names of the notes assigned to it; *sol* is for the lower, *re* for the near-higher, and *ut* is related to the far-higher notes. Likewise, in the fold <note>original: "sinu"; the inner joint</note> of the pinky is placed *a. la, mi, re*,

<column-break/>

*a* is the name of the key; *la, mi, re* are the names of the notes assigned to that key; *la* is assigned to the lower, *mi* to the near-higher, and *re* to the far-higher notes. Likewise, at the pulp or the tip <note>original: "fronte"; literally the 'forehead' or top</note> of the pinky is situated *b fa, ♮ mi*. *b* and *♮* <note>original: "♮"; the square-b or natural sign</note> are the names of the keys, though they are taken in different ways: for *fa* is represented by the "round b" <note>original: "b rotundum"; the flat sign ($\flat$)</note>, and *mi* is represented by the "square b" <note>original: "♮ quadratum"; the natural sign ($\natural$)</note>. Likewise, at the tip of the ring finger is placed *c sol, fa, ut*. *c* is the name of the key; *sol, fa*, and *ut* are the notes assigned to it; *sol* serves the far-lower, *fa* the near-lower, and *ut* the higher notes. Likewise, at the tip of the middle finger, *d la, sol, re* is located; *d* is the name of the key; *la, sol*, and *re* are the names of the notes; *la* is compared to the far-lower, *sol* to the near-lower, and *re* to the higher. Likewise, at the tip of the index finger is placed *e la, mi*. *e* is the name of the key; *la* and *mi* are the names of the notes assigned to the key; *la* is assigned to the lower, *mi* to the higher. Likewise, in the fold of the index finger, *f fa, ut* is located; *f* is the name of the key; *fa* and *ut* are the names of the notes; *fa* is added for the lower, *ut* for the higher. Likewise, in the middle of the index finger, *g sol, re, ut* is imprinted; *g* is the name of the key; *sol, re*, and *ut* are the names of the notes assigned to it; *sol* is assigned to the lower, *re* to the near-higher, and *ut* to the far-higher. Likewise, in the middle of the middle finger is placed *aa. la, mi, re*. *aa* <note>original: "$^\text{a}_\text{a}$"; representing the double-a of the higher octave</note> is the name of the key; *la, mi*, and *re* are the names of the notes; *la* is assigned to the lower, *mi* and *re* to the higher, but with this difference: if they are continuous <note>occurring in direct sequence</note> above the "round b," it will be called *mi* in the said *aa. la, mi, re*; if, however, they are continuous after the "square b," it will be called *re* in the said *aa. la, mi, re*.

# THE SUMMARY OF MUSIC.

Likewise, in the middle <note>original: "gremio"; literally "lap," referring to the middle joint</note> of the ring finger <note>original: "medici"</note> is placed **B fa, ♮ mi**; both **b** and **♮** are the name of a single key, but they are used differently. If it is a "round b" <note>original: "b rotundum"; our modern flat sign ♭</note>, it is called **fa**; if it is a "square ♮" <note>original: "♮ quadratum"; our modern natural ♮ or sharp sign #</note>, it is called **mi** alone. Likewise, in the bend <note>original: "sinu"</note> of the same ring finger, **C sol, fa** is situated; **C** is the name of the key, while **sol** and **fa** are the names of the notes. Both of these are compared to the lower notes; **sol** is placed nearby, and **fa** descends to those placed further away. The last one, **d la, sol**, is rooted in the tip <note>original: "sinu," here referring to the top joint-crease</note> of the ring finger; **d** is the name of the key, and **la** and **sol** are the names of the notes. They are compared to the lower notes differently: **la** to the keys placed far away, while **sol** wants to be joined to those placed nearby.

Among other things, it should be known that the seat or joint itself is said to be "on a line," such as **C, B, D**, etc.; whereas a joint is likewise said to be "in a space," such as **A re, C fa, ut**, and similar ones. A key of any joint is said to be "on a line" because it is the beginning of a line, which maintains the name of that joint all the way to the end, or until it changes. Similarly, a key is said to be "in a space" because it is the sign of a joint and the beginning of a space, which is named after that joint until the end of the space, or until it changes perceptibly. A space is called the surface that designates an even-numbered joint from **C ut** up to <unclear>d</unclear> **la, sol**. From this, it should be seen that above **la, sol** and below **C ut** <unclear>d</unclear>, there is no "notable space" as was said, because a space in music is nothing other than a surface enclosed between two nearby lines, whether actually or

<column-break/>

mentally. I say **mentally** because it sometimes happens that the highest or lowest of the four lines is actually drawn, and another that *could* be drawn, but is not, is understood to be there; and such an interposed space is said to be "notable"—that is, assignable to notes.

It should also be known that the ancients first found **A re** among the keys, and afterwards **B mi**, and so ascending according to the order of letters in the alphabet. However, they later considered that some chants descend even as far as **A re**, such as the antiphon *O Sapientia* <note>A famous "Great O" Antiphon sung in late Advent</note> and similar ones; but there could not be a notable space unless it was enclosed by certain limits. For this reason, they invented **Gamma ut** <note>The Greek letter Γ, marking the bottom of the scale</note>, which shows that repeating a supposed [system] is an error: for anyone who either ignores or does not set a limit to his journey or his labor seems to wander. Furthermore, it should be considered that the keys assigned to the said joints are distinguished by three boundaries. The first boundary contains these keys: **G, A, B, C, D, E, F, G**; and these are called **graves** <note>low or heavy</note> because they use a low and, compared to the others, a blunt sound. The second boundary also contains **a, b, c, d, e, f, g**; and these are called **acute** <note>high or sharp</note> because they are accustomed to rendering a high sound compared to the previous ones. The third boundary contains these keys: <gloss>a b c d</gloss> **aa, bb, cc, dd**; and they are called **peracute** <note>very high</note> because they are higher than the high ones. Let these remarks concerning the keys suffice for the present.

# JEAN DE MURS

->**IOANNIS DE MURIS**<-

<meta>catchword: CHAPTER-</meta>

Join the ten joints of the fingers with nine more,
These have distinguished the notes and are full of song.
They placed the Greek **Gamma ut** <note>original: "Gamma ut"; the lowest note of the medieval scale, represented by the Greek letter Γ (Gamma)</note> at the tip of the thumb;
**G** serves as your key <note>original: "clavis"; the letter representing the pitch</note>, and as the note <note>original: "nota"; the solmization syllable</note> is made, so it will be right.
In the middle <note>original: "gremio"; literally "lap" or "bosom," referring to the middle joint</note> of the thumb, the earlier teachers placed **A re**;
**A** is the key, and **re** becomes the note; thus they taught the younger students.
The base [of the thumb] gives **B mi**. **B mi** marks the division;
**C fa ut** follows from here, and it shall stand at the base of the index finger.
**C** becomes your key, **fa** looks to the lower notes:
While **ut**, the note which follows, looks only to those behind.
So it is in the rest: the letter is the first key.
Of the notes, some ascend, while others seek the depths.
From this, however, you should except high **g sol fa** and **d la sol**,
Since they could not add a leap above themselves.
These keys only look backward as they step;
Where the path fails, there is no escape but to turn back.
In **b fa ♮ mi** <note>original: "b. fa. ♮ mi."</note>, however, it does not seem to be so.
For there, a double **b** is held as a double key:
The soft, round **b** <note>original: "b molle rotundum"; the flat sign ♭</note> commands **fa** to be there;
If the **b** is squared <note>original: "b quadratum"; the natural or sharp sign ♮</note>, it likewise requires a hard **mi**.
And whether it be round or square, the line provides for it;
Music owes a space to the soft **b**, and a line to the hard.
When the joint number is even, it will hold a space;
If it is odd, then it shall have the name of a line.
And there are nine spaces, but the tenth line is abundant,
Beyond which it is no trouble for you to seek a space.
Let the space be enclosed either in the mind or in practice,
Even if it lacks every touch of the notes' covering.
When you are wise, know the end of the paths beforehand;
If you walk toward that end, confusion will harm them.
A line or space runs like a whole page,
As the key has taught, which is not far from the key [signature].
It is asked why the line is not varied on the palm,
Though a page often allows this when it is written. (a)
The answer is given for the whole: because the palm stands only as a whole,
And a fourfold line could not easily provide the song.
Whether many can do more than few is not doubted;
Hence it is in great matters that a crowd of men is asked for.

# SUMMA OF MUSIC.

## CHAPTER IX.

### *Why the hand is used as an instrument rather than any other limb.*

Considering the arrangement and utility of the musical hand or palm, it is no wonder if one asks why the first teachers did not base the principles of music on some external instrument, but rather on the hand, which is taught to be an organ and part of the human body? But let this first question be solved first by interpretation and secondly by reason; for it is not true that these principles are known only through the hand, but also through the monochord <term>monochord: a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to measure musical intervals mathematically</term>. However, a monochord is not owned by everyone, nor is it always at hand; these principles are held more conveniently and readily through the hand, and are also practiced through it. Therefore, the aforementioned teachers considered that, as Aristotle says, among all the senses only two are found to be "disciplinary" <note>original: "disciplinares"; meaning senses through which one can be taught or disciplined</note>, namely sight and hearing, both of which apprehend instruction. This is achieved through the hand; for one who sees and hears this, and pays diligent attention to it, makes great progress. For through sight, one dis-

<column-break/>

cerns the shapes, the differences, and the distances of the joints; and through hearing, one discerns and compares the diversity of sounds. Hence Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*: *we know the legitimate sound by finger and ear.* <note>original: "legitimumque sonum digito callemus & aure"; Horace, Ars Poetica, line 274. It suggests that rhythm is felt by the finger and pitch is judged by the ear.</note>

It should also be noted that music is of value to a sighted person who is deaf, but only slightly—for instance, if they had the use of hearing before their deafness and were not ignorant of music then. Similarly, this art is useful to a blind person who can hear, because by a preliminary touch they can learn the hand, even if they did not know it before. But if a person is deaf and has never heard, neither music nor the hand is of any use to them, because, as Aristotle says, a blind man does not reason about colors; and thus we can add that neither does a deaf man reason about sounds. For the proper subject of hearing is sound, just as the proper subject of sight is the colored object. Regarding external musical instruments, it must be said that they are of no use to the deaf, even if they were previously skilled in the art of playing them. A blind person who can hear, however, can use some musical instruments, but others not at all—which is easy to recognize and requires no examples.

### *A Poem on the Same Subject.*

->This hand is taught to be more useful than the rest,<-
->As it is always held more ready and available.<-
->The primary senses benefit with the help of this art:<-
->Hearing by touch, and sight by means of position.<-
->This is of no use to the deaf, yet the blind man works with it,<-
->Learning and teaching, since he is known for singing.<-
->Present a sound to the deaf, or a color to the blind,<-
->If you wish to perhaps waste your labor in vain.<-
->Many blind people carry resonant instruments,<-
->But let the deaf recite supported by no melody.<-

# JOHN OF MURIS

<meta>catchword: nus,</meta>

## CHAPTER X.
### On the species of intervals.

Having spoken of the joints, which are also called the seats of the notes, and having dealt with the notes assigned to those joints—according to which one, two, or three notes (and no more) must be ascribed to each joint, which is nothing other than a single striking or "beat" of sound—we must further consider what a melody composed of two notes should be called, and in how many ways it may vary. It should be noted, therefore, that this combination of notes is called by the general name **interval** <term>interval: the distance in pitch between two sounds</term>. There are nine species of intervals: namely, the unison, semitone, tone, minor third, major third, fourth, fifth, minor sixth, and major sixth; finally, the octave is joined to these.

The **unison**, however, is as it were the first and the foundation of intervals. It is not strictly one of the nine intervals because it does not consist of an ascent or descent of notes; hence it is called "unison" because several notes sound uniformly while they are held continuously on the same line or in the same space—such as *re, re*; *fa, fa*; *sol, sol*, and the like. It is called "unison" from the "unity of sound."

Conversely, we must speak of the **semitone**. In this context, a semitone is less than a tone and exists in the manner of a "privation" <note>privation: a philosophical term meaning the absence of a quality that should normally be present; here, the semitone is seen as an "incomplete" tone</note>, whereas the tone exists in the manner of a "habit" <note>habit: in medieval philosophy, the presence of a full quality or state</note>. And since a privation is not recognized except through the habit, we must first say what a **tone** is. However, the name "tone" is used for many things. In grammar, a tone is an accent, which by the ancients was di-

<column-break/>

vided into the acute, circumflex, and grave; but the moderns divide it into the acute, moderate, and grave. In music, "tone" is still used equivocally <note>original: "aequivoce"; meaning a word that has multiple distinct meanings</note>; it is divided into the tone of two notes, the tone of many notes, the "minor" tone, and the "major" tone.

The **minor tone** <note>here referring to the interval of a major second</note> is nothing other than the first and perfect consonance of two dissimilar notes, and this consonance is called an **interval**, acting as a gap or distance. It is called a consonance—meaning "sounding together"—because if the melody of the tone is split by too long a gap of time, it loses the power and nature of a tone and should not be called such. Therefore, in this definition, "consonance" is taken as the general category. The phrase *of dissimilar notes* is used so that the unison is excluded. The word *perfect* excludes the semitone, and the word *first* excludes the minor third and the other species of intervals that follow.

It should be known that "semitone" is not derived from *semis* (which means half), but from *semus, sema, semum* (which means "imperfect"), because it is not a "perfect" tone—for it is actually more than half of a tone <note>This refers to Pythagorean tuning, where the "minor semitone" or limma is slightly different from a mathematical half</note>. Thus it was said of the Trojans: *Half-man Phrygians* <note>original: "Semiviri phryges"; a quote from Virgil's Aeneid (Book 12), used here to show that "semi-" means "incomplete" or "lacking full status"</note>, and again, *Us half-man Phrygian*, etc. This was because they wore clothes in the manner of women, which is why they were called "half-men."

Having said these things about the minor tone, it remains to speak of the **major tone** <note>here referring to a musical Mode or "Tone" in the sense of Gregorian chant</note>. The major tone is the melody of the many notes of a single chant; its property is most observed at the end. But lest there be an interruption for one who is hurrying along, let mention of this cease for the present, because many things will be said about it later. The **minor third** <note>original: "semiditonus"</note> is named from *semis* (meaning "imperfect") and *ditonus* (major third)...

<summary>This page defines the various musical intervals, categorizing the unison as a foundation rather than an interval and distinguishing between different meanings of the word "tone" in grammar and music. It provides a technical definition of the tone as an interval and uses classical etymology to explain that a "semitone" is an "imperfect tone" rather than a literal half.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the classification of musical intervals used in medieval music theory. Having already defined the unison, semitone, and tone, the author now describes the larger intervals—the thirds, fourth, fifth, sixths, and finally the octave—using the "Guidonian Hand" (a mnemonic system where notes are mapped to the joints of the fingers) to explain their distances.</meta>

# THE SUM OF MUSIC

<sig>D d 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Ditonus (Major third)</meta>

... [minor] third, just as *re, fa*, and conversely. The **major third** <term>ditone: an interval composed of two whole tones</term> is so called as if it were a "double tone," such as *mi, ut*, or vice versa. The **fourth** <term>diatessaron: from the Greek 'dia' (through) and 'tessaron' (four)</term> is named from *dia*, which means "of" or "through," and *tessaron*, which means "four," or "square," because it proceeds from the fourth joint <note>joint: the 'articuli' or segments of the fingers on the Guidonian Hand used to track the musical scale</note> to the fourth, such as *la, mi*; *fa, ut*; *mi, la*; *sol, re*; and vice versa. The **fifth** <term>diapente: from 'dia' (through) and 'pente' (five)</term> is named from *dia*, which means "of," and *penta*, which means "five," as if made from five notes, as appears in *re, la* and similar instances. The **minor sixth** is called a "semitone with a fifth" because a semitone is joined with a fifth, just as if a movement is made from *fa* (which is in middle c. *sol-fa-ut*) to *mi* (which is in low E. *la-mi*). The **major sixth** is a "tone with a fifth," a consonance consisting of a whole tone and a fifth, just as if *la* in middle a. *la-mi-re* is joined with *ut* which is in low C. *fa-ut*; and so for the others.

<column-break/>

The ninth and final interval is the **octave** <term>diapason: from 'dia' (through) and 'pan' (all)</term>, and it is named from *dia*, meaning "of," *pan*, meaning "all," and *son*, meaning "sound," as if containing all consonances <note>The octave was considered the "perfect" container of all other musical ratios</note>, because it passes through all the joints of all the other consonances. Others say it is called *dia-pasin*, which means "of the similar" or "equal," because it proceeds from like to like; for although the joints are different, each initial letter of a joint (which is its "key" <note>clavis: the letter-name of a note</note>) has another letter similar to itself an octave above or below. This indeed constitutes an octave, just as low C. *ut* has middle c. *sol-re-ut*; low A. *re* has middle a. *la-mi-re*; low B. *mi* has middle b. *fa* ♮ *mi*, and similar cases. Thus, a sound passing from any key to its likeness, whether ascending or descending, as has been said, constitutes an octave.

---

### Verses on the Same Subject.

Each of the joints possesses one, or two, or three
Notes; none of them contains more.
A note is made, and made as many times as a sound is struck
To this end. Even a continuous sound is not called a "note."
It happens that notes are doubled; if they are doubled,
Know that nine intervals are formed, and no more.
The unison is first, which the semitone accompanies,
The tone follows this, yet it is varied equivocally <note>equivocally: the author implies the word "tone" has multiple meanings in music, such as a whole step, a chant mode, or an accent</note>.
A "tone" is an accent, a specific modulation of notes,
Either minor or major; let the minor be only of two <note>Referring to the semitone as the "minor" version of the tone</note>.
Because they are dissimilar, perfect, and continuous,
The semitone is smaller, and does not differ from these equally.
While the tone is larger, it will hold more notes,
Reaching for the end, from which it shall have its name.

# JOHN DE MURS

> The **major third** <term>ditone: an interval of two whole tones</term> precedes this, but a **minor third** <note>original: "semi... sociatur"; literally "a half is joined," referring to the semitone that turns a major third into a minor third</note> is nevertheless associated with it.
> The **fourth** <term>diatessaron</term> joins the fourth [note], with the fourth-species coming from this.
> You may join the **fifth** with the fifth [note], and it will become a **fifth** <term>diapente</term>.
> Immediately following is the **minor sixth** <note>original: "cum semitono diapente"; a fifth plus a semitone</note>.
> Suddenly the **major sixth** <note>original: "diapente tono iungens"; a fifth joining with a whole tone</note> follows the eighth [note].
> The ninth species is the **octave** <term>diapason</term>, either because it contains all these others, or because it contains similar ones joined to itself.

### CHAPTER XI.

->**Why there are no more than nine intervals, and no more than nineteen joints.**<-

Since two notes can be combined in nine ways so that nine intervals are formed from them, someone might not absurdly ask: since notes can be joined in many more ways both above and below the octave, why is the musician content with only nine intervals? To this it must be said that it is so in every art: whatever hinders the goal of the art should, by greater right, be removed from that art. Just as in **grammar**, which ultimately intends correct speech, **barbarisms** <term>barbarismus: an error in the form of a single word</term> and **solecisms** <term>solœcismus: a grammatical error in the arrangement of words</term> are said to be errors, and what is more remarkable, even **cacophony** <term>cacophaton: an unpleasant-sounding sequence of words</term> is avoided.

So too **logic** <note>original: "dialectica"</note>, which intends to create certainty from a doubtful matter, while it hunts for **syllogistic necessity** <note>the logical requirement that a conclusion must follow from its premises</note>, it disentangles useless combinations of propositions—such as the conjunction of two premises in the "second figure"—and other such **illogical fantasies** <term>paralogisticas phantasias</term>; and one may find something of this sort in every single art. So also in **music**, since it especially intends delight, it drives away and despises whatever seems contrary to that goal. Moreover, the pairings of notes—specifically those that do not constitute one of the nine

<column-break/>

aforementioned intervals—rightly ought to be avoided by the musician, because they are not part of genuine melody, but instead produce an hateful dissonance, which are judged contrary to the purpose of music. Such is the **fa** in the "soft B" <note>original: "b. molli"; B-flat</note> in the high register when compared with the **E** <note>original: "E. la, mi"</note> in the lower or higher register, if it were joined to it as an interval <note>this describes the "tritone" or augmented fourth, a famously harsh dissonance in medieval music</note>. Such is the low **A** <note>original: "a. la, mi, re"</note> with the **B-natural** <note>original: "b. mi"</note>, and vice versa; and a similar judgment should be held for similar cases.

But something must be said regarding the interval that sounds as an octave; likewise that nineteen **joints** <note>original: "articuli"; the segments of the fingers on the mnemonic "Guidonian Hand"</note> or "seats" of notes were maintained by the ancient teachers. One might ask whether more can or should be found. To this it can be said that nineteen suffice, though more could certainly be had. For since song is divided into the **low** <term>gravis</term>, **high** <term>acutus</term>, and **very high** <term>peracutus</term>, and since eight keys serve the low, seven the high, and four the very high, it hardly happens that anyone has a voice of such vigor that they can run through these keys in singing without a change of voice; and even more notes would ascend beyond this, if they were invented. But if by chance some singer did not begin the song low enough at an appropriate pitch, but by starting it unsuitably high ascended into the upper keys until he ran out of notes, let him not complain that he has a lack [of notes]; for in place of the first key he sought and did not find, let him simply take a lower one...

<summary>John de Murs explains why music is limited to nine specific intervals and nineteen notes, arguing that any other combinations produce "hateful dissonance" and that the human voice is naturally limited to this range.</summary>

...the next letter serving the same, and through the **octave** <term>diapason: the interval of an eighth</term> he will find the desired sound in it; this is evident in musical instruments, which have only seven or eight differences of notes, within which any song is found.

Some attribute the aforementioned **nineteen** <note>original: "decem novenarium"; referring to the 19 notes of the standard medieval scale</note> to the nineteen joints of the hand itself; they say that because no more joints are found on the hand, no more positions for notes can be found. But to judge such things so seems foolish, because different and distinct shapes of joints exist outside the hand just as they do inside. It should also be known that **Guido** <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the monk who developed the precursor to modern staff notation and the "Guidonian Hand" as a memory aid</note> in his music added three notable joints to the aforementioned nineteen. He named the highest *C* "c. sol, fa, ut" and the highest *D* "d. la, sol, re," and he further added the keys "f. fa" and "g. sol." He assigns this reason: since we have an octave in the **low notes** <term>graves: the lowest range of the medieval scale</term> from *G. ut* up to *G. sol, re, ut*, and similarly in the **high notes** <term>acutes: the middle range</term> from *G. sol, re, ut* (which is the end of the lows) up to *g. sol, re, ut* (which is the end of the highs), Guido said that just as many joints should be held in the **very high notes** <term>peracutes: the highest range of the scale</term> so that the octave can also be completed in them; otherwise, music would suffer a defect in this part. To this it can be answered, as we said before, that since we can do without those three aforementioned joints, they seem to be added somewhat superfluously. For just as Art desires to supply what is lacking, so it is also Art's role to cut away whatever is superfluous.

## CHAPTER XII.

### On the signs of intervals as they are ordered in different ways by different people.

From what has been said, it is clear that the intervals found in song proceed according to **ascent and descent** <term>arsin & thesin: the upward and downward movement of a melody</term>; therefore, it is necessary that they be measured by certain limits, otherwise there would seem to be no difference between a smaller distance and a larger one. Thus, signs were invented through which the species of intervals might be recognized. Something, therefore, can be said about musical signs. However, the signs for notes on sounding musical instruments behave differently according to the various properties of the instrument. For larger wind instruments do not have a continuous range except for the **whole tone and semitone** <note>original: "tonum & semitonium"</note>, according to how they are arranged and ordered progressively. Such are **organs, pipes, horns, bagpipes, panpipes, recorders** <note>original: "organa, tibiae, cornua, musae, siringae, flaiota"</note>, etc. Certain stringed instruments are also tuned progressively, such as **citharas and psalteries, the hurdy-gurdy, the monochord** <note>original: "citharae & psalteria, organistrum, monochordum"</note>, and the like; and these have the proper signs of their own notes. There are also sounding vessels, which are recognized according to their position and order, such as **bells** <term>cymbala: specifically small sets of tuned bells used in the Middle Ages</term>, and the like. There are other stringed instruments that are discerned by ear alone, tuned by the harmonies of the **octave, the fourth, and the fifth** <term>diapason, diatessaron, & diapente</term>, and by different placements of the fingers, craftsmen form for themselves tones and semitones, and so on for others. But the one who sings holds the joints of the fingers and the

<column-break/>

differences of sounds in the hand itself as signs. However, those who wish to write on a page or in a songbook, or to learn what is written, or to sing, clearly need signs that certify the quantity of the sounds; the ancients used different signs in different ways.

To make what follows clear, it must be noted that the first teachers used to form the **keys** <term>claves: the letter-names that identify a specific pitch or "clef"</term> of all the finger-joints in various ways. For they marked the low G with the Greek **Gamma** <note>original: "Γ. graecum"</note>, but later they placed the simple letters A. B. C. D. E. F. G. for the keys, and they assigned these to the **low notes** <term>gravibus: the lowest octave of the medieval scale</term>. Following those, for the **high notes** <term>acutas: the middle octave</term>, they made the letters capital <note>The text says "capitales," but medieval terminology often swapped the usage of capital and lowercase letters compared to modern standards; here it refers to the middle register</note> a. b. c. d. e. f. g. Finally, they formed four keys for the **very high notes** <term>peracutas: the highest register</term> using a **double-bellied shape** <gloss>a b c d</gloss> a. b. c. d. <note>original: "duplo ventre"; referring to the cursive "double" letters like 'aa' used to denote the highest octave</note>. From these, it is certain that the key for each joint of the hand kept its own proper form. From that point, some of the ancients—wishing to jot down music for themselves rather than for others—wrote the shape of the key itself in place of a note, without using staff lines. How a song was noted down with letters over the words can easily be seen from what has been said. But it is established that this way of singing, using a double labor, possessed too much difficulty.

Regarding the difficulty or diversity of keys invented by the ancients, we say that it is not necessary for all keys to be shaped so differently. For although both the low and high notes are written with simple letters after the C, this works well enough to show the difference: that the letter or key which is in the low range is on the line,

<column-break/>

and how the next note following it ought to begin. Let him also examine his melody outside of the intervals, or determine which <term>mode</term> <note>The melodic scales (like Dorian or Phrygian) that governed medieval composition.</note> it belongs to. And if he does not have a flexible voice, but is dissonant, and if he should perhaps lose the favor or even the direct assistance of a teacher, let him bestow care upon it and practice musical instruments and use them often—such as the <term>monochord</term> <note>A one-stringed instrument used to teach the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note> or the <term>symphonia</term> (which is called an <term>organistrum</term>) <note>An early form of the hurdy-gurdy.</note>; let him also labor to sing with the organ. Indeed, on these instruments a note cannot easily go astray or be distorted far from its proper sound, because the notes can be easily observed through certain and marked keys and can be brought forth promptly without a companion or a master singer.

## CHAPTER XIV.
### On the discovery of the tones, and their number.

It was said above that this name "tone" <note>original: *tonus*</note> is equivocal <note>A word with multiple meanings.</note> as it refers to both the major tone and the minor tone. We have already spoken about the minor [tone] <note>The interval of a whole step.</note>. Now it follows to speak of the major [tone] <note>In this context, the author refers to the church modes or "tones," such as the Dorian or Phrygian modes.</note>. Hence we must see what it is and how it is divided. It was partially touched upon above what it is, because, as has been established, the major tone is a regular melodic arrangement of a song consisting of many small notes, which is primarily observed toward the end. "Melodic arrangement" <note>original: *modulatio*</note> is used as the general category; **regular** is added to distinguish it from a song that extends [erroneously] above or below the diatonic scale; **of many small notes** is said to distinguish it from the minor tone, which consists only of the melody of two notes. **Which is primarily observed toward the end** is added to refute the opinion of those who think a song should be judged by its beginning.

Having the definition of the tone, it remains to see how it is divided. Hence it should be known that the ancient teachers of music divided the tone into four parts: namely, into the <term>protus</term>, <term>deuterus</term>, <term>tritus</term>, and <term>tetrardus</term> <note>These are Latinized Greek terms meaning first, second, third, and fourth.</note>, that is, the first, second, third, and fourth. But it may be asked: for what reason were they

<column-break/>

led to place a grouping of four <note>original: *quaternarium*</note> in the aforementioned species? To which it must be said that these same teachers studiously and carefully considered that music is founded upon a very great and wonderful harmony of sounds. Therefore, it was reasonably discovered according to the number and proportion of those things which are proven to have a friendly, greatest, and primary harmony in worldly matters—which are the elements, whose binding and mutual "harmonious discord" <note>original: *concors discordia*; a classical concept where the universe is held together by the balance of opposing forces.</note> constitutes the <term>macrocosm</term>, that is, the greater world. For fire is exceedingly hot, air moist, earth dry, and water cold. Drawing the reason for their number from this, the first teachers divided the musical tone by four. This same grouping of four, also caused by the elements but not arranged in the same way, is found in the <term>microcosm</term>, that is, the lesser world, which is man. For he consists of four humors: namely, <term>cholera</term> <note>yellow bile</note>, <term>blood</term>, <term>phlegm</term>, and <term>melancholy</term> <note>black bile</note>. And these share the four aforementioned elemental qualities, but they are not arranged according to the order of "above" and "below" [as the elements are]. However, the elemental makeup and even the order is found in the four quarters of the year, the month, and the day.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter XIV regarding the definition of musical "tones" (modes). The previous page established that a major tone (a mode) is a melodic arrangement primarily defined by its ending. This page moves into the specific final notes of the modes and the expansion from four to eight modes.</meta>

# JOHANNES DE MURIS

They also established that the melody of the *protus* <note>The first category of modes, corresponding to the Dorian and Hypodorian.</note> should take its end in **D sol re**; the *deuterus* <note>The second category, corresponding to the Phrygian and Hypophrygian.</note> in **E la mi**; the *tritus* <note>The third category, corresponding to the Lydian and Hypolydian.</note> in **F fa ut**; and the *tetrardus* <note>The fourth category, corresponding to the Mixolydian and Hypomixolydian.</note> in **G sol re ut**. But it may be asked why the song is more properly ended on these notes and not others, such as higher or lower ones, and why on consecutive notes rather than ones spaced apart? To this, it must be said that music was primarily invented for delight; for this reason, it entrusts its end to the low notes <note>original: *graves* — the lower register of the medieval scale.</note> rather than the high <note>original: *acutis*</note> or very high <note>original: *peracutis*</note> ones, because it intends to finish this work in a rational and delightful way. But some seem to intend the opposite of this, since they appear to ascend a fifth <note>original: *diapente* — an interval of five notes.</note> from the final note. To which it must be said that this happens by accident—namely, to adorn the end of the song in the low register, which is what is principally intended. As evidence of this: while many can firmly maintain a song in the low register, few can ascend a fifth; if the reverse occurs, it is proven to be irregular. Since, therefore, the songs of all the tones regularly end in the low register, they admit the higher keys of the low range rather than the lowest ones; because, as will be said later, a song very often descends below its final note, which would not be permitted if it attempted to end on the very lowest notes of the scale. Furthermore, the reason they end not on one note but on four—and not separated, but consecutive—is because the elements to which the tones are compared are not similar, but have four places: earth is the lowest; water is second; air is third; and fire is fourth. Thus, the elements are joined not separately but continuously, and so too are the tones.

<column-break/>

After the four inventors of the tones mentioned above, others followed who were more perceptive than the ancients. They considered that the melodies of the four aforementioned tones sometimes ascend a great deal and sometimes descend a great deal. To avoid confusion, they distinguished each of them into two: the *protus* into the *authentic protus* and the *plagal protus*; the *deuterus* into the *authentic deuterus* and the *plagal deuterus*; the *tritus* into the *authentic tritus* and the *plagal tritus*; and the *tetrardus* into the *authentic tetrardus* and the *plagal tetrardus*. "Plagal" is named from *plaga*, which means a position or a lowering <note>From the Greek *plagios*, meaning "sideways" or "slanting," used here to describe the lower-range version of a mode.</note>, because it dwells mostly among the lower notes. "Authentic" is said as if "extended high" <note>original: *alte extentus*</note>, because it ascends more into the higher keys; or "authentic" is used as if meaning "authoritative" <note>original: *authenticus*</note>, because it is worthier than the plagal and is, as it were, its master. And it should be noted that every authentic tone is odd-numbered, and if it is even-numbered, it is plagal. Thus, the *authentic protus* and the *plagal protus* have the same final key, **D**, and these are the first and second modes. The *authentic deuterus* and the *plagal deuterus*—that is, the third and fourth modes—have **E**. The *authentic tritus* and the *plagal tritus*—the fifth and sixth—have **F**. The *authentic tetrardus* and the *plagal tetrardus*—the seventh and eighth—have **G**.

And perhaps someone may ask what the reason is for this set of eight, and whether there is something else in the natural world upon which this number and its property are founded? To this it must be said that this set of eight is required by the same cause as the aforementioned set of four, but sought in a different way. For although there are four elements, and only four...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the four primary musical modes (protus, deuterus, tritus, and tetrardus) expand into eight distinct modes. ...just as with the primary elemental qualities: one of them belongs to an element principally, while another belongs to it less properly and not as its primary trait. For example: fire is principally hot and secondarily dry; earth is principally dry and subsequently cold; but water is found to be properly cold and accidentally moist; air is said to be principally moist and secondarily hot. From this analogy, the previously mentioned eightfold number of tones <note>The "tones" here refer to the church modes.</note> is derived. And just as one quality is primary and the others secondary to the same element, so too do two musical modes share one "final" note: one mode is the primary (authentic) and the other is secondary (plagal). <note>In medieval music theory, "authentic" modes have a higher range, while "plagal" modes share the same ending note but have a lower range.</note>

### The Same in Meter

The ancients spoke of four types of tones,
From which the total number of them was revealed.
The elements of the greater world <note>The macrocosm or the universe.</note> are contained in this number;
Add the humors of the smaller world <note>The microcosm or the human body.</note>,
And the parts of the year, the month, and the great day.
To these, you can compare the tones of the same kind;
They have parts that are touching and in a fixed order.
Consider, then, the four types of tones discovered.
They hold the highest keys of the low register <note>original: *gravium claves* — the notes D, E, F, and G in the medieval gamut.</note> as their end;
By their own right, they cannot be finished elsewhere.
They noted that young men first erred in the number of tones,
Who would sound now with a low voice, now with a high one.
They said that any of the mentioned tones, whether "authentic"
Or "plagal," would not be the same.
This tone is called **authentic**, as if it were "held high" <note>original: *alte tentus* — a medieval folk etymology for the word "authentic."</note>;
Then the **plagal** will be "pressed down," because it is slow to climb.
The plagal is even-numbered, a servant who walks and creeps;
The authentic is odd-numbered, a master who flies on wings.
Thus the number grows, thus the eightfold count emerges;
For one tone covers two, as if under a veil.
The even and odd tone hunt for the same ending note,
So that they may conclude the song together at last.
Although they do not share their meals or their burdens,
The master and the servant are accustomed to stay the night together. <note>A metaphor for the two modes sharing the same final note.</note>
Having said why there were twice two, let it now be told
Why there are now eight: because the number is doubled.
A tree produces large, primary branches,
But a large one is sometimes split into two smaller ones.
Just as fire is made hot, and then dry thereafter,

### CHAPTER XV.
#### *Which are the final keys and the substitute keys of the tones.*

It has been said that the **Protus** <note>The first and second modes.</note> ends in **D. sol, re**; the **Deuterus** <note>The third and fourth modes.</note> in **E. la, mi**; the **Tritus** <note>The fifth and sixth modes.</note> in **F. fa, ut**; and the **Tetrardus** <note>The seventh and eighth modes.</note> in **G. sol, re, ut**. These keys are properly and regularly owed to the tones already mentioned. I say "properly" because a song is sometimes terminated "improperly." For it sometimes happens that a song which should regularly and properly end in the low register is ended higher up in the high register <note>original: *acutis* — refers to the "acute" or higher-pitched section of the medieval gamut.</note>; and this is done primarily because of a necessity arising from the **semitone** <note>The half-step. Medieval singers shifted the ending note of a song to a higher position (transposition) if the original position didn't allow for the correct arrangement of half-steps required by the melody.</note>. For if such a song were placed in the low register, it would either lack a semitone where it ought to have one, or have one where it ought to lack it. Since such a song finds its desired ascent and descent in the high register, and is not hindered by the semitone, the low notes are set aside and it is placed in the high notes. But this is by favor, not by right; furthermore, this license is not granted except to the **Protus**, **Deuterus**, and **Tritus**, because **D. sol, re**, which is the proper key of the **Protus**, has its very similar substitute in **a. la, mi,**

<column-break/>

**re**. Also, **E. la, mi**, which is the property of the **Deuterus**, has a substitute in the **hard-b** <note>original: *b. durum* — B-natural.</note> in **b. fa. ♮ mi**. So too **F. fa, ut**, which is proper to the **Tritus** in the low register, has a substitute in **c. sol, fa, ut** in the high register. The **Tetrardus**, however, does not avoid its own end in **G. sol, re, ut**, because due to the proximity of the semitone above and below, it does not face the necessity found in the others, and therefore it ought not to have a substitute; hence its proper duty is exercised in its own place. If, therefore, a song of the **Tetrardus** sometimes seems to wander out of place, let it be attributed to the ignorance of either its first singer or perhaps the scribe, and it is subject to the correction of a skilled singer.

And so that no example of the aforementioned necessity be lacking: the song of the **Protus** fails in the low register in this antiphon of the second tone, *"Great mystery of inheritance,"* <note>original: *magnum hæreditatis mysterium*</note> which necessity compels to end in **a. la, mi, re**. And it should be noted that if a song ends higher up, the translation <note>The "transposition" or relocation of the melody.</note> of this song ought to begin higher up as well, according to the requirement of the end; as is often done because of the lack of a semitone.

...often, as has been said, it happens to occur. ...in the low register, let us seek help from the high register. Since the **Protus** <note>The first and second modes.</note> cannot reach its end in the low register at **D. sol, re** in this responsory: *Holy and immaculate are you, O Virgin* <note>original: *Sancta & immaculata es virgo*</note>; ascending to the high notes, it asks for a substitute ending for itself at **a. la, mi, re**. If anyone begins and sings all these in the substitute <note>original: *vicariis*</note> or "affinity" keys, they will reach the end without error; however, the **Tetrardus** <note>The seventh and eighth modes.</note> will not change its own seat.

### Chapter XVI.
***What the initial keys of the tones are, and how and how much they ascend or descend.***

It has been said that the chant of each tone is especially observed, and even indicated, near the end: and this is to say, that although some chant has special properties of a certain tone at the beginning, and in the middle is even more similar...

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of musical modes, moving from the "final" notes (the notes on which a melody concludes) to the "initial" notes (where a melody begins) and the melodic range (how high or low the notes go).</meta>

<page-num>222</page-num>
<header>JOHANNES DE MURIS</header>

...to the same; yet at the end, it is especially adapted to it. And since we have spoken of the keys <note>The term *clavis* (key) here refers to specific pitch positions on the medieval musical scale.</note>—which and how many are the finals of the tones <note>The "tones" are the eight modes of Gregorian chant.</note>—now we must speak further about the initial keys of their chants, and how many notes they pass above or below their final.

But one might ask: why were the final keys of the chants of the tones discussed before the initial keys, or before those notes observed in the middle of a melody? To this it must be said that this is done because of the greater dignity of the end; for a chant is less easily identified by its beginning or middle than by its conclusion. Thus, the **Authentic Protus** <note>The First Mode, which typically concludes on D.</note> has four proper initial keys: **C, D, F,** and **a**. For every chant of the first tone either properly begins on **C. fa, ut**, as in this antiphon: *After the departure of the most blessed* <note>original: *post excessum beatissimi*</note>, etc.; or on **D. sol, re**, as in this antiphon: *Behold the name of the Lord* <note>original: *Ecce nomen Domini*</note>, etc.; or on **F. fa, ut**, such as: *He found the light* <note>original: *Invenit lumen*</note>; or on **a. la, mi, re**, such as: *Go out quickly* <note>original: *exi cito*</note>, etc. The beginning of this tone does not start on **E. la, mi** or **G. sol, re, ut**. And the chant of the first tone is found to descend as far as **A. re**—four notes below its final—as in the beginning of the Responsory: *Let every age rejoice* <note>original: *lætetur omne seculum*</note>, etc. It ascends to the letter **g**, specifically ten keys above its final, as in the same Responsory at the words: *eternal love* <note>original: *æternus amor*</note>, etc. Some, however, judge this same chant to be irregular because of its improper ascents; to whom it can be answered that this ascent is delightful, and thus does not exceed the purpose of music, which was invented primarily for delight.

The **Plagal Protus** <note>The Second Mode, which shares the final note D with the First Mode but has a lower range.</note> has four beginnings

<column-break/>

or starting notes: **A, C, D, F**. **A. re**, as in: *Behold, he comes* <note>original: *ecce advenit*</note>, etc.; **C. ut**, as here: *It was for a time* <note>original: *fuit ad tempus*</note>, etc.; **D. ut**: *O Wisdom* <note>original: *O sapientia*</note>, etc.; **F. ut**: *Be comforted* <note>original: *consolamini*</note>. And the chant of this tone descends to **C**—which is not found in others—as in *They gathered* <note>original: *collegerunt*</note>, and at the start of the sequence *Come, tell us* <note>original: *Eia dic nobis*</note>, etc.; and it is found to ascend to high **d**, as in the Responsory: *All fullness* <note>original: *omnis plenitudo*</note>, etc., seven keys above its final.

The **Authentic Deuterus** <note>The Third Mode, which concludes on E.</note> has three proper beginnings: **E, F, G**. **E**, as here: *This is she who knew not* <note>original: *hæc est quæ nescivit*</note>, etc.; **F**, as in *O glorious* <note>original: *O gloriosum*</note>; **G**, as in: *You, always the same* <note>original: *te semper idem*</note>. And it descends only to **C**, as in this Responsory: *A great mystery* <note>original: *magnum mysterium*</note>, etc.; and it ascends to high **G**, as in this Responsory: *With great power* <note>original: *Virtute magna*</note>, at the word: *testimony* <note>original: *testimonium*</note>. The **Plagal Deuterus** <note>The Fourth Mode, sharing the final note E.</note> has five initial keys: **C, D, E, F, G**. **C**, as in: *Deal your bread to the hungry* <note>original: *frange esurienti*</note>; **D**, as in: *Your [mercy], O Lord* <note>original: *tuam domine*</note>; **E**, as in: *Be watchful in spirit* <note>original: *vigilate animo*</note>; **F**, as in: *Thou art all fair* <note>original: *tota pulchra*</note>; **G**, as in: *After childbearing, O Virgin* <note>original: *post partum virgo*</note>. Moreover, it descends to **B. mi**, as in this Responsory: *For so long a time* <note>original: *tanto tempore*</note>. It ascends to high **C**, as here: *Arise* <note>original: *Exurge*</note>, etc.

The **Authentic Tritus** <note>The Fifth Mode, which concludes on F.</note> has three proper initial keys: **F**, as in: *A multitude of pagans* <note>original: *paganorum multitudo*</note>; **a**, as in: *Destroy the temple* <note>original: *solvite templum*</note>; **c** on the line, as in: *Holy, holy, holy* <note>original: *sanctus, sanctus, sanctus*</note>. And it ascends to **g** on the line, as in this Responsory: *Which, when he had heard* <note>original: *quod cum audisset*</note>, etc. Below its final, however, it descends only rarely, which is not found in the others. The **Plagal Tritus** <note>The Sixth Mode, sharing the final note F.</note> sometimes ascends to the highest reached **d**, but then it is improperly terminated on the substitute key **c** in the high register, as in the sequence: *The Word born of God* <note>original: *Verbum de Deo natum*</note>; however, when it is terminated in the low register, it has two initial keys, **D** and **F**. **D**, as in: *Today you shall know* <note>original: *hodie scietis*</note>.

Nothing moves below [the final note], and it is found in the high **g**. <note>This refers to the Fifth mode discussed at the end of the previous page.</note>
The sixth mode, taking its end in **F**, will take **D** as its first note.
Or it may have **F** as its beginning; descending, it seeks **E** as its lowest.
From here come the introits *Today* <note>original: *Hodie*</note>, *Witnesses* <note>original: *testes*</note>, and the *Benedictus*.
The keys are changed upward when **a** or **c** are taken.
So it is done in these chants, if by chance it is necessary.
But you shall not move the Tetrardus <note>The "fourth" pair of modes: the Seventh and Eighth.</note> from its proper seat;
You will always see it finished in **G** everywhere.
The seventh begins on **G**, and you will also join **♮** <note>B-natural</note>, **c**, and **d**.
The chants *This is the head* <note>original: *Hoc caput*</note>, *He sent* <note>original: *hoc misit*</note>, *The people* <note>original: *populus*</note>, and *All* <note>original: *omnes*</note> bear witness to this.
It presses upon **F**, its neighbor, and climbs to the high **g**,
*The Angel* <note>original: *Angelus*</note> and *All* <note>original: *omnes*</note> will make your singing sure.
The eighth is richer than the others in its beginnings;
If it seeks a "lodging," <note>An opening note.</note> it looks to six [notes] in its progress.
It enters on **C** or **D**, and at the same time requires **F**, **G**, and **a** or **c**.
It descends to **E**, but it reaches up to the heights of **a**.
*Wisdom* <note>original: *sapientia*</note> gives this, and *Have mercy* <note>original: *miserere*</note> provides that.

### CHAPTER XVII.

<margin>How much the authentic modes ascend and descend, and how much the plagals.</margin>

We have spoken specifically about the course and law of the <term>tones</term> <note>In this context, "tones" refers to the eight musical modes of Gregorian chant.</note>; according to this, the neighbor can be held by general rules and by approving the course or law in a chant's certain ascent or descent through the keys. That is to say, how much each of the modes can be stretched upward or relaxed downward, which is to say, how much they can properly or improperly ascend or descend—according to the rule or by permission. It should be noted, therefore, that an <term>authentic</term> <note>The odd-numbered modes (1, 3, 5, 7) which typically have a higher range.</note> chant can rarely ascend through a <term>diapason</term> <note>An octave (eight notes).</note>, that is, up to eight notes above its final note; by license, however, it may go up to the ninth, and even the tenth, but this is rare. For what one possesses by right, one may use frequently; however, a wise man uses granted favors cautiously and rarely. A <term>plagal</term> <note>The even-numbered modes (2, 4, 6, 8) which have a lower range, often centered around the final note.</note> chant rarely

<column-break/>

can ascend through a <term>diapente</term> <note>A perfect fifth (five notes).</note> and up to the sixth key; by license, however, it may go up to the seventh, and even to the octave, but rarely. Furthermore, the plagals descend as far as four notes, that is, through a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>A perfect fourth (four notes).</note>, and even to the fifth, but rarely, below their final note. The authentic modes, however, descend as far as a fourth, which belongs to the plagals. The third mode is an exception, as it does not pass below the next lower note, as is the fifth, which is not required to descend at all below its final note. It must also be considered that although it has been said that the authentics ascend through an octave and sometimes further, and the plagals through a fifth and sometimes further, it is not to be understood that it always happens thus, but that it *can* happen in this way. Just as we say that a Bishop may celebrate both major and minor orders during the <term>four seasons</term> <note>The "Ember Days" (Quatuor Tempora), specific times in the liturgical calendar set aside for fasting and ordinations.</note>, it is not understood that he must do this in all four seasons, but that he is able to.

</columns>

### THE SUMMARY OF MUSIC.

### *A Poem on the Same Subject.*

->Believe that you know the law or the course of the modes,<-
->When you know by how much of a range their course precedes.<-
->The Authentic modes may rightly climb an octave,<-
->One or perhaps two notes may be added as extra figures.<-
->It suits the wise man to use these concessions rarely;<-
->It is proven better to use the proper notes securely.<-
->By right, a Plagal mode has the power to climb by a fifth,<-
->Grace grants one or two notes—three only slowly.<-
->A Plagal mode shall have four notes <note>original: *bis binas*, literally "twice two"</note> below the final note;<-
->One more may be added, but it will rarely see five.<-
->Give four to the authentic ones, though the third is an exception,<-
->Joining itself to one, while the fifth is associated with none.<-
->No one should think that this ascent or descent<-
->Always happens, but should note that it *can* happen.<-

### Chapter XVIII.
#### How authentic chant is distinguished from plagal by distinguishing keys.

Since there are four proper keys for the modes—namely **D**, **E**, **F**, and **G**—I call them "proper" because, when necessity urges, the *Protus*, *Deuterus*, and *Tritus* <note>The first, second, and third pairs of modes.</note> have "vicarious" or substitute keys for themselves at the interval of a fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note>, as if having a shared agreement with them: the high **a**, **♮** <term>B-natural</term>, and **c**. Through these, the defect is excused which occurs in the low **D**, **E**, and **F** mentioned before. Someone might doubt how the first mode can be discerned from the second, since both take their end in **D** <term>sol-re</term> <note>These are the solmization syllables for the note D in different hexachords.</note>. Similarly, one might ask about the third and fourth, whose end is the low **E**; and likewise for the seventh and eighth, both of which adopt **G** as their end. But since knowing and being able to assign the difference in the aforesaid matters is both good and difficult, it is proven that one needs the help of art. Aristotle also says that to assign a difference between things that are very dissimilar

<column-break/>

is not difficult, but it is difficult between those things which seem to agree the most.

To this, it must be noted that just as there are four final keys, so also there are four <term>distinguishing keys</term> <note>original: *claves discretivæ*; these are the notes that help a singer identify which mode a melody belongs to.</note> of the modes. What the final keys are has been stated many times above. The distinguishing keys of the modes are contained on the little finger <note>A reference to the "Guidonian Hand," a mnemonic tool where parts of the hand represent different notes.</note>, which are **F** <term>fa-ut</term>, **G** <term>sol-re-ut</term>, **a** <term>la-mi-re</term>, and **♮** <term>B-natural</term> <term>durum</term>. There are four of them, neither more nor fewer, because since there are eight modes, each distinguishing key works to differentiate two modes: for **F** <term>fa-ut</term> discerns the first from the second, **g** the third from the fourth, **a** the fifth from the sixth, and **♮** <term>B-natural</term> the seventh from the eighth.

Perhaps someone asks: why were these distinguishing keys established and not others? To this, it must be said that Plagal chant travels more through the lower keys, and Authentic through the higher ones, and for this reason, the distinguishing keys are rightly ordered in this way.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how to distinguish between "authentic" (high) and "plagal" (low) modes. This page provides specific rules based on the distribution of notes relative to a "distinguishing key" for each of the four mode pairings.</meta>

# JOHN OF MURIS

...so that the last two of them belong to the low notes, and the first two belong to the high notes. Therefore, through this rule—with a certain exception to be mentioned shortly—you may learn to distinguish an authentic chant from its plagal counterpart. If a chant of the *Protus* <note>The first pair of modes (1 and 2), ending on D.</note> has more notes above **F-fa-ut**, it is, as far as this is concerned, authentic and of the first mode; if it has more below, it is plagal and of the second. And if a chant of the *Deuterus* <note>The second pair (3 and 4), ending on E.</note> has more notes above **G**, it is authentic and of the third mode; if more below, it is plagal and of the fourth. Likewise, if a chant of the *Tritus* <note>The third pair (5 and 6), ending on F.</note> has more notes above **a-la-mi-re**, it is authentic and of the fifth mode; if more below, it is plagal and of the sixth. Likewise, if a chant of the *Tetrardus* <note>The fourth pair (7 and 8), ending on G.</note> has more notes above **♮-durum** <term>B-natural</term>, it is authentic and of the seventh; if indeed it has more below, it is plagal and of the eighth.

And it must be noted that this qualification, "as far as this is concerned," is added because the aforementioned abundance of notes above the distinguishing key—insofar as it is able—pulls the chant into the property of the authentic mode. However, an abundance of notes found below the distinguishing key—insofar as it is able—pulls the chant into the property of the plagal mode. I say "insofar as it is able" because, as has been said, this occurs if the *trope* <note>In this context, "trope" refers to the melodic character or specific melodic formulas of the mode.</note> agrees with the "course" <note>The overall range or melodic path.</note> of the chant. If the trope and the course of the chant disagree, it is necessary for us to yield to the trope and set aside the course.

But since it has not yet been stated what a trope is—about which enough will be said later—for the present it should be noted that an authentic chant essentially and gradually

<column-break/>

descends toward the end; for the end defines the act. <note>A philosophical maxim: the purpose or conclusion of a thing determines its nature.</note> Because of this, these antiphons are judged to be of the first mode and not the second: *Volo pater* <note>original: "I will, Father"</note>, *Reges Tharsis* <note>original: "The kings of Tharsis"</note>, and *Circumdantes* <note>original: "Surrounding"</note>, even though they have more notes below **F-fa-ut** than above. A plagal chant, however, tends toward the end by falling or plunging more sharply, such as by a <term>semiditone</term> <note>A minor third.</note> or by some other larger interval; and thus, by detracting from the authentic, it pulls the chant into the property of the plagal mode, as happens in the song *Tu puer propheta* <note>original: "You, child, [shall be called] a prophet"</note>. Odo and Guido also say something noteworthy regarding the difference and distinction of the modes: if a chant strikes the fifth <note>original: *diapente*</note> above its final note five or more times, it should be ascribed to the authentic and not the plagal, even if its course runs against the law of the plagal. This is clear in the antiphon *Ecce tu pulcra es* <note>original: "Behold, you are beautiful"</note>, and in the Response *Sicut omnium* <note>original: "As of all..."</note>, and in many others. Yet this rule is not found to be universal in all cases; we have mentioned it, however, so it may be known that a plagal chant should rarely reach the fifth. This is done so that the prerogatives of ascent may be seen as attributed to the authentic keys as if they were the masters of the plagal ones. It should also be noted that a chant which is called "doubtful" by some—where it is less clearly known whether it is authentic or plagal—will always be called authentic. For by right, the designation is taken from the more worthy, as is evident in the antiphon *Circumdantes* and similar ones, and in the Introit *Deus in adiutorium* <note>original: "O God, [come] to my assistance"</note>. This is said to be of the seventh mode rather than the eighth; for greater and more powerful honor is to be attributed to the master, and not the servant.

### Verse on the Same Subject <note>original: "Metrum de Eodem"</note>

Just as four notes are said to be the final keys, <note>The notes on which a chant ends: D, E, F, and G.</note>
So also four "distinguishing" keys are properly found;
The low ones are ***F*** and ***G***, but the high ones we call ***a*** and ***b***. <note>In medieval notation, lowercase 'a' and 'b' (specifically B-natural) represent the notes in the higher octave.</note>
This number is sufficient, because each key serves two modes.
The distinction of the modes is made by these four.
The first mode wants more notes to be above ***F-fa-ut***,
And the second properly wants more to be below it.
The third differs from the fourth, with ***G*** as the mediator:
The fifth also differs from the sixth with the help of the ***a*** key.
The seventh is taught to differ from the eighth by the ***♮*** <term>B-natural</term>.
The odd mode <note>The authentic modes: 1, 3, 5, 7.</note> stays above, but the even <note>The plagal modes: 2, 4, 6, 8.</note> is held lower.
If you count correctly, the rule given is certain enough,
Provided a concordant final **neuma** <term>melodic phrase</term> is found.
If perhaps near the end the chant begins to move differently,
The prior law of the authentic mode perishes, and it is placed in the plagal.
It happens equally if that section dwells there more lingeringly.
The plagal law departs when the second-to-last **neuma** covers it.
Thus *Nisi Dominus* <note>A reference to the chant for Psalm 126/127, "Unless the Lord."</note> is titled as the first mode,
Thus the **neuma** is proven to grant the mode based on the end.
However, **Odo** and **Guido** <note>Odo of Cluny and Guido of Arezzo, the two most influential medieval music theorists.</note> report that if it happens to be sung
And the chant is weighed down under the plagal law by its movement,
Yet if it is drawn upwards as far as a **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>
Or does so many times, it is rightly called authentic.
Lest the rule fail, it is finally verified thus:
If the final **neuma** is known to be concordant with the authentic.
If a chant should be doubtful, and if you cannot know which it is
By the notes alone, it desires to be authentic.
For it is fitting that an interpreter, in ambiguous cases, confirms the 
Better part, while disregarding the lesser. <note>In medieval thought, authentic modes were considered more "noble" or "better" than their plagal counterparts.</note>
So I wish it to be, even if it falls under the law of the first plagal.
This the final **neuma** of the chant also achieves.
And briefly, if the end does not recede from the law,
You will easily be able to know the mode which the chant obeys.
But if the notes disagree with the end, let it be believed honestly:
The law yields to the end, which does not take such things poorly.
