## CHAPTER XIX.

### *Concerning the trope, the tenor, and the tail, which are observed in song.*

Having addressed the question of the tones in that they all properly end in the "low" notes—though by happenstance some end in the "high" notes, except for the seventh and eighth modes, which do not change their location—three other properties must be noted in song as it is usually sung in the church. Their names are these: trope, tenor, and tail, <note>In this context, John de Muris is defining technical parts of a melody. *Tropus* (trope) here refers to a melodic "turning" toward a mode; *tenor* refers to the sustaining or reciting note; *cauda* (tail) refers to the closing melisma or concluding notes.</note> at least insofar as they are named from the end. For "trope" signifies many things ambiguously: the grammarian and the rhetorician call a trope a "figure," a manner or a certain figurative way of speaking. But a trope in music is a certain proclamation of the voice which is sung in a specific tone, adapted especially around whatever the end may be; even when it is the beginning or the middle of the song, the intention of the skillful singer always turns the melody back to the proper end of some specific and specifically intended tone. This "turning back" or proclamation is called a "trope" in song, acting as a "conversion" toward the tone intended by the singer. 

This trope sometimes begins at the very start of the song and never deviates from the law or course of the mode, as in the antiphon: *To all who fear God* <note>original: "Omnibus Deum timentibus"</note>; in such cases, either no one or only fools seem to doubt the tones. Sometimes the trope arises in the middle of the song, and sometimes not far from the end, as is evident in this Responsory: *Prepare your hearts for the Lord* <note>original: "Praeparate corda vestra Domino"</note>; in the beginning it seems to belong to the "authentic protus" (that is, the first mode), but in the end it finishes in ***E-la-mi*** <note>The note E in the medieval hexachord system.</note> and is assigned to the "protus deuterus" (that is, the third mode). Also in the Responsory *Rejoice, Mary* <note>original: "Gaude Maria"</note>; in the beginning and mid-

<column-break/>

dle it belongs to the "authentic deuterus" (that is, the third mode), but in the end it is given to the "plagal of the third" (that is, the sixth mode). For as Aristotle says: *The end is the best part of a thing*; and likewise: *The end is that for the sake of which a thing exists*; thus it rightly happens in song that it is best recognized by its end. Therefore, let him who does not wish to repent after his judgment beware of judging too quickly. Whence Solomon says: *My son, be quick to hear, but slow to judge.* <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 5:11: "Be swift to hear, but be slow to speak."</note>

It should also be noted that certain songs are turned away from the property of one tone toward another by some people—not by reason, but by a certain custom—and by others they are finished in a different way and through a different key. In such cases, as has been said, to avoid the controversy of litigants, we ought to follow or at least tolerate the customs of the local churches. This occurs because, in such a song, different people will perceive things differently in comparison to the various tones. For example, this antiphon: *And looking back* <note>original: "Et respicientes"</note> is finished by some as if it were in the third mode, and by others as if it were in the eighth. Just as some finish the end of an antiphon, such as *Do good* <note>original: "Benefac."</note>, sometimes so that it is in the fourth mode, and sometimes so that it is in the eighth. Likewise this antiphon: *It has budded* <note>original: "Germinavit."</note> is sometimes finished as if it were in the first mode, sometimes as the fourth, and sometimes as the eighth. Because examples of these are easy even for a singer to find, we do not include them in the text.

From the aforesaid, it is manifest to the diligent observer that the division of a song regarding the diversity of tones happens in two ways: for sometimes the final line in the song is the same for both points of division, and then there is doubt...

<summary>John de Muris explains the concept of the "trope" in music as a melodic turning point that defines a chant's mode, emphasizing that the end of a piece is the ultimate decider of its classification. He also acknowledges that local church customs often lead to the same chant being categorized or performed in different modes.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how to classify melodies into specific modes or "tones." The previous page introduced the concept of the trope as a melodic "turning" that guides a song toward its proper ending. Here, the author addresses ambiguous chants that seem to sit between two modes and introduces the concepts of the tenor (the reciting note) and the "tail" (a concluding melodic flourish).</meta>

<page-num>229</page-num>
<header>THE SUMMARY OF MUSIC.</header>

...whether a chant is contained within the <term>authentic mode</term> <note>The "authentic" modes are the four primary scales in medieval music (Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian), which typically have a higher range than their "plagal" counterparts.</note>, or within its <term>plagal mode</term> <note>The "plagal" modes share the same final note as the authentic ones but sit at a lower pitch range.</note>; and in these cases, the sheer number of notes usually makes the distinction. Sometimes, however, there is doubt regarding a chant that some people assign to one "final" <term>key</term> <note>original: "clavem... finalem"; referring to the concluding note of the melody.</note>, and thus it is reduced to the mode proper to that ending. Among others, the same chant—using a different final key, and indeed a different starting key—is judged by the mode that is "at home" with that ending.

For example, regarding this <term>antiphon</term> <note>A short chant usually performed before and after a psalm.</note> *Glorious Princes* <note>original: "Gloriosi principes"</note>, there is doubt whether it belongs to the sixth or eighth mode, depending on whether it begins and ends on *F-fa-ut* or on *G-sol-re-ut* <note>These are names for notes in the medieval "hexachord" system: F and G.</note>. However, it more properly belongs to the sixth. This is similar to what happens with the antiphon *No one has condemned you, woman* <note>original: "nemo te condemnavit mulier"</note>: for if it begins and ends on *F-fa-ut*, it becomes the sixth mode; but if it begins and ends on *G-sol-re-ut*, it becomes the eighth, and it is more properly the eighth. Likewise, for the response *For the sinful nation* <note>original: "Genti peccatrici"</note>, the chant is ambiguous... and in these cases, one must yield to the custom of the Church and consult the book or the mark of the master.

The term **Tenor** is also used for many things; the "tenor" of a speech is called its summary. However, in music, the **Tenor** is a certain fitness of the melody that holds the chant within the boundaries of its mode. The tenor of a chant is observed through these two words, *World without end, amen* <note>original: "seculorum amen"; these are the final words of the "Gloria Patri," used to determine the reciting note of a mode.</note>, and especially through these and not others, because they are the end of the <term>versicle</term>, which is very frequently performed. 

There is a difference between the **trope** and the **tenor**, because the trope itself sometimes begins at the start of a chant, sometimes in the middle, and sometimes near the end. It is also clear that the "final neuma" <note>A neuma is a melodic phrase or group of notes; the "final neuma" is a specific melodic gesture used at the end of a chant.</note>, which was mentioned above, and the trope are the same thing; and every mode has its own trope near the end—I say "near the end,"

<column-break/>

and not *at* the end, because a plagal mode and its authentic partner share the same final note; therefore, they cannot be distinguished by that note alone. And although there are as many tenors as there are modes, the beginning of one tenor is sometimes shared by several in succession, and sometimes not, according to the beginning of the second tenor. Sometimes the "high a" <note>original: "a. vero acuta"; referring to the pitch A4 in modern notation.</note> is the beginning of the tenor for the first, fourth, and sixth modes; "high c" for the third, fifth, and eighth; "high d" for the seventh, and so on.

But someone might ask: why do the second and seventh modes, above all others, have special letters for their starting notes? To this it must be said that this may be done to signify that these two modes behave far differently than the rest. For the second mode descends further than the others, and the seventh, in its entirety, ascends more than the others. I say "in its entirety" because the sixth mode is found to touch the highest "d" in some places, though rarely (as stated above), but it is often found to be lower than the seventh.

The **Tail** <note>original: "Cauda"; a melisma or concluding flourish of notes.</note> or **End** in a chant is a certain melody that is usually performed once a chant is finished to distinguish its mode and to honor its tenor. And because a "tail" is the end of an animal, and the name "end" seems to be derived from the nature of the thing, this "end" or "tail" is usually added to the final antiphon. For this reason, in the office of <term>Compline</term> <note>The final prayer service of the day in the Divine Office.</note>, since there is only a single antiphon over the psalms, it ought not to have a tail; for if it is not present where it is most expected, it should not be where it is less expected. And because of this—that the antiphon in Compline over the psalms should not have a tail, nor the one over the *Song of Simeon* <note>original: "nunc dimittis"</note>—the antiphons in the other <term>Hours</term> <note>The various prayer services throughout the day.</note> should likewise not have tails.

->*Verses on the Same Subject.*<-

Having said what a mode is and where it may go,
The wise singer must yet know three other things.
He should distinguish what a trope or tenor is, and what the final tail signifies;
Let him see the ambiguity that music requires.
In song, a "trope" <note>original: "tropus"; here referring to a melodic turning point or formula that characterizes a mode.</note> is a certain turning of the voice,
For I believe it touches upon the intended end of the chant.
Sometimes it arises early, sometimes near the end;
Through this means, the chant is accustomed to seek its harbor.
This latter trope may be known as the final <term>neume</term> <note>original: "neuma"; a group of notes sung to a single syllable, often forming a melodic phrase.</note>,
Which wins for itself the right to be the conclusion of the aforementioned mode.
Whatever precedes it, carrying its former weight,
When the trope arrives, the trope must give the name.
There is a tenor of words, and a tenor of voices is taught;
By it, the chant is held within the boundaries of the mode.
The words *World* <note>original: "Secula"; the first word of the concluding phrase of the Gloria Patri, "Seculorum Amen."</note> give it its name, if *Amen*
Is now joined to it, but I deprive it of song <note>A poetic way of saying the author is focusing on the technical term rather than the melody itself.</note>.
More often than the rest, this is the voice in the singer's mouth;
It ought therefore to enjoy the honor of its name.
The trope comes before the end, and the tenor accompanies the end.
It approves the mode itself as if it were held to be legitimate.
To each mode let its own trope and tenor be assigned;
And let the "tail" <note>original: "cauda"; a concluding melodic flourish or melisma.</note>, the final modulation, duly follow.
It does not prick from behind with the point of a deceitful weapon.
Whatever it does in front, if it is found to be a faithful friend 
Behind, it should not be called wicked.
A "tail" sometimes denotes evil, or the ruin of fraud;
The peacock, the capon, and the bird of prey are adorned with the same.
So it is in song: because the "tail" knows not how to harm,
It proves the chant, it adorns it; thus it ought rightly to please.

---

### CHAPTER XX.
### *How and where the* GLORIA *is begun, and concerning the semitones and the differences of the modes.*

Since the tenor of any mode, which is the *world without end, amen* <note>original: "seculorum amen"; the standard melodic formula used to end a psalm verse.</note>, is the end of the little verse which is the *Glory be to the Father* <note>original: "Gloria patri"</note>; from what has been said, it is clear how the aforementioned verse is finished. From this, therefore, we must see how it ought to be be-

<column-break/>

-gun, and especially according to how the psalm ought to be. For the Church must use <term>psalmodizing</term> <note>The practice of singing psalms according to set melodic patterns called "tones."</note> very frequently, and this is to investigate how the psalm is to be sung according to the tenor of each mode.

It should be known, therefore, that the *Gloria* of the first, fifth, and sixth modes begins on *F-fa-ut* <note>This refers to the note F in the medieval system of solmization syllables.</note>; the second on *low C*; the fourth on *low E*; the third and eight-

...of the eighth mode on *G. sol, re, ut*; of the seventh mode on B-natural <note>original: "♮. duro"; referring to the "hard" or B-natural pitch in the medieval hexachord system</note>. And it must be noted that although we have assigned only one *seculorum* <note>original: "seculorum"; the musical formula for the conclusion of the Gloria Patri, named after its final words "saeculorum. Amen"</note> to each mode as its tenor, nevertheless the tenor of each mode has either one <term>difference</term> <note>original: "differentia"; a melodic variation at the end of a psalm tone designed to lead smoothly into the beginning of the specific antiphon that follows</note> or several; except for the second mode, where the tenor itself is sufficient without any difference. The reason one tenor has more differences than another is because the beginnings of the antiphons in one mode are more varied than in another, and therefore it requires more differences so that the approach to the start of the antiphon is made more easily, the psalmody being situated according to this or that tenor or difference. However, according to the various customs of different churches, more or fewer differences are assigned to the tenors; hence the saying: "If you are in Rome, sing in the Roman manner; if you are elsewhere, sing as they do there" <note>A musical adaptation of the famous proverb attributed to St. Ambrose</note>.

It should also be noted that just as there are eight modes and eight tenors of those modes, so also there are eight <term>half-stops</term> <note>original: "hemitonia"; in this context, it refers to the middle cadence or "mediant" of a psalm verse where the singer takes a breath</note>, which are named from *hemis*, meaning "half," and *tonus*. For just as the melodic movement of a mode is considered around the beginning and the end, so it is also considered regarding its middle. However, more by custom than by theory, two beginnings and two half-stops are given to the eighth mode, because the differences for the antiphon *Nos qui vivimus* <note>original: "we who live"; a famous antiphon usually associated with the "Tonus Peregrinus" or wandering tone</note> and similar ones are assigned a special half-stop that differs from the half-stop of its own tenor and its other differences. These half-stops are also sung differently

<column-break/>

in the second, seventh, and eighth modes according to the different regions of various churches. This should not seem strange, since even the exchange of clothing and social customs varies. Among all people, it should please a person to adapt to those with whom he chooses to live; for a wise man changes his habits according to the times without it being a crime.

It must also be considered that in the *Benedictus* <note>The Song of Zechariah, used in the morning service of Lauds</note> and in the *Magnificat* <note>The Song of Mary, used in the evening service of Vespers</note>, the half-stops differ from the half-stops of the psalms in the first, fourth, sixth, and eighth modes; in the remaining modes, they agree with the half-stops of the psalmody. Examples of these would be placed in the text if it were not so tedious to mix the music in with the prose. But use your own wit to grasp more from my words; if you wish to gain practical experience in these matters, turn yourself to a "tonary" <note>original: "libellum tonorum"; a reference book that categorized antiphons by their modes and endings</note> and practice your studies there, even once you have learned the art, until the skill is transformed into a fixed habit. It should also be observed with diligent attention that just as the melodies of the psalms vary according to the variety of the modes, so also do the verses of the <term>Responsories</term> <note>a type of chant where a soloist's verse is followed by a choral response</note>. Likewise, the psalm and the *Gloria* of the <term>Introit</term> <note>the chant sung during the entrance of the ministers at Mass</note> vary according to the different modes. But because such things are demonstrated plainly to the eye in almost any church by the tonary, it is proper that we should omit whatever might be determined more diffusely about them, because as Horace says: "You shall not linger around the common and trivial circle" <note>A quote from Horace's "Ars Poetica," advising writers to avoid the obvious or over-explained</note>.

<header>SUMMARY OF MUSIC.</header>

### CHAPTER XXI.

**How and in how many ways error occurs in singing.**

Since the proper nature of chant is often not observed by everyone, we must see in how many and which ways error occurs in singing. For error happens sometimes from inability, sometimes from negligence, sometimes from stubbornness, and sometimes from carelessness. From inability, the elderly, children, and the sick sing poorly, and this is pardonable, because a natural inability excuses such people; concerning this, Persius <note>A Roman satirist (34–62 AD)</note> teaches: *a natural flaw is not to be mocked*. From negligence, those who are drunk sing poorly, as do those who are lazy, or those who despise practicing the chant more diligently; it also includes those who judge the whole from a part without foresight; these people are hardly excused, or are not worthy of pardon at all. Regarding the first of these, Aristotle says: *the drunkard shall be punished with a double penalty* <note>original: "ebrius duplici pœna punietur"; a reference to Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics regarding crimes committed while intoxicated</note>; regarding the others, it is well said: *because he who is ignorant shall be ignored* <note>original: "quia ignorans ignorabitur"; a reference to 1 Corinthians 14:38</note>; against the last group, it is said: *I hope he lacks success, whoever thinks deeds should be judged by their outcome* <note>original: "careat successibus opto, quisquis ab eventu facta notanda putat"; a quote from Ovid's Heroides</note>. For it happens that different chants start in the same way but end differently, such as these <term>Antiphons</term> <note>short chants sung with psalms</note>: the antiphon *Blessed be [the name of the Lord]* <note>original: "Benedictum sit"</note> and *Glorious princes* <note>original: "Gloriosi principes"</note>; and this one: *The saints were singing* <note>original: "cantabant sancti"</note>; and this one: *Under the throne of God* <note>original: "sub Throno Dei"</note>; as well as these: *This child* <note>original: "Iste puer"</note> and *In the fragrance* <note>original: "In odore"</note>. Yet all these differ according to the <term>modes of the reciting tones</term> <note>original: "tropos tenorum"; the melodic formulas used for psalm verses</note>, which is clearly recognized from the ending.

<meta>ANCIENT WRITERS ON MUSIC. VOL III.</meta>

<column-break/>

From stubbornness, those sing poorly who, having abandoned the proper law of chant because of their own emotional impulse, exceed the limits and pervert what has been properly composed; they teach such perversions to others and lead them into incorrigible habits, to the point that not their use, but rather their abuse, seems to be held as authority. Against such people it is said: *he who sins by teaching to sin, sins twice: against himself, who is guilty, and against those whom he makes guilty*. Of such people Aristotle says: that some are born to contradict; and these types exult most when they defend their own perverse opinion with shouting.

From carelessness, those sing poorly who, either affected by boredom or exhausted by labor, depress <note>sing lower than intended</note> those parts which should be raised in the chant, sparing not the chant but themselves; or, led by a certain impudence, they inappropriately raise those parts which should be depressed, and finish the chant clumsily in comparison to what preceded it. An example of the first is the <term>Gradual</term> <note>a responsorial chant sung after the first Scripture reading of the Mass</note> *You who sit, O Lord* <note>original: "Qui sedes Domine"</note>; there, at the words *above the Cherubim* <note>original: "super Cherubim"</note>, when they ought to sing higher, they sing lower and err. Likewise another: *When princes persecuted* <note>original: "Cum principes persecutis"</note>, there at the word *he desired* <note>original: "concupivit"</note>; for they ought to sing higher on <term>acute c</term> <note>a high note in the medieval hexachord system</note>, but they sing on <term>soft b</term> <note>b-flat</note>. Likewise another Gradual: *You have proved, O Lord* <note>original: "probasti domine"</note>, there at *fire me* <note>original: "igne me"</note>; for when they ought to begin on <term>acute e</term>, they begin on <term>grave F</term> <note>a low F</note>. Equally, they raise some things which should be depressed, as in the antiphon *When the Lord approached Jerusalem* <note>original: "cum appropinquaret dominus Ierusalem"</note>, there at *if you also had known* <note>original: "si cognovisses & tu"</note>. Just as in the word *Awesome* <note>original: "terribilis"</note> at the phrase *and the gate of heaven* <note>original: "et porta cæli"</note>; for it must be sung in the low notes, but they inappropriately raise it.

Also, those sin through carelessness who, by beginning the chant with a tasteless and crude voice, twist it from its legitimate course; this usually happens in these antiphons: *When they brought in the child* <note>original: "Cum inducerent puerum"</note>. *When John had heard* <note>original: "Cum audisset Iohannes"</note>—

# JOHANNES DE MURIS

...tones; for since they are of the first mode, if a note is inflected too much, they seem to harmonize with these: *He who is of the earth* <note>original: "qui de terra est"; an antiphon for the Monday after Low Sunday</note> and the antiphon *When you were born* <note>original: "Quando natus es"; an antiphon for the Feast of the Circumcision</note>, which belong to the third mode. Likewise, through carelessness, scribes commit most harmful sins and cause very many others to sin; they do not observe the initial and final clefs <term>claves: the musical signs at the beginning or end of a staff that determine the pitch of the notes</term> of the chant. While they begin the chant clumsily, they cannot reach its legitimate end; they either corrupt it in its course, or distort it from its own proper ending, and sometimes they even force it into another mode. As an example of this sin, let another chant be recalled which by necessity is transposed from the low notes to the high notes <term>gravibus ad acutas: shifting a melody from a lower register to a higher one, often by a fifth</term>; if anyone were to begin this differently, he would wander astray in his writing, and later in his singing.

Likewise, those who believe and say that "the note does not err" sin through carelessness. Such people attribute a single tone to everything; they seem to neigh like horses or bellow like oxen rather than actually sing anything.

<column-break/>

Regarding such people, Horace says in his poetry that *he is laughed at who always blunders on the same string.* <note>original: "ridetur, chorda qui semper oberrat eadem"; a quote from Horace’s Ars Poetica</note> Such people are ignorant of the fact that a note performs the same function in chant as a figure does in poetic meter. For the intention of the composer <note>original: "actoris"</note> in chant and the composer in meter is the same in kind: namely, that the voice should harmonize with the subject matter of its text. If the subject matter of the text in the chant is joyful, the note ought to be light and happy, such as in the chants for St. Mary, St. John the Baptist, Epiphany, the Resurrection, and similar feasts. If, however, the text signifies something laborious, either according to virtue or according to appearance, the note ought to be heavy, and move from B-flat <term>b. molli: literally "soft B," the origin of the musical flat symbol</term> to B-natural <term>♮ durum: literally "hard B," the origin of the musical natural and sharp symbols</term>, and vice-versa. This is clear enough in the chants *Fabian*, and *They gathered together* <note>original: "collegerunt"; likely the Responsory "Collegerunt pontifices" for Passion Sunday</note>, and in the length of the verses of the Responsories for St. Stephen, and others like them. When the subject matter is of a middle sort, the chant ought to behave in a middle way; yet fools think this lacks a rational basis.

## CHAPTER XXII.

### *How new song is to be made and diversified.*

Once the property of song is known, it will not seem enough to anyone that he can sing only those things which were discovered by others previously; but perhaps, led by the alacrity of his own virtue or by the prayers of others, he will take care to compose a text <term>dictamen: a formal written composition or poem</term> with fitting notes, or at least to join a suitable melody to a text received from elsewhere.

Therefore, this singer must consider how he may adapt his own song to its pre-determined tone <term>tono: used here to mean musical mode</term>, because just as not all men take delight in the same foods—but some in sweet, some in bitter, and some in those that hold a middle way—so also in song: it delights some to hear nothing but the lingering and final wanderings of the first tone;

<column-break/>

others, however, delight in the precipitous and obscure depths of the second tone. To some, the almost severe and indignant leaping-forth of the third tone is more pleasing; some the sound of the fourth tone draws in, as if soothing and flattering. Others are soothed by the wanton playfulness of the fifth tone; others are moved by the sixth voice as if by a certain sweet lament of lovers, or like the song of the nightingale <note>original: "philomelæ"</note>. To others, the free leaps of the seventh tone seem joyful; others gladly attend to the seriousness of the eighth tone as if it were a general or primary teaching above the rest.

Whence also Terence, considering the different intentions of different people, said: *There are as many opinions as there are heads; each has his own way.* <note>original: "Quot capita, tot sententiæ, suus cuique mos est"; a classic proverb from Terence's play Phormio</note>

Therefore, if a musician composes a song at the request of another, if he wishes to satisfy the intention of the petitioner, he shall inquire from that person in which species of song he especially delights, and according to this, he shall adapt the song to the proposed tone. But if the character of the petitioner...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on musical composition from Chapter XXII, moving from the general desire to create new melodies to the specific rules of matching musical character to the emotional content of a text.</meta>

# JOHANNES DE MURIS

->He should not pay as much attention to the property of the material itself as he considers what Horace says in his *Art of Poetry*, because *one single way of measuring verse does not suit every subject.*<- Hence he says: *Strong wars rejoice to be told in the Maeonian foot* <note>original: "Fortia mæonio gaudent pede bella referri"; the Maeonian foot refers to the dactylic hexameter used by Homer for epic poetry</note>; and again: *He sins against Andromache, who acts the part of Thais* <note>original: "peccat in Andromachem, Thaida sis quis agit"; meaning it is a mistake to play a tragic, noble figure like Andromache in the style of a comic courtesan like Thais</note>. So also in composing a song, a similar caution must be applied, so that a song's own proper melody is joined to the subject matter of the text. For if the material is sad, the song should properly be humble and low, as in the Responsory <term>℟</term> *Deliver me, O Lord* <note>original: "Libera me Domine"</note>, and in the antiphon that suggests the lament of David: *I grieve over you* <note>original: "Doleo super te"</note>; and similarly in the lament of Dido: *O glory, O of the Libyan kings* <note>original: "O decus o Lybiæ regum"</note>. For this reason, the Tract <note>a reflective chant that replaces the Alleluia during penitential seasons</note> of the Mass in the second mode, as well as the eighth, should be sung either in the Mass, or for the departed, or on a day of fasting; and in these, the song will either be properly mournful, or at least serious. Because of this, these modes are by right assigned to these Tracts above all others. If, however, the material is joyful, the song should also conform itself to the same in high notes. This is done at Easter, when the *Alleluia* is sung, and *The good shepherd has arisen* <note>original: "surrexit pastor bonus"</note>; along with *King of glory* <note>original: "rex gloriæ"</note>, and similar pieces. But if the material is happy and playful, a song with leaps is appropriate, as in the Epiphany *The old man* <note>original: "Veterem hominem"</note> etc.; for Saint John, *Because of the inseparable* <note>original: "Propter inseparabilem"</note> etc.; and for Saint Mary: *Rejoice, O Mother* <note>original: "Gaude mater"</note>. If the material is of a middle sort, the song should properly conform itself to that middle way. For it happens that a song is made by some in such a way that it runs through every mode. Thus its first small part is rendered in the first mode, the second in the second, and so on for the others; and this is done so that the musician may show the skill of his mastery in song, or because they consider that "sameness is the mother of boredom," while

<column-break/>

diversity stimulates the appetite. A second cause for this diversity can occur when consideration is given to the subject matter, in which there are some prosperous things and some adverse things, as is clear in the chant for Saint Catherine, for Saint Gregory, for the Transfiguration of the Lord, and similar ones.

It should also be noted that certain inventors of song apply some special sign to their melody; hence some grant a special lower note to repetitions which the preceding part did not have at first, as in the Responsory <term>℟</term> *He descended from heaven* <note>original: "Descendit de cælis"</note>. Such is the chant of Saint Lambert throughout. Others do not wish to build the structure of their song except upon the bases of rhythm or meter, examples of which easily occur to anyone who looks. Others declare the "tenor" <note>the reciting tone or structural pitch</note> of the mode of an antiphon through the verse that accompanies the antiphon. This is seen in the chant of Saint Lawrence, Saint Paul, and the Holy Trinity. It is also useful to the composer of song, if he wishes to compose and arrange a melody delightfully, to arrange pauses in the song where the text itself requires a time for pausing; this doctrine is well observed in this antiphon: *When she was betrothed* <note>original: "Cum esset desponsata"</note> etc., as in that one: *When they brought in the child Jesus* <note>original: "Cum inducerent puerum Iesum"</note>; and let similar judgments be made of similar cases. Otherwise, when the meaning of the text seems to hinder the note, and vice-versa, weariness is brought not only to the singer but also to the listener. Let the inventor of song also note that the intervals of the fourth <term>diatessaron</term> and the fifth <term>diapente</term> are delightful, which is clear through the *Alleluia, the voice of exultation* <note>original: "vox exultationis"</note>; and these can be placed quite often. Even the octave <term>diapason</term>, if its extremes are firmly observed, is interspersed with delight; but because of its difficulty, it should be placed rarely.

# THE SUMMA OF MUSIC

### A Verse on the Same Subject

There is a certain type of person who knows how to sing, and sings willingly; it is enough for him that he knows how to sing decently. Yet it is not enough for another to simply walk along a certain, established path—he wishes to spend his time wandering through a shady valley <note>The author uses the "shady valley" as a metaphor for creative exploration or perhaps a lack of disciplined focus on the established rules of the art.</note>. He who desires to sing what no one has heard before must realize that if he does not sing with art, he will be as nothing to me as a singer. 

Let the musician who cares to fashion a song pay close attention to the proposed melody, which the formula <term>formula: the set of rules governing a musical mode</term> rightly shapes. The virtue of the prose's subject matter teaches this beforehand: he who follows the song should proceed according to what the text suggests. A sad subject produces a sad and low-pitched song; a joyful subject produces a joyful one. He who remains in the middle—dealing with neutral subjects—commands the song to be quiet and temperate.

When a **Tract** <term>Tract: a reflective, melismatic chant used in the Mass during penitential seasons like Lent</term> fashions a lament or at least treats serious matters, the second mode will rightly be used, as will the eighth "touch" <note>original: "tactus"; referring to the melodic range or specific modal characteristics</note>. When a festive king wishes to have the *voice of one exulting* <note>original: "Vox exultantis cum rex."</note>, he surely intends to teach the greatest joys through his song.

But yet, not every mouth praises every flavor: a voice which one person flees, another approves and teaches to be the better one. There is something else special regarding the tone <note>original: "tono"; here referring to the musical mode</note> that one person loves; while another, loving something else, asks the song to provide that specific gift. Therefore, a musician who does whatever he is asked does not always follow the natural character of the subject matter he is singing. He might excuse himself by saying he is only following the requests of his patron; but I praise more the manner of the man who fears to commit any artistic sin.

Sometimes a singer is a "new" composer while he fashions his poems; he gathers the tones himself and paints them all throughout the work. He does this, however, in such a way that the first mode holds the first seat for itself, and the others follow in order until he reaches the lowest. Perhaps they show this because they are talented in this art, or otherwise because many different things are pleasing; I prove this by the analogy of diners at a feast. In this way, bitter things <note>original: "Pontica"; literally "things from Pontus," often used by classical poets to refer to bitter herbs like wormwood or the sorrows of exile</note> are joined to sweet things, and sad things to the joyful; just as the rose stands with its thorns, or the fir tree among the brambles of the hazel.

Some believe their song will be worthy of praise and rejoice to show their own "sign" or signature style within it. Indeed, writers of books of verse sometimes attach a special and decorative sign to their work. We are taught that **Persius** <note>A Roman satirist known for his difficult and distinct style</note> and **Petrus** <note>Likely referring to a medieval poet like Peter of Blois, known for his rhythmic verse</note> observed this practice, as they are seen to adorn their verses through their own unique signs.

# JOHANNES DE MURIS

### CHAPTER XXIII.
#### *Which vices are to be avoided in a new song.*

From what has already been said, it is clear how a new song is to be discovered and how its proper subject matter ought to be intended—unless perhaps it is formed otherwise for some external reason. But as Aristotle testifies in the *Topics*, it is of the same character to love one’s friends and hate one’s enemies, just as it is to attend to the properties which are rightly due to a song and to avoid the vices which corrupt a song by depraving it. Since a thing is not easily avoided unless it is known, it is appropriate that those things which are faulty in a song be carefully and studiously avoided by the master of a new song.

Therefore, let the new master of song take care lest a contrary melodic trope be joined to the course of any mode <note>original: "tonus"; the author uses this to refer to the eight ecclesiastical modes</note>. That is, let a melody that is appropriate for one mode at its beginning and middle not be assigned to a different mode at the end. This doctrine was formerly observed in the chant for the Trinity <note>likely referring to the Introit *Benedicta sit sancta Trinitas*</note>; however, it is handled poorly in the Communion *Princes have persecuted me* <note>original: "Principes persecuti sunt me"; Psalm 119:161</note>, which follows the law and course sometimes of the third mode, sometimes of the sixth, and finally has the trope of the first, and thus remains in the first mode. That vice in music is proportionally likened to a **solecism** <term>solecism: a grammatical mistake or absurdity</term> in grammar, which is caused by the incoherence of the accents of the words.

Likewise, another vice in a new song must be avoided: that there should not occur in it an irregular interval, or any other than the nine intervals assigned above. This would be as if a 

<column-break/>

transition were made from the note **E-la-mi** to **B-flat** <note>original: "B. molle"; this transition creates the tritone, famously called the "devil in music" (diabolus in musica)</note>, or vice versa. This vice is likened to a false proposition, which is greatly avoided by the logician. Irregular music of this kind is rightly called **false music** <term>musica falsa: the use of pitches outside the standard hexachord system, often involving accidentals</term>, and it should be strictly avoided. Likewise, in the formation of a new song, the useless repetition of the same interval should not be applied, as is found in this Tract: *He who dwells* <note>original: "Qui habitat"; Psalm 91</note> and *my refuge, my God*, and similarly in this Introit: *have mercy on me, Lord*. It should be known, however, that an interval or a musical phrase is heard with delight through a single repetition; therefore, it can be repeated once, but rarely, as in the Alleluia, *The good shepherd has arisen* at the words *for his sheep* <note>original: "pro ovibus"</note>, and in the chant for Saint Nicholas, *Clementiam*. Consider that this vice is similar to **trifling** <term>nugatio: a rhetorical term for the useless repetition of words (tautology)</term>, which the rhetorician detests most of all.

Likewise, the new singer should diligently avoid both mutilated brevity and tedious prolixity. These two vices seem to have a similarity to ellipsis and excessive wordiness <note>original: "eclipsi & macrologia"</note>. Horace removes these two from a good poet, where he says: *I labor to be brief, I become obscure; those following light things fail too much.* <note>original: "brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio: Sectantes levia nimium deficiunt"; from Horace's Ars Poetica</note> But if some or all of the aforesaid vices are seen daily in the ecclesiastical books, let such excess be blamed on their first composers, who can to some extent be excused by their own authority. Yet modern composers must know that they are not permitted everything that was permitted to the ancients; this is clear in the books of the ancients, both in the construction of prose and in the figures of meters.

### Verse on the Same Subject.

Having said what is fitting when a song is begun,
Let this be held alongside: what might stain the song.
For the prudent traveler at least wishes to know the pit,
So that the lover of the straight path may leap over it.
Let no melodic trope unjustly push the course from its seat <note>The "seat" refers to the final or tonic of the mode; the author warns against wandering into a different mode.</note>.
It is better that what is concordant be with it always and everywhere.
There is another vice: the leap, which the rule rejects;
Let him who sees such things say this method is false.
And note that the same note should never be repeated more than twice,
Excepting the unison <note>original: "unisonum"; here referring to repeated strikes of the same pitch</note>, because this is repeated more often.
Both the too short and the too long note recede without praise:
One song moves nothing here, while the other harms through boredom.
Virtue, seen in the middle of vices to be pleasing,
Teaches us to rightly hold the middle ground in song as well.
There is another who asks: why are such things forbidden now,
When they are noted as having been observed well enough by the ancients?
Let him hear this: many things are not permitted to the moderns,
Which the ancients previously set down in their four-fold writings.
For they indeed often employed many ways of speaking,
Which are now a vice, because they are faulty for singing.

### CHAPTER XXIV.
#### On polyphony.

Thus far we have spoken of simple song <note>Plainchant or monophony</note>, which is called "simple" because it is sung either by one person, or by many in one single way. Now, however, proposing to bring an end to this work, lest we seem entirely ignorant of polyphony, we shall say a small thing about what it is and how it is divided.

Polyphony is named from *poly* (<term>πολυς</term>: many), which means plurality, and *phone* (<term>φωνης</term>: voice), which means sound, because it is nothing other than a way of singing by several people observing different melodies. It is divided into three species: namely, **dyphonia**, **triphonia**, and **tetraphonia**—that is, into double, triple, and quadruple song.

<column-break/>

**Dyaphonia** <note>Also known as organum; the singing of two distinct parts</note> is a way of singing in two modes; and it is divided into **basilica** and **organica**. **Basilica** is a way of singing a melody in two parts such that one voice holds one note continuously, which is like the base <note>original: "basis"</note> of the other singing companion; the other partner begins the song either at the fifth (<term>diapente</term>: an interval of five notes) or at the octave (<term>diapason</term>: an interval of eight notes), sometimes ascending and sometimes descending, so that at the pause <note>A cadence or resting point</note> he accords in some way with the one who observes the base. **Organica dyaphonia** is the melody of two or more people singing in two parts in such a way that one voice ascends while the other descends, and vice versa; yet in pausing they agree especially either on the same note, or the fifth, or the octave. It is called or-

<meta>The catchword "au-" indicates the next word is likely "autem" (however) or "authentica" (authentic).</meta>

--- Page 252 ---
<meta>This page continues the transition from monophonic plainchant to the complexities of polyphony (multi-voiced music). The previous page ended while explaining that "simple" song remains simple even if many people sing the same melody; this page introduces "organic" music, where voices move in different parts.</meta>

...[single melody]; **organic** <note>original: "organica"; referring to organum, an early form of polyphony</note> music, however, is named from the organ, which is an instrument for singing, because in such a species of song the singer labors much.

**Triphonia** <note>literally "three-sounding"; music for three voices</note> is a melody or manner of singing by three or more voices; and it is performed in three ways: namely, so that one or more voices hold a single note continuously as a base; and by another one or more, the same melody is begun at the **fifth** <term>diapente: the musical interval of a perfect fifth</term>, and is sung in that same course until the end; and by a third one or more, the same melody is begun continuously at the **octave** <term>diapason: the musical interval of an octave</term>, and is lawfully finished in the first voice of the course of the same song. This manner of triphonia is begun just like a *basilica* <note>likely referring to a "stately" or church-style of polyphonic beginning</note> triphonia. **Organic triphonia** is a melody or manner of singing by three or more, divided into three ways so that one or more voices hold the base in the low notes of the pauses; by another one or more, an organic *distertius* <note>original: "distertius"; likely a technical term for a third voice part moving in relation to the others</note> song is begun at the fifth, or perhaps at the **fourth** <term>diatessaron: the musical interval of a perfect fourth</term>; and by a third one or more, an organic diverse <note>original: "diformis"</note> song is begun at the octave, with the third part meeting the second organic part. When the first part uses some concordant pause either at the fifth or at the octave, it can also happen that an organic and dissimilar triple note is sung by these three parts together; and this manner is rightly called organic triphonia.

<column-break/>

The teaching is similar concerning **tetraphonia** <note>literally "four-sounding"; music for four voices</note>, in which four different parts vary: the lowest part indeed begins in the low notes; the second part begins the same melody at the fifth; the third, with respect to the first, begins at the octave; and the fourth, with respect to the second, begins at the octave similarly. Thus, the four parts, running through the melody together, pause together and finish the song together, so that each part follows its aforementioned manner. **Organic** music, as has been said, took its name from the vocal organ, because different organs <note>the author puns on the musical instrument and the human vocal apparatus</note> resonate in different ways, just as individual humans have different individual forms. Organics is nothing other than the disparate concord of a melody meeting itself in different ways; for while in such a species of song one part ascends greatly, another indeed descends greatly, and vice-versa; and they pause together, as has been said, either on the same pitch, or at the fifth, or at the octave. If, however, it happens that they pause elsewhere—which is seen to happen rarely—one should not hold the note for long, but should quickly spring back from the pause. Yet it often happens in organic song that the lower part while pausing has few notes while the upper part has many; in that case, the few notes are drawn out slowly, while the many are to be sung quickly, until at last they meet at the end either on the same pitch, as was said, or at the fifth, or at the fourth.

### Verse on the Same Subject.

> Simple song is that which is noted by the rules above,
> Nor should it be joined to double, triple, or quadruple parts.
> If the manner is single, it is called "simple" of voice,
> Which is not changed even if there are many singers.
> It is called "double" not because there are two singing in this way,
> Rather, the "double" manner is that which those practicing the art observe.

One part holds the note, while the other harmonizes aptly,
And this pleases the ear, captured by its great sweetness:
Or each part sings, both discordant and concordant with its companion.
You might call this the **organic genre** <term>Organicum genus: a style of polyphony (organum) where voices move in relation to each other, rather than just in unison</term> of such a melody.
From there, a three-part song grows with a triple melody,
It does not swell merely because three people sing in a larger number,

### CHAPTER XXV.
#### *The allegorical covering of music.*

According to the philosopher <note>original: "teste philosopho"; a standard medieval reference to Aristotle</note>, like rejoices in its like and rejects its opposite. Since, therefore, we have spoken of music—by whom and how it was invented, what it is, what its properties are, and what its purpose is—it does not seem unfitting that an example from other things be added to the aforementioned, to which music may seem similar. For music, to speak **symbolically** <term>tropologice: an interpretive method searching for moral or spiritual allegories</term>, appears to be similar to the Church, because it is evident that in both cases, their forms are rooted in the same types of numbers.

Musical science is one, although it is founded upon diverse parts; just as, although there are many members of the Church, the Church

<column-break/>

is nevertheless one, rooted in the unity of the Catholic faith. Hence Solomon says in the Song of Songs:
> *One is my dove, my beautiful one* etc. <note>original: "Una est columba mea, formosa mea"; quoting Song of Solomon 6:9</note>

For he spoke thus figuratively of the Holy Spirit, and of the holiness and unity of the Church. In music, a **binary** <term>binarius: the number two, or a twofold division</term> quality is found, in that it is divided into **mundane** <term>mundana: the "music of the spheres," or the mathematical harmony of the universe</term> and **human** music; just as a binary quality is proven to exist in the Church, in that it possesses two Testaments <note>The Old and New Testaments</note> for him who reads and considers by comparison, through which the Church works and joins their "walls" together through a cornerstone, which is Christ, by way of intimation. Likewise, there is another binary in music, in that it is divided into **natural** and **instrumental**; just as another binary is found in the Church, in that it utilizes both the **contemplative** and **active** lives: natural music is likened to the contemplative life, and instrumental—

Music is also likened to the contemplative life, since one who has made it a habit is able to practice it in the heart and without books; just as music is also likened to the active life, because without external instruments, such as books, a singer cannot practice. Regarding this, however, it is said that "she has chosen the best part for herself, which shall not be taken away from her" <note>A reference to Luke 10:42, where Jesus describes Mary's contemplative listening as superior to Martha's active serving.</note>: so too the use of music is not taken from one who preserves it through habit. And just as the life of Martha, which signifies the active life, is more perilous than that of Mary, because it seems to be subject to greater danger, so too those who do not know the song without books are subject to a swifter loss; for if the books are not present or ready, they appear to fall silent and know almost nothing of the song. But since "it does not happen to every man to visit Corinth," <note>original: "non cuivis hominum contingit adire Corinthum." Furthermore, the **binary** <term>binarius: the number two or a grouping of two</term> is still found in music, according to whether the song is either **authentic** <term>authentus: the four higher-register modes of Gregorian chant</term> or **plagal** <term>plagalis: the four lower-register "side" modes paired with the authentic ones</term>; just as there is a similar binary in the Church: namely, the love of God, which is like the authentic, and the love of neighbor, which is like the plagal. This is because love [of God] and the authentic song look toward those things which appear to be above; but the love of neighbor and the plagal song are assigned to the lower things.

Moreover, the **ternary** <term>ternarius: the number three or a grouping of three</term> is found in music; for song is divided into the low, the high, and the very high: <note>original: "gravem, acutum & superacutum." These refer to the different pitch registers (hexachords) used in medieval music theory.</note> just as in the Church there is found a threefold contrition of the heart (compared to the low notes), confession of the mouth (compared to the high), and satisfaction through works (compared to the very high), because just as these three relate to each other, so do those according to a comparison of degrees. Likewise,

<column-break/>

there is another ternary in music, according to whether instrumental music consists of **percussive** <term>vasalibus: literally "vessel-like" instruments, referring to bells or drums</term>, **wind** <term>foramininalibus: literally "with holes," referring to flutes, pipes, or organs</term>, or **stringed** <term>chordalibus</term> instruments. Just as there is another ternary in the Church—namely, Faith, Hope, and Charity—in which the Church solemnizes when they are properly in harmony, and rejoices festively in the manner of a harper. Likewise, a third ternary is found in music, insofar as a beginning, an end, and a middle are considered within it: just as it happens that one finds a ternary in the Church, in which the Father as the first, the Son as the second, and the Holy Spirit as the third is believed and proven to be; none of whom exists, or will be, or was without the other; and just as these three constitute one song, so these three constitute one substance of God alone.

Furthermore, in music there is the **quaternary** <term>quaternarius: the number four or a grouping of four</term>, insofar as the tones are divided into the **Protus, Deuterus, Tritus, and Tetrardus** <term>The four "maneriae" or parent-modes of the medieval system, each containing an authentic and a plagal version</term>. So too in the Church, the quaternary is the number of the virtues: namely, Prudence, Temperance, Fortitude, and Justice. In significance of these, Moses made veils and curtains for the outer decoration of the Tabernacle in four colors: purple, fine linen, hyacinth, and scarlet. Likewise, in music it is most often the custom that four lines are drawn in the upper part of the composition, without which the notes cannot guide the singer with certainty: <note>Medieval music was typically written on a four-line staff, unlike the modern five-line staff.</note> so too in the Church is the quaternary of the four principal Gospels, through which the actions of the faithful are directed toward blessedness.

Likewise, in music there are seven **final keys** <term>claves finales: the notes (D, E, F, G, etc.) on which a chant melody can end</term>; just as in the Church there are seven **canonical hours** <note>The set of eight (sometimes grouped as seven) prayer times that make up the daily Liturgy of the Hours.</note> of the office. Furthermore, in music there are seven initial letters of all the joints...

Likewise in the Church there are seven Sacraments, which are named in this way either from their effect, or because they sanctify the church, or because they are signs of a sacred thing; for one thing is perceived by the bodily senses, and another sacred thing is understood beneath it. Likewise in the Church, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit are contained in a grouping of seven; for there is the Spirit of Fear, Piety, Knowledge, Fortitude, Counsel, Understanding, and Wisdom.

Furthermore, the number eight is found in music in the tones <note>In this context, "tones" refers to the eight church modes or "tonoi."</note>, which are founded upon the aforementioned fourfold system of tones; just as in the Church there are eight Beatitudes, which are rooted in the four virtues mentioned a little before <note>The four cardinal virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance.</note>. For it is clear to anyone considering it diligently that each one of the Beatitudes preached by the Lord can be reduced to one of these four stated virtues.

Furthermore, in music nine intervals of sounds are distinguished, about which it was appropriately spoken above—both what they are and how they are distinguished from one another. Likewise, nine orders of angels are recognized by the Church, and how they are distinguished from each other: namely, angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, virtues of the heavens, Cherubim, and Seraphim. Also, in music there are nine spaces <note>The "spaces" between the lines of a musical staff.</note>, just as in the Church—at least regarding what is most frequently and generally found—there are nine readings, nine responsories, and nine psalms. This

<column-break/>

frequency of occurrence, I say, is because of the customs of the monks, who turn an ancient custom into a greater one.

Furthermore, ten lines can be seen in music <note>Refering to the "Great Staff" or the total range of the musical system used at the time.</note>: just as in the Church the Decalogue, that is, the contents of the ten commandments of the Law, is found. These are written and read here for the sake of the ignorance of the less advanced; for to expert readers many things seem equally useless, or even superfluous, which are useful to those who are less advanced. "You shall have no other gods before me," that is, you shall have me alone as God. "You shall not take the name of your God in vain," that is, you shall not swear easily or unnecessarily. "Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day," that is, hold it as holy and do no servile work on it. "Honor your father and your mother," namely by attributing reverence and service to them. "You shall not kill," adding "by your own will or hand or counsel or consent," for the sentence of a judge is permitted to do this. "You shall not commit adultery," that is, you shall not know any woman carnally or affectionately who is not your lawful wife. "You shall not steal," adding "by will or deed, taking others' property secretly and wrongly." "You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor," from which it is never permitted to do so. "You shall not covet your neighbor's wife"; if it is not permitted to covet her, it is not permitted to have her. "Nor his servant, nor his handmaid, nor his ox, nor his ass, or whatever is his, whether mobile or immobile," namely, do not desire them.

Furthermore, in music there are nineteen articles <term>articuli: the specific joints on the "Guidonian Hand" used to teach the musical scale</term>, eight in the low notes, seven in the...

# JOHN DE MURIS

<page-num>244</page-num>
<header>JOHN DE MURIS</header>

<columns>2</columns>

...high <note>original: "acutis"</note>, and four in the highest <term>peracutis: the highest register in the medieval gamut, typically from G above middle C to the high E or F</term>: just as in the Church there are certain lower ranks, certain higher ranks, and indeed certain middle ranks among the aforementioned, in which God is continually served by the orthodox. The first rank is that of the faithful and the laity remaining in charity; the second rank is that of travelers, pilgrims, and so on; the third is the Order of the Brothers of the Sword <note>A military order active in Livonia</note>; the fourth of the Templars; the fifth of the Hospitallers; the sixth of the Order of the Holy Trinity; the seventh of the House of the Teutonic Knights; the eighth of the Order of Lepers <note>Likely the Order of St. Lazarus</note>; and these eight points seem comparable to the low notes <term>graves: the lowest notes of the musical scale</term>. Likewise, there are seven orders in the Church similar to the seven points in the high notes <term>acutis: the middle register of the medieval scale</term>: the first is the order of secular clergy; the second of St. Augustine; the third of St. Benedict; the fourth of St. Bernard <note>The Cistercians</note>; the fifth of the Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>; the sixth the Order of St. William; the seventh of St. Francis: these now-mentioned are deservedly compared to the high notes, because they are higher than the low ones. Likewise, there are ranks comparable in the Church to the four highest <term>peracutis</term> musical points: the first is of the barbarians <note>Likely referring to recent converts or those on the frontiers of Christendom</note>, the second of the anchorites, the third of the hermits, the fourth of Christians captured by pagans or heretics; these bear a resemblance to the highest notes, because they surpass the others in tribulation and in the austerity of their punishments. The keys <note>Clefs or pitch-markers</note> in music are the signs of their specific

<column-break/>

points: so also in the Church there are the specific habits <note>The distinctive clothing of religious orders</note> of the said orders, by which the aforementioned orders are distinguished from one another.

Likewise, music ultimately intends delight, just as the Church sighs and says every day for that delight which is found in blessedness alone: *Thy kingdom come*; concerning which delight Paul added: *I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ*. In music there is a discrete middle key dividing the plagal song from the authentic <term>plagal and authentic: the two classifications of church modes, where authentic modes have a higher range and plagal modes a lower, "sideways" range</term>; just as in the Church, Christ is the mediator dividing the goats from the lambs, the evil from the good. It is also worthy of consideration in music what the beginning or the middle effects: in song, the trope <term>tropus: here referring to the musical mode or the specific melodic character</term> gives the song its name, and preserves it in the property of its tone: just as in the Church, however the beginning or middle of a human life may be, the final intention <note>The state of a person at the end of their life</note> either blames or commends it, and confirms a person's good or bad state. Likewise, music by its natural virtue preserves one from an immanent sickness, cures a present one, and turns demons to flight by terrifying them: and all these things can be clearly seen in the Church. Since, therefore, music has a resemblance to the Church in such things, and in so many and great ways, it is no wonder if the use of music and its solemn remembrance is observed in the Church.

# THE SUMMARY OF MUSIC

<page-num>245</page-num>
<header>THE SUMMARY OF MUSIC.</header>

A second binary <note>original: "binarius"</note> is seen in this art, by which music is held to be either natural or instrumental. This teaches us that the life of the Church is twofold: the contemplative life and the active life, which you may see joined together in equal measure. 

From here, there is a third binary, for song is divided into the "authentic" and "plagal" <term>authentic and plagal: the two forms of medieval modes; authentic modes have a higher range, while plagal modes sit lower around the same final note</term>. Thus, in the Church, we "solfa" <note>sing the notes of the scale</note> a double love: God requires the first love, but our neighbor requires the latter.

Following this, a ternary <note>original: "trinarius"</note> is found in both systems. For the high register <term>acutus</term> follows the low <term>gravem</term>, and the highest register <term>peracutus</term> follows that. In the Church, the first step is contrition of the heart, grieving for having sinned; from this comes the work of penance, which leads down to the final result. Three things give honor to the musical art: the vessel <note>the body of the instrument</note>, the string, and the air-hole. But the three virtues are faith and hope, if you join love to them. Just as a psalm has a beginning, a middle, and an end; so there are three: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

The *Protus* <term>Protus: the first of the four "maneriae" or mode families in medieval theory, encompassing the Dorian and Hypodorian modes</term> has its companions, making four in total; so too there are as many books of the Gospels in the Church. We recognize four proper clefs <note>original: "claves"</note> for these modes; recognize also as many virtues of good men. Let him be prudent, just, brave, and moderate <note>The four Cardinal Virtues: Prudence, Justice, Fortitude, and Temperance</note>, who desires to be blessed through these virtues. This is signaled by the scarlet, the blue, the purple, and the fine linen—each of these was a color sent for the coverings of the Tabernacle.

Seven small letters are the keys of the joints <note>referring to the seven note names A-G mapped onto the joints of the Guidonian Hand</note>. Say that this same number represents the sacraments in the Church: the Body of Christ <note>the Eucharist</note>, Baptism, Confirmation, Anointing, and Holy Orders; then sacred Marriage, and finally I give my Confession. There are seven keys which suffice for the high notes; so God gives to the Church his seven gifts of salvation <note>The Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit</note>.

Observe the eight tones, if they have been correctly numbered; thus in the Church I know there are eight beatitudes. What we call Music holds nine intervals of sounds; there are also as many holy ranks of good spirits <note>The nine choirs of angels</note>. Just as a line is associated with ten joints <term>articulis: the specific spots on the fingers used in the "Guidonian Hand" mnemonic system to track the musical scale</term>, so the book of Moses serves as many commandments.

Join nine to ten, and thus you will number nineteen joints <note>The full musical gamut was often mapped to 19 or 20 locations on the hand</note>. By just as many ways will you now distinguish the different types of people in the Church: there is the layman, the pilgrim, the knight of the sword, the good host...

That you are the prince of nature is made clear through your deeds;
What nature denies, she wonders at, and finally does not know.
In you, contraries are seen to be joined,
Not as mixtures usually do, which result in a middle ground <note>In medieval philosophy, mixing two opposites usually creates a "mean" or "medium." The author argues that in Christ, the opposites (human and divine) remain fully themselves without being diluted into a third thing.</note>.
Christ is proven to be true man and true God:
Thus it is known that neither this part nor that is diminished.

O gracious Spirit of the Father and the Son, you are the fountain
Of piety; you are the principle through which grace is given freely.
You are the light in darkness, you are the sustainer of light;
Consoling the wretched, you are the repairer of the broken.
You call back the wandering, and give rest to the weary.
You lead and bring the poor into the joys of the harvest.

Grant, Father, that by virtue we may be rebels against vice;
Thus, O just judge, you will drive away punishment from us.
Grant, Son, that with the cloud of the foolish mind put to flight,
Your servants may know this: that they belong to a blessed lot.
Come, gracious Spirit, rain down the dew of goodness
Upon our breasts, lest they remain parched in a sterile way.

These [three] are not the same person, yet I believe they are three, not three gods <note>original: "tres, non tria"; a standard Trinitarian formula meaning three Persons but not three essences or three Gods.</note>.
May the royal road hold me thus, nor shall I recede from it.
How these things come to be, you shall see in the stronghold of the Father;
Believing simply, you shall remain silent for now in this valley <note>The "valley" refers to the earthly world, contrasted with the "stronghold" or "citadel" of heaven.</note>.

And whatever remains of the eating of the Passover lamb,
You shall burn with fire; the law prescribes this as a warning <note>A reference to Exodus 12:10. Allegorically, it means that what the human mind cannot "digest" (understand) about divine mysteries should be left to the "fire" of faith or the Holy Spirit.</note>.
Commit to faith whatever doubt arises;
That which is beyond your strength cannot harm you if you do so.
And give to the Holy Spirit whatever presses hard upon you:
Believe me, if you believe in Him, the believing mind will rise.
We speak these things often, but such a gift is through all things;
That we may believe well, may the Three and One grant to us.

The port is near, the anchor holds the prow, the boat is moved.
But whenever the waves arise, let it be asked to open.
The boat is indeed fragile, for it is the poor boat of John <note>original: "Iohannis"; referring to the author, John de Muris.</note>,
Which is leaky, lacking ribs, and patched with rags.
At first it burned for you, O blessed Virgin and Mother,
And with your help, it was brought back with prosperity.
The weight was great, and it was unequal to those strengths:
But you, pious and ready when asked, resist the shipwreck.
You beat back the sea, the final darkness, and the waves.

### JOHANNES DE MURIS’S SUMMARY OF MUSIC.

<page-num>248</page-num>
<header>JOHANNES DE MURIS’S SUMMARY OF MUSIC.</header>

And it is no wonder if the **Star of the Sea** <note>original: "stella maris"; a traditional title for the Virgin Mary, often invoked by sailors and writers seeking safe passage through the "waves" of life or intellectual labor.</note> rules over the waves.
Through your mediation, whatever was done concerning you came to be;
Guide me, save me; for this I ask as my pact with you.
From here, the little boat <note>The "navicula" or little boat is a common medieval literary trope representing the author’s book or the process of writing reaching its conclusion.</note> has carried its paper and its light burden,
Which the grace of the said Lady, and also of the Lord, has sheltered.
In that place, writings teach in various ways; what a letter requires,
And what a formal composition <note><term>dictamen</term>: the medieval art of formal prose and letter-writing. De Muris suggests that music, like rhetoric, follows specific rules of "composition."</note> is, which a witness does not know how to produce.
This third labor <note>The author refers to this work as his "third labor," suggesting it was part of a larger planned series of treatises on the arts.</note> concerning song serves friends,
Not the wicked, but the simple and modest boys.
For the wicked man disapproves, and unjustly bites back at what is said:
Ancient things hardly please one to whom all recent things are foul. <note>A commentary on the "Ars Nova" period, where traditionalists clashed with those pursuing "recent" musical innovations.</note>
Whenever he sees any of these works of ours,
He will never be able to find fault with the intent of the mind.
At a meager table, a rich mind dines on rich things.
The serene mind of the author itself brightens this work.
Grant, O God, that the writer and all kind readers
May become worthy of the heavenly song in your presence.
Grant us to live justly now with a pure mind;
Grant us afterwards to sing to you in heaven with a joyful voice.
A detractor will perhaps [bring harm] to this art,
When weighing this work and the narrowness of the time spent.
Four months brought this forth from its beginning,
Yet they were not a cause for ceasing from study.
There are eight hundred and sixty verses here:
The book itself shows this, looking back from the first leaf.

### TREATISE ON MUSIC BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

<page-num>249</page-num>
<header>TREATISE ON MUSIC BY THE SAME AUTHOR.</header>
<columns>2</columns>
<sig>OLD WRITERS ON MUSIC. PART III.</sig>
<sig>I i</sig>
<meta>catchword: pro-</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal woodcut band featuring stylized floral or sunburst motifs at the center and repeating scrollwork across the width.</image-desc>

### From the Melk Manuscript compared with the Vienna Manuscript.

It can be gathered from manifold experience that music promotes the affections of the soul; for those who are afraid sometimes sing out of fear, so that they may grasp courage from the song. Likewise, someone in a disagreeable state, recalling to memory a melody which they sang with delight in prosperous times or heard being sung, will sigh, and the mind is measured by movements similar to when they were actually singing it. Likewise, the troubled begin to sing, trying to turn themselves away from sadness through song. Likewise, those pulling ships and other heavy weights incite themselves more impetuously to pull with sociable song. Likewise, doves have been seen to fly toward those playing the cithara <note>The cithara was a stringed instrument of the lyre family, often associated with Orpheus and the power of music to tame nature.</note>. Likewise, birds in cages, otherwise silent, begin to sing upon hearing melodies. Likewise, infants in cradles and boys who do not yet understand anything frequently form certain sounds for themselves, taking delight in them.

**First petition:** <note>original: "petitio"; in this context, a "petition" refers to a postulate or a foundational logical axiom.</note> *Every doctrine and every discipline arises from pre-existing knowledge.* <note>This is a direct reference to the opening of Aristotle’s "Posterior Analytics."</note>
**Second petition:** *No other knowledge is found prior to sensory cognition.*
**Third petition:** *To rest in manifold experience as if at the end of a process.*
**Fourth petition:** *Experience regarding sensible things creates an art.*
*That Pythagoras handed down to us the art of sounds.*

This Pythagoras, the ancient prince of numbers

<column-break/>

and master of proportions, to whom throughout his whole life number was so obedient that he looked into individual things through the power of the science of numbers; remaining for a long time in anxiety over how he might find a rational basis for the art of melodies, once by divine will, while passing by the workshops of smiths and turning this thought over in his mind, heard certain hammers striking upon the anvil emitting a wonderful harmony. Turning toward them as a fervent seeker of truth, he ordered the hammers to be swapped among the workers in silence, doubting lest such a great melody might come from the strength of the men. When they were alternated, the same symphony returned as before. From this he concluded that such concordances were contained not in the arms of the men, but in the nature of the hammers, by reason of number, measure, and weight. However, a fifth hammer was cast out because, when compared to any of the others, it sounded discordant and was useless. Having considered the weights of the others, they were found in double <term>dupla</term> <note>The 2:1 ratio, which produces the octave.</note>, one-and-a-half <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>The 3:2 ratio, which produces the perfect fifth.</note>, and one-and-one-third <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>The 4:3 ratio, which produces the perfect fourth.</note> proportions. And in whatever other things—drums, bells, and others containing these proportions—he found the same harmonies: thus he rested in this experience through the cause. From these experiences, the principles of musical reason were detected through the fourth [petition].

### To join the power of numbers to harmony.

Pythagoras [found] the consonances of sounds through...
