### SPECULATIVE MUSIC.

But I wonder not a little about this: that among us Christians, those two genera—namely, the chromatic and the enharmonic—have never come into use. Instead, in the diatonic genus, we see all ecclesiastical chant and all music measured by time <note>A reference to "mensural music" or polyphony, where notes have specific rhythmic values.</note>—such as in square notation, organ music, songs, and other forms—as well as every sound made by all instruments and by lay men and women, young and old. Where then in the world do these two aforementioned genera lie hidden? I believe it is for no other reason than that they are restricted, being almost against the natural inclination of human voices for singing. For I know that the human voice would never, or scarcely ever, be in harmony within these two genera, nor would it ever be certain of itself; yet, on an instrument, it is possible. Still, I have no doubt that such music would be very harsh, rough, and <note>original: "non concordans"</note> discordant to men steeped in the third genus, as we are. <margin>(a) *Bern MS:* That music of those modes would be harsh and unpleasant to men steeped in the third genus, namely the diatonic, as we are, etc.</margin> Furthermore, I am not unaware that the fourth <term>diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term> can be divided into five semitones, both by major and minor intervals, and by commas. But this would be to exceed the tetrachord in the diagrams on both sides of the aforementioned types.

->*Thus I agree with the monochord of Boethius.*<-

Since, therefore, these three genera always meet in the fourth, but vary in their modes, there should be no doubt to anyone that 

<column-break/>

once the monochord is divided according to the diatonic genus, it is also divided according to the other genera. Therefore, we must deal with the division of the monochord in the diatonic genus; in its entire division, nothing is placed except either a whole tone or a minor semitone. I will mark the divisions of the monochord line with letters, and in its description on the flat surface, I will provide the names of the strings <note>The "strings" here refer to the specific pitches or positions on the monochord, traditionally named using Greek terminology (e.g., *Proslambanomenos*).</note> which the ancients assigned, and the numbers to which the proportion of the consonances refers. And since Boethius <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "Fundamentals of Music" became the standard textbook for a millennium.</note> maintains that a longer string has more parts and a greater space than a shorter one, he therefore assigns to it the greater, low sound, and to the smaller string a smaller number and a high pitch. <margin>(b) *Bern MS:* To the shorter string a smaller number and place, although well etc.</margin> This could be done just as well the opposite way for the longer string—because it contains fewer vibrations than the shorter one—if one gave it a smaller number, and gave more numbers to the shorter string because it has more vibrations, as he himself suggests; whichever way it is done, the proportion never varies.

But first I will set down the division of the diatonic monochord according to Boethius, in which there is only a double octave. <term>bis diapason: a range of two octaves, the standard Greek "Greater Perfect System."</term> <margin>(c) *Bern MS adds:* As far as the proportion of numbers is concerned, although it is not inconsistent with three or four octaves.</margin> And since from what has been said before we have seen how the double and single octaves and the other consonances were discovered, it is clear that nothing remains but to describe the figure upon the flat surface, and the monochord will be seen most clearly in it immediately. <margin>(d) Here ends the Bern manuscript.</margin>

->*But I wish to clearly describe such a monochord.*<-

Following that division which Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "Fundamentals of Music" was the standard textbook for a millennium.</note> gives for the division of his monochord <term>monochord: a musical and scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge, used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of intervals</term>, I wish likewise to divide the monochord, (a) only by changing the position of the strings and their number. This is because the primary manner of singing, which flourished in his time, has in our own time been varied—only incidentally—in its numbers, so that it is much more pleasing than it was to the ancients. Thus, music is a very subtle thing; for through the practice of modern people, it is advanced not only by the help and invention of literate men studying this field, but even the common people—especially youths and women—are moved to it, by what power I know not, unless it be by a natural industriousness. (*)

<column-break/>

I divide this monochord of mine in the following way: let *a. b.* be a string placed upon a flat surface, divided through the middle at point *i.* Therefore, from *i* to *b. a.* <note>the distance compared to the whole</note> the consonance of the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note> is found to be the best. Likewise, if *a. i.* is divided into equal parts at *q.*, then from *q.* to *b. | a.* the **double octave** <note>original: "bis diapason"</note> will sound, being of that same better kind. Likewise, if *a. i.* is again divided into equal parts, there will arise for you an octave of the same multiple kind. And thus the last part may be divided as long as one pleases, and the ear will be able to judge the consonance. In this, the power of the intellect surpasses that of the senses. Thus, the better consonances will have been known, and they stand in the first degree of certainty. Others, however, follow them in this way: let the string *a. b.* be divided again into three parts, of which one part is *a. f.* and the other two parts, containing the rest, extend to *b.*

Read by the same in the aforementioned Gymnasium in the year of grace 1593, while the sun was entering the 20th degree of Aquarius.* What follows, only the Paris manuscript contains.</note>

### SPECULATIVE MUSIC

**N n 2**
<meta>Catchword: OF</meta>

**b. f.** the better [ratio] outside the genus of multiples is resolved into a <term>fifth: the musical interval of a fifth, known in Latin as the diapente</term>; therefore the <term>fourth: the interval of a fourth, or diatessaron</term> has now necessarily been found, which does not differ from the <term>octave: the diapason</term> except by the middle of a fourth, for the first and second strings **e. i. a. f.** but thus you will find this in **a. b.** When the string **a. b.** is cut again into four equal parts, one part becomes **b. e.** and with the other containing **a. e.** to **a. b.**, a fourth will resound.

The harmonies having thus been discovered and confirmed, it remains to find the tones and semitones through which the ascent and descent to the aforementioned harmonies are made. Let **c. d. e.** be a part of string **a. b.** and then **a. d.** to **a. b.** will be a manifest <term>major third: an interval of two whole tones, or ditonus</term>. And now truly in the strings **a. e.** a <term>minor semitone: the smaller of the two semitones in the Pythagorean system</term> becomes known, and consequently **a. e.** to **a. b.** is a major third with a minor semitone, which by a single name is called a fourth. Consequently, you now have a <term>tritone: an interval of three whole tones</term> with a semitone in **a. f. a. b.**, namely in the diatonic scale.

Furthermore, let part of the string **a. f.** | **a. b.** be made equal to **f. g.**; then **a. g.** to **a. b.** will be a tone, and the semitone is found. Likewise, **a. b. b. i.** is made equal, returning **a. i.** to **a. b.** as the octave noted before, in the division of which there are five tones with two minor

<column-break/>

semitones, as has been seen. Therefore, since the octave has been divided once according to its internal parts, it is necessary in the same way, by repeating the process, to divide the double octave. Moreover, this instrument contains 19 strings, or a double octave plus a fifth <note>original: "bis diapason cum diapente"</note>, although it is possible to increase it further: and it is in the shape of a right-angled triangle as far as two of its sides are concerned. But the third side cannot fall under one and the same straight line, but rather approaches a circumference described over three points: it can, however, be described in other figures, both square and oblong, circular, concave, or flat. And just as this instrument contains all instruments within its power, I wish to describe for you the figures into which this instrument can be transformed, for the sake of example: the figures of which are written down in this order. (a)

This instrument, shaped in divided figures of squares, quadrangles, triangles, and circles, denotes all musical instruments.

*Here ends the Speculative Music according to Boethius, abbreviated by Master John de Muris in Paris at the Sorbonne. In the year of our Lord 1323.*

# ON THE NUMBERS,
## WHICH HOLD MUSICAL HARMONIES, ACCORDING TO PTOLEMY OF PARIS.
<note>Johannes de Muris (c. 1290–1351) was a prominent French philosopher and music theorist. "Ptolemy of Paris" likely refers to the medieval reception of the ancient Greek theorist Claudius Ptolemy within the University of Paris circle.</note>

->*From a Paris Manuscript*<-

And since we spoke above concerning the discovery of music—how it was found from the weights of hammers—it is now time to demonstrate by which numbers this was achieved, and how the harmonies always remain within those specific numbers.

Therefore, just as there were four hammers, so there are four numbers found from their weights, which contain almost every property of music. These are **6, 8, 9,** and **12**. In these four numbers, you will find just as many <term>proportions: the mathematical relationship between two quantities</term>, and through these, just as many harmonies. They are as follows: <term>double: a 2:1 ratio</term>, <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio, or "one and a half"</term>, <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio, or "one and a third"</term>, and <term>sesquioctava: a 9:8 ratio, or "one and an eighth"</term>.

The **double proportion** exists whenever a larger number, compared to a smaller one, contains that smaller number twice within itself, such as **12 to 6**. For the number twelve contains six twice. In this numerical proportion consists the harmony of the <term>diapason: the musical interval of an octave</term>. If you test this on a <term>monochord: a single-stringed instrument used for measuring musical intervals</term>, or with pipes, or with bells, or indeed with any objects capable of producing sound, such that one object is double and the other is its half, the octave will undoubtedly always occur for you.

The **sesquialtera proportion** exists whenever a larger number, related to a smaller one, contains the whole of it and additionally its half, such as **12 to 8**. For the number twelve contains eight within itself plus its half, which is four. From this

<column-break/>

proportion, the harmony of the <term>diapente: the musical interval of a fifth</term> arises for us. Generally speaking, wherever these are produced, the lower voice will always contain the whole of the other within itself plus its half.

The **sesquitertia number** occurs whenever a larger number, compared to a smaller one, contains the whole of it and its third part, such as **12 to 9**. For twelve contains nine and its third part, which is three. In this numerical agreement consists the harmony of the <term>diatessaron: the musical interval of a fourth</term>; for the lower voice will always contain the whole of the other within itself plus its third part.

The **sesquioctava number** is also found when a number, compared to another, contains the whole smaller number and its eighth part—that is, a single unit <note>original: "unitatem"</note>. In this agreement, therefore, exists the <term>tone: a whole step in a musical scale</term>. For wherever you find this, you may not doubt that the lower voice contains the whole of the other within itself plus its eighth part.

These, therefore, are the numbers that were found from the weights of the hammers. By a certain divine, rather than human, providence, they are so fitted and, in a sense, bound to the aforementioned harmonies that wherever those numbers are present, the said harmonies will be there also; and conversely, where these harmonies exist, you will undoubtedly find these same numbers. And as was said above, it is through these specific numbers, and not just any others...

# ON THE NUMBERS.

...through these the monochord is divided; through these, cymbals and little bells <note>original: "cimbala & tintinnabula"</note> are formed; through these, pipes or reeds, or stalks are measured; through these, harps and lutes <gloss>f. barbiton</gloss> resound. Finally, whatever a musician plays in this world will in no way deviate from these numerical proportions. However, the three remaining <term>consonances: harmonies that sound pleasing to the ear</term>—that is, the <term>ditone: a major third</term>, the <term>semiditone: a minor third</term>, and the <term>semitone: a half-step</term>—are separated from these specific numerical proportions. It is not that they do not fall into any proportions at all, but rather that they involve such difficult ratios that the intellect of philosophers can scarcely comprehend them; for this reason, we have decided they should be removed from this specific numerical comparison. We have, however, taken care to describe the remaining harmonies with their numbers in the figure below (a).

### The Subject of Music.

What is the subject of music? Number related to sound; or, conversely, sounding numbers are the subject of all music, whether it be <term>plainchant: unmeasured, monophonic church music</term> or <term>mensurable: music with a rhythmic pulse or "subalternate" structure</term>.
What is a number? A collection of units, or a heap poured out from units, as **Hugo** <note>likely Hugh of Saint Victor (c. 1096–1141), a prominent theologian and philosopher</note> says. Therefore, music, both plain and measurable, consists of num-

<column-break/>

-bers, which are difficult numbers because they are infinite.

->*From where the word "Music" is derived.*<-

Etymologically, **Music** is said to be as if "protecting those who sing through use" <note>original: "muniens usu canentes"</note>; hence **Boethius** <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook for a millennium</note> says:
> Because music protects those who sing through use, it holds
> This name, and gives a favorable omen to the singers from then on.

Another view: Music is named as if "moysica," from *moys* meaning water, and *ycos* meaning science <note>This is a common medieval folk etymology; "moys" is a Greek-influenced interpretation of the Hebrew word for water, famously linked to the name Moses</note>.
Another view: Music is named after the poetic **Muses**.
Another view: Music is named after the **Musa**, an instrument of shepherds, as has been seen.
Another view: Music is the mistress of all arts, containing the principles of all methods, established in the first degree of certainty, proportionally bred into the nature of all things in a marvelous way. It is delightful to the intellect, lovely to the ear, making the sad joyful, making the greedy generous, confounding the envious, comforting the weak, making the wakeful peaceful, and waking the sleeper; it nurtures love and honors its possessor, if it attains its proper end, being ultimately established for the praise of God.

->**Bartholomew** says concerning music:<-

> This music sits, this music arranges the heavenly songs:
> In her sight every musician rises,
> Who was powerful either by nature or by art.
> Here first is **David**, woven into the hymns
> Sung together, teaching with harp and psaltery.
> Here is **Pythagoras**, and that sacred **Boethius**,
> The authors and eternal fathers of this art.
> **Orpheus, Amphion, Chiron, Vocasus, Arion**,
> Each of these touches his own strings with his thumb.

<column-break/>

# TREATISE ON PROPORTIONS.
->From the Paris Codex.<-

---

Those who desire to obtain knowledge of musical proportions handed down by Master **Johannes de Muris** <note>Johannes de Muris was one of the most influential mathematicians and music theorists of the 14th century</note>, of venerable memory and most expert in the science of music, should skillfully direct their attention to the following things. These are the pre-supposed principles in the general "Tree of Proportions" that follows, declared more specifically through exemplary divisions. There are, in fact, five distinct genera of proportions between themselves, under which and in which all proportions are generally contained, and they are these: <term>multiple: where the larger number contains the smaller multiple times (e.g., 2:1)</term>, <term>superparticular: where the larger contains the smaller plus one part (e.g., 3:2)</term>, <term>superpartient: where the larger contains the smaller plus several parts (e.g., 5:3)</term>, multiple superparticular, and multiple superpartient.

The first of these genera, namely the **multiple**, occurs when the larger number contains the smaller number within itself exactly multiple times, so that nothing is lacking or remains over—namely twice, or three times, or four times, and so on, and thus further unto infinity. Hence, if the larger part of the number contains the smaller number twice, it is exactly a **double** <note>original: "dupla"</note> proportion, such as 2 to 1, 4 to 2, 6 to 3, 8 to 4, and so on for others. And under this proportion is the <term>diapason: the interval of an octave</term> consonance; for this consonance was found in the numbers of weights 12 and 6—namely, that a weight of 12 compared to a weight of 6 produced the diapason consonance, as will appear more clearly below.

<column-break/>

Regarding these matters and those written below, it must be known that for any of the five aforementioned genera of proportions of larger numbers to smaller ones, the smaller numbers can just as well be proportioned to the larger ones by using the preposition **sub**. For it follows: if the larger number contains the smaller twice, then the smaller number is contained twice in the larger. If, therefore, 2 to 1 relate to each other in a double proportion, 1 to 2 will relate to each other in a **sub-double** <note>original: "sub dupla"</note> proportion, and so on for the others in the same way. Thus, there is a **sub-multiple** genus when the smaller number is contained exactly within the larger multiple times—namely twice, three times, or four times, etc.—as was described above regarding the larger to the smaller.

If, however, the larger number contains the smaller number exactly three times, it is called a **triple** proportion, such as 3 to 1, 6 to 2, 9 to 3, and so on for others. And under this proportion is the consonance of the <term>diapason with diapente: an octave plus a fifth, or a compound twelfth</term>. For 12 to 6 make a double proportion, in which is the diapason; but 18 to 12 make a <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio</term> proportion, in which is the <term>diapente: the interval of a perfect fifth</term>, as will be more fully declared below. But 18 to 6 relate to each other in a triple proportion, as has just been said; therefore, the diapason with

...along with the <term>diapente: the musical interval of a perfect fifth</term> consonance, it exists in a triple proportion. These things will be seen more clearly below.

If the larger number contains the smaller four times, it is called a **quadruple proportion**, such as four to one, eight to two, 12 to 3, 16 to 4, 20 to 5, and 24 to 6, and so on. And under this proportion is the <term>double diapason: a musical interval of two octaves</term> consonance; for 12 to 6 have a relationship making a <term>diapason: the musical interval of an octave</term> in double proportion; similarly 24 to 12 make another diapason in double proportion; therefore 24 to 6 make a double diapason in quadruple proportion.

Similarly, if the smaller number is contained in the larger three times, it is called a **sub-triple proportion**, such as one to three, two to six, three to nine, and so on. If the smaller number is contained in the larger precisely four times, it is called a **sub-quadruple proportion**, such as 1 to 4, | 2 to 8, | 3 to 12, | and so on. The same should be understood in the same way for the quintuple, sub-quintuple, sextuple, sub-sextuple proportions, and so on, unto infinity.

The second genus is called **superparticular**, or sub-superparticular. It is a superparticular genus when the larger number contains the smaller only once, and one <term>aliquot part: a part that divides the whole without a remainder</term> of it precisely. The sub-superparticular genus is when the smaller number, along with one of its aliquot parts precisely, is contained once in the larger. Regarding this, it must be noted that an "aliquot part" is that which multiplies a number, or when taken a certain number of times, returns its whole precisely; or whose repetition

<column-break/>

can precisely return the whole of which it is a part, just as the number one [unity] can return any similar number, and the number two can return any even number.

Hence, if the larger number contains the smaller in its entirety plus its second part—that is, its half—it is called a **sesquialtera** proportion <note>original: "sesquialtera"; this is a ratio of 3:2</note>, such as 3 to 2, | 6 to 4, | 9 to 6, and so on. And under this proportion is the **diapente** consonance; for this consonance was discovered in the numbers of weights 9 and 6, namely that a weight of 9 resonating against a weight of 6 produced the diapente consonance <note>This refers to the legendary discovery of musical ratios by Pythagoras using hammers of different weights</note>; about which more is said below. Similarly, if the smaller number with its second part (or half) is contained in the larger, it is called a **sub-sesquialtera** proportion, such as 2 to 3, | 4 to 6, | 6 to 9, and so on.

If indeed the larger number contains the smaller once in its entirety plus its third part, it is called a **sesquitertia** proportion <note>original: "sesquitertia"; this is a ratio of 4:3</note>, such as 4 to 3, | 8 to 6, | 12 to 9, and so on. And under this proportion is the <term>diatessaron: the musical interval of a perfect fourth</term>; for it was discovered in the numbers of weights 8 and 6, namely that a weight of 8 against a weight of 6 made a diatessaron. More specifically on this below. Similarly, if the smaller number with its third part precisely is contained in the larger, it is called a **sub-sesquitertia** proportion, such as 3 to 4, | 6 to 8, | 9 to 12, and so on.

If the larger number contains the smaller and its fourth part, it is called a **sesquiquarta** proportion <note>original: "sesquiquarta"; this is a ratio of 5:4</note>, such as 5 to 4, | 10 to 8, etc. And if reversed, it will be a **sub-sesquiquarta** proportion. You can proceed further in the same way. For if it is a fifth part, it is called sesquiquinta, and...

### JOHANNES DE MURIS
### Page 288

...and conversely, the sub-sesquiquintal; if it contains a sixth part, it is the sesquisextal, and conversely the sub-sesquisextal; if a seventh, the sesquiseptimal, and conversely the sub-sesquiseptimal. If, however, it contains an eighth part, it shall be called a **sesquioctave proportion**, such as 9 to 8 | 18 to 16 | 27 to 24, and so on for others. And within this proportion stays the <term>tone: the interval of a major second</term>, because it was discovered in the numbers of the weights 9 and 8; so that a weight of 9 against a weight of 8 produced a tone, as will be made clear and manifest below. <note>This refers to the legendary discovery of musical intervals by Pythagoras, who allegedly weighed blacksmiths' hammers to find the ratios of the octave, fifth, and fourth.</note>

The third genus is called **superpartient** or sub-superpartient. It is a superpartient genus when the larger number contains the smaller within itself once, and furthermore a certain <term>aliquant part: a part that is not a single unit fraction (like 1/2 or 1/3) but a combination of parts (like 2/3 or 3/4)</term>—or rather, some <term>aliquot parts: exact divisors</term> which, when taken together, do not form a single aliquot part. The sub-superpartient genus is when the smaller number is contained entirely once within the larger, along with its aliquant (not aliquot) part. Regarding these, it must be noted that an "aliquant part," as it is used here, is the opposite of an "aliquot part." For an aliquant part is that which, when multiplied by any number, does not precisely return its whole, but results in more or less. And the species of the superpartient are these: namely the superbipartient, supertripartient, superquadripartient, and so on to infinity, just as the species of the multiple genus are double, triple, quadruple, etc., and the species of the superparticular genus are sesquialter, sesquitertial, sesquiquartal, and so on. Thus, if the larger number contains the smaller within itself entirely once, and furthermore two of its parts which, when taken

<column-break/>

together, do not make a single aliquot part, it is called a **superbipartient proportion**, such as 5 to 3 | 7 to 5; and if it is done conversely, it will be a sub-superbipartient proportion, such as 3 to 5 | 5 to 7, etc. <note>A superbipartient ratio $1 + 2/n$. For example, $5:3$ is $1 + 2/3$. The "two parts" are two-thirds.</note>

And here it must be observed which parts these are: namely, thirds, fifths, or sevenths, and so on. In the first case, it will be a "superbipartient thirds" proportion, such as 5 to 3. In the second case, it will be a "superbipartient fifths" proportion, such as 7 to 5—which is smaller than the former, because a third part of something is larger than a fifth of the same thing. Thus, the proportion is to be named further according to the quantity of the parts and their number.

If indeed the larger number contains the smaller entirely once, plus three of its parts, it is called a **supertripartient proportion**, such as 7 to 4—which is "supertripartient fourths"—and 8 to 5, which is "supertripartient fifths," etc.; and conversely the sub-supertripartient, such as 4 to 7, etc. If, however, the larger number contains the smaller once plus four of its parts, it is called a **superquadripartient proportion**, such as 9 to 5 (which is "superquadripartient fifths") and 11 to 7 (which is "superquadripartient sevenths"), and so on for others. Conversely, the proportion will be sub-superquadripartient, such as 5 to 9, and one should proceed in a similar manner for any further genus.

The fourth genus is that which is joined from the multiple and the superparticular, and it is called **multiple superparticular**, or sub-multiple superparticular. It is a multiple superparticular genus when...

### ON PROPORTIONS

...when the larger number contains the smaller within itself multiple times, and additionally some <term>aliquot part: a part that divides the whole exactly, like 1/2 or 1/3</term> of it, or several parts that are not aliquot but which, when taken together, form one aliquot part. <note>The author is describing the Fourth Genus, the Multiple Superparticular, such as 5:2 (two and a half).</note> Conversely, the **sub-multiple superparticular** genus is when the smaller number and some aliquot part of it is contained multiple times within the larger. The species of the **multiple superparticular** are these: **double sesquialter**, **double sesquitertial**, and so on; similarly **triple sesquialter**, **triple sesquitertial**, etc.; **quadruple sesquialter**, etc., proceeding thus unto infinity. 

Hence, if the larger number contains the smaller twice plus its half-part, it is called a **double sesquialter proportion**, such as 5 to 2 | 10 to 4 | 15 to 6 etc. <note>5 contains 2 twice, with 1 left over; 1 is half of 2.</note> If it contains a third part, it is called **double sesquitertial**, such as 7 to 3 | 14 to 6 etc. If done conversely, they will be **sub-double sesquialter** proportions, such as 2 to 5, and **sub-double sesquitertial**, such as 3 to 7. If, however, the larger number contains the smaller three times and its half-part, it is called **triple sesquialter**, such as 7 to 2 | 14 to 4 etc. If a third part, it is called **triple sesquitertial**, such as 10 to 3 | 20 to 6 etc. And so conversely, for the sub-proportioning of smaller numbers to larger; and so for others unto infinity.

The fifth genus is called **multiple superpartient**, or **sub-multiple superpartient**; and it is a multiple superpartient genus when the larger number contains the smaller whole multiple times, and additionally some <term>aliquant part: a part that is not an exact divisor, but a combination of parts</term>—not just one aliquot part, but several, which when taken together do not make a single aliquot part. And according to the

<column-break/>

multiplicity, quantity, and number of the parts, the proportion must be named: such as double, triple, quadruple and beyond; or as bi-partient, tri-partient, quadri-partient and beyond; or as thirds, fourths, fifths, etc. unto infinity, all of which are species of this genus. 

Hence, if the larger number contains the smaller twice and two of its parts, it is called **double superbipartient**, such as 8 to 3 | 16 to 6, which is specifically **double superbipartient of thirds** <note>8 contains 3 twice (6), with 2 left over. Since 2 is two-thirds of 3, the ratio is 2 and 2/3.</note>; if it contains three parts, it is called **double supertripartient**, such as 11 to 4 | 22 to 8 etc., which is **supertripartient of fourths**. If, however, the larger number contains the smaller three times and two of its parts, it is called **triple superbipartient**, such as 11 to 3 | 22 to 6 etc.; but if three parts, it is called **triple supertripartient**, such as 15 to 4 | 30 to 8, and so for others unto infinity. 

Conversely, following what was said above, smaller numbers can be sub-proportioned to larger ones, because the **sub-multiple superpartient** genus is nothing other than when the smaller number and its aliquant (non-aliquot) part is contained multiple times in the larger. For 3 to 8 stand in a **sub-double superbipartient** proportion; 4 to 11 in a **sub-double supertripartient** proportion; 3 to 11 stand in a **sub-triple superbipartient** proportion; and 4 to 15 in a **sub-triple supertripartient** proportion. And let these suffice for the genera of proportions in general, all of which—regarding the larger numbers proportioned to smaller—you may see more clearly in the following figure.

### JOHANNES DE MURIS

# Genus
<note>Latin: *Genus*. In this context, it refers to the primary classification of mathematical ratios or "types" of proportions.</note>

- **Multiple**
    - Double
    - Triple
    - Quadruple
    - When the larger number contains the smaller within itself entirely:
    - twice, as in 2. 4. 6. 8. 10.
                      1. 2. 3. 4. 5.
    - thrice, as in 3. 6. 9. 12.
                      1. 2. 3. 4.
    - four times, as in 4. 8. 12. 16.
                           1. 2. 3. 4.

- **Superparticular** <note>original: *Superparticulare*. A ratio where the larger number contains the smaller once, plus one <term>aliquot part: a part that divides the whole exactly, like 1/2 or 1/3</term>.</note>
    - <term>Sesquialter: a ratio of 3:2, representing the musical interval of a perfect fifth</term>

IOANNES DE MURIS

# THE SECOND BOOK.

## HERE FOLLOWS WHAT MASTER JOHANNES DE MURIS
## SAYS CONCERNING THE PRACTICE OF MUSIC, OR CONCERNING MENSURABLE MUSIC.
<note>original: *de mensurabili*. This refers to music with a definite, measurable rhythm, as opposed to "plainchant" which had a more fluid, unmeasured rhythm.</note>

->*From the same Parisian Manuscript.*<-

Since in the preceding discourses we touched upon music theory lightly and briefly, it now remains to inquire more extensively into its practice, specifically that part which is mensurable, since various practitioners hold different views concerning it. As was shown in the first book, the voice is generated with motion, since it belongs to the category of successive things; therefore, while it is being made, it exists, but once it has been made, it is no more. Succession does not exist without motion. Time inseparably implies motion. Therefore, it is necessary for the voice to be measured by time. Time, moreover, is the measure of motion. But here, time is the measure of the voice produced with continuous motion: and the same definition is assigned to both time and the unit of measure.

Time is either greater or lesser: greater, which has a more prolonged motion; lesser, which has a shorter motion, other things being equal, according to one calculation. These do not differ in species, for "more" and "less" do not change the nature of the species. In all time of measured voice, the ancients reasonably assigned a certain mode of perfection, positing that such time could receive division by the number three <note>original: *per ternarium*. This reflects the medieval preference for triple meter, which was considered "perfect" because of its association with the Trinity.</note>, believing that all perfection exists in the ternary number. Because of this, they established "perfect time" as the measure for any song, knowing that in art, it is not fitting for the imperfect to be found—although some moderns

<column-break/>

have believed themselves to have found the opposite (far be it from them!), whose intention will be more clearly explained in what follows. <note>Muris is referring to the *Ars Nova* composers who were beginning to use "imperfect" (duple or binary) time signatures, which he initially views with skepticism.</note>

->*Also by the same Johannes de Muris.*<-

That all perfection rests in the ternary number is evident from many probable conjectures. For in God, who is most perfect, there is unity in substance and trinity in persons; he is therefore three-in-one, and one-in-three; thus, there is a greatest harmony between unity and trinity. In the primary intelligence, we say that the divided, the concrete, and the composite are found under the number three. In the first of the bodies, the heavens, there is the mover, the mobile, and time. There are three things in the stars and the sun: heat, ray, and splendor. In the elements: action, passion, and matter. In individuals: generation, corruption, and the subject. In all finite time: a beginning, a middle, and an end. In every curable disease: an increase, a peak, and a decline. There are three operations of the intellect; three terms in a syllogism <note>The basic unit of logic: major premise, minor premise, and conclusion.</note>; three figures of argument. There are three intrinsic principles of natural things. Three powers of an un-deprived being. Three relative differences of place. In the entire universe, there are three dimensions <note>original: *lineæ* (lines).</note>. The ternary is the first odd number, the first and uncomposite number, and a cube is generated by the drawing of it into itself three times. No two lines, but three, enclose a surface. Among polygon figures, the triangle is the first of

# PRACTICAL MUSIC

...of all those rectilinear figures, the triangular is the foundation. Every body has three dimensions, otherwise it could never sustain itself.
<note>The author is likely concluding a geometric proof here, arguing that three is the minimum number of dimensions required for a physical object to exist in space.</note>

Since, therefore, the number three <term>ternarius<gloss>the ternary or the number three</gloss></term> presents itself in all things in some way, its perfection ought no longer to be doubted. By its opposite, the number two <term>binarius<gloss>the binary or the number two</gloss></term>, because it recedes from the ternary, is left imperfect, since even the number two is so ill-reputed.
<note>In medieval number theory, odd numbers were often associated with stability and the divine, while even numbers—especially the number two—were seen as unstable because they could be divided, representing a "falling away" from unity.</note> 
But indeed, any number composed in such a way that it has a correspondence to the ternary can deservedly be considered perfect. For unity, being continuous, is divisible not only again into ternaries, but into infinity without ceasing.

Since, however, the voice measured by time comprises a union of two forms—namely natural and mathematical—it follows that by reason of the mathematical, division would not cease; yet because of the division of other voices, it is necessary for it to be terminated somewhere. For just as a limit is set for all things existing in nature, and a reason for their magnitude and growth, so it is for their smallness and its diminution. For they demonstrate naturally that nature is bounded by a maximum and a minimum. The voice, moreover, is essentially a natural form joined accidentally to quantity; therefore it must have limits of division <note>original: *fractionis*</note>, the breadth of which no voice, however fleeting, is able to cross. These limits we wish to understand by reason.

A voice uttered and measured by a certain time does not only project itself into the air according to a point, or a line, or a surface, but in a conical and spherical manner, in the likeness of a sphere, like light in a transparent medium; this is evident through

<column-break/>

six ears <note>referring to the six directions of spatial perception: up, down, before, behind, left, and right</note> arranged according to the six differences of proportion. Since this voice is so weighed down by the power of the impeller <note>the person singing or speaking</note>, which is finite because it proceeds from a finite heart, it must have limits to its duration or continuation, since a voice can be generated neither in infinity nor in a mere instant. These limits are as follows:

All music, especially mensurable music, is founded on perfection, encompassing number and sound within itself. Now, the number in music which is considered perfect by musicians is the ternary, as is clear from the things said previously. Music, therefore, takes its origin from the ternary of numbers, which ternary, multiplied by itself, generates nine <term>novenarius<gloss>the number nine</gloss></term>. Within this nine, in a certain way, every number is contained, since beyond nine there is always a return to unity; therefore, music does not transcend the number nine. 

If nine is again multiplied by itself, it produces 81. This product is measured by the ternary in a triple dimension, in the manner of the voice. For three times three, twice three, three times nine, and the products again multiplied by three always: just as three times three produces nine, and three times nine is 27, and three times 27 always generates 81. 

Therefore, from unity—which is the third part of the ternary, which is perfect—to 81—which is likewise perfect—it is surely worthy to be bounded from the greatest to the least of any voice. And its entire length is included between these limits; within which four distinct degrees of perfection can be notably assigned, and this is how:

No musical perfection exceeds the ternary, but it embraces and instructs the ternary. Perfection is that according to which, or that by which, something is said to be perfect.

He explains that sound moves spherically in space and must have finite limits because it is produced by a finite human heart.</summary>

# JEAN DE MURS

That is perfect which is divisible into three equal parts, or into two unequal parts where the smaller is surpassed by the larger. 
<note>De Murs defines perfection through the ability to divide a unit into three, a reflection of the Holy Trinity and geometric stability.</note>

Unity, however, is indivisible, and can be called neutral; therefore, the category of division must be maintained in these things, and similarly for indivision. Indeed, the number three <term>ternarius<gloss>the ternary or the number three</gloss></term> is perfect in this regard. The number four is binary <term>binarius<gloss>the number two or its multiples</gloss></term> and in this respect is imperfect. Its unity is 27, which "imperfects" the perfect while "perfecting" the imperfect, and is distinguished into three parts. 
<note>The number 27 (3 to the power of 3) was a cornerstone of De Murs's system, representing the total number of the smallest time units in a "perfect" Long note.</note> 
The first degree goes from 27 to 9; the second from 9 to 3; the third from 3 to 1; and the fourth—in any of which one can find the perfect, the imperfect, and the neutral in the numbers 3, 2, and 1. There are, therefore, four degrees, neither more nor fewer.
<note>These four degrees correspond to the levels of medieval rhythmic measurement: Maximodus, Modus, Tempus, and Prolatio.</note>

### On the Drawing of Note Shapes

It also remains to be seen by which figures, signs, and note-shapes the things we have spoken of ought to be appropriately assigned or designated, and by what words or terms they should be called; for in our own time, our teachers of music argue with one another about this every day. And although signs are chosen by convention <term>ad placitum<gloss>at will or by agreement</gloss></term>, nevertheless, since all things harmonize with one another, more suitable signs for designating the sounds ought to be discovered by the musician. Regarding their invention, the ancient wise men long ago unanimously agreed or conceded that geometric figures should be the signs for musical voices. They chose to call these "points" <term>puncta<gloss>notes or dots</gloss></term>, not in the sense of an indivisible geometric point, but in the way a doctor uses the term for a "day" <note>This likely refers to a "critical day" or a specific unit of measurement in medical prognosis.</note>. The figure of the written note is a four-sided surface, since it is produced from the *e, la, mi* line alone, in which

<column-break/>

every musical note begins, as if within a genus, through a cause which—by essential forms, that is, natural ones—is of an essential shape. For by varying the sign of the note's shape, every mode of any song is explained. Indeed, the musical note and the quadrilateral figure signify, by convention, a continuous sound measured by time. There are nine distinctions of this form: the **rectangle**, the **equilateral**, the **tailed**, the **point**, the **position**, the **right**, the **left**, **upward**, and **downward**, as will be seen in the following figure.

Concerning the figure of the first and fourth degrees, the ancients spoke little, but they treated the figures of the second and third degrees rationally, although their voices extended to wider degrees; for what they uttered with their mouths, they imagined in their minds. The reason for this is left silent: yet they gave us the method for making progress. What they did was incomplete: they designated the third and second degrees with a similar figure, but designated unity with a dissimilar one, because the binary is closer to the ternary than unity is. However, those things which properly belong to the intellect allow that transition is easier among those things that share a symbol, and vice versa. 

From the ternary to the binary—that is, from the perfect to the imperfect—and vice versa, the transition is easier than from the binary to unity. Therefore, a more similar figure should not be adapted to them in the assumption of any degree, the distinction of which is not perceived in themselves, but is rather manifested in relation to another. According to the ancients, the figure is quadrilateral, equilateral, rectangular, and tailed...

<meta>The catchword "dex-" indicates the next page will likely begin with "dextrorsum," meaning "to the right," referring to the direction of a note's tail.</meta>

...to the right, upward or downward, in the second degree it signifies the imperfect and perfect equally—that is, the ternary <term>ternarium<gloss>the number three or triple division</gloss></term> and binary <term>binarius<gloss>the number two or duple division</gloss></term>. The same figure without a tail signifies unity, but when signifying unity in the second degree, it signifies the ternary and binary in the third.
<note>De Murs is explaining how the presence or absence of a "tail" (stem) on a note changes its mathematical value depending on which level of the rhythmic hierarchy—the "degrees"—the music is in.</note>

The quadrilateral figure, equilateral and obtuse-angled, signifies unity in the same degree.

They spoke of the first degree as far as the binary and unity, but they omitted the ternary, or they suggested it should be understood through a similar figure; in the fourth degree, they completely abandoned unity, or they figured it implicitly in ligatures <note>Ligatures are groups of notes joined together in a single pen stroke, a common feature of medieval notation.</note>—specifically the quadrilateral, equilateral, obtuse-angled figure with an upward tail, and this is the last of the fourth degree. But the first is similar to the second, namely a quadrilateral, inequilateral, right-angled figure with a tail to the right, upward or downward.

### The Differences of the Four Degrees.
The differences of the first degree: equilateral, inequilateral. The differences of the second: with a tail, without a tail. The differences of the third: right-angled, obtuse-angled. The differences of the fourth: obtuse-angled without a tail, obtuse-angled with a tail.

<column-break/>

### On the Names of the Note Shapes.
It remains to inquire about the names of the figures, which are called <term>notulæ<gloss>little notes or marks</gloss></term>. In the first degree, we can name them thus: triple long, double long, simple long. In the second, following the names of the ancients: perfect long, imperfect long, breve. In the third, by analogy with the preceding: perfect breve, imperfect breve, semibreve—not from an equal part, but from a greater or lesser part, so that the binary is called the major part, and unity the minor; and this semibreve is called "minor" by the ancients. 
<note>The "ancients" refers to earlier theorists of the 13th century, like Franco of Cologne, whose system De Murs was expanding.</note>
In the fourth, following the previous names: perfect semibreve, imperfect semibreve, least semibreve <term>minima<gloss>literally "the smallest"</gloss></term>.

They are named differently by others, though the same meaning remains. Omitting the first degree, which is appropriately named: long, semi-long, breve, semibreve, minor, semi-minor, least; or thus, and fittingly: long, longer, longest—that is, great, greater, greatest <term>maxima<gloss>the largest note value</gloss></term>, taking the start of the comparison from the unity of the first degree. Then in the second: perfect, imperfect, breve, shorter, shortest—that is, small, minor, least. (a)

### *The Distinction of the Five Ways.*

Since it has been stated that the same figure represents both the perfect and the imperfect—just as the same general matter can take on many forms—a distinction between them is assigned by authors in five ways. This is evident in the second degree <note>The "second degree" refers to the relationship between the *longa* and the *brevis*.</note>, of which they had greater knowledge. For instance: a long before a long is perfect; a long before two shorts, a long before three shorts, a long before a dot <term>punctum<gloss>a mark used to divide or increase a note's value</gloss></term>, and a long before a long rest is always valued as three beats <note>original: "trium temporum"</note>. And this distinction is taken from the site or position of the notes.

The imperfect is recognized in two ways: with a unit <note>A "unit" refers to a *brevis* or short note.</note> placed before it or following it. What has been said regarding the second degree should be understood for the other degrees in its own way. In any of these degrees, these species of singing can be assigned: one consisting of all perfect notes; another from a preceding binary <term>binarius<gloss>a group of two or a double value</gloss></term> and a following unit, and let the rests be similar to this first mode. The second species has a unit preceding and a binary following. The third is collected from the first and second—namely, from a preceding perfect note and two following units, the last of which represents the sign of a binary; the fourth species is the opposite; the fifth is made of all units and their fractions.

### *On Rests.*

Regarding rests <note>original: "pausis"</note> and ligatures <note>notes tied together in a single stroke</note>, more could be said elsewhere; but let it suffice for them what has been said in the rules of the ancients, except that rests can now be arranged here as examples, and this in four degrees, as above.

<image-desc>A musical notation diagram featuring a five-line staff. On the staff, there are various vertical bars of different lengths representing "rests" categorized into four rhythmic levels (degrees). Below the staff, there are small square musical notes positioned beneath the corresponding rests to demonstrate their value: a long bar for the long rest, and progressively shorter bars for the brevis, semibrevis, and minim rests.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

At the end of this little work, it should be noted that it happens that a song can be made of perfect notes in imperfect time <note>This refers to mixing triple-time notes in a duple-meter framework.</note>, such as three shorter notes; and of imperfect notes in perfect time, such as two short notes <note>original: "breves"</note>. For two binaries and two ternaries are made equal in totals of 6, 12, 16, 24, and so on by adding 6. There are, however, two perfect binaries from imperfect time; just as there are two imperfect ternaries from perfect time, and they revolve into one another and are finally made equal by an even proportion. And one sings from perfects in perfect time, and from imperfects in imperfect time, as is appropriate.

Likewise, it is possible for perfections <note>A "perfection" is a complete triple-beat unit.</note> to be separated and disjointed rather than continued; for example, a single short note might be found between two perfect notes. However, once the collection of short notes is made, the whole is reduced to a perfection, because just as it can be brought forth by the mouth, so can it be named. There are, moreover, many other novelties hidden in music, which will appear quite doubtful to those who come after us.

In this musical art, some things are included as if hidden within, which, if they were explained outwardly, many people who are constantly arguing over certain conclusions would immediately stop. It is our concern that—out of love for them rather than for the sake of novelty—we wish to appropriately approve some conclusions over which doubt has arisen among the masters. Let no envious critic rise up against us if we are compelled to say what has been commanded, preserving the modes of the voices and their appearances, while always following the limits of the ancients.

### *These are the Conclusions.*

1. That a long note <note>longa</note> can be made imperfect by a short note <note>brevis</note>.

He concludes by defending his modern refinements of musical theory as being in harmony with ancient traditions.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Jean de Murs' technical explanation of rhythmic "imperfection." On the previous page, he established how the same note shape can represent different values. Now, he provides a list of rules for how larger notes are "imperfected" (reduced from a triple value to a double value) by smaller notes.</meta>

<page-num>297</page-num>
->**PRACTICAL MUSIC.**<-
<sig>P p</sig>
<meta>catchword: fe-</meta>

2. That a short note <term>brevis<gloss>the standard unit of time in this system, often worth three beats when "perfect"</gloss></term> can be made imperfect by a half-short note <term>semibrevis<gloss>a note worth one-third of a perfect short note</gloss></term>.
3. That a half-short note can be made imperfect by a minimal note <term>minima<gloss>the smallest rhythmic unit, worth one-third of a perfect half-short</gloss></term>.
4. That a long note <term>longa<gloss>a note usually worth three short notes</gloss></term> can be made imperfect by a half-short note.
5. That a short note can be made imperfect by a minimal note.
6. That a minimal note cannot be made imperfect <note>Because there is no smaller note value below it to "take away" a portion of its time.</note>.
7. That a second short note <term>altera brevis<gloss>a short note that is doubled in value to fill out a triple measure</gloss></term> can be made imperfect by a half-short note.
8. That a second half-short note can be made imperfect by a minimal note.
9. That time can be divided into any number of equal parts.

I. That a perfect long note <note>original: "longa perfecta"</note> can be made imperfect by a short note is granted by all musicians as self-evident, as if by oath. Everything that is perfect is reduced to the imperfect when its third part is removed; for the "perfect" is divisible into three equal parts, while the "imperfect" is divisible into two. According to the authors <note>original: "actores," referring to established music theorists like Franco of Cologne</note> who divided the notes this way, the short note is the third part of a perfect long note. Therefore, a perfect long is rendered imperfect by a short note. It does not matter if it comes before or after, since whenever a unit is subtracted from a group of three, an imperfect group of two always remains; this is also clear from musical works.

II. III. From these points, it is clearly concluded that a short note can be made imperfect by the half-short of the ancients, and a half-short by a minimal note. All imperfection <note>In medieval music, "imperfection" is the technical term for a note losing 1/3 of its value to a neighboring smaller note.</note> occurs by reason of a third part being removed by the musicians. A half-short is the third part of a short note, and a minimal note is the third part of a half-short: therefore, each

<column-break/>

of these makes its whole imperfect. Furthermore: just as the short note relates to the perfect long, so the half-short relates to the short, and the minimal note to the half-short: in each case, there is a triple proportion <note>original: "proportio tripla," meaning a 3:1 ratio</note>. A short note makes a long imperfect, as has been said; therefore a half-short does so to a short, and a minimal note to a half-short. The same logic holds for two shorts between two longs, and for two half-shorts between two shorts, and for two minimal notes between two half-shorts; for in every degree of the hierarchy, the "third mode" <note>A specific rhythmic arrangement in medieval theory.</note> applies. But if a division of the mode <term>divisio modi<gloss>a vertical stroke or dot used to separate rhythmic groups</gloss></term> is placed between two short notes, both longs will be rendered imperfect by a short note according to the authors. Therefore, similarly, if a dot is placed between two half-shorts or minimal notes, both the shorts (by the half-shorts) and the half-shorts (by the minimal notes) will necessarily be sung as imperfect.

> [Even the perfect and the imperfect are designated by the teachers <note>original: "doctores"</note> with a similar figure <note>The visual shape of the note (the "figure") remains the same even if its rhythmic value changes.</note>. It is possible for a melody <term>tropo<gloss>literally "trope" or "turn," here referring to the musical phrase</gloss></term> to be perfect or imperfect; but the perfect is expressed through the short note; therefore the imperfect is also possible; therefore it is possible for a short note to be imperfect. But the imperfect, by having its half added back to it, returns to the perfect; therefore an imperfect short note, when its half (which is a half-short) is added back to it, returns to being perfect: thus a half-short note added to a short note "perfects" it, and likewise "imperfects" it when removed. The difference in the shape of the figure is no obstacle, because one shape does not imperfect another shape, since every shape is formally perfect in itself: rather, that which is signified by the name of one figure imperfects that which is imported by the name of another. The figure is the sign; the musical reality is the thing signified. The sign is perfect...

<page-num>298</page-num>
<header>JOHN DE MURS</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...perfected <note>original: "fectum," continuing from "perfectum" on the previous page</note> through its primary form, and likewise marked by its sign; one happens to the other, both making a single unit by joining together, which is called a <term>notula<gloss>a musical note</gloss></term>. For a note is a four-sided figure of a numbered sound, measured by time according to the will of those who mark it. A note therefore includes two forms: the four-sided figure, which is primary, and the marking <note>original: "signatio," the specific rhythmic value assigned to the shape</note>, which is secondary. It is the marking, moreover, that is made "perfect" or "imperfect," not the physical figure itself. 

Just as in grammar one voice does not depend on another, nor does it create a construction on its own, but rather the relationship of the ways they are shaped does; so too between one figure and another there is no musical proportion, but rather the musical consonance is caused by the proportion of the musical *things* <note>original: "rerum musicalium," referring to the actual durations or sounds represented by the shapes</note> being either perfect or imperfect. For a figure is not diminished or increased by another figure, but rather the "thing" designated by the name of the figure is. For one unit of time is understood to contain three units of time, and in this, it is "perfect." It is said to be "imperfected" when a third part is taken away, and "perfected" again if it is added—this does not happen to the shapes, but to the things they represent. One must also imagine the <term>ternary<gloss>a group of three</gloss></term> being reduced to a <term>binary<gloss>a group of two</gloss></term>, or vice versa, regarding their substance and not their outward form; wise mathematicians understand this.

**IV.** From the preceding points, we now have a way to prove that a **long** can be made imperfect by a **semibreve**; for that which makes the part imperfect, also makes the whole imperfect. A semibreve makes a breve imperfect; a breve is a part of a long (as shown previously); therefore, a semibreve makes a long imperfect. Furthermore: every integral whole is made imperfect by its part, provided it is placed under a

<column-break/>

ternary classification. A semibreve is a ternary part of a long, for it is the third part of a breve, and a breve is the third part of a long; therefore, a semibreve is the third part of the third part of a long; thus, it can make a long imperfect. 

This is even more compelling and more beautiful for the musician: everything that is uttered by the voice in a straight, whole, and regular way when singing, the wise musician ought to represent through the proper small notes; for figures are like the signs of voices in grammar. If art did not vary the nature and the figure of the song, the opposite would happen; for we can sing without figures, provided it is sung naturally and appropriately from the mouth. Sometimes 8 or 5 semibreves are uttered under a single breath and a single continuous accent: therefore, it ought to be shaped by the musician into one "body." Thus, a long—whether it is a "perfect" or "imperfect" long of breves—is rendered imperfect by a semibreve, whether placed before or after, since the whole body of the long, which is one, is made perfect by reason of the breves, and not the breves themselves.

To see the distinction between the imperfection of a "perfect long" and an "imperfect long," one must use such terms as these: a note is divided thus: one is **perfectly perfect**, another **perfectly imperfect**, another **imperfectly perfect**, and another **imperfectly imperfect**. For example, let this be shown in one grade for all: a long is called **perfectly perfect** when it includes three time-units of its grade, such as three breves, and it is recognized in five ways, as seen before; but it is called **perfectly imperfect** when it includes two time-units of its kind or grade, such as two breves. It is called **imperfectly perfect** when it includes three time-units that are not perfect, but...

# PRACTICAL MUSIC

## ON THE RECOGNITION OF NOTES

...the other of them is sung as imperfect, either at the start or the end—for instance, as two whole <term>breves<gloss>the standard 'short' note, which can be divided into three semibreves</gloss></term> and a third imperfect one. This is recognized in five ways: if a <term>long<gloss>a long duration note, equal to three breves in 'perfect' time</gloss></term> is placed before another long without any <term>semibreve<gloss>the smallest standard note value in this system</gloss></term> of the same level coming between them, the first is called "imperfectly perfect" <note>original: "imperfecte perfecta"</note>. However, if there is a dot, and it is before two breves, or even before three, or before a rest—if it is possible to make it perfect in that way. For everything that is performed is said to be "figured" <note>represented by a shape or symbol</note>, and what is figured, even if it is difficult, must be capable of being performed; for art never extends itself to the impossible. 

"Imperfectly imperfect" is recognized in two ways: such as if a long is placed before a single breve with nothing of its own kind in between, but with an interposed semibreve which belongs to another level, or the reverse, or both. In such cases, it is called "perfected imperfectly" from the front, or "imperfectly perfected" before and after, and in many other varying ways which will appear in the following figures.

We must, however, be careful of a common objection raised by those whom we are arguing against in this work: they believe, without fail, that all imperfect notes can be made perfect by a dot, since the dot is the sign of <term>perfection<gloss>the state of being complete or having the value of three</gloss></term>. But if a dot is added to a note that is made "imperfect" by a semibreve—specifically a long—it becomes unknown whether that long is now "perfect" by a value of three breves or only two. Yet the "Old Art" <note>original: "ars antiqua," referring to the 13th-century style of Franco of Cologne</note>, which we wish to oppose, says it will be a perfection of three, even though it would have been possible to perform it with the value of two breves. Before the addition of the dot, the first note was "imperfectly imperfect," worth five semibreves; through the addition of the dot, it is rendered "perfectly perfect," worth nine semibreves, whereas

<column-break/>

it ought not to be worth more than six—that is, the dot should not create perfection out of more than was there, because the note had been imperfect. Therefore, this is a poor rule. A similar objection is raised so that a breve cannot be made imperfect, as seen in this description:

<image-desc>A musical notation example on a four-line staff. It is divided into two parts. The first part shows a square breve followed by three lozenge-shaped semibreves. The second part shows the same sequence, but with a dot placed after the square breve.</image-desc>

The first breve was imperfect before the addition of the dot, and the long was "perfectly perfect," worth three breves; the last breve was also "altered" <note>doubled in value to fill out a triple measure</note>. But once the dot is added—which is possible—all of these relationships are destroyed. The dot placed there signifies a <term>division of the mode<gloss>a marker showing where one rhythmic group ends and another begins</gloss></term>; therefore, this latest error is worse than the first. If, therefore, this is more impossible, the other choice should be preferred: thus, it is not only a long that is affected by a semibreve. But the second breve can in no way be placed as imperfect. 

To these two points, a single response must be given: one must be careful with the dot, for although it is the smallest in size, it is nevertheless the greatest in power <note>This is a famous medieval maxim: "minimus in quantitate, sed maximus in potestate."</note>. The wise men of old, wishing to show the perfection of the same genus or level (such as a long in respect to a breve), added a tiny dot to the right side, without denying others, or the perfection of a note of another genus. The first is called "perfect" because of the three similar notes following it; we now call this "immediate" or "near" perfection, since it is fulfilled by parts that are near to it or of its own level, and we assign this to any level of note, as was shown before.

But because they [the ancients] remained silent about the perfection of another level—which is now said to be a "new" thing—they entirely omitted the sign for that perfection, which we call "mediate" and "remote" <note>Jean is defending the innovations of the *Ars Nova*, which allowed for more complex rhythmic relationships between different levels of time (prolation and mensuration).</note>. However, when new things arrive, one must use new innovations; therefore...

# JEAN DE MURS

## ON THE RECOGNITION OF NOTES

If it pleases musicians, let us be in agreement on this: that we sometimes grant a dot the sign of perfection <note>original: "puncto... signum perfectionis"</note>. Like the ancients, let it be placed not to the right but above—that is, on the upper part of the note to be perfected—to signify the perfection of the following genus, which defines the category; below, however, it signifies the third genus from the one given, and placed before the note if the process continues further.

It should be noted that not everything can be made perfect by a dot when another form has already been introduced there; unless something is subtracted, a first <term>long<gloss>a note of long duration, typically equal to three breves</gloss></term> cannot be dotted, for a <term>breve<gloss>the standard "short" note</gloss></term> would then be superfluous, provided the song is regular. A <term>regular song<gloss>cantus regularis</gloss></term> is one where the perfections that begin together also end equally as they continue. An <term>irregular song<gloss>cantus irregularis</gloss></term> is one where the notes are accumulated in time through the shapes of the figures, according to how the performer chooses to arrange the voice. It sometimes happens that two songs are regular in themselves and absolutely, but are irregular when compared to each other, such as when an imperfect part is sung against a perfect one. From what has been said regarding the previous objections, the solution is clear; therefore, we must marvel at those men who, for fear of sublime reasoning, are forced to abandon the truth, even when two more difficult arguments have been brought to the opposite side.

V. & VI. From these same reasons, it appears that a <term>breve</term> can be made imperfect by a <term>minim<gloss>the smallest note value in this system, whose name means "the least"</gloss></term>; for as the <term>semibreve<gloss>a note value between a breve and a minim</gloss></term> relates to the long, so the breve relates to the minim, since in both cases a nine-fold proportion <note>original: "proportio nontupla"; this refers to a 9:1 ratio, such as when one long contains nine semibreves</note> is created. A long can be made imperfect by a semibreve, as has been shown; therefore, a breve can also be made imperfect by a minim. From their opposite, it is clear that a minim cannot be made imperfect, since it is indivisible; one cannot give less than the least.

<column-break/>

VII. & VIII. By the preceding arguments, which proved that an imperfect long is made imperfect by a semibreve, it can be shown that the "altered" breve <note>In certain contexts, the second of two notes is "altered" or doubled to fill out a triple measure</note> is made imperfect by the same: for although it differs from the long in its shape, it is the same in its significance; and things signified are those to which their own properties are due. And by a similar logic, one must hold that the "altered" semibreve is made imperfect by a minim. If any objections are raised, they have been resolved in the preceding sections.

IX. That time can be divided into any number of equal parts is clear from this: Every <term>continuum<gloss>a continuous sequence where parts are joined together, like time or a line</gloss></term> is divisible into any number of parts of the same proportion, such as two, three, four, and so on. Time belongs to the category of continua; therefore, it can be divided into any number of equal parts. Thus, a song can be made of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, or 9 equal semibreves of the same shape; however, it is not very well possible for the human voice to go further. A song consists of three equal parts and of two. Two and three are five, twice two is four, twice three are six, four and three are seven, twice four are eight, three times three are nine; all these are equal; therefore, a song can be made from just as many equal parts. A musician would be praiseworthy and skilled if, over the same equal measure of time, by dividing it now by two, now by three, and so on through the other parts, he could sing the whole in <term>discant<gloss>a style of polyphony where a melody is sung against a fixed base</gloss></term> <note>original: "discantaret"</note>.

Under these nine declared conclusions lie many other special conclusions, which will become clear to students through practice. However, regarding these few things we have said, if anything is included that seems inconsistent with the truth, you...

We ask you, venerable musicians, whom we have loved from our youth because of the art of music—for whoever knows it well, no other knowledge remains hidden—that you might wish to correct our failings out of love for this labor, and support us kindly. For it is not possible for the whole truth of any science to rest in the head of one man, unless he possesses an angelic intellect. For perhaps through the passage of time, the same thing will happen to us as happened to the ancients, who believed they had reached the end of music. Yet let no one say that we have touched the fixed state and the final end of music. For opinions and the cycles of science run back in a circle, as it has pleased the supreme will of Him who, not out of necessity, created all things in this world, and will voluntarily set all things apart.

## ALSO BY JEAN DE MURS
### QUESTIONS ON THE PARTS OF MUSIC.
->*From the same Paris Codex, compared with another from St. Blaise.*<-

<margin>(a)</margin> How many are the parts of <term>prolation<gloss>the system of rhythmic relationships between note values</gloss></term>? Five. Which ones? The <term>maxima<gloss>the largest note value, often called a "large"</gloss></term>, the <term>longa<gloss>a "long" note</gloss></term>, the <term>brevis<gloss>a "short" note, or breve</gloss></term>, the <term>semibrevis<gloss>a "half-short" note</gloss></term>, and the <term>minima<gloss>the "smallest" note value, or minim</gloss></term>.
What is the maxima? It is twofold. In what way? For it is called either the "longest" or the "longer."
What is the "longest"? That which is measured under one accent by three long <term>times<gloss>tempora; the basic units of duration</gloss></term> (b).
What is the "longer"? That which is performed under one accent in two long times. (c)
What is time in general? The measure of a voice brought forth under one continuous motion.
What is a long time? That which is separated into three (d) parts down to the smallest voice.
What is the "smallest" <note>original: "minimum"</note> in the voice? That which is naturally indivisible.

How many <term>minims<gloss>the smallest rhythmic units</gloss></term> are in the <term>perfection<gloss>a grouping of three units, considered "perfect" in medieval theory</gloss></term> of long times? 27. These reach an indivisible unity through a threefold division <note>3 x 3 x 3 = 27</note>.
What is the "number of numbers"? (e) 81. These determine every perfection and imperfection of any continuous voice <note>81 represents the total number of minims in a "perfect" maxima: 27 x 3 = 81</note>.
What is perfection? That by which something is perfect.
What is imperfection? That according to which something is imperfect.
What is perfect? That which is divisible into three parts (f), or into two unequal parts, where the smaller is completely exceeded by the larger <note>This refers to a 1:2 ratio within a triple grouping</note>.
What is imperfect? That which is divided into two equal parts.

<meta>This page continues Jean de Murs' pedagogical "Questions and Answers" on music theory, following his introduction to the five parts of prolation. The previous page ended with the definition of the Maxima; here, he moves into the Long, the Breve, and the smaller divisions of time.</meta>

# JEAN DE MURS

What is the neutral? That which makes a <term>perfect<gloss>in medieval music, "perfect" refers to divisions of three, symbolizing the Holy Trinity</gloss></term> note <term>imperfect<gloss>divisions of two, considered "incomplete" compared to three</gloss></term> through subtraction, and makes an imperfect note perfect through addition.
What is a **Long**? It is twofold. In what way? For it is properly named either perfect or imperfect. 
Why is it called **properly**? To distinguish it from other parts; for although "perfect" and "imperfect" apply to them as well, they claim other names for themselves and not these. 
What is a **perfect Long**? That which is measured under one <term>accent<gloss>beat or pulse</gloss></term> as three <term>brief times<gloss>the "brevis" or breve note value</gloss></term>.
What is an **imperfect Long**? That which is measured under one accent as two brief times <note>The St. Blaise manuscript adds: "perfect or imperfect."</note>.
What is a **brief time**? <note>The St. Blaise manuscript labels this "imperfect."</note> The third part of a long time <note>St. Blaise: "of a perfect time."</note>, divisible by the same division as the whole; otherwise, it is that which, being a part of the greatest and the whole of the least, stands at an equal distance from both.
How many **minims** are in a brief time? <note>St. Blaise: "in a perfect [time]."</note> Nine. Why? Because taken three times they constitute a perfect value, and taken twice—or assigned as such—they constitute an imperfect one. What is perfect and imperfect has been said before.
What is a **Breve**? It is twofold. In what way? For it is called either a "straight" breve or a "shorter" breve.
What is a **straight breve**? That which is performed in its entirety under one continuous time.
Why is it called **entirely**? Because of the parts of the time, which are not called a single entire time.

<column-break/>

What is **one time**? The definition of time and the designation of "one time" are the same.
Of what measurement <note>St. Blaise uses the word "duration."</note> is one time? Double. In what way? Either voluntary or artificial.
What is **voluntary**? That which is formed slowly or quickly according to the whim of the performer.
What is **artificial**? That which, when performed, is divided into two <note>St. Blaise: "is divided into three equals."</note> equal parts, any of which may be similarly divided by a single division; otherwise, it is that which is divisible into nine equal minims while it is being completed <note>St. Blaise: "while it is being performed."</note>.
What is the **shorter [breve]**? A breve that occupies two parts of the time <note>St. Blaise: "of a perfect [time]."</note>.
How many minims are in the shorter breve? Six. Which ones? Those whose half, when added to the whole, completes a straight breve.
What is a **Semibreve**? It is twofold. In what way? For it can be suitably called either "small" or "lesser."
What is the **small [semibreve]**? A third <note>St. Blaise: "A third part of a third of a breve."</note> of a straight breve, whose threefold division comes to rest in the voice of the minim.
What is the **lesser [semibreve]**? A semibreve which contains two parts of the "small" one.
Where does the word **semibreve** come from? It is named from *semis*, which means <note>St. Blaise: "a half, by which an entire part is named."</note> a part of a whole.
Why is it called a semibreve? From the greater or lesser part of a breve <note>St. Blaise: "from the thirds."</note>, but not from an equal half, as in the case of a <term>semitone<gloss>literally "half a tone," though in this period it often meant an "incomplete" tone</gloss></term>.
What is a **Minim**? It is undivided. Why? Because it is not possible to give anything smaller than the smallest.
