# MUSICAL QUESTIONS

What is the absolute minimum? That which is the meter and measure of all things contained within the same category.

What is measure? That which, being repeated as many times as the thing being measured, is finally made equal. <note>(a) The St. Blaise manuscript adds: "and equated."</note>

What does it mean for the *measure to be equated to the thing measured*? <note>(b) The St. Blaise manuscript reads: "to say measured, is measured, and equated."</note> That multiple melodies, through a multitude of voices, are joined together in good musical proportion.

What is music? Music is the mistress of the arts, containing within itself the principles of all methods, established in the first degree of certainty in the nature of all things, and in a wondrous way, proportionally inborn; it is delightful to the intellect, pleasing to the ear; it gladdens the sad, <note>original: "avaros amplificans" — literally "enlarging the greedy," likely suggesting that music makes the miserly heart generous</note> enriches the humble, confounds the envious, comforts the weak, lulls the wakeful to sleep, awakens those who sleep, nurtures love, and honors its possessor; if it attains its proper end, it is ultimately instituted for the praise of God. Alternatively: Music is that which teaches the art and method of singing correctly by means of properly shaped notes.

What is a <term>note<gloss>original: "notula," the symbol representing a specific sound</gloss></term>? A four-sided figure of a numbered sound, signifying time measured according to choice.

What is a four-sided figure? That which is contained by four angles.

What is an angle? An angle is threefold. In what way? Right, obtuse, and acute.

What is a right angle? That which is caused by a perpendicular line falling upon a straight line.

What is an obtuse angle? That which is greater than a right angle.

What is an acute angle? That which is smaller than a right angle.

<column-break/>

How many properties belong to the figures? One. (*as written*)

Which? By sign only.

How many signs of the figures are there? Five. Which? <term>Maximas<gloss>the largest note value</gloss></term>, <term>longs<gloss>long notes</gloss></term>, <term>breves<gloss>brief notes</gloss></term>, <term>semibreves<gloss>half-breves</gloss></term>, and <term>minims<gloss>the smallest notes</gloss></term>.

Give the value for maximas. 81. <note>In this system of "perfect" triple division, one Maxima equals 81 Minims (3x3x3x3).</note>

Give for longs. 27.

Give for breves. 9.

Give for semibreves. 3.

Give for minims. 1.

Give for those beyond the last. Nothing.

In how many ways are notes varied? In as many ways as the figures themselves. How many figures are there? Some figures are equilateral or unequal-sided, right-angled or obtuse-angled, tailed or untailed, pointed upwards or downwards, with a dot or without, before or after, and frequently arranged to the right or to the left.

How are maximas made? A four-sided, unequal-sided, right-angled figure, tailed to the right, either upwards or downwards, is called a maxima.

How is a Long shaped? Like a maxima, except it is shaped with equal sides.

How is a Breve shaped? Like a long, except it is written without a tail.

How is a Semibreve shaped? Four-sided, obtuse-angled, equilateral, and without a tail. <note>This refers to the "diamond" or lozenge shape of the semibreve.</note>

How is a Minim? Like a semibreve, except it is tailed upwards.

How is the <term>perfect<gloss>triple division</gloss></term> shaped? Just like the <term>imperfect<gloss>duple division</gloss></term>.

Where can these be distinguished? In the placement or the order in which the figures are set.

In how many ways is the perfect recognized? In five ways. By which? When either a similar figure...

The aforementioned small notes are of what form? Simple. Why? Because they are distinct from one another and are in no way joined together.

Give the compound forms of these. <term>Ligatures<gloss>from the Latin "ligatura," meaning a binding; two or more notes written as a single connected symbol</gloss></term>.

What is a ligature? The proper joining of notes according to their position above or below.

How many kinds of ligatures are there? Two. Which ones? Straight and oblique.

What is a straight ligature? It is divided into two. How? For one is ascending, when the first note is lower than the second; or descending, when the first note is higher than the second.

How many parts does a ligature have? Two, and sometimes three. Which ones? The beginning, the middle, and the end.

How is the beginning recognized? In three ways. How? With propriety,

<column-break/>

without propriety, and with opposite propriety.

Every descending ligature that has a stem descending from the left side, as here <image-desc>musical notation: descending binary ligature with a downward stem on the left of the first note</image-desc>, and every ascending ligature lacking a stem, as here <image-desc>musical notation: ascending binary ligature without any stems</image-desc>, is said to be **with propriety**.

Every descending ligature lacking any stem, as here <image-desc>musical notation: descending binary ligature without any stems</image-desc>, and every ascending ligature having a stem descending from the right side, as here <image-desc>musical notation: ascending binary ligature with a downward stem on the right of the first note</image-desc>, is said to be **without propriety**.

However, every ligature, whether ascending or descending, having a stem ascending from the first note on the left side, as here <image-desc>musical notation: ascending and descending binary ligatures, each with an upward stem on the left of the first note</image-desc>, is said to be **with opposite propriety**.

How is the end recognized? In two ways. Which ones? With perfection and without perfection. Every square note situated directly above the second-to-last note or below the second-to-last note, as here <image-desc>musical notation: two examples of vertical square-note stacks</image-desc>, is said to be **with perfection**; if, however, it is to the side and indirect, as here <image-desc>musical notation: two examples of square notes side-by-side</image-desc>, which only happens when ascending, it is said to be **without perfection**.

What is an oblique ligature? That which is formed from slanted shapes, as here <image-desc>musical notation: two examples of oblique ligature shapes</image-desc>; the final note of any slanted shape is called a <term>breve<gloss>a "short" note value</gloss></term>.

Every ligature "with propriety" makes the first note a breve; every ligature "without propriety" makes the first note a <term>longa<gloss>a "long" note value</gloss></term>.

### MUSICAL QUESTIONS

Every <term>opposite property<gloss>original: *opposita proprietas*; a specific rule in notation where an upward stroke at the start of a ligature changes the rhythmic value</gloss></term> makes the first note a <term>semibreve<gloss>half-short</gloss></term>.

Every <term>perfection<gloss>the state of being triple or "complete" in medieval rhythmic theory</gloss></term> makes the last note a <term>long</term>, while <term>imperfection<gloss>the state of being duple or "incomplete"</gloss></term> makes it a <term>breve</term>.

All middle notes are breves, unless they are joined with an opposite property, as seen here: <note>The original manuscript contains a small rectangular musical notation mark representing a ligature.</note>

In every <term>oblique body<gloss>a single symbol representing two notes, drawn as a thick diagonal bar rather than square blocks</gloss></term>, the first point without a tail is called a long; if it has a tail descending to the left, it is a breve; if it has an ascending tail, it is a semibreve. In <term>ligatures<gloss>groups of notes tied together</gloss></term>, longs are made imperfect in whatever way was shown for simple figures.

->*Concerning the Modes.*<-

What is a <term>mode<gloss>original: *modus*; here referring to rhythmic patterns rather than melodic scales</gloss></term>? It is an arrangement of note shapes demonstrating various moods of the soul in songs.

How many modes of singing are there? Many. Of which the first is when a third part of its own value is placed after a figure; the second is the opposite. The third is when a second part, or a third, or the figure itself is placed before a figure. The fourth is the opposite. The fifth involves all of these mixed and varied.

In how many ways is a "perfect" note made "imperfect"? In as many ways as it happens to be separated by a three-fold division, whether mediately or immediately.

Why is it called *immediately*? Because of the "near parts." And *mediately*? Because of the "remote parts."

What are the near parts? Those of which three together perfectly restore the whole. <note>In triple time, three "near" smaller notes (like three breves) equal one larger note (like a long).</note>

What are the remote parts? Those of which more than three are required to make a complete whole.

By how many names is the complete "whole" called? Four. Which ones? Perfectly per-

<column-break/>

fect, perfectly imperfect, imperfectly perfect, and imperfectly imperfect. <note>These terms describe the relationship between different levels of time (e.g., how a Long relates to a Breve, and how a Breve relates to a Semibreve).</note>

How are they recognized? Through those things that were said above.

How is an "imperfect" note made "perfect"? Imperfection is twofold: immediate and mediate.

Immediate is such as a long [perfected] by a breve, a breve by a semibreve, and generally every "whole" by a third part of itself; the sign of this perfection is a dot added to the right.

Mediate is such as a long [perfected] by a semibreve, or a breve by a <term>minim<gloss>the smallest standard note value of the period</gloss></term>; and generally every "whole" perfected by a third part of its own third part. The sign of this perfection is a dot added above. And so it proceeds proportionally through the corners or sides of the note.

->*Concerning the Dot.*<-

How many meanings does the <term>dot<gloss>original: *punctus*</gloss></term> have? Several. Which ones? It signifies perfection, the marking of time, the separation of perfections, and sometimes the division of a mode, according to <term>Hugo<gloss>likely referring to the theorist Hugo von Reutlingen (1285–1359)</gloss></term>. The second dot, which is added to a note or a division of a mode, does three things, like a preposition added to a case: it either completes, changes, or diminishes.

In how many ways is song created in general? Two. Which ones? For there is <term>regular song<gloss>cantus regularis</gloss></term> and <term>irregular song<gloss>cantus irregularis</gloss></term>.

What is regular? When the song is made of perfect time against perfect, or imperfect against imperfect, and the perfections begin and end at the same time.

Irregular is named by the opposite.

In what way? When a song is made of perfect...

### *On Discant and Consonances.*

There are six species of <term>discant<gloss>original: *discantus*; a style of medieval polyphony where a voice is added above a plainchant melody</gloss></term>, through which every discant can be made plain and melodious. The first species is the <term>unison<gloss>two voices singing the same pitch</gloss></term>, and it occupies one line or one space, except for *b-flat and b-natural* <note>original: *b. fa ♮ mi*</note>, in which there are two different sounds on the same line or in the same space, though they do not create a unison. The <term>semiditone<gloss>minor third</gloss></term> is the second species, and it consists of one whole tone and a semitone. The <term>ditone<gloss>major third</gloss></term>

---

<margin>(a)</margin> *In the lower margin of Blasianus's text, these notes are added:* These aforementioned six species are called "simple" because they are contained within the <term>diapason<gloss>octave</gloss></term> inclusive. Every simple <term>consonance<gloss>a harmonious combination of notes</gloss></term> is embraced within the octave, and whatever lies outside it can be described by repeating these. It was not necessary in this work to set down more species than those mentioned; for a tenth is considered the same as a third, because it is composed of an octave (or double) and a third; a twelfth,

<column-break/>

is the third species, and it contains two full tones. The <term>diapente<gloss>fifth</gloss></term> is the fourth species and contains three tones and a semitone. The fifth species is that which contains one whole and perfect tone along with a fifth <note>This describes a Major Sixth.</note>. The sixth species is the <term>diapason<gloss>octave</gloss></term>, and it contains eight notes, so that the semitones <note>original: *mi fa*</note> are interposed twice; it occurs from <term>D la re</term> to <term>mi la re mi</term>, namely from *Gamma-ut* to *G-sol-re-ut*, or from *A-re* up to *A-la-mi-re* <note>These are names for specific pitches in the medieval "Guidonian Hand" system, used to navigate the scales.</note>.

<margin>(a)</margin> Of these aforementioned species, some create a "perfect" consonance and others an "imperfect" one. The unison, the fifth, and the octave create a perfect consonance. The other species—namely the minor third, the major third, and the major sixth <note>original: *tonus cum diapente*</note>—create an imperfect consonance. These tend to "strive" to ascend or descend into the aforementioned perfect species: specifically, the minor third toward the unison, the major third toward the fifth, and the major sixth toward the octave, by ascending or descending in sequence. And what I have ordained regarding the minor third, major third, and fifth above the unison, you should understand the same way regarding those above the octave.

It should also be known that a discant ought to have its beginning and its end on a perfect consonance. We must also avoid, as much as we can, two perfect consonances joined in a sequence while ascending or descending <note>This is an early rule against "parallel fifths" or "parallel octaves," which became a standard rule in classical harmony.</note>. It is notably important to know that we cannot place two notes...

that is, an octave with a fifth, is considered a fifth; a thirteenth is like a sixth; and a "double-double" or an octave-plus-octave (which are the same) is like a simple octave; and so on for the others. Whatever was said above regarding the simple species of discant is understood in the same way for those composed from these simple consonances.

This is very beautiful in discant. Also, it should be known that *mi* against *fa* <note>original: "mi contra fa"; this refers to the "tritone," a harsh dissonance that was strictly forbidden in perfect consonances</note> does not harmonize in the perfect species, such as in the fifth, octave, tenth, twelfth, and in the unison; but in the imperfect species—namely in the third, sixth, and eleventh—one can be placed against the other by license.

It should also be noted diligently that when the simple melody or tenor (which is the same thing) moves in the highest register, such as in the third register, if we wish to provide a discant for that simple melody, we devise voices

It should also be known that when we wish to sing by <term>false music<gloss>original: "falsa musica"; the use of accidentals or "musica ficta" to alter notes outside the standard medieval hexachord system</gloss></term>, it is necessary that in singing the discant we take this voice, as in *D. la sol re*, and *re* in *E la mi re*, and *mi* in *F. fa ut*, and *fa* in *G. sol re ut*, and *sol* in *a. la mi re*, and *la* in *b. fa. ♮ mi*. Hence, we can certainly sing discant through the whole "hand" by false music, as long as the tenor does not harmonize with <term>true music<gloss>original: "verae musicae"; music that stays within the traditional "natural," "hard," and "soft" hexachords</gloss></term>. But when we are able to sing discant through true music, it is unlawful to sing through false music.

(a) What is the difference between an <term>altered note<gloss>a note that is doubled in value to fill out a triple measure</gloss></term> and an <term>imperfect note<gloss>a note whose value is reduced from three units to two</gloss></term>, since the altered note in <term>perfect mode<gloss>triple meter</gloss></term>, time, and measure is the same as the imperfect one? The answer is: they are the same regarding time, mode, and measure, but they differ in their figures <note>the visual shapes of the notes</note>. The reason why? Because a <term>large</term> as well as a <term>long</term>, <term>breve</term>, and <term>semibreve</term> can be made imperfect from the front and from the back. And always the note which is made imperfect is made imperfect by a note of a smaller form or a smaller value, and the imperfect note has a larger body or form that is also varied. And because of this, the note which is altered is in a similar form to the one that causes it to be altered; therefore [it is different]. And alteration occurs in the second place from the front, and not from the back, but this is not so in a note...

## ADMONITION.

*In the often-cited Parisian manuscript, the following things are joined by the same hand, which are undoubtedly by the same author, even if he occasionally reports the opinions of another, namely **HUGO**, whom he had already cited just above. Therefore, we provide them here in the order in which they follow in the said manuscript, especially since after them, the art of <term>discant<gloss>the practice of singing a melody against a fixed plainchant</gloss></term> by the same JOHANNES de Muris occurs again.*

The proportional numbers follow according to Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Neoplatonist whose writings on the "Music of the Spheres" were standard in medieval education</note>, which numbers indeed come together to create music. These are six, namely: <term>epitritus<gloss>4:3 ratio</gloss></term>, <term>hemiolius<gloss>3:2 ratio</gloss></term>, **double**, **triple**, **quadruple**, and <term>epogdous<gloss>9:8 ratio, the Pythagorean whole tone</gloss></term>.

**Epitritus**, which by another name according to Boethius <note>The most authoritative Roman writer on music theory, whose works formed the basis of the medieval curriculum</note> is called *sesquitertius*, occurs when between two numbers the larger contains the whole smaller number within itself, and its third part besides, such as four to three, or 8 to 6. And it is called *epitritus* from *epi* <note>original: "ἐπι"</note> which is "upon," and *trite* <note>original: "τριτη"</note> which is "third," as if a number containing another tone and a third part of it besides. From this is born the <term>consonance<gloss>original: "symphonia"; a harmonious sounding together</gloss></term> which is called the **fourth** <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>.

**Hemiolius**, which by another name is called *sesquialter*, occurs when between two numbers the larger contains the whole smaller number, and its half besides, such as three to two. And it is called *hemiolius* from *hemi* <note>original: "ἡμι"</note>

<column-break/>

in Greek, which is "half" in Latin, and *holon* <note>original: "ὅλον"</note> which is "whole," as if containing the whole and half of its own whole. And from this is born the consonance which is called the **fifth** <note>original: "diapente"</note>.

The **double** number occurs when between two numbers the smaller is measured twice in the larger, such as 4 to 2; and it is named from "two" and "fold," as is evident, and from this is born the consonance which is called the **octave** <note>original: "diapason"</note>.

The **triple** number is when between two numbers the smaller is measured three times in the larger, such as 3 to 1. It is evident why it is so called. And from this is born the consonance which by composition is called the **octave with a fifth** <note>original: "diapason cum diapente"; modern musicians call this a twelfth</note>.

The **quadruple** number is when between two numbers the smaller is measured four times in the larger, such as 4 to 1. It is evident why it is so called. And from this is born the consonance which is called the **double octave** <note>original: "bis diapason"; modern musicians call this a fifteenth</note>.

An <term>epogdous<gloss>original: "epogdous"; a Greek-derived term for a ratio where a number contains the whole of a smaller number plus one-eighth of it</gloss></term> number is one that contains within itself a smaller number twice and additionally its eighth part <note>The text likely means "contains the whole of a number plus one-eighth," referring to the 9:8 ratio</note>, as in the case of 9 to 8. This number is otherwise called, according to <note>Boethius was a 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music textbook for a thousand years</note> Boethius, the <term>sesquioctave<gloss>a Latin term for the 9:8 ratio</gloss></term>; and it is called *epogdous* from the Greek *epi* <note>original: "ἐπὶ"</note> which means "above," and *okto* <note>original: "ὀκτὼ"</note> which is "eight," as if it contains the whole and additionally its eighth part. From this ratio, according to musicians, the **tone** is born. However, the ancients wished to call a sound smaller than a tone a **semitone**. But this should not be understood as if it were a literal "half-tone," just as we do not take a <term>semivowel<gloss>In Latin grammar, letters like L, M, N, R, S, X, F which have a sound but cannot form a syllable without a vowel</gloss></term> in literature to be half a vowel. Finally, by its very nature, a tone does not allow itself to be divided into two equal parts; for since it consists of the number nine, and nine can never be divided equally into whole numbers, the tone refuses to be divided into two equal halves. That is, it does not have any middle point that maintains an equal proportion to the extremes, because a tone is divided into two unequal parts: the <term>minor<gloss>the "limma" or Pythagorean semitone</gloss></term> and the <term>major<gloss>the "apotome"</gloss></term>. But they called the sound smaller than a tone a "semitone," which was found to differ from a tone by as much as these two numbers differ from each other: namely, 243 and 256—a difference of 13. This number (13), when multiplied eight times, does not seem to reach the halfway point of 243. For those 13s, by reconciliation, make 104, which in no way will contain the middle of 243 <note>The author is using medieval arithmetic to prove that you cannot simply split the 9:8 ratio into two equal whole-number ratios</note>. The ancient Pythagoreans used to call this semitone a **diesis**. But later usage decreed that a sound smaller than a semitone should be named a *diesis*. Plato called the semitone a **limma**. But having considered all these things, it is clearly evident in what follows:

### *Concerning what a tone is according to various considerations, and concerning its partition and parts.*

Next, the semitone should be discussed; but because a semitone is less than a tone, etc. (a)

It is defined otherwise: a **tone** is the space between two unisons, containing within itself two semitones, or the space of two semitones. Otherwise: a tone is the ascent or descent of one voice to another nearby voice, dividing it thus, such as *re, re ut* <note>The author uses Solmization syllables—the ancestors of Do-Re-Mi—to illustrate a step</note>.

Otherwise: a tone is the **rule** which judges every ecclesiastical song at the end, and not the beginning, for this reason: because the final note is more excellent than the other notes; and for another reason, because <term>antiphons<gloss>short chants sung before or after a psalm</gloss></term> and <term>responsories<gloss>chants with a call-and-response structure</gloss></term> and other church songs are not as truly or perfectly known at the beginning as at the end, according to what <note>Ptolemy was a 2nd-century mathematician and astronomer whose work "Harmonics" influenced musical theory</note> Ptolemy says: that everything is to be named from its end.

It follows yet further, what a tone is according to the text called the *Enchiridion* <note>Handbook</note> of <term>Hucbald<gloss>A 9th-century monk and music theorist</gloss></term>. A tone is when a voice is deflected or raised from another, whether in a low or high sound, by a modest interval, like the distance of a single point, so that the hearing altogether easily notices their division. And a tone is the **space** of those two voices so clinging to each other, not the voices themselves—which are nothing other than sounds—according to the interval that is between them. In any...

<header>JOHN DE MURIS</header>

You have an example of this in any musical instrument between the first two strings, provided they are well-tuned, or in the <term>hydraulia<gloss>a water organ; an ancient pipe organ powered by water pressure</gloss></term> between the first two pipes; likewise, you can test this in the <term>antiphon<gloss>a short chant in Christian ritual, sung as a refrain</gloss></term> *Go tell John* <note>original: "Ite dicite Iohanni"; a reference to the Gregorian chant based on the Gospel of Luke 7:22</note>. Furthermore, a **tone** is a certain unbroken striking of the air reaching the hearing, moving from low to high—specifically from the note *G* to *a*—and vice versa; its name is derived from "to sound" or "to thunder" <note>original: "a tono tonas"; the author is making a folk-etymological connection between the noun 'tonus' and the verb 'tonare'</note>. Alternatively: a tone is the rightful space of high or low pitch between one sound and another, containing within itself two semitones, but not <term>equal semitones<gloss>the author stresses that a tone cannot be divided into two exactly equal halves in the Pythagorean system</gloss></term>. Alternatively, as <note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) was the primary authority on music theory in the Middle Ages</note> Boethius says: A tone is said to consist of two minor semitones and a **comma**. For if a whole tone consists of an <term>apotome<gloss>the "major semitone" in Pythagorean tuning</gloss></term> and a semitone, and the semitone differs from the apotome by a comma, then an apotome is nothing other than a minor semitone plus a comma. Therefore, if someone removes two minor semitones from a tone, a comma is what remains.

### On the parts of a tone.

These are the parts of a tone: the **diesis**, the **limma**, the **asma** (or minor semitone, which is the same thing), the **comma**, the **apotome**, the **major semitone**, and the **diaschisma**. A diesis or minor semitone contains within itself two diaschismas. A comma contains within itself two **schismas**. An apotome contains a diesis and one comma. Furthermore, according to the sayings of <note>Likely Hugo of St. Victor or a similar scholastic author; "Nepos" refers to a specific, though now obscure, treatise</note> Hugo in his book called *The Grandson*, a major semitone contains within itself a diesis and one schisma—that is, the half of a comma along with a diesis. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>Usually referring to Aristotle, though here citing general musical philosophy</note> encompasses these spaces and those smaller than them with the following definitions:

> A **diesis**, he says, is the space by which the <term>sesquioctave ratio<gloss>the 9:8 ratio that creates a whole tone</gloss></term> is greater than two schismas and two diaschismas, or one apotome.

<column-break/>

> A **comma** is the space by which the sesquioctave ratio is greater than two dieses and two minor semitones. A **schisma** is half the space of a comma.
> 
> A **diaschisma** is half of a diesis—that is, smaller than a semitone. From these things it is gathered that a whole tone is primarily divided into a minor semitone and an apotome; it is also divided into two minor semitones and one comma, which results in it being divided into four diaschismas and one comma. A complete half of a tone, which is called a **major semitone**, consists of four diaschismas, or of two dieses (which make one minor semitone) and one schisma (which is half the space of a comma).

### Also Hugo on the division of the tone.

Since a whole tone is joined from two minor semitones and a comma, if anyone wishes to divide that whole, let him make one minor semitone into two diaschismas, and half of a comma into one **asma**. Rightly, therefore, it has been said that the complete half of a tone can be broken down into two diaschismas and one schisma. Thus, the complete half of a tone—that is, the major semitone—differs, or is seen to differ, from the minor semitone by one schisma. The apotome, however, differs from the minor semitone by two schismas; for it differs by one comma, if two schismas complete one comma.

### Also the same Hugo on the division of the tone.

Note that a whole tone is divided into a minor semitone and an apotome. To have an understanding of this division, it should be noted—

# CONCERNING TONES.

It must be noted that a whole tone can be divided into eight <term>diaschisms<gloss>the smallest theoretical division of a tone in this system, representing one-eighth of a tone</gloss></term>, from which two complete or major semitones are formed. But note that a major semitone is one thing, and a minor semitone is another. To understand this division, note that two diaschisms make one <term>schism<gloss>one-fourth of a tone</gloss></term>, and one schism makes a <term>diesis<gloss>here used to mean a minor semitone, though its meaning varied among medieval theorists</gloss></term>, which is the same as a minor semitone. And two minor semitones make one major semitone, because from the division of the diaschisms, a major semitone is formed from four diaschisms: and thus from two major semitones, a whole tone is completed.

But a *semitonus* is one thing and a *semitonium* is another: a *semitonus* <note>original: "semitonus"</note> is called an "imperfect tone," and its name is derived from the words *semis, sema, semum* <note>Latin terms implying "incomplete" or "mutilated"</note>, which means the same as "not full"; likewise, a "semi-ditone" is like an imperfect <term>ditone<gloss>an interval of two whole tones, similar to a major third</gloss></term>. But a *semitonium* <note>original: "semitonium"</note> is named from the indeclinable word *semis* <note>meaning "half"</note>, as is clear from the definition of a tone. For a tone is defined thus, as appears above: a tone is the legitimate space of high or low pitch between one sound and another, containing within itself two "half-tones" [*semitonia*] and not "imperfect tones" [*semitonos*]. And this same point is evident through <note>An influential 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook for medieval music theory</note> Boethius and also through <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the inventor of modern musical notation</note> Guido, who says: a tone took its name from "intoning," because it establishes nine steps for the larger voice—that is, the tone of nine <note>Referring to the 9:8 numerical ratio of a whole tone</note>—and eight steps for the smaller voice—that is, the semitone of eight. And just as there is said to be a major and minor semitone, so too there is said to be a major and minor tone.

> *Likewise the same Hugo, and he intends to say that in the <term>fourth<gloss>diatessaron</gloss></term> and the <term>fifth<gloss>diapente</gloss></term> there is a major semitone.*

Having seen what a tone is, how many and what kind of parts it has, what a major semitone is

<column-break/>

and what a minor one is, what a *semitonium* is and what a *semitonus* is, and what a major and minor tone are; it appears that the voice, sound, or space that exists between the major and minor tone—that is, in the <term>sesquioctave ratio<gloss>the ratio of 9 to 8, which defines a whole tone in Pythagorean tuning</gloss></term> or "nine-fold" tone—is called a tone. A major semitone of this tone, by a right interval, holds exactly the middle, as is clear from the aforementioned things and as will be made manifest later according to the sayings of certain men. And although the true doctors, to whom I yield, and my master <note>Likely referring to St. Thomas Aquinas, who discussed the harmony of the spheres and the soul</note> Thomas say: the <term>octave<gloss>diapason</gloss></term> is composed of two proportions, namely the fourth and the fifth; and the fourth consists of two tones and a minor semitone, while the fifth consists of three tones and a minor semitone: therefore the octave consists of five tones and two minor semitones, which do not make a full tone—and those who understand otherwise are in error. Thus, I do not contradict such a great man or his sayings, nor is it my intention to contradict him; he and the experienced ones must truly be yielded to; for I am not able to reach the depth of his words—these are the words of <note>Likely Hugh of Saint Victor, a 12th-century mystic and scholar who wrote on the "arts" including music</note> Hugo. But as certain things can be conceived according to certain teachers, so they can also be brought forward: hence this seems possible to be proven through the number related to the position, as is clear on the <term>monochord<gloss>a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge used to demonstrate the mathematical ratios of musical intervals</gloss></term>, that there is a major semitone there, or a complete half of a tone such as has been described. And so that this might be seen more clearly, we have wished to explain the tones, the semitones, and their parts. Whatever may be said here, however, I agree with the sayings of the experts: and these things stated above are the sayings of the venerable Hugo.

A **formal tone** <note>original: "Tonus formularis"</note> is defined as the interval of a single voice [pitch step], containing within itself two semitones.
A **nine-fold tone** <note>original: "Tonus novenarius"</note> is that which is created by a note of nine parts <note>Referring to the 9:8 ratio of the Pythagorean whole tone</note>.
A **middle tone** <note>original: "Tonus meses"</note> is one that possesses neither an authentic [higher] rise nor a plagal [lower] fall <note>Refers to the classification of church modes</note>.
A **continuous tone** is so called because, through the use of **B-flat** <note>original: "B. rotundum," the "round B" used to signify a flat</note>, it compels G to sound as the *protus* <term>protus<gloss>the first mode category, usually starting on D; B-flat allows it to be transposed</gloss></term>, A as the *deuterus* <term>deuterus<gloss>the second mode category, usually starting on E</gloss></term>, and itself as the *tritus* <term>tritus<gloss>the third mode category, usually starting on F</gloss></term>.

# HERE BEGINS THE ART OF DESCANT <term>descant<gloss>the medieval practice of singing a new melody over a fixed plainchant</gloss></term> PROVIDED BY MASTER
## JOHN DE MURIS, IN ABBREVIATED FORM.
### *From the same Parisian Manuscript.*

Aristotle, the prince of philosophers, states in the prologue to his *Metaphysics* (a): "The sure sign of one who possesses knowledge is the ability to teach." In any art, those who understand the theory are able to teach, whereas those who only practice without being experts might know *that* a thing is so, but they do not know the *reason why* <note>original: "propter quid"</note>. They do not act through the science of what they say—just as a fire burns [by nature, not by knowing why]. However, we believe that understanding and knowing in every art comes more from the art itself than from mere experience. Therefore, we judge the master-craftsmen to be wiser than the merely experienced. For this reason, we consider the art to be more of a science than experience is. The former can teach, while the latter cannot.

Since, however, art deals with universals, and experience deals with particulars, and universals presuppose particulars, it follows that art presupposes experience. Experi-

-> # ON PROPORTIONS. <-

Pythagoras, wishing to rely on the judgment of the ears regarding consonances <note>In medieval music theory, a "consonance" is a combination of notes that sounds pleasing or "stable" to the ear.</note> (since it is not surprising for anyone to be deceived concerning that which is not their own, for the ear judges the sound but does not comprehend the proportion at all): remained for a long time in a state of anxiety, seeking how he might rationally find the science of consonances. On one occasion, while passing by the workshops of blacksmiths, he heard hammers emitting a certain wonderful consonance, and immediately, as if thunderstruck, he turned toward them. Doubting whether the melody arose from the strength of the men, he ordered the hammers to be swapped; and feeling the same result as before, he realized that the consonance was contained within the nature of the hammers, arranged in such a fashion. The number of hammers was five, but the fifth was rejected because it sounded dissonant. Four hammers therefore remained, whose weights were found through sensory experiment to be in the proportions of **double**, **one-and-a-half** <term>sesquialtera<gloss>A ratio of 3:2, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its half.</gloss></term>, **one-and-a-third** <term>sesquitertia<gloss>A ratio of 4:3, where the larger number contains the smaller plus its third.</gloss></term>, and **one-and-an-eighth** <term>sesquioctava<gloss>A ratio of 9:8, which defines a whole tone in Pythagorean tuning.</gloss></term>. Finding this same proportion in the "infancy" of ancient instruments—those with strings, holes, wind, and others—he tested it. From these experiments running together in his memory, he grasped a single universal principle, which became for him the beginning of the art and science.

And so that what has been said may appear more clearly, let the proportion of the hammers be shown in the numbers to which the proportion first applies. Let the weights of the hammers be **12, 9, 8, and 6**. Therefore, **6** compared to **12** in a **double proportion** is considered a **diapason** <term>diapason<gloss>An octave; the interval where the frequency or weight ratio is 2:1.</gloss></term>. Then, **12** to **9** and **8** to **6** in a **one-and-a-third proportion** demonstrate the **diatessaron** <term>diatessaron<gloss>A perfect fourth; the interval defined by the ratio 4:3.</gloss></term>. Next, **12** to **8** and **9** to **6** in a **one-and-a-half proportion** resound as a **diapente** <term>diapente<gloss>A perfect fifth; the interval defined by the ratio 3:2.</gloss></term>. Finally, **8** to **9** in a **one-and-an-**

<column-break/>

**eighth proportion** forms a **tone**; for only these species of multiples have a place in consonances. Simple consonances are made in simple proportions, and composite ones in composite proportions. Hence, the **octave-and-a-fifth** <note>original: "diapason & diapente"</note> was in a **triple proportion**, which arises from the **double** and the **one-and-a-half**, such as **2, 4, 6**. The **double octave** <note>original: "Bis diapason"</note> is a **quadruple proportion**, which is born from the **double**, such as **2, 4, 8**. The **fourth** and the **fifth** together return an **octave**, for the **double** arises from the **one-and-a-half** and the **one-and-a-third**, such as **2, 3, 4**. The **fifth** is made from the **one-and-a-half** and the **one-and-a-third**, as in **6, 8, 9** <note>In this sequence, 6 to 9 is 3:2 (fifth), 6 to 8 is 4:3 (fourth), and 8 to 9 is a tone.</note>. The **fourth** consists of two tones and a semitone; the **fifth** consists of three tones and a semitone. But these two added together make an **octave**; therefore, the **octave** consists of five tones with two semitones. However, those two semitones do not reach the perfection of a full tone, as is proved in the following.

Because it has been said that the **octave** consists of five tones and two semitones, which do not reach the perfection of six full tones; it remains to be shown that a **semitone**, according to the voice, is not truly a half of a tone, as some in ancient times estimated. Any half, when doubled, ought to return its whole integrally; but a semitone doubled does not return the whole integrally, which is evident in the ordered numbers **243** and **256**, which return the semitonal proportion <note>This ratio, 256:243, is known as the Pythagorean "limma" or minor semitone.</note>. For **256** compared to **192** in a **one-and-a-third proportion** completes a **fourth**, from which, if two tones are subtracted, a **semitone** remains. Therefore, the difference between **243** and **256** is **13**, the double of which is **26**, which is added...

...then upon 243. If it is a true semitone <note>In this context, a "true semitone" refers to a mathematical value that is exactly half of a whole tone. Johannes is using the Pythagorean ratio of 256:243 to show it does not perfectly divide the tone.</note>, it ought to yield a whole tone in the **one-and-an-eighth** <term>sesquioctava<gloss>A ratio of 9:8, which defines a whole tone in the Pythagorean system.</gloss></term> proportion, which is 269. But it does not do so, because if one-eighth part were added to 243, the resulting number making a tone in the 9:8 ratio would be 273 and 3 eighths, which is greater than the preceding number; therefore, it is not a true semitone.

Furthermore, by the rule of arithmetic: if two numbers exist in a certain proportion, the products created from them will remain in that same proportion. For example, 2 and 3 relate to each other in a **one-and-a-half** <term>sesquialtera<gloss>A ratio of 3:2, the mathematical basis for the musical interval of a perfect fifth.</gloss></term> proportion; the products created from these are 4, 6, and 9, among which the same 3:2 proportion is maintained. Therefore, just as 243 multiplied by itself is 59,049, so 243 <note>The text here likely contains a scribal error; to follow the logic of the squares, this should be 256, as 256 times 256 equals 65,536.</note> extended by itself generates 65,536; that which is produced from the multiplication of one root by the other is the proportional middle, namely 63,408 <note>original: "63408"; mathematically, 243 multiplied by 256 is actually 62,208. These calculations were often difficult for medieval copyists to maintain accurately.</note>. Just as there is a semitone proportion between the roots, so it is between the products; but let these be two [intervals]. Therefore, if it were a true semitone, the distance from the greatest to the least would be a whole tone; which

<column-break/>

is however not the case; for if an eighth part of the first number were added to it, it would exceed the third; therefore, there was no true semitone between the first and second, nor between the second and third, and so they could not complete a whole tone. Therefore, similarly, between the roots—which are 243 and 256—there was no true half of a tone, but rather less: which is the point I set out to demonstrate. And let these things concerning the theory of music suffice for the listener for the sake of brevity.

Nevertheless, subsequent inventors of music have organized it in various ways: some on stringed instruments, some on reed instruments, and others on wind instruments. Certain later inventors, however, organized it for voices using the joints of the hands <note>This refers to the "Guidonian Hand," a popular medieval mnemonic where singers used the joints and tips of their fingers to find and remember different notes of the scale.</note>, by the letters of the alphabet distinguished by steps, and by making "mutations" <note>A "mutation" was the process of shifting between different hexachords (six-note scales) to reach higher or lower notes in a melody.</note> of one step into another, as the description placed below demonstrates.

<note>This table illustrates the system of hexachords—six-note scales (ut-re-mi-fa-sol-la). Because a single melody might exceed six notes, singers had to "mutate" or switch between these seven overlapping columns to reach higher or lower pitches. The letters on the left represent the absolute pitches, while the syllables (ut through la) represent the functional roles of those notes within a specific hexachord.</note>

# A LITTLE TREATISE
## ON THE DIFFERENCES AND KINDS OF SINGERS PUBLISHED BY
## MASTER ARNULPH OF ST. GHISLAIN.

->*From a Parisian Manuscript.*<-

I believe that in these times there are four principal types of singers. The first type is commonly found among the common folk who are completely ignorant of the art of music. Lacking any benefit of natural talent, and driven by the rash daring of their foolish presumption—even though they do not yet know plainchant—they nonetheless strive to gnaw at and "devour" musical harmonies <note>The author uses "consonantia," which refers to the sounding together of different notes, a precursor to harmony.</note> everywhere with greedy bites as they lead the singing. In the barking of their own brawling, they bray louder than a donkey and make a terrible noise like a brutal trumpet-blast. They vomit out a *cacemphaton* <gloss>(a) <note>original: "cacemphaton"; a technical term for an unpleasant sound or a foul-sounding pronunciation.</note></gloss>. When they attempt to sing polyphony <note>original: "organizantes"; performing *organum*, an early form of harmonized singing.</note>, they commit a "barbarism" in music by doing the exact opposite of the rules. Blinded by the false shell of their own execrable presumption, they boast to themselves that they can surpass or lead the most excellent singers. They impudently offer to correct or direct others with their voices <note>original: "tuba," literally "trumpet," here used metaphorically for a loud, piercing voice.</note> so that they might appear to be musicians to other men. Yet they do not even know enough about music to be led by others; they are always singing out of tune with those in harmony, and they defile whatever is produced according to the rules with their unlearned faults. Indeed, they are as intolerable and harmful to singers as weeds <note>original: "zizania"; a reference to the biblical "tares" or weeds that choke the wheat.</note> that grow up and choke the first harvest. Silence cannot be imposed on them—which in itself is considered a vice in them—but instead they stubbornly 

<column-break/>

cry out all the more greedily. They are not ashamed to trample under their feet the musical pearls of harmony, which are more precious than gold. These are surely the ones whom the authority of music irrevocably banishes from its borders; indeed, they are the ones upon whom the favor of indignant music itself spits.

The second type is evident in those laypeople who, although they are unskilled in the entire art of music, are nevertheless led by a zeal for its sweetness. They lend their delicate ears to any musical sounds, following and associating with musicians most attentively. Like the panther of the "good scent" <note>According to medieval bestiaries, the panther possessed a naturally sweet breath that would attract all other animals to follow it.</note> which all animals follow, or like the bee that diligently pursues flowers for the sake of the honey's sweetness, they follow those set upon study. They gather handfuls from the harvest of musical gleanings so that they may sing along more gracefully with the singers. By frequent practice, they become skilled and experienced in many musical matters, so that what they lack in formal art is supplied by use and natural industry. Among these we see some clerics who, on musical instruments, discover and pass on the most difficult musical patterns—which the human voice would hardly dare to express—through a miraculous prodigy of innate musical inventiveness. Others, however, who [simply perform] what has been so created and passed down...

# ON THE DIFFERENCES OF SINGERS.

<column-break/>

...they remember [the music] only slightly less laudably, and sometimes the grateful diligence of the one remembering matches the praise of the original inventor. These are truly from the "marketplace of music," and to them it is certainly granted to be favored; indeed, by her promised mercy, Music does not exclude them but adopts them as sons of her own house and special family.

The third type is clearly proven in those who possess glorious treasures of musical art and discipline within the shrines of their hearts, acquired laudably through the virtue of study. Even if they suffer a defect in their physical "organ" <note>In this context, *organum* refers to the voice or the vocal apparatus itself.</note> for worthily bringing forth the high notes they understand, the living knowledge of the art nevertheless compensates for their natural inability. That which they cannot produce by themselves through harmonious singing, they see to it is done through their disciples, by teaching those placed under them according to the rules. They share their musical riches and reveal secrets to those worthy of the worthy "numbers" <note>Numbers here refers to the mathematical ratios that define musical intervals.</note> of music. From their hearts flow not only the theoretical streams of musical doctrine, but they also manifest this through practical deed and work. Thus, the ear and eye of a wise person recognize a practical musician worthy of praise. For what he possesses as an internal habit, he exhibits for hearing and contemplation in action; such people do not engage in "musical sophistry" <note>Meaning they do not use deceptive or shallow techniques.</note>, but profess a real and substantial music. Although they may weary their listeners when singing, their eloquence redeems this defect whenever they speak the rules of the art through verbal instruction.

The fourth type in order—though first in dignity—is seen to shine gloriously in those whom natural instinct, supported by the vocal 

<column-break/>

organ of a honeyed voice, renders figuratively like nightingales <note>original: "philomelicos"</note>. Yet they are much better than nightingales by the gift of their voice, and not inferior to larks in praise. In these singers, the noble acquirer of the vocal art directs the natural organ regularly according to mode, measure, number, and color. With wondrous modulation, they vary the shifts in harmonies, and through a multiform variety of modes, they bring material for new recreation to the soul of the listener. Furthermore, through the grace of a superior delivery, they take any unpolished or unsuitably presented musical works back to the "forge of their creator," and by remodeling them, return them to a more graceful form. For who would not wonder that, through the mastery of performance, a musical proportion that was dissonant in its original tradition might become sweet before the audience through artful delivery, and be brought back to the grace of harmony? Indeed, a true happiness—both of nature and of art—decorates these "surpliced" <note>original: "superpellatos," likely referring to clerics or choir members wearing a surplice.</note> singers. Nature herself, cooperating with the "daughter of Arithmetic" <note>Music was traditionally classified in the Middle Ages as the daughter of Arithmetic, as both belong to the mathematical arts of the Quadrivium.</note>, has crowned them with a more blessed diadem and, having nourished them with the milk of her sweetness, led them to the peak of perfection.

Furthermore, these are the ones whom the third class of singers—exercising the authority of judicial power in music and sitting upon the tribunal of the musical court—judges to be justly preeminent. They are seen as powerful in ability, action, and habit (the things which perfect a graceful singer), since they are not found to be lacking in any respect. Of these, there is another part: namely, the favored female sex. This group is as precious as it is rare; while in the epiglottis of a sweet-sounding throat, she divides the tones with balance in...

# ARNULPH ON THE DIFFERENCES OF SINGERS.

...semitones, and semitones into indivisible parts <note>Likely referring to microtones or the smallest possible melodic intervals that cannot be further divided.</note>, it chatters with an ineffable and playful melody, which you would think more angelic than human. From this, it is fitting for women—or more truly, for earthly Sirens <note>In medieval thought, Sirens symbolized the seductive and dangerous power of music that could lead a soul to ruin.</note>—to fill enchanted ears with such a sleepy intoxication, stealing away the soul by an invisible theft. Once stolen and made willing, they subjugate it to their slavery and lead the earthly shipwrecked soul, alas, into how great a Charybdis <note>A mythical, inescapable whirlpool; used here as a metaphor for spiritual or moral ruin.</note> of a prison, in which no kind of redemption or price holds place. 

Whence, though nature precedes [art] in dignity and priority, in this at least Music seems to honor nature: that in such work, art has wonderfully, in a way, preceded nature. For that which nature by itself does not wish to do, art perfects when aided by the service of training. What does it take away from or diminish in nature if it is decorated by the help of artistic genius? For we sometimes see several people of an inferior physical form who are more graceful through their acquired virtue, whereas the beauty of naturally handsome people becomes cheap when they lack the decoration of character and acquired virtue.

Therefore, the first [kind of] singers—if they should even be called singers since they are not themselves musicians—Music damns as unworthy of any degree of comparison. Struck by the sentence of anathema <note>A formal curse or excommunication; Arnulph uses the language of the Church to heighten the severity of his musical judgment.</note>, Music 

<column-break/>

condemns them as if they were reckless invaders of her most holy and injured majesty, and pronounces them excommunicated from all communion of singers. 

However, those who are singers according to the second difference—because industry places the arrangements of nature within them, whence they bring forth innate music through the exercise of use—are held as "good" in the grade of singers and worthy of the status of those set before them. 

Furthermore, those whom the third difference describes—because they excel those who rely on rote learning through art and science—are justly granted to be established as "better" in the comparative degree. 

Truly, those whom the fourth difference proclaims—since they are perfect, being those to whom nature denies nothing when the service of art is supplied—are elevated by a more just estimation as "best" musicians in the superlative degree among singers.

Saving the opinion of a sounder judgment, finally, in the series of this little work, let the diligent observer consider in which difference or in which grade among singers he ought to conduct himself, so that each person who has a taste for music may more often delight in singing in his own grade, always deferring to those to whom seniority is due; and let the ignorant person, howling like a woman, learn to restrain his own tumult.

->*Here ends the treatise of Master Arnulph. (a)*<-

# JOHN KECK
## INTRODUCTION TO MUSIC.
### *From the Tegernsee autograph.*

### A NOTICE.
*I found the* Introduction to Music *by* John KECK *in the Tegernsee monastery, written in the author’s own hand, as was clearly evident to anyone comparing it to the certificate of profession still preserved in that monastery. We insert that certificate here, because there have been those who doubted his monastic profession.* <note>The editor is providing "proof" that Keck was a monk at Tegernsee to settle a scholarly dispute about his identity.</note> > “In the name of Christ, amen. I, Brother John Keck of Giengen, a priest of the Diocese of Augsburg and a professor of arts and sacred theology, for the honor of almighty God and the most blessed Virgin Mary, and of our most blessed father Benedict and all the Saints, by the tenor of these presents, promise stability, the conversion of my life, and obedience according to the Rule of the same Saint Benedict, before God and his Saints, in the name of the holy martyrs Quirinus, Chrysogonus, and Castorius, and the other Saints whose relics are in this present church, in the presence of the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Lord Caspar, abbot of this monastery in Tegernsee, and before you fathers and brothers here present, in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, amen. In testimony of which, I have written this present certificate with my own hand in this venerable place of Tegernsee on the feast of the glorious and immaculate Virgin Mary, Mother of God <note>The Feast of the Immaculate Conception.</note>, which was on Saturday, the eighth day of the month of December, in the year of our Lord one thousand four hundred and forty-two.”

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, which introduced John Keck, a 15th-century priest and monk at Tegernsee, this page begins his actual treatise on music. # OF JOHN KECK

I believe no one doubts that various people are affected in different ways by musical melody, unless perhaps he is someone who, like a deaf man, has never recognized himself as a disciple of experience, the mistress of all things. For who does not know that by the sound of the trumpet, not only soldiers, but even the horses they ride are strengthened with wondrous boldness in war? They are encouraged to attack and join the conflict, so much so that you would marvel at how they are drawn toward those terrible things by the sweetness of music, led not so much by freedom of will as by a certain natural necessity. Finally, by this musical melody, guests at a feast are refreshed with such wonderful sweetness that sometimes some of them even forget to eat, and as if captured by a thread <note>original: *filo*; the text suggests a correction to *philtro*, meaning a "love potion" or "charm"</note>, they sometimes lose themselves and rise to play like little dogs. Aristotle expressed this well in his *Politics* (Book 8, chapter 4), saying that music is naturally delightful to every age and to all characters.

There are also those who are shaken with fear by the melody of a song; thus we read in Exodus (Chapter 19) that the children of Israel, when the Law was given, were filled with no small terror by the blast of the trumpet. Gideon himself is recorded in the Book of Judges <note>The text cites Judges 17, but Gideon’s victory with trumpets occurs in Judges 7.</note> to have struck his adversaries with the greatest fear by such a blast. There are also some who, at the time of funerals, produce mournful sounds through the service of flutes, by which the multitude of bystanders is often seen to be moved to pious tears. Therefore, the Philosopher [Aristotle]—who observed that so many men are affected by musical harmony in just as many ways—rightly decreed (in *Politics*, Book 8, chapter 6) that melody, according to the different musical modes, leads to different states of character.

<column-break/>

Who, then, could fully describe the benefits of music, which is proclaimed magnificent by the greatness of such effects? It is known to be naturally implanted even in the beasts themselves. Hence the nightingale <term>philomela: a poetic and mythological name for the nightingale</term> strives to give the thirsty ears of men a drink from the honeyed cup of her voice. Hence the swan, desiring to satisfy its own hungry ears, does not cease to "cook" the food of sounds in the pot of its throat, until it finally seems to exhale its last breath.

You see, therefore, O Father Abbot! that I have failed to sufficiently praise music—she who, not content with the praise of both human and animal natures, ascends to the heavens and makes them her subjects. She presumes to demand certain tributes from them by the authority of Divine Majesty, since the movement of the heavens is constrained with wondrous sweetness by the rigor of musical discipline, as Scipio testifies in Cicero's writing <note>original: *De beatorum musica*; Keck is referring to the "Dream of Scipio" in Cicero's *On the Republic*, which discusses the "Music of the Spheres."</note>. I pass over one of her most excellent privileges: namely, that she rises above every physical creature in a wondrous way, so much so that in the heavenly homeland, the throats of the celestial citizens are believed to be intoxicated by her nectar. This is according to the testimony of the royal prophet [David], who says (Psalm 149): "The high praises of God are in their throat."

In this matter, we must consider with what great care we should embrace this science, which is seen to be placed above other human sciences by so many gifts of privilege. For music takes away sadness from labor, as the Philosopher says (*Politics*, Book 8, chapter 15); it puts evil spirits to flight, for as the history of the Kings testifies (1 Samuel 16), when David played the lyre, the evil spirit departed from Saul. This is the science that brings about a rapture in the soul of man...

<summary>John Keck argues for the profound psychological and spiritual power of music, citing its ability to embolden soldiers, soothe diners, and even move animals and the celestial spheres. He draws on authorities like Aristotle, Cicero, and the Bible to position music as a divine science superior to others.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle's Politics, music of the spheres, David and Saul, nightingale, swan song, psychological effects of music, biblical trumpets, musical modes</keywords>

# INTRODUCTORY TO MUSIC.

man, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> again testifies (*Politics*, Book 8, chapter 6), so that he may be able to hear the secrets of the third heaven with Paul—secrets, I say, which it is not permitted for a man to speak. Music delights the performer even more than the listener, and it offers no small help toward moral virtues, as Aristotle sang (*Politics*, Book 8, chapter 5). For this reason, James said in his canonical epistle: "Is any among you sad? Let him pray. Is he cheerful? Let him sing psalms" <note>James 5:13</note>. Here, the gloss <note>A standard medieval biblical commentary</note> states: by the frequent sweetness of psalmody, one drives away the harmful plague of sadness, and consequently brings in joy and gladness. Correct then was the Psalmist when he said: "My lips will exult when I sing to you" <note>Psalm 71:23</note>.

However, this singing that gladdens the human mind should not be high-pitched, but rather very deep and grave, so that it can scarcely be distinguished from the speaking voice. For Aristotle forbade in the *Politics* (*Politics*, Book 8, chapter 9) that old men should sing harmony rigidly; for high-pitched harmony often distracts human minds and burdens the body so much that souls are weighed down by its heaviness, preventing them from being lifted up into exultation by the flight of contemplation. Yet this exultation of the mind is the goal of psalmody, for which purpose it was instituted, as Augustine says (*Confessions*, Book 10, chapter 3). Therefore, the singing of religious men—who can be understood by the name "elders," since they ought to possess the gray hairs of the elders of whom it is said, *a man's understanding is his gray hair* <note>Wisdom 4:9; original Latin: "cani sunt sensus hominis"</note>—should by no means be rigid. Instead, it should sound forth with a modest gravity in the manner of those speaking, sweetly and mournfully without <term>discant</term> <note>original: *discantu*; here referring to complex, high-pitched polyphony that might obscure the text or solemnity</note>, so that as they sing to the Lord, their lips

<column-break/>

may deserve to exult without end, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, who is blessed forever.

->*The prologue ends.*<-

->*The introduction begins.*<-

This book is called the "Introductory to Music" because it encompasses the proportions of all sounds with wonderful brevity. It also demonstrates several things he proposes that are unknown to the simpler brothers, so that students might not only be required to believe, but that it might also make them knowledgeable in musical proportion, instructed by mathematical <term>acribology</term> <note>original: *acribologia*; from the Greek for "exactness" or "precise treatment"</note>. Thus, they may not only become skilled in Gregorian chant, but rather be able to penetrate all musical consideration more clearly with an illuminated intellect.

->*The introduction ends.*<-

Chapter I. On the invention of music.
Chapter II. On the various proportions of sounds or voices.
Chapter III. On the representation of sounds or voices.
Chapter IV. On the consonance and dissonance of sounds or voices.
Chapter V. Demonstrates certain things mentioned above and brings the book to an end.

->*The Chapters end.*<-

## CHAPTER I.
### On the invention of Music.

Wise men say that music is threefold: one kind is metric, another is rhythmic...

--- Page 334 ---
<meta>This page continues Keck’s discussion on the types of music. Having transitioned from the spiritual effects of music on the previous page, he now begins the technical treatise. He dismisses the "trivial" divisions—likely mundane and human music—to focus on "harmonic" music, which belongs to the Quadrivium, the higher division of the seven liberal arts.</meta>

# JOHN KECK

...and placing the third as "harmonic." But lest we be misled by an ambiguity of the word, we cut away the first two kinds of music from our consideration—since it is clear they are of common concern—and we will proceed further only with the third, which is truly part of the *quadrivium* <note>The "four ways"—the mathematical arts of Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astronomy.</note>. Indeed, some claim this is named after *Moys* <note>original: "Moys", an Egyptian word for water</note>, which means "water"; however, we believe more truly that Music drew its name from the *Muses*. Different people have identified different inventors of this art. For the history in Genesis mentions Tubal <note>Genesis 4:21; Tubal-cain is often confused with Jubal in medieval texts as the father of musicians.</note> as the first inventor of Music; others name Amphion <note>A son of Zeus in Greek myth whose music could move stones.</note>, while others—as do the greater part of philosophers—name Pythagoras. As they tell it, while passing a blacksmith's shop by chance, Pythagoras heard four hammer blows that produced the proportions of his sounds: the <term>tone</term> <note>a whole step</note>, the <term>diapente</term> <note>a perfect fifth</note>, the <term>diatessaron</term> <note>a perfect fourth</note>, and the <term>diapason</term> <note>an octave</note>. But he suspected that perhaps this proportion of sounds rested in the strength of the arms of those working; so, having swapped the hammers, he ordered them to strike again. There, despite the swapping of the hammers, the original proportions of the sounds remained with each of them. Thus, with experience as his teacher, he learned that this proportion of sounds resides in the weight of the hammers. When he explored their weight more diligently, he found their weights to be according to these four numbers: 6, 8, 9, and 12. He found that the <term>diatessaron</term> exists between 6 and 8, the <term>diapente</term> between 6 and 9, the <term>tone</term> between 8 and 9, and the <term>diapason</term> between 6 and 12. Therefore, in these four numbers, he established the principle of all music as something known by experience, namely that the fourth is said to consist in the <term>sesquitertia</term> <note>a ratio of 4:3</note> proportion, the fifth in the <term>sesquialtera</term> <note>a ratio of 3:2</note>, the tone in the

<column-break/>

<term>sesquioctava</term> <note>a ratio of 9:8</note>, and the octave in the <term>dupla</term> <note>double, or 2:1</note> proportions. We have decided that these must be assumed as a starting principle in the following sections.

### CHAPTER II.

#### *On the various proportions of sounds or voices.*

All voices that have a proportion of equality produce a <term>unison</term>. But since it happens that one may deviate from equality—as from the middle point of virtue—in many ways, or rather infinitely, it follows that different sounds could be assigned infinite species according to infinite variations of unequal proportions. However, very few of these are approved by the judgment of the ears; the great, or rather the largest part of them, produces a dissonance detestable to the ears. Therefore, they must be rooted out from the field of musical science like thistles.
We come, therefore, to those species of different sounds which musicians find either concordant or, at the very least, not so harshly dissonant. Let us say first that the <term>tone</term>—which, as we said above, consists in the <term>sesquioctava</term> <note>9:8</note> proportion—is found and exists between any two adjacent voices of those six, namely *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la* <note>The six syllables used in medieval solmization, the ancestor of do-re-mi.</note>, except for *mi* and *fa*. Between those adjacent voices, you find the <term>minor semitone</term>, which the wise have called a <term>diesis</term>. I said "minor" to distinguish it from the <term>major semitone</term>, which is called an <term>apotome</term> or "cutting." Indeed, a tone is not understood to be cut through the middle into equal halves, such that equal semitones would create middle tones; rather, as we shall demonstrate in the later sections, it is cut into unequal parts so that the larger or smaller unequal semitones...

### INTRODUCTION TO MUSIC

...might be produced. From which it can be inferred that the <term>semitone</term> <note>original: *semitonium*</note> is not named from "half" [*semis*] as a literal half of a tone, but from "imperfect" [*semis*] as an incomplete tone. It is concluded, therefore, that the difference between a whole tone and a minor semitone produces a major semitone; the difference between these two semitones musicians have baptized with the name <term>comma</term>.

Furthermore, those searching more subtly, not satisfied with these small sections, created the <term>diesis</term>, which is the minor semitone divided into two equal parts, to which they gave the name <term>diaschisma</term>. The ancients indeed called this diaschisma a "diesis," but the half of a comma they called a <term>schisma</term>. The <term>semiditone</term> <note>the minor third</note> is so called as if it were an "imperfect ditone," because it is completed by a minor semitone and a tone, just as one finds between the syllables *re* and *fa*, or *sol* and *mi*, when the notes are closest to each other. The <term>ditone</term> <note>the major third</note> is so called because it is gathered from the joining of two whole tones, as you can see between the closest notes *ut* and *mi*, or *fa* and *la*. You complete a <term>diatessaron</term> <note>the perfect fourth</note> with a ditone and a diesis (that is, a minor semitone), just as we see occurring between the closest notes *ut* and *fa*, or *re* and *sol*, or *mi* and *la*. If you add a tone to this, you will see a <term>diapente</term> <note>the perfect fifth</note> result, as we are accustomed to practice between *ut* and *sol*, or *re* and *la*. The <term>dysemiditone</term> <note>literally "two-semiditones," likely an augmented fourth or diminished fifth depending on the tuning system</note> also consists of a ditone and two dieses (that is, two minor semitones); the <term>tritone</term> consists of three whole tones.

Thus, hurrying toward the end of the chapter, let us collect the proportions of sounds of which musicians have treated, and we shall find: the unison; the schisma (which is half of a comma); the comma; the diaschisma (which is half of a minor semitone); the diesis (which is the minor semitone); the <term>apotome</term> <note>the major semitone</note> or "cutting off"; the whole

<column-break/>

tone; the semiditone; the ditone; the diatessaron; the dysemiditone; the tritone; and the diapente. To these, add the semitone with a diapente, the tone with a diapente, the semiditone with a diapente, and the ditone with a diapente. If we join a semitone to this last one, the <term>diapason</term> <note>the octave</note> will result, the most perfect consonance of all and the most similar to the unison. Moreover, you may add all those proportions of sounds prior to the diapason to the diapason itself (if you wish), and it will be like a replication of them, since it is established that the diapason is like a second unison.

### CHAPTER III.
->*On the representation of sounds or voices.*<-

Having enumerated the proportions of sounds or voices, it remains to represent them artificially. Since musicians have not been accustomed to represent the proportions of inequalities smaller than a semitone—because their difference can scarcely be distinguished by the ears—they have therefore disdained to take them into use for this reason.

Therefore, setting aside the proportions of the schisma, comma, and diaschisma, and hurrying to the representation of the others, we say that the minor semitone is represented by **Square B** <note>B-natural</note> and **low C**; or **low E and F**; or **high a and Round b** <note>B-flat</note>; or **Square B and high c**; also **high e and f**; and again **super-high a and Round b**; and finally **Square B and super-high c**. You will gather, therefore, that there are seven minor semitones usually represented.

Here you have certain points worthy of wonder for those new to music (though not to the truly learned): first, that there is a greater difference between high round B and high square B than between high A and high round B, or even between high square B and high C. This is evident: for between A and square B there is a whole tone, since they are the neighboring notes *re* and *mi*. That tone is divided into unequal parts by round B, which is a strong *fa* <note>solmization syllables help singers find the correct pitch relative to a central note</note>, both between A and square B, and between high A and highest A, and the top *mi*; consequently, between A and round B there is a **minor semitone** <term>semitonium minus: the smaller of two types of half-steps in ancient tuning systems</term>. It is necessary, therefore, that the remainder of that tone, which lies between round B and square B, be a **major semitone** <term>semitonium maius: the larger half-step, often called an "apotome"</term>. Likewise, between round B and C, since they are *fa* and *sol*, there is also a whole tone, which is itself divided by square B into unequal parts. One of these is a minor semitone—namely between square B and the middle C—since they are *mi* and *fa*. It follows then that the remainder of that same tone, which lies between round B and square B, is a major semitone.

Second: that the difference between the boundaries of a **diminished fifth** <term>dysemiditoni: a "double-minor third," functioning here as a diminished fifth</term> is smaller than that of a **tritone** <term>tritono: an interval of three whole tones, an augmented fourth</term>, despite the fact that the boundaries of the diminished fifth are five steps apart, while the tritone is only four. This is evident: for the boundaries of the diminished fifth are separated by two whole tones and two minor semitones, which, when taken together, cannot equal a full tone,

<column-break/>

and thus it is necessary that the diminished fifth be smaller than the tritone. You see, therefore, that the proportions of sounds cannot be understood merely by the distance between places through the arrangement of margins and lines, as many people mistakenly believe. However, we will discuss these matters more extensively in the final chapter, God willing.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### *On the consonance and dissonance of sounds or voices.*

Some of these proportions of sounds are called "perfectly consonant" because they create a perfect agreement of harmony: namely the **fourth** <term>diatessaron</term>, the **fifth** <term>diapente</term>, and the **octave** <term>diapason</term>. Others, however, harmonize imperfectly, such as the minor third <note>original: semiditonus</note>, the major third <note>original: ditonus</note>, the minor sixth <note>original: semitonium cum diapente</note>, and the major sixth <note>original: tonus cum diapente</note>. All remaining intervals we call dissonant. It is for this reason that **counterpoint** <term>contrapunctus: the art of combining different melodic lines</term> is said to consist of these—namely the perfect and imperfect consonances. Indeed, the proportion of equality is the simplest; therefore, the **unison** <term>unisoni: two voices on the same pitch</term> creates the simplest proportion of voices. But after the proportion of equality, the "multiple" proportion is simpler, and among the multiples, the "double" ratio <note>2:1</note> reaches the superlative degree of simplicity. After the multiple proportions, the "superparticular" is simpler than the "superpartient"; and among the superparticulars, the **one-and-a-half ratio** <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio</term> holds the primacy of simplicity, followed by the **one-and-a-third ratio** <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio</term>, then the **one-and-a-fourth ratio** <term>sesquitertia: a 5:4 ratio</term>, and so on.

Thus, from the double ratio is born the octave, the simplest consonance of different sounds and the one most similar to the unison. Then, from the one-and-a-half ratio, the fifth arises, sweet- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing to the next page.</note>
