### Chapter V.

*Which demonstrates some of the things related above and brings the book to an end.*

It remains for us to demonstrate some of those things we mentioned in our narrative above, so that all ambiguity concerning them may be removed for the brothers. Thus, with the night of ignorance banished, they may deserve to become knowledgeable instead of ignorant as the serene day of musical knowledge dawns. To achieve this, it is necessary to recall to memory what we set forth as a principle at the beginning of this work: namely, that the octave rises from a **double** <note>ratio of 2:1</note> proportion; the **fifth** <term>diapente</term> from a **sesquialter** <note>ratio of 3:2</note>; the fourth from a **sesquitertian** <note>ratio of 4:3</note>; and the **whole tone** <term>tonus</term> from a **sesquioctave** <note>ratio of 9:8</note> proportion. 

And since in the root of the sesquioctave proportion (which consists of the terms 8 and 9), we cannot extend a **ditone** <term>ditonus: an interval of two whole tones, roughly a major third</term>, we therefore first multiply the first number of this root by itself, and three terms of the same proportion will result: namely 64,

<column-break/>

72, and 81. In these terms, two tones are perceived: one between the first two numbers [64 and 72], and another between the last two [72 and 81]. A ditone, however, is found between the outer terms [64 and 81]; this falls short of a fourth, because the difference between those two outer terms is less than a third part of the smaller one.

However, since the smaller number, namely 64, does not have a third part, these three numbers must be multiplied by three, and three other terms of the same proportion will result: namely 192, 216, and 243. Regarding these terms, the judgment is entirely the same as was said of the three immediately preceding ones: namely, that you may know there is a sesquioctave [9:8] proportion between any two adjacent ones, and consequently you should not doubt that a tone exists there. Therefore, a ditone will necessarily resonate between the outer terms. If you also add to the first term of that proportion [192] its own third part, namely 64, the number 256 will result, which has a sesquitertian [4:3] proportion to the first term; consequently, it must resonate as a fourth with that same first term.

You have, therefore, four terms: 192, 216, 243, and 256. The outer ones [192 and 256] will sound a fourth; the first and second [192 and 216] a tone; the second and third [216 and 243] likewise a tone; and the first and third [192 and 243] a ditone. Multiply these three terms again by 8, and to the product of the third term add its eighth part; this produces four more terms, namely 131,072, 139,968, 157,464, and 177,147. Between the first and second, a **major semitone** sounds; between the second and third, a **tone**; and between the third and fourth, a **tone** similarly. If you multiply these terms by 4, and from the product of the fourth term you subtract its fourth part, and set the remainder as the second term <note>Keck is performing complex arithmetic to find the common denominator for even smaller intervals</note>, you will have these five terms: 524,288, 531,441, 559,872, 629,856, and 708,588. Between the first two, there is a **comma** <term>comma: the Pythagorean comma, a tiny interval resulting from the difference between twelve perfect fifths and seven octaves</term>; the second and third are a **minor semitone**; the first and third are a **major semitone**; and the second and fifth are a **fourth** <term>diatessaron: the interval of a perfect fourth</term>;

<column-break/>

the third and fourth are a **tone**; the third and fifth are a **ditone** <term>ditonum: a Pythagorean major third, made of two whole tones</term>; and the fourth and fifth will most certainly sound a **tone**. Furthermore, if from the second term you successively descend by three **tones**, and from the last term of this descent you ascend again by a **fourth**, you will have (including that aforementioned second term) these six terms: 373,248, 419,904, 472,392, 497,664, 524,288, and 531,441. Between the outer terms of these, there is a **tritone** <term>tritonum: an interval of three whole tones, often considered dissonant</term>; the first and second are a **tone**; the second and third are likewise a **tone**; the first and third are a **ditone**; the third and sixth are likewise a **tone**; the second and sixth are a **ditone**; the third and fourth are a **minor semitone**; the first and fourth are a **fourth**; the fourth and fifth are a **minor semitone**; the fourth and sixth are a **major semitone**; and the fifth and sixth sound a **comma**. Thus, the difference of the **comma**—that is, the difference between the last two terms—is 7,153. The difference of a **tone** (the third and sixth terms) is 59,049. The difference of a **major semitone** (the fourth and sixth terms) is 33,777. But the difference of a **minor semitone** (the fourth and fifth terms) is 26,624.

It is clear, therefore, that a **minor semitone** is larger than three **commas** and smaller than four; a **major semitone** is larger than four **commas** and smaller than five; and a **tone** exceeds eight **commas** but is exceeded by nine. All these things are evident; for the difference of a **comma** taken three times is exceeded by the difference of a **minor semitone**, and taken four times, it exceeds it. The same must be said of the others in their own way.

INTRODUCTORY WORK ON MUSIC.

You see, therefore, that the semitone within the fourth <term>diatessaron: an interval of a perfect fourth, which has a ratio of 4:3</term> is a smaller part than half of a whole tone. Since the fourth consists of the 4:3 ratio <term>sesquitertia: a ratio of 4 to 3 (or 8:6)</term> and differs from the fifth <term>diapente: an interval of a perfect fifth, with a ratio of 3:2</term> only by a single tone—because the 3:2 ratio <term>sesquialtera</term> exceeds the 4:3 ratio by a 9:8 ratio <term>sesquioctava: the ratio of a standard whole tone</term>, as is clear in these three terms: 6, 8, and 9—it will be manifest that the fifth also contains this minor semitone. Furthermore, since it is manifest that the double ratio <note>the octave, or 2:1 ratio</note> consists of the 3:2 and 4:3 ratios (as seen in the terms 6, 9, and 12), it is necessary that the octave <term>diapason</term>, the fifth, and the fourth be considered together;

<column-break/>

and consequently, the octave contains six tones minus a comma <term>comma: specifically the Pythagorean comma, the tiny mathematical discrepancy discovered when comparing twelve fifths to seven octaves, or six whole tones to one octave</term>.

Behold, by God's favor, we are now released from the obligation of the promise made above. You will find below, on another part of the leaf, the individual proportions of the sounds on the string of the monochord <term>monochord: a scientific instrument with a single string and a movable bridge used to measure musical intervals</term> set before you as if in a mirror. By contemplating them, you may marvel at the things we have said; from these, you will also be able to draw out even deeper matters than those we have set down, provided you are not at all lazy in applying your diligence.

*The introductory book on Music by Brother Johannes Keck ends.*

### NOTICE.

*The name of ADAM is still celebrated among the people of Fulda. He calls himself a "ducal musician" in the dedication of this work on Music, which I have found nowhere else but in a single manuscript in the city library of Strasbourg. This codex shows such age, unless I am mistaken, that it could be the author's own original manuscript. It appears from this very work that he lived in meager circumstances within a certain community of musicians. The author indicates the year he wrote it at the very end: 1490.*

# THE WRITINGS OF ADAM OF FULDA

[The author] confirms that we should ask for honorable things from friends and perform honorable deeds for their sake. I was moved by the words of Jerome <note>original: "Hieronymi verba"</note> saying: *do not rush headlong into writing, lest you be led by a light madness; learn for a long time what you would teach.* But it was always my intention to obey you no less; therefore, I was ready in all things to submit to your will, even though I have withheld my hand from the pen for so long; for many obstacles often tend to stand in the way of good works. I could not, therefore, fulfill this until now, I confess, though I promised so many times. But hear the reason: when I recently departed from Passau <term>Patavia: the Latin name for the city of Passau in Bavaria</term>, as you know, I betook myself to the monastery of Vornbach <term>Formibacense: Vornbach Abbey (or Formbach), a Benedictine monastery on the Inn River</term> for the sake of finishing this work. In that place, your letters reached me a second time requesting the same thing. Indeed, I was prompt in following your commands, for I completed two or three small notebooks <term>sexterniculos: quires or small gatherings of parchment/paper</term> right there.

When I recently discovered that these had been stolen from me and poorly transcribed <note>Adam is complaining about an unauthorized or "pirated" copy of his drafts</note>, I did not wish to give you a book equal to those stolen transcriptions, fearing that an uncorrected labor might reach you first; for it never pleased me that something should be sought after which, once found, would only cause annoyance.

But there was no leisure for correcting them then, since enough of a burden had been placed upon me in the service of my princes. I decided, therefore, to take the papers with me and finish them in the court, if there should be any leisure; for he who serves princes does not live for himself, but for them. And believe me, military camps are no harsher than the courts of princes, where there are always envies, backbiting, rivalries, insults, and almost infinite injuries, so that he may be called happy who lives far from the tumults of courts and is content with his lot—

<column-break/>

—and is content with his lot; for all service is wasted if you do not, for once, rightly learn to despise such things. Furthermore, regarding the little dwelling—not to say hut—where several of us live together in one house while composing, ants are scarcely as cramped in their tunnels as we are living in one hut. There is such "silence" there <note>Adam is being sarcastic about the noise</note> that you would think you were hearing magpies or crows in the mud, or frogs in the marshes. Yet no work is so arduous, nor any noise so loud, that it could separate me from the love I have begun to feel for you. For Socrates says: *one should have short speeches with a friend, but long friendships.* I will not speak of a friendship that desires words without deeds, but I wished to satisfy you with both words and deeds, choosing rather to presume beyond my strength than to deny anything to charity, which overcomes all things.

Receive kindly this small gift from a poor house; you will weigh its small price against our usefulness. For it is established that nothing is more dear to the most serious men than that which is bought with prayers. Moreover, it does not matter what is given, but with what mind, as Seneca says in his book *On Benefits* <note>original: "de beneficiis"</note>. I am pleased to say with Peter: *Silver and gold I have none* <note>original: "argentum & aurum non eſt mihi" — a quote from Acts 3:6</note>. Yet he who grants a little, but does so willingly, equals the wealth of kings in spirit; for that which is given with a ready hand comes much more gracefully than that which is given with a full hand. What else, then, could I give you, since you seek not gold nor silver, but art? I would have wished, however, that this burden had been entrusted to another’s yoke, who could have written better than I; for you are not one whom mediocre things befit, nor am I one who can provide the sublime. I confess that I have assumed a heavy burden, and unless you assist me with your shoulders—

<summary>In this introductory letter, Adam of Fulda apologizes to his patron for delays caused by the theft of his drafts and the chaotic nature of life at a princely court. He emphasizes that despite his cramped and noisy living conditions, his devotion to his friend and to the "art" of music compels him to finish the work.</summary>

### *Preface to the First Part.*

As I am about to write on music, I fear lest while I wish to be of use to others, I may begin to fail myself, or while instructing others, I might be rebuked for ignorance and incur the vice of infamy; for the saying of the philosopher Cobaris <note>likely a reference to a minor classical or medieval authority</note> comes to mind: *each man is duller in his own business than in another’s.* But on the contrary, Isocrates says: *He who acts wrongly in his own affairs will never advise fittingly in those of others.* Yet a man does not weigh his own things as modestly as he does those of others.

<column-break/>

Looking also at this and other matters, I fear lest I be convicted by my rivals of the vices of rashness and arrogance—even if I have shown as much diligence as I was able—since few, if I may not say none, are found among modern musicians (whether fear, or labor, or ignorance has hindered them) who have thoroughly taught or shaped this art. And on the other hand, I must fear lest, while I might seem to agree with the words of my rivals (who repeatedly call me "half-voiced," mute, and for the most part tongue-tied), I fail to comply with my friends who ask and desire this of me, or lest in pleasing the former, I displease the latter.

I have decided, therefore, to please those desiring worthy things more than to listen to the words of disparaging rivals; for to be disliked by the wicked is to be praised. When a certain man cursed the philosopher Antisthenes, he replied: *It is the habit of a superior person to suffer this, but of an inferior to do it.* Therefore, lest I seem to them to have remained silent as one altogether ignorant of the art (for Ovid says: *no one can teach what he knows least*; and the Satirist <term>Satyricus: the Roman poet Persius</term> also says: *your knowledge is nothing unless another knows that you know it*), I have wished to undertake these things for the honor of all, not because I judge myself more fit than others, but while others are sleeping. And as Cicero says: *honor nourishes the arts, and we are all kindled toward study for the sake of honor; but where honor is lacking, there study also fails.* I do not doubt that many will remain who, as is characteristic of the men of our age, will not cease to strike me from behind as one greedy for empty boasting—that is, to provoke me, despising the work before they read it, and annihilating it before they understand it—men who wish to be seen as musicians rather than to actually be so, not governed by rules or...

# ADAM OF FULDA

...or obeying precepts, neither following authors nor reasons, but asserting that whatever pleases their own whimsical head is "musical" and "artistic." Perhaps they are imitating the sentiment of Maro <note>original: "Maronis"—referring to the Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note>: *In art, each is drawn by his own pleasure* <note>original: "in arte trahit sua quemque voluptas"</note>; or they certainly delight in the verse of Persius the Satirist: *Each has his own will, and one does not live by a single prayer* <note>original: "velle suum cuique est, nec voto vivitur uno"</note>; or they use the words of Terence the comic poet without any sense, as he says in *Phormio*: *As many men, so many opinions; each has his own custom* <note>original: "Quot homines, tot sententiæ, suus cuique mos est"</note>. Boethius <term>Boethius: An early 6th-century philosopher whose "De institutione musica" was the standard textbook for medieval music theory</term> rebukes their madness enough and more; but alas, he labors in vain, since they all claim to imitate him, or Johannes de Muris <term>Johannes de Muris: A 14th-century mathematician and music theorist influential in the development of mensural notation</term>, or Guido <term>Guido d'Arezzo: The 11th-century monk credited with inventing the musical staff and solmization (do-re-mi)</term>, although there are many who have neither seen nor read their books. I say nothing of the far greater number of those lacking understanding who do not even know the names of authors—not only in Germany, but everywhere among nations: in France, Italy, and the surrounding regions—who contend that the art of music is subordinate to instruments. *For those who merely repeat what they hear are easily called masters*, as Marcus Varro says in his book on morals. But do not lend your ears to these people, who, while they lead others astray, are also led astray themselves. Perceive how easy it is to convict these magpies <note>Magpies were often used as a metaphor for people who chatter without understanding or who merely mimic sounds</note> and, as it were, crush them between your fingernails. Believe the authors, and give more trust to the learned and skilled than to the illiterate. Nor should you be led astray by those philosophers who think little of the art—I call them "philosophers" because they do not desire what they are unable to learn; for it is foolish to desire what cannot be achieved, as "the lyre is played for the ass in vain" <note>original: "fruſtra enim lyra aſino canitur"—a common Latin proverb meaning to waste words or art on someone who cannot appreciate it</note>. Therefore, embrace the art and receive this little book, since with your love it has taken its beginning and its end by the will of God.

<column-break/>

->*Here begins the first part.*<-

As I was about to begin the first part, I thought to myself that it would need to be completed only if the imploring of divine aid preceded all other things, as Truth itself testifies: *Without me you can do nothing* <note>original: "Sine me nihil potestis facere"—referring to the words of Jesus in John 15:5</note>. I have decided, therefore, in the name of the holy and individual Trinity to give a beginning to this little work, to whose honor I wish to undertake these things; to whom be praise, honor, blessing, brilliance, and thanksgiving forever and beyond. Amen.

Since, therefore, in these days the books of the ancient philosophers are little read—not only in music, but also in the other mathematical arts <term>mathematicalibus: the Quadrivium, the four "mathematical" subjects of the liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy</term>—it has happened for that reason that they are much dreaded as if they were unintelligible or too difficult. For some, full of envy, wish to communicate what they know to no one; others, having little confidence in themselves, fear to introduce error; thus it happens that everyone remains silent. But, as are the words of Naso <note>original: "Nasonis"—the Roman poet Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso)</note>: *There is little virtue in keeping silence about things* <note>original: "Exigua est virtus præstare silentia rebus"</note>; and elsewhere: *What is hidden is unknown; there is no desire for the unknown* <note>original: "quod latet, ignotum est, ignoti nulla cupido"</note>. However, so that it may come into the light, it seemed good to me to briefly extract a small treatise from the music of Boethius and others, according to the strength given to me by the holy and inestimable Trinity, and to share it with each person who finds pleasure in this little work.

I will, therefore, give the little book four parts in the aforementioned name, and each part divided into its own chapters. In the first part, I shall speak of the authors and the utility as well as the description of the art. In the second part, I shall tell of the method of learning the art. In the third part, I shall treat of mensural or figurative song <term>mensurali vel figurativo cantu: "measured" music where the shape of the note indicates its specific duration, as opposed to the unmeasured rhythm of plainchant</term>. # THE FIRST PART OF MUSIC

...musical or harmonic paths will be opened, with some discussion of arithmetical and geometrical proportions. Therefore, for the first point:

### Chapter I

This is the definition of music: Music is the art that teaches how to form voices, and how to accent those formed voices through sound with right proportion. Or thus: it is a liberal science providing the power of singing truly and according to rule. It is called "music," as Isidore <term>Isidore of Seville: A 7th-century scholar whose "Etymologies" served as an encyclopedia for the Middle Ages</term> records in the first book of his *Etymologies*, as if it were the "science of the Muses"; or from *musan* <note>original: "a musan"—referring to a Greek term for a musical instrument</note>, a musical instrument suited to all others; or it is named from *madusica*, that is, from "modulation," which exists only in the proper consonance of voices. But Augustine <term>St. Augustine: The 4th-5th century theologian whose "De Musica" linked musical rhythm to the divine order</term> says to Jerome: music is the science of sense, or of sensing how to modulate well for the contemplation of great things, granted by the bounty of God even to mortals possessing rational souls. Virgil seems to touch upon this in the *Eclogues* <note>original: "Buccol."—referring to Virgil’s Bucolics or Eclogues</note> where he says: *From Jove is the beginning, Muses, all things are full of Jove.* <note>original: "a Iove principium, Musæ Iovis omnia plena"</note>

Music is twofold: natural and artificial. Natural music is "worldly" and "human." Worldly music <term>musica mundana: Often called the "music of the spheres," this was the ancient belief that the movement of celestial bodies produced a divine harmony inaudible to human ears</term> is the resonance of the super-celestial bodies from the motion of the spheres, where the greatest harmony is believed to exist; and mathematicians consider this type. Human music exists in the body and soul, in the spirits and the temperament of the limbs; for while harmony lasts, man lives, but when its proportion is broken, he dies. And physicians consider this type, of which we say nothing for the present.

Artificial music: musicians hold to this type. It is either instrumental or vocal. Instrumental music is sound caused by various instruments, which, although it is vocal, nevertheless

<column-break/>

its voices are material. *Common vocal music* <note>original: "Vocalis usualis"</note> is the emission of the voice lacking the principles by which it ought to be governed, such as the singing of the common people, which can be compared not only to humans but even to beasts by natural instinct. *Regulated vocal music* <note>original: "Vocalis regulata"</note> is a most sweet modulation, constructed regularly and artistically according to ascent or descent, and it is itself fourfold, as follows. *True regulated* music is that which proceeds by a straight path through the keys <note>original: "claves"—the structural notes of the musical scale</note>, without the transposition of voices, content within its own limit. *Fictional regulated* music <term>musica ficta: The practice of using "accidental" notes (sharps or flats) that lie outside the standard hexachord system to avoid dissonances or create sweeter harmonies</term> is when voices are transposed in the keys; for instance, in all those where "fa" is not locally placed, "soft B" <note>original: "B. molle"—the origin of the modern "flat" symbol (♭)</note> can be placed; similarly in all keys in which "fa" is locally placed, "hard B" <note>original: "♮. durum"—the origin of the modern "natural" (♮) and "sharp" (♯) symbols</note> can be placed by the driving force of the tone and by necessity. For just as the whole soul is delighted by the fitting together of modulations, so on the contrary it withdraws itself from the pleasure of hearing if it perceives anything corrupted within it. *Simple or plain regulated* music is that whose figures suffer neither increase nor decrease, as happens in Gregorian chant. *Mensural or figurative* music is that whose figures can be increased or decreased in signs according to form and species, and this occurs in the primary degrees of music, namely mode, time, and prolation <term>mensural notation: A system of musical notation where the shape of a note determines its duration relative to others</term>. Both simple and mensural music can be either "true" or "fictional."

### Chapter II

This one of the seven liberal arts <term>Liberal Arts: The medieval curriculum consisting of the Trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the Quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, astronomy)</term> brings no small utility among the others, as Aristotle witnesses in his *Problems* <note>original: "P. 19. problemate 10."</note> where he says: *Music gladdens the sad, and compels the happy to rejoice more and more.* And likewise in the 8th book of the *Politics*: *The soul*, he says, *naturally delights in music.*

# ADAM OF FULDA
<meta>catchword: „Mu-</meta>

...is changed; for it makes souls so intent that they think of nothing else, as Cassiodorus <term>Cassiodorus: A 6th-century Roman statesman and monk whose writings on the "liberal arts" helped preserve classical knowledge for the Middle Ages.</term> suggests. Rufus Constantinus <margin>(a)</margin> affirms the same in his *Viaticum* <note>original: "Viatico" — a medical handbook by Constantine the African, often called Rufus here.</note>, where he relates that Orpheus, through his music, changed the hearts of princes from sadness to joy; for it rouses those who sleep, makes those who are awake drowsy, and heals melancholy. Thus the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the 8th book of the *Politics*: music is a friend to every age, and significantly to youth. For the young especially ought to be educated in music, lest they be given over to lewdness. For in the 6th book of the *Ethics*, the philosopher says: it is natural for us to take delight in those things in which we began to take delight from infancy; if, therefore, young people find in music that same satisfaction which they usually seek in vanities, it will then easily appear to them how to leave behind those things that are vain and apply their minds to a greater satisfaction.

I judge this art not undeservedly worthy of praise, since it is the oldest of the arts, discovered before the Great Flood, and was once held in great honor among the Greeks: nor was it believed that anyone was sufficiently educated unless he was especially imbued with music. Themistocles, the Greek general, when invited to a banquet and having refused the lyre, was considered less learned. Socrates, the fountain of philosophers, did not fear to be instructed in the lyre in his old age, believing that if music were lacking to him, the summit of the sciences would be lacking. The army of the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedaemoniorum"</note>, instructed in musical modulations, brought back victory. Proclus <note>original: "Broccus (f. Proclus)" — a 5th-century Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>, the foremost orator of his time, wished for music to sound in harmony with himself.

<column-break/>

What praise Empedocles won from it is clear in the prologue of Boethius. When Pythagoras heard a certain young man from Tauromenium <note>original: "Taurinum" — a common reference to the "Tauromenian youth" story found in Boethius and Cicero.</note>—as Cicero says in his book on counsels—raving with lust at the door of his mistress, he healed him with the stroke of the psaltery. The physician Asclepiades cured a madman by singing. Although Lycurgus gave the Spartans the harshest laws, he cultivated music. But the ancients also used to sing the praises of heroes and gods to the lyre at banquets. What of *that Ioppas from Virgil? Does he not sing of the wandering moon and the labors of the sun?* <note>original: "nonne canit errantem lunam solisque labores?" — a quote from Virgil’s Aeneid describing the bard Iopas.</note>

Plato extols it with these words: music is the art of arts, the science of sciences, through which the insane are healed, demons are put to flight, and even the gods are appeased: which Ovid also testifies to when he says: *An angry God is swayed by a pleading voice.* <note>original: "flectitur iratus voce rogante Deus"</note> Cicero affirms the same: for he says that music is when we linger in the knowledge of divine things. Behold how much importance music had among the pagans. For it was the custom of the Pythagoreans that when they went to bed, or when they rose in the morning, if there were any sadness, they would dissolve it with the sweet sounding of the lyre; for it penetrates the ears with a hidden sweetness of the mind. Among the Hebrews, however, the walls of Jericho fell completely at the blast of the trumpet: as the prophets sang, Saul prophesied: as David played the harp, the demon was restrained: at the touch of the psaltery, Elisha received the spirit of prophecy.

For the preservation of the body and for retaining a teachable mind, this art is seen to be very useful. Through its equal and just proportion of numbers, music naturally inclines men toward justice, equity of character, and the proper governance of the state. ### CHAPTER IV.

These arguments seem great, and I do not say they are small; but I dare to respond as Dametas did in Virgil: <note>Dametas is a character in Virgil’s 'Eclogues'.</note>

The first is delight; for the human mind, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> pleases, necessarily requires some external delights for its own strengthening, without which it can hardly live; but having these comforts, it is drawn toward performing virtuous works. The second is the dispelling of melancholy. Since it is more difficult, as stated in the first book of the *Ethics*, to bear sadness than to abstain from pleasures (for melancholy often induces tyranny or desperation in great men), it is necessary for emperors, kings, princes, consuls, and others governing the state—who suffer a constant influx of melancholy due to the burden of labor—to dispel it through musical modulation and delights. ### CHAPTER V.

To respond to what follows: every art is good, but the abuse of an art is worst; therefore all things are to be received in a better light, since it is not an evil to know evil, but to do evil. But since music is of the best kind, why should we not be allowed to imitate it—that which the holy fathers and prophets eagerly imitated for the exercise of divine praise? We have in the Old Law Moses, and his sister Miriam, Joshua the son of Nun, King David, and many musicians among the prophets whom it would be tedious to recount. In our Law <note>The Christian era.</note>, we have the most holy Popes Gregory and John, the divine Jerome with the others, Saint Bernard, Isidore, Boethius, Odo, Berno, Guido, Hucbald, Regino, Otto, Notker, Robert King of France, Hermann the nephew of Emperor Henry, and many more whom I omit for the sake of brevity. Among the pagan philosophers, however, we find Pythagoras, Xerxes, Aristoxenus, Archytas, Philolaus, Ptolemy, Anicius <note>Boethius</note>, Linus of Thebes, Mercury, Orpheus, Amphion, and many more whom it would be difficult to count.

# ADAM OF FULDA

...Nevertheless <note>original: "Pra-" (catchword), continuing from "wor..." [words] on the previous page</note>, the talkative voice does not belong to the elderly unless it is a vibrant voice; and a man with a poor voice always wishes to sing. For the nature of things, as it pleases the nobleman Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus (c. 340–402 AD), a Roman statesman and orator known for his refined Latin style</note>, is such that those who stutter speak more, for they affect an abundance of speech out of shame for their defect; I could say the same of these critics. Furthermore, we concede that there will be many who use this art not for the honor of God, but for their own pleasure; yet it seems inappropriate that the art should therefore be shunned. Nor is the Holy Scripture any worse simply because heresies have occasionally proceeded from it. Far be it from us, therefore, that all should be brought to nothing because of a few, because, as Augustine says to Licentius <note>Licentius was a student of St. Augustine; this refers to their dialogues on music and poetry</note>, singing has its own cheerfulness, even if one does not move one's limbs to it, when it is sung with a modulation full of charity. For although headstrong people may possess this art, the art is nonetheless good in itself. Indeed, there is a common proverb: "as many heads, so many opinions." Not everyone can be well-mannered, since no artist is perfect in that regard; yet one must maintain an honorable custom for those who ask, and indeed neither singers nor musicians deny this.

However, to prove those liars who deny that music exists for the sake of earning one's bread <note>original: "de pane lucrando"—a common medieval phrase for a trade practiced only for survival or profit</note>, it is fitting to say: has not every assembly of the churches been instituted and founded to sing the praise of God? Regarding this, a certain author says: among all the institutions of the Church, none is more pleasing to God than the continuous singing of psalmody; and elsewhere: "The Levites shall cry out to me, and I will hear them." Who would not understand that music is the cause of every Prelacy <term>Prælaturæ; the high-ranking offices of the Church, such as bishops or abbots</term>? But setting these things aside, let us see how much music is valued in our own times. Does not our most 

<column-break/>

holy lord, Pope Innocent VIII <note>Pope from 1484 to 1492; this helps date the manuscript’s context to the late 15th century</note>, cherish, observe, and honor musicians, following the footsteps of his predecessors? For all the Roman Pontiffs were either musicians themselves or delighted in musicians, whom they honored with the greatest favors and gifts. What the most invincible Emperors of the Romans and the most serene Kings have done is a matter of public record. There is no one who does not know what the most Christian King of the Franks, and the Kings of England, Aragon, Spain, Hungary, and Apulia, and many princes, distinguished prelates, and free cities throughout Italy, Gaul, and Germany have done and continue to do for the musicians of our age.

### Chapter VI.

Behold how music has been honored and variously praised among the gentiles, the Hebrews, and the Christians. It neither lacks honor now, nor is it despised, except by the ignorant; for the only enemies of art are the ignorant. Therefore, let those dull-witted "two-legged asses" <note>A common insult in humanist writing for those who lack appreciation for the liberal arts</note> who go against nature yield and acknowledge that they are defeated; let them stop speaking evil, lest their own misdeeds be recognized, as the Comic Poet says. For music itself provokes frogs, dolphins, and indeed all other living creatures to the hearing of its modulation, as Isidore <note>St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD), whose "Etymologies" was a primary source for medieval musical theory</note> says; for birds sing incessantly if they hear singing. Thus, sweet-sounding birds emit voices from their modulating throats, singing continually. Even the fish gather for melody; whence Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author of the "Attic Nights"</note> reports that Arion, having been cast into the sea, was carried to port and saved by dolphins, because he had performed a sweet sound on his lyre and a song to console his misfortune before he was submerged. ### CHAPTER VII.

Wishing to designate the inventors of the musical art, I have desired to recount those things handed down to me by others and those things I have read, desiring to satisfy everyone. That music comes from God is known to all; Aurelius <note>Aurelius Augustine (354–430 AD), known as St. Augustine, who wrote the influential treatise *De Musica*.</note> records that this reminder of a great thing was granted to mortals by God; and Licentius also says to him:

> Who was it that gave number to the tones, and explained
> how to sing to the world’s Thunderer, and to lead the matching dances? <note>Licentius was a student of Augustine; these lines are from a poem he addressed to his teacher regarding the divine order of the cosmos.</note>

Virgil noted this: *The beginning of the Muse is from Jove.* <note>original: "a Iove principium Musæ." A reference to Virgil’s Eclogues, suggesting that all inspiration and art begin with the king of the gods.</note>

But it is now fitting to speak of the inventors. Since many people are said by many sources to have been the inventor, I shall share with everyone what seems right to me. The Greeks report that Pythagoras the philosopher first weighed the art of music from the sound of hammers; for hearing the disparity of sounds and the melody caused by the hammers, he con-

<column-break/>

-cluded rightly that harmony could be achieved even more fully by the human voice: an opinion to which Boethius and Macrobius <note>Boethius (c. 480–524) and Macrobius (c. 400 AD) were the primary authorities through whom medieval scholars learned Greek music theory and the story of Pythagoras’s discovery at the blacksmith's forge.</note> allude. But no one among the experts can bear this opinion of the pagans with an even mind, since there is no poet who does not call Orpheus most skilled in music; he preceded Pythagoras not merely by years but by centuries, even though Boethius says in his book on music <note>original: "l. m. musicæ," likely *De institutione musica*.</note> that Pythagoras found the first music among the Greeks through the unequal weights of striking hammers, through the unequal tension of strings, and through the unequal length of reeds. Others, however, say that Jubal was the inventor of music, which seems truer to me: for it is said that before the flood, the art was written by him on two columns—one of brick and the other of marble—for fear of fire and flood. <note>Jubal is mentioned in Genesis 4:21 as the "father of all those who play the harp and flute." The legend of the two pillars was a popular medieval tradition used to explain how antediluvian knowledge survived Noah's flood.</note> Josephus <note>Titus Flavius Josephus (37–100 AD), the Romano-Jewish historian.</note> affirms this, saying that they have remained in the land of Syria until now. The most holy Jerome agrees with this, as does Moses himself in Genesis 4, for he calls Jubal the father of musicians.

Furthermore, some wish Moses to be the inventor of the art, and say that he first weighed harmonies from the sound of waters; for music is said to be named from *moys* in Greek, which is *aqua* [water] in Latin, because it is said to have been found near waters. <note>This is a common medieval "false etymology" popularized by Isidore of Seville, incorrectly linking the Greek *mousa* (muse) to the Egyptian/Hebrew *moys* (water).</note> Again, there are some who say that harmonies took their origin from the movements of the heavens, asserting that a great melody arises from the motions of the heavens by reason of the friction of the celestial bodies, in which the greatest concord is believed to exist, as Empedocles <note>A Greek pre-Socratic philosopher who theorized about the elements and the forces of Love and Strife.</note> taught. Plato is said to have been closest to this opinion, for he thought that one siren stood upon every celestial sphere. But Aristotle rejects their opin- <note>The catchword "pi-" at the bottom of the previous page indicates the word "opinionem" (opinion) continues here.</note>

Therefore, whatever the truth may be, we must consider that there were many inventors of the art according to the variety of places and times, and the distances between regions. We believe that among the Hebrews, Jubal the son of Lamech began it before the flood; then Moses; among the Greeks, Pythagoras—to whom, as Horace says, the Muse gave the power to speak "with a well-rounded mouth" <note>original: "ore rotundo"; a quote from Horace's *Ars Poetica* referring to the eloquence and polished style of the Greeks</note>; and among the Latins, Boethius. But if we ask who among all was the very first, I think it was Jubal himself, for he preceded the others in time; for Holy Scripture records him as the inventor, and no other.

It was not granted to me to dwell upon

## THE LITTLE PREFACE OF ADAM OF FULDA, MUSICIAN, TO THE SECOND PART BEGINS HAPPILY.

### Prologue.

We believe that the interests of men are diverse; some introduce their writings to others, and each person strives to adorn his poems as best as he is able. If I bring forth the fables or histories of the ancient poets, I do not think I have detracted anything from my own examples or from the truest histories. It is the custom to return like for like; thus it happens that when the books of the poets and philosophers agree with this art of ours through all their fables or histories, we do not fear to introduce ancient histories and the fables of poets for a greater understanding of the art. For as Cicero <note>original: "Tullius"</note> says, we make the listeners attentive if we demonstrate that those things we are about to say are new, great, and useful. Indeed, as Varro says, the most excellent kind of teaching is the placement of examples; but I choose to use those introduced as true, not merely fictions.

We shall give our trust to Boethius: all others have imitated him as a leader, though they may have added something at times, mindful of the opinion of Marcus Varro, who says: "He will teach nothing magnificent who has invented nothing from himself." Use what has been invented, but labor for things yet to be found; for it is not so much a matter of praise to have found something as it is to be finding it—for the former belongs to another, while the latter is one's own gift. "If you wish to be taught, teach; and lacking teachers, you shall be taught by practice. Construct the things you know through readings, but acquire those things you have not yet learned through disciplines," says Isocrates.

I, however, although unequal in learning, am nonetheless not unmindful of the opinions of these men...

"Let each man practice the art he knows"; this is a Greek proverb. For these musical matters are such that men, while they teach, they also learn; as Guido says in the prologue to the rules of antiphons: there are many more things that we come to know through our own senses than those we have learned from a master. We make ourselves briefly teachable if we set forth the essence of the matter aptly and concisely. For what is more foolish than not to learn what you have not yet mastered, as Seneca testifies? Therefore, as long as you live, you must keep learning; for it befits a lover of knowledge to act vigorously, as Isocrates pleases.

Thus, I dare to replicate the form of <term>unmeasured music</term><note>original: "Musicae... immensuratae"; this refers to Gregorian chant or "plainchant," which does not have a fixed rhythmic beat like modern music.</note>, and to add to what has already been added—not because I consider myself an author suitable for completing such works, but so that I might meet the doubts of modern musicians and their opinions, and satisfy them as far as I am able.

It is always my intention to adhere to the rudiments of Boethius and Guido. Even if rivals bear this poorly, attributing more to others, I shall not be moved; for I prefer to imitate the <term>learned negligence</term> of Boethius and Guido rather than the useless diligence of others.

### CHAPTER I.

There are, first of all, seven things to be considered, through which—as if through the most principal elements—the path into the art lies open, namely:

<column-break/>

the hand, the song, the voice, the key, the mutation, the mode, and the tone. For Guido of Arezzo, the abbot of the Cross of St. Leufred, was the first to teach that the inflections of the notes must be learned by the **hand** <note>The "Guidonian Hand" was a mnemonic device where different parts of the hand represented different pitches, helping singers learn to sight-read.</note>, rightly concluding that a <term>pentachord</term> <note>A five-note scale.</note> could not suffice. He added the <term>Gamma</term> ($\Gamma$) below the <term>proslambanomenos</term> <note>The lowest note of the ancient Greek system; Guido added one note lower, the "Gamma," from which we get the word "gamut."</note> and four "super-excellent" notes beyond the <term>nete hyperboleon</term> <note>The highest note of the Greek system.</note>, dividing the threefold song sevenfold by seven letters, twenty keys, and six syllables <note>The six syllables are the "solmization" syllables: Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</note>. Johannes, however, maintains that the Gamma ($\Gamma$) was invented before Guido. But in the course of time, more modern teachers of music, not content with these keys, concluded by necessity that three strings—namely the <term>trite</term>, <term>paranete</term>, and <term>nete hyperboleon</term>—must have an octave added above them. Similarly, an octave was added below the <term>lichanos</term>, <term>hypate</term>, and <term>parypatemeson</term> for the sake of <term>mensural music</term> <note>Music with a fixed, "measured" rhythm, as opposed to plainchant.</note> invented by the venerable Guillaume Dufay. His composition gave to our people the great beginning of "formality," commonly called <term>manerum</term> <note>Likely referring to "mannerism" or a specific structured style of polyphony.</note>. For he himself, though first content with the rules, not undeservedly overstepped the limits in transposition, since it is very useful for instruments and those who know them—for whose sake we believe more was admitted. We, however, are content with the rules, nor shall we obey the ancients less than the moderns, although we have attained more subtlety; yet there is no one among all of them who does not boast that he has received something from the ancients.

Concerning the division of the <term>monochord</term> <note>A scientific instrument with a single string used to measure musical intervals.</note>, many people say many things, holding various opinions, and one person rebukes the division of another—such as Ptolemy, who rebuked the divisions of Aristoxenus and Archytas as a revenge for music.

Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), a Roman philosopher whose works on music theory were the standard textbooks for the Middle Ages.</note> eventually brought to light a division of the scale that was not unsuitable, which everyone thereafter imitated. But Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033 AD), the monk credited with inventing modern musical notation and the "hand" mnemonic.</note>, driven by necessity, went beyond those limits and added further notes; therefore, modern musicians, trusting in Guido’s boldness, did not hesitate to add further necessary notes to those already added. The <term>monochord</term><note>A scientific instrument with a single string used to measure the mathematical ratios of musical intervals.</note> is named from the Greek *monos* <note>original: "μονος"</note>, which means "one" or "alone," because it is an instrument of a single string. ### CHAPTER II.

"Song"—which the Greeks call *oda* <note>original: "odam"</note> and we sometimes call "praise"—is melody produced from sound, tone, and mode by the living voice. It is, therefore, technically said incorrectly that one "sings" on organs, trumpets, or harps. It is not my place, however, to reprimand anyone, especially the holy Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note>, since he says very often that the Hebrews "sang" with the trumpet. But if the definition of song is strictly true, it is said incorrectly because those voices are material <note>Meaning they are produced by physical objects rather than the human soul/breath.</note>; yet it is more beautifully said that they "sang with a trumpet" than that they "trumpeted."

<column-break/>

The ancients wished this song to be threefold: namely, <term>natural</term>, <term>soft</term>, and <term>hard</term>. But after the teachers discovered the "Hand," and additionally the location of letters along with the voices <note>The syllables Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La.</note>, it was found that "song" should be understood in two ways: namely, generally and specially. Generally: and the first division remains; for there are three types of song in general, namely natural, <term>soft B</term> <note>original: "b. mollaris"; refers to the hexachord containing B-flat.</note>, and <term>hard B</term> <note>original: "♮. duralis"; refers to the hexachord containing B-natural.</note>. Specially: and there will be seven songs <note>Or hexachords.</note> within the Hand: two natural, two "soft B," and three "hard B." For the voices are found seven times within the Hand: from which it happens that wherever *ut* is placed, another "song" begins there. There are, however, some who attribute two voices to each type as if they were suited to them; for they give *ut* and *fa* to the soft B, *re* and *sol* to the natural, and *mi* and *la* to the hard B, the order of which the following figure sufficiently explains.

The beginning of singing psalms in the Church started in imitation of the shepherds, who wished to pay praises to God during the performance of sacrifices. Elsewhere, however, we read that it was introduced by the most blessed martyr Ignatius <note>St. Ignatius of Antioch (c. 35–107 AD).</note>, who heard angelic voices singing to the Lord and brought that custom to his church; thus the rite of singing spread into various churches. Many, however, maintain that among the Latins, St. Ambrose, the bishop of the Church of Milan, was the first to give the method of singing psalms to the Western Church. We, however, hold Gregory as our author, from whom the simple song has received the name "Gregorian."

### CHAPTER III.

Voice is sound, formed by the "pick" <note>original: "plectro"</note> of the tongue through the striking of the teeth and the clashing of the two lips in the manner of cymbals, with the aid of the hollow of the throat and the lungs, which receive and release air like a bellows. There is, however, a certain species of both voice and sound, and another of sound but not voice; indeed, sound is threefold in nature through the echo of sounds: **harmonic**, which consists of the songs of voices; **organic**, which subsists on breath <note>Meaning wind instruments like the organ or flute.</note>; and **rhythmic**, which receives its proportions <note>original: "numeros," literally 'numbers' or 'rhythms'.</note> from the management, tension, and striking of strings. One type of sound is discrete, which creates consonance and is accepted in music; the other is indiscrete, which produces dissonance and is rejected.

A <term>Symphony</term><note>In this medieval context, "symphonia" refers to a pleasing concord or "sounding together" of intervals, rather than a large orchestral work.</note> is a tempering of modulation with concordant sounds, whether in the voice, in breath, or in striking. Moreover, the human voice stands out as specified by musicians, which is musically located in six voices or syllables

<column-break/>

by which every song is governed through mutations. These are thought to have been taken by Johannes <note>Likely referring to Johannes Afflighemensis (John Cotton), though the system is more famously attributed to Guido of Arezzo.</note> from the hymn: *Ut queant laxis etc.* <note>The Hymn to St. John the Baptist, used by Guido of Arezzo to name the notes of the scale. The first syllable of each line—Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La—formed the hexachord.</note> There are six voices: *ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.*

### CHAPTER IV.

A <term>Clef</term><note>original: "Clavis," literally "key." In medieval theory, the "key" unlocked the specific pitch of the lines on a staff.</note> is truly a "local letter" rectified by the voices, twenty of which are placed upon the Hand, namely Gamma-ut, A-re, etc. Of these, only three are usually placed <note>Meaning used as clef signs on a staff.</note>, namely **C. sol, fa, ut; F. fa, ut; and G. sol, re, ut.** Others are placed very rarely or never. They are comprised under seven letters, called "local letters," doubled in the higher order, namely A, B, C, D, E, F, G. Truly, there are five species of Clefs: namely Low <note>original: "Graves"</note>, Final, High <note>original: "Acutæ"</note>, Excellent, and Super-excellent. If a voice or note should occur outside these species, it must be judged according to its <term>diapason</term><note>The interval of an octave.</note> above or below. ### CHAPTER V.

Mutation <term>Mutatio: the technique of switching between the three types of hexachords (hard, soft, and natural) to reach higher or lower notes.</term> is the variation of one voice <note>original: "vox", here meaning a solmization syllable like ut, re, mi.</note> into another in the same key <note>original: "clavis", the pitch or letter-name of the note.</note>: however, I do not think the voice is the sound, because the sound in the same key

<column-break/>

does not vary. I wish, however, for the voice to be the "song" <note>original: "cantus", referring to the specific hexachord system currently in use.</note>, because the song is changed in the key, [moving from] hard ♮ <note>original: "♮. duralis"</note> into natural, or natural into hard ♮, or soft b <note>original: "b. mollem"</note>, and so on.

->OF ADAM OF FULDA<-

Mutation is of two types: extrinsic is when a voice <note>In this context, "voice" refers to the solmization syllables: ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la.</note> is openly changed into another voice, such as *fa* into *sol*, *sol* into *re*, and vice versa. Intrinsic is when the voice that ought to be changed is left behind, as happens in mensural song <note>Measured music with specific rhythmic values, as opposed to the unmeasured flow of plainchant.</note>.

Two things are required for mutation: do not mutate unless it is necessary—that is, to skillfully change one voice into another—and that the keys <note>Clefs or pitch-letters on the staff.</note> be inspected, along with the joined notes <note>original: "conjuncta"</note>, on account of the *synemmenon* <term>synemmenon: a Greek term for the "tetrachord of the conjuncts," here referring to the use of B-flat</term> in transposition.

<column-break/>

I did not wish to add those childish rules regarding the falling of notes in mutation to this small work of ours, since this is not a specialized study for the common wandering students <note>original: "bacchantria" - referring to the *vagantes* or traveling scholars known for rowdy behavior and simplified learning</note>, where such things might not be continuously practiced. Let the knowledge of the species, or the modes, of which we shall speak later, suffice.

How mutation behaves in the keys, or how many mutations each key has, the following figure demonstrates.

| Every Key | Number of Voices | Resulting Mutations | Verse |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **One voice** (four instances): Γ. *ut*; A. *re*; ♮. *mi*; e. *la*. | 1 | They have no mutation. | If the voice is single, no mutation shall occur. |
| **Two voices** (eight instances): C. *fa, ut*; D. *sol, re*; E. *la, mi*; F. *fa, ut*; e. *la, mi*; f. *fa, ut*; c. *sol, fa*; d. *la, sol*. | 2 | They have two mutations. | If the voice is double, a double mutation shall occur. |
| **Three voices** (six instances): G. *sol, re, ut*; a. *la, mi, re*; c. *sol, fa, ut*; d. *la, sol, re*; g. *sol, re, ut*; a. *la, mi, re*. | 3 | They have six mutations. | If the voice is triple, a sixfold mutation shall occur. |

### CHAPTER VI.

There still remains *b-flat fa* / *b-natural mi*, as well as its octave <term>diapason: the interval of an octave</term> *b-flat fa* / *b-natural mi*, because in these no mutation occurs; for we cannot change *fa* and *mi* into one, since they are separated by a semitone. For a semitone is like a half tone; indeed, the ancients wished to call a sound smaller than a tone a "semitone": but it is to be understood

<column-break/>

in such a way that it is not thought of as a literal half of a tone, just as we do not take a "semivowel" in writing to be exactly half of a vowel, nor can a whole tone be made from two equal semitones. Because of this, Plato wished to call this very thing a *limma* <term>limma: in Pythagorean tuning, the "leftover" interval that is slightly smaller than a true semitone</term>, and the Greeks called it the *synemmenon* "round b" <note>original: "b. rotundum", the symbol for B-flat</note>, that is, the "added" note.

### THE SECOND PART OF MUSIC.

Yet many, without knowledge of this art, seem to want to sing well by mere habit; however, when questioned about number or interval <note>In the medieval Quadrivium, music was studied as the science of numbers in relation to sound.</note>, they do not know how to respond. Truly, they do not grasp the words of the philosopher Democritus, who says: the voices of the unskilled are in the same place as the sounds released from the belly; for what is the difference if the latter howl downwards and the former howl upwards? I myself saw a certain man who wanted to be held as an authority and composer of this art, who cared neither for the rhythmic number in prolation nor for the position of the clefs. I asked why he omitted these things; he replied that they were not a necessity, even though they are the most necessary things of all. And there was another who, when he wished to begin the service of the sixth tone <note>One of the eight church modes or scales used in Gregorian chant.</note> with his pupils, sang the first tone instead. Yet this man was a musician of great fame; for as Horace says: "the foolish public also often gives honors to the unworthy," and I believe fame seduced him. We also knew a certain Andrechinus of Basel, who, by running here and there, proclaimed himself the servant now of this Prince and now of that, and among the ignorant he was regarded as the greatest musician, though he hardly understood himself. This one thing, however, he had learned in the school of philosophy: to flee from the learned entirely, lest his ignorance be worn down by debate.

This class of men is so perverse and so stiff-necked that they wish to be seen to possess more of the art than they actually have. They think nothing is right except what they have made themselves, not obeying the authorities. They wish to believe in <insert>experience</insert>, rather than in reason, the mistress of all, even though the judgment of both ought to be sought. Let them, therefore, share in the portion of reason. Perhaps the wretched men do not know—

<column-break/>

—that there is a great difference between a singer and a musician. Or perhaps they have not read Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the most influential music theorist of the Middle Ages.</note> in the second *Micrologus* of music, where he says:

> *Between musicians and singers, the distance is great:*
> *The latter speak, the former know, that which music composes.*
> *For he who does what he does not understand is defined as a beast.*

Nor have they heard Boethius saying in the first book of *Music*, chapter 3: "He is a musician who, having weighed reason, assumes the science of singing not by the service of work, but by the command of speculation <note>original: "speculationis" – here meaning intellectual contemplation or theoretical study.</note>." For the science of music is as much more noble in the cognition of reason than in the work of doing and the act, as the body is surpassed by the mind. For the speculation of reason does not need the act of working; for the works of the hands are nothing unless they are led by reason. From this it follows that how great the glory and merit of reason is can be understood here; for bodily craftsmen, so to speak, take their names not from the discipline itself, but rather from the instruments themselves: for the lutenist <note>original: "citharœdus"</note> is named from the kithara, the piper <note>original: "tibicen"</note> from the pipes, and the organist from the organ.

Three types of people are occupied with music: one works with instruments; another composes songs; the third judges both. The first, which performs with instruments, spends its whole labor there and is separated from the understanding of the science of music, because it serves and brings nothing of reason, but is devoid of all speculation.

The second, which composes songs, belongs to the poets; it is led to song more by a certain natural instinct than by speculation and reason, and therefore it must be set apart.

# ADAM OF FULDA

<column-break/>

Pardon Boethius, then, since you too are a poet, and do not think his work was done for nothing; for he does not speak merely of the art of humanity <note>original: "humanitatis arte"; likely referring to the humanities or the more superficial aspects of human culture as opposed to the rigorous mathematical science of music.</note>.

The third type of musician is the one who takes up the skill of judging, who can weigh the rhythms, the melody, and the whole song; however, since this is situated entirely in reason and speculation, it will be properly assigned to the science of music. Let them learn, therefore, that there is a difference between musicians, singers, and instrumentalists. Let them not arrogantly despise the art and its authors, but trust the ancients, who brought forth more reason than these people can even understand.

Many, however, take my words—I fear—in a negative way, and interpret my recounting of the vices of many as if I wished to overshadow my own ignorance. But my conscience is my witness that they think ill of me; for I remember the words of Jerome to Rusticus, where he says: <note>original: "inuenti ſunt ſcioli tantum ad detrahendum, qui eo ſe doctos oſtentare volunt, ſi cunctorum dicta lacerent."</note> *half-knowledgable people have been found only for the purpose of disparaging, who wish to show themselves off as learned by tearing apart the words of everyone.* And also Cicero in the second book of his *Tusculan Disputations*: <note>original: "ſtultitiæ proprium eſt, aliorum vitia cernere, ſuorum obliviſci."</note> *it is the property of folly to see the vices of others and forget one's own.* I am not such a man; rather, other causes move me: I pity the art, which, although it was most laboriously invented by the ancient philosophers worthy of all praise, is in our age corrupted, torn apart, and confused by the basest novices <note>original: "beanis"; a medieval academic slang term for "yellow-beaks" or raw freshmen who have not yet been "purified" by education.</note>. Oh, if Boethius were alive, certainly moved by pity he would rather lament music than translate it. You would not only say, O Guido! <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), the inventor of modern musical notation and the "ut-re-mi" system.</note> that singers are fools, but you would think they were all masters; for without masters they presume to do everything they want. Oh, rash 

<column-break/>

audacity! Oh, cursed presumption! We who are barely twelve years old already fear to learn, or if we have learned a few minor precepts, we weigh them as if they were the innermost secrets of the art; and understanding little, we affirm that we know everything. We wish to be subject to no one's correction, so that the truth appears written in us regarding the music of Pope John <note>Likely referring to the theorist John Cotton, though cited here as "Johannes Papa."</note>: they do not know and do not wish to know, and they flee from those who do know; when questioned, they shamelessly make noise, they resist the truth, and they defend their error with the greatest effort. They are like those possessed by spirits, neither seeing by themselves nor obeying the leadership of those who can see, even though no thing is learned without a master. Even mute animals and herds of wild beasts follow a leader, but our people care for neither leader nor master, believing they understand everything by themselves: (a) whom I would compare to no one better than a drunkard, who indeed returns home, but does not know by which path he returns. Even a millstone sometimes gives off a distinct screeching, yet it knows nothing of what it is doing. 

Oh, pitiable art! Oh, art to be lamented! which all the unlearned claim for themselves everywhere; already the disciples assume the office of judging, but alas! they are less than disciples—that is, common laymen who know neither art nor letters. Having attained a tiny bit of skill on instruments, they judge everything, they tear everything apart and confuse it: so that music now seems to be not one of the liberal arts <note>The seven "Liberal Arts" were the higher academic disciplines (like Logic and Astronomy); music was part of this elite group.</note>, but one of the mechanical arts <note>The "Mechanical Arts" were manual crafts or trades, considered lower in status than theoretical sciences.</note>. Let them consider, therefore, if the art is to be pitied; let them pity it themselves and admit that I have spoken the truth. If they do not, the blame will be pushed back on me, though unjustly. But it pleases me now to proceed and follow what has been begun.

# SECOND PART OF MUSIC

## Chapter VII

A **mode** <note>original: "modus"; here referring to a melodic interval rather than a scale</note> is the melodic rising or falling of voices or notes; or defined thus: a mode is the distance or interval between a high and a low sound. An interval of notes created by depth or height, rising or falling, is called a "mode" by musicians, as is the relationship of voices to one another; from this, we understand the movement of the notes.

Now, there are twelve modes, although some list only nine, not counting the semitone with a fifth, the minor third with a fifth, and the whole tone with a fifth, because these rarely occur in **Gregorian chant**; however, we use them more frequently in **mensural** <note>Music with a specific, measured rhythm or meter.</note> or **figured song** <note>Early polyphonic music involving multiple independent voices.</note>. I have decided, therefore, that they should be counted with the others, and later I will indicate their description—how they are raised or lowered, strongly or weakly—using two diagrams to help trace their harmonic form.

Since a mode is the melodic rising or falling of voices, one must first know the properties of voices, followed by the species of the modes.

Among voices, some are *unison*, which when struck individually return one and the same sound. Others are *equisonant*, which when struck together create a single, simple sound out of two, such as the <term>diapason</term> <gloss>octave</gloss> and the double octave. There are *consonant* voices, which produce a sound that is composite and blended, yet sweet, such as the <term>diapente</term> <gloss>fifth</gloss> and the <term>diatessaron</term> <gloss>fourth</gloss>. There are *emmeles* <note>From the Greek meaning "in tune" or "suitable for melody."</note>, which are not consonant themselves but can be correctly fitted into a melody, such as the whole tone and other types of intervals. *Dissonant* voices

<column-break/>

are those which do not blend their sounds, but strike the sense harshly. There are also *ecmeles* <note>From the Greek meaning "out of tune" or "unmelodic."</note>, which are not accepted in the joining of harmonies to create a melody, such as the **tritone** <note>An interval of three whole tones, often called "the devil in music" for its instability.</note> and the diminished fifth. This division is found in the works of **Odo** in the *Enchiridion*, and in the music of **Hermann the German** written in the form of a dialogue.

There are twelve modes, or types of leaps. A *unison* is the repetition of the same pitch in the same voice. A *semitone* <note>A half-step.</note> is a leap from *mi* to *fa*, and vice versa. A *tone* <note>A whole step.</note> is a leap from one pitch to the next; it contains two unequal semitones. A *semiditone* <note>A minor third.</note> is a leap from line to line, or space to space, including a semitone. A *ditone* <note>A major third.</note> is a leap to the third, excluding a semitone. A *diatessaron* is a leap to the fourth, generally consisting of two tones and a semitone, unless it is a tritone. A *diapente* is a leap to the fifth, including three tones and a semitone, unless it is a diminished fifth. A *semitone with a fifth* is a leap to the sixth voice consisting of [three] tones and two semitones <note>A minor sixth.</note>. A *tone with a fifth* is a true leap to the sixth with four tones and one semitone <note>A major sixth.</note>. A *semiditone with a fifth* is a leap to the seventh consisting of four tones and two semitones <note>A minor seventh.</note>. A *ditone with a fifth* is a leap to the seventh consisting of five tones and one semitone <note>A major seventh.</note>. The *diapason* is a leap to the octave, the greatest among the consonances. You will find the proportional form of these modes clearly set out in the final part concerning proportions.

The proportionality of all the "periphones"—that is, the consonances—through...

->ADAM OF FULDA<-

These modes are sought out, along with the <term>diaphony</term> <gloss>the sounding of two voices together</gloss> arising from the circuit or progression of the musical strings. For **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524), whose "De institutione musica" was the fundamental music theory textbook of the Middle Ages.</note>, the preeminent author of this art among the Latins, established fifteen musical strings, spanning from the <term>proslambanomenos</term> <gloss>the lowest note in the Greek system</gloss> to the <term>netehyperboleon</term> <gloss>the highest note</gloss>, encompassing a quadruple or double-octave, which he called the "greatest symphony." **Johannes de Muris** <note>A 14th-century mathematician and music theorist.</note>, who is practiced here and there in the schools, followed him in this. After this came **Guido** of the Italian nation <note>Guido of Arezzo (c. 991–1033), credited with inventing the musical staff and the "Guidonian Hand."</note>, a musician of no small renown, who rightly concluded that the species of the **monochord** <note>A single-stringed instrument used to measure musical intervals.</note> could be expanded further. Not content with fifteen strings, he added the low "Gamma" (Γ) <note>original: "Proslambanomenos Γ"; this added a note below the traditional Greek scale.</note> and the "excellent" notes above the <term>netehyperboleon</term>, establishing twenty-four strings in total. He instituted a method for learning these more easily by using the **hand**; it is believed that this was later perfected by **Odo of Cluny**, the monk.

As time passed and human wit increased, musicians began to be even more subtle. No longer content with the "Hand" or the precepts of Guido, but transposing the song as often as necessary, they found that more voices should be added below Gamma and, similarly, more voices should be associated above high E-la. I believe the venerable **Guillaume Dufay** <note>A famous Burgundian composer (c. 1397–1474) who bridged the gap between Medieval and Renaissance styles.</note> was the inventor of this expansion, and all modern musicians imitate him. Many, however, obey their own will rather than authority; many of them follow practice without a knowledge of the art, since the use of the musical art is innate to many. But just as wisdom without eloquence is of little use, and eloquence without wisdom is not only useless but often harmful, so art without practice is of little value, and practice without art is nothing.

<column-break/>

I wished to prove by reason that these additions ought to be set down, for authority preceded them. Since music—one of the four arts of the <term>Quadrivium</term> <note>The higher division of the liberal arts, comprising arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy.</note>—rejoices in measure, number, and proportions, and since all proportions, whether geometrical or arithmetical, tend toward infinity, why should the harmonic proportions of voices or sounds not also tend toward infinity, provided they can be reached by the human or material voice? For experience, which is the mistress of all things, teaches us this.

### CHAPTER IX.

Since it has become a widespread custom among composers to create **canonical songs** <note>Canons; pieces where one melody is followed by one or more imitations of the same melody.</note>, in which some believe the entire art is tied up as if in a knot, the foolish believe other fools. Many of these composers, when they wish to obscure things for others, so overshadow themselves that they can scarcely see at noon, like one-eyed men. For they use strange syllables and non-musical terms, and they waste much time on a matter of little fruit, or they set forth a tiny bit of imagination in many verses of text in place of a <term>canon</term> <gloss>a rule or instruction for a musical riddle</gloss>. To them I would say: "If you do not wish to be spoken of, do not speak." <note>original: "si non vis dici, non dicaris." A play on words suggests that if they don't want their music to be deciphered/understood, they shouldn't bother presenting it.</note> But alas, there are many who rejoice more in *appearing* to be musical theorists than in actually *being* so; having failed to master it in their youth, they are afraid to learn in their old age. I wish they would accept the counsel of fate and imitate **Cato**, who in his old age wished to be instructed in Greek literature; or **Solon**, who learned even as he was dying; or **Socrates**, who devoted himself to music as an old man. When some asked Socrates if he was not ashamed to study in his old age, he replied: "It is a greater shame to be ignorant in old age than to study in old age." And the lofty Homer did not fe- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing on the next page; original: "fe-" likely for "ferebat" or similar.</note>

...should be followed, who, when he could not solve a problem proposed to him by fishermen, threw himself headlong into the sea, as the story goes. <note>This refers to a legend about the death of the poet Homer, who supposedly died of frustration after failing to solve a riddle about lice posed by young fishermen.</note> Let them learn, therefore, to seek the art of music more than they trust in themselves, and to make use of vocal music and strings rather than those belonging to others.

<margin>(a) See the music of Ægidius of Zamora <note>Gil de Zamora, a 13th-century Spanish Franciscan theorist.</note> above in Part II, page 382.</margin>
For Boethius <note>The most influential musical authority of the Middle Ages.</note> established fifteen strings, to which he gave Greek names, perhaps taken from Pythagoras, as has been said and as the following figure declares. Nicomachus reports that music was at first simple, consisting of only four strings; the aforementioned Boethius, in Book I of his *Music*, chapter 2, says this lasted until the time of Orpheus. This four-stringed system, the <term>tetrachord</term> <gloss>a scale of four notes</gloss>, was invented by Mercury from the shell of a rotted fish. <note>In traditional mythology, Mercury used a tortoise shell; the Latin here uses "piscis" (fish), likely referring to a shell-bearing sea creature.</note> Corebus, the son of Atys, added a fifth string; Hyagnis the Phrygian a sixth; Terpander of Lesbos a seventh; Licaon of Samos an eighth; Prophrastus of Periotes a ninth; Histiaeus of Colophon a tenth; and Timotheus of Miletus the eleventh.(a) Guido, however, added one low string and four "super-excellent" <gloss>very high</gloss> ones; then, more modern thinkers stepped beyond these boundaries and added further notes above and below, as touched upon before. Since Guido and his followers left these added or "super-added" notes unnamed, I wished first to complete Guido’s work. I call the string added in the bass, namely $\Gamma$ <note>Gamma-ut, the lowest note of the medieval system.</note>, the *hyponomenon*, which means "low sound," because it is the deepest in the hand <gloss>the Guidonian Hand mnemonic</gloss>. For the four super-excellent notes—namely the doubled *b, c, d, e*—I call the first *b* the *epitrite diahyperboleon* <gloss>the super-extended fourth</gloss>, that is, "superexcellent," with the *trite hyperboleon* as two notes; then followed by the *epiparanate diahyper-*

---

<column-break/>

*boleon* and the *epinete diahyperboleon*, remaining according to the preceding form. The very last note, namely natural, I call the *la orexion*, which means the "newest sound" in the hand. Regarding the additions of the moderns, since they lack names, I have chosen to call all those in the "hypothesis" (that is, the lower placement) the *hyperaxiapathones*, meaning the deepest or ultimate sounds. Similarly, in the "hyperboleothesis" (that is, the superexcellent high placement), I have chosen to call all the additions together the *origneoboleones*, meaning those "sounding above the last," as the following figure indicates.
