### CHAPTER X.

Now that we have spoken of the modes of the strings, or of <term>periphonia</term> <gloss>concordant sound</gloss> and <term>diaphonia</term> <gloss>discordant sound</gloss>, it is fitting to learn of the <term>consonances</term> <gloss>intervals that sound pleasant</gloss> and <term>dissonances</gloss> <gloss>intervals that clash</gloss> within the modes; for the whole of music is learned for the sake of symphony and harmony.

Therefore, some consonances are "perfect," namely: the unison (the same voice), the <term>fifth</term> <gloss>original: diapente</gloss>, and the <term>octave</term> <gloss>original: diapason</gloss>, along with their equivalent sounds: the octave, the twelfth, and the double-octave. Others are "imperfect," such as the <term>major third</term> <gloss>original: ditonus</gloss> or the <term>minor third</term> <gloss>original: semitiditonus</gloss>, and likewise the major sixth (a tone with a fifth) or the minor sixth (a semitone with a fifth), along with their equivalent sounds, the tenth and the thirteenth. As for the rest, even if they could be measured unto infinity, they are merely repetitions of these.

Furthermore, some say the <term>fourth</term> <gloss>original: diatessaron</gloss> is a perfect consonance, and some say it is imperfect; but we say it is a "semi-dissonance," meaning it does not concord well by itself alone. Johannes de Muris <note>A famous 14th-century mathematician and music theorist.</note> even denies that it is a consonance at all...

# ADAM OF FULDA

...unless a perfect consonance precedes it; however, with perfect or imperfect concords, it is moderated, and it creates consonance not of itself, but in respect to others. This is what musicians of the nations have begun to call *faulx bordon* <note>original: "faulx bordon"; Fauxbourdon is a technique of musical arrangement using parallel harmonies, which Adam seems to find "grim" or "foul" compared to traditional counterpoint.</note>, because it renders a grim sound. All other voices, besides those already mentioned, are for the purpose of dissonance—that is, they are in disagreement with all others.

From the prescribed consonances, every <term>symphonia</term> <gloss>harmonious composition</gloss> is composed through <term>arsis and thesis</term> <gloss>the rising and falling of the voice</gloss>. This includes not only the simple <term>neuma</term> <gloss>a group of notes sung to one syllable</gloss>, which Berno <note>Berno of Reichenau, an influential 11th-century music theorist.</note> calls a *distrophe* <gloss>two notes of the same pitch</gloss> or *tristrophe* <gloss>three notes of the same pitch</gloss>, but also, I believe, a song of double and triple concordant ratios. Since, therefore, a faulty habit—as Berno testifies—can hardly or in no way be uprooted from customary work and from the mouths of singers, certain rules of composition were invented by the teachers so that no one should be led by their own whim. I have chosen to insert some of these here because, alas, we see music corrupted everywhere by composers. This happens because a most wretched habit has grown among instrumentalists who, though they scarcely understand two rules, oh the sorrow! wish to compose songs. And if only they were just songs—but they even presume to handle great works through mere practice. Furthermore, others, scarcely understanding the shapes of the notes and having attained only a small bit of the art, "correct," tear apart, and corrupt every song, and falsify what was rightly composed. I remain silent about the many who, although they were well-taught by their masters, err just as often because they have not soundly committed individual things to memory, whether through their own fault or that of their teachers. There are many more who have learned more through sheer knack

<column-break/>

than through art; they consider whatever they do to be the law, and they hurl insults at one another. One fool confounds another, and if there were a thousand of them, barely ten would agree. The first says, as Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo, the inventor of modern musical notation.</note> reports, "Master Bruno taught me thus." Another says, "I learned it this way from my master Albinus." A third says, "Truly, my master Odo <note>Likely Odo of Cluny, another major musical authority.</note> informed me differently." Thus it happens that while each person prefers his own master, there are as many diversifiers of composition as there are masters in the world. And it happens to us according to that saying of *Nasonis* <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the Roman poet Ovid.</note>:

> *As many as the habits in hearts, so many are the*
> ->*figures in the world;*<-
> ->*While each person is pleased with himself, the gullible*<-
> ->*crowd is but smoke.*<-

Truly, whoever prefers to cling to a corrupt habit rather than obey the truth should learn that mimes and jesters will be the composers of the future.

### CHAPTER XI.

It has pleased me here to provide the more useful rules of the ancients—especially ten that seem most useful to me—for the common methods of composition, so that men are not led by a slight madness, and so that no one is drawn by his own whim without instruction.

First: In every song, at least one voice is said to be adapted to the true <term>tone</term> <gloss>one of the eight church modes</gloss>. To adapt to the tone means to beautifully and locally place the eight tones—that is, the <term>clausulae</term> <gloss>musical endings or cadences</gloss>. For just as the accent of prose is adorned by a punctuation mark, so is the tone adorned by the eight.

Second: Every composer should learn to adorn a song distinctly with pauses, because they create variety. For it is no less praiseworthy to pause than to sing, nor is the accent of prose made without a pause.

### MUSIC PART TWO.

Third: every dissonance must be avoided as much as possible, as should the <term>tritone</term> <gloss>the interval of three whole tones, considered unstable</gloss> and the <term>semidiapente</term> <gloss>a diminished fifth</gloss>. This is because the discrepancy of the semitone is forbidden, except in musical movements where a perfect consonance immediately follows it. I do not say "semidiapente" <note>literally "half-fifth"</note> in the same way Virgil (Maro) speaks of the "half-men of Phrygia," <note>original: "semiviri phryges"; Adam is making a pun on Virgil's *Aeneid* (12.99). He is arguing that a "semitone" is not mathematically exactly half of a whole tone in the tuning systems of his time.</note> because a semitone is not actually half of a tone.

Fourth: a composer must look ahead carefully to the true position of the keys when transposing a tone, because there one encounters the meeting of <term>conjuncts</term> <gloss>joined scales</gloss>, which the Greeks called *synemmenon* and our own musicians have chosen to call *musica ficta* <note>original: "musica ficta"; "fictitious" or "false" music, referring to the use of sharps and flats that lie outside the standard medieval hexachord system.</note>.

Fifth: every composer should simply commit to memory the twelve articles of the art, for without these no song can be composed.

Sixth: all composers should have special regard for the first three degrees of music: namely, <term>mode</term>, <term>time</term>, and <term>prolation</term> <gloss>the three levels of rhythmic division in medieval notation</gloss>. This is for the sake of the numbers, so that they may assign to each what belongs to it—that is, the correct sign for recognition and the <term>tactus</term> <gloss>the steady pulse or beat</gloss>.

Seventh: no perfect consonance is allowed to follow its own identical perfect consonance in <term>arsis and thesis</term> <gloss>the rising and falling of the melody</gloss>. Instead, any perfect consonance ought to be followed worthily by a different perfect consonance—for example, a <term>diapente</term> <gloss>perfect fifth</gloss> after a unison, or a <term>diapason</term> <gloss>octave</gloss> after a perfect fifth.

Eighth: although the ancients once forbade more than three or four imperfect consonances from following one another, we moderns do not forbid it, especially with <term>tenths</term>, since they provide ornament, provided there is an intermediate voice.

Ninth: the <term>diatessaron</term> <gloss>perfect fourth</gloss> must never be placed alone, unless it is moderated by either a perfect or imperfect consonance.

<column-break/>

But it is also not permitted for voices to ascend or descend together [in parallel fourths], unless it is, as mentioned before, *faulx bordon* <note>original: "faulx bordon"; a technique of parallel harmony that Adam views with some suspicion compared to stricter counterpoint.</note>. Some think this can be done in the *hypothesi* <gloss>the lowest register</gloss> and in the *hyperboleothesi* <gloss>the highest register</gloss>; but reason does not recommend this, because it would go against the preceding rule.

Tenth: let every composer learn to place perfect consonances against the tenor in the *hypothesi* (that is, in the lower notes) rather than imperfect ones—with the exception of the <term>third</term> and its equivalent intervals, which is a sound tempered by an equal resonance of consonance. Horace seems to speak of this when he says:

> It is not enough for poems to be beautiful; let them be sweet. <note>original: "Non satis est pulcra esse poëmata, dulcia sunto"; quoted from Horace's *Ars Poetica*.</note>

If I had added musical figures to all these points or attempted to clarify them more brilliantly, it would have brought weariness to the readers rather than pleasure. Therefore, I chose to omit everything else, so that the reader's mind would not be confused by an excessive craving for reading.

### CHAPTER XII.

These ten precepts, therefore, have seemed necessary to all composers of songs according to the will of the ancients. But among the moderns—who, as Priscianus says, "the younger they are, the more clear-sighted they are" <note>original: "quanto iuniores, tanto perspicaciores sunt"</note>—there are many more rules. Thus, if I may say so without causing offense, there is no true composer unless he knows all the precepts of this little book. For it is not enough for a composer to be a singer; he must also be a perfect musician. When he wishes to compose for others to sing, he himself should know what he is doing, so as not to labor in vain. For Seneca says: "it is shameful to speak one thing and think another"; but it is even more shameful to do one thing and feel another, because the first...

Finally, if a composer wishes to use proportions, let him use musical ones, because the others, with few exceptions, lack harmony <term>symphonia</term> <gloss>the agreeable concord of different sounds</gloss>. Let him, therefore, strive to establish them cautiously, lest he substitute one for another, because one leads to error and the other to disgrace. For many, while they love obscurity, are a laughingstock to experts, because rarity of obscurity is seldom without error. But I myself have used this [obscurity], to tell the truth, showing my own ignorance more than providing information about the art; yet it is said to be the mark of a very poor mind to use only things already invented rather than things yet to be discovered. Therefore, let everyone do as much as he worthily can; for if you do well, you will give authority to your own person, as Socrates says. I have wished to say these things while maintaining peace, being neither deceptive nor secretive, for I cannot please everyone. Yet I have not undertaken this without the judgment of very grave men, on whose au-

### CHAPTER XIII.

A tone is the discernment or knowledge of the beginning and end, and the ascent and descent, of any regular melody; or thus: a tone is a rule teaching the perfect end of regular harmonies <term>symphoniae</term>. However, I do not consider a tone to be modal—that is, a harmony of a song captured within the modes—but rather I consider a tone to be melodic or formal. Some call tones "tropes" <note>original: "tropos"</note> from a suitable turning; some call them "modes" from the act of moderating; the Greeks call them *phthongos* <note>original: "phthongos", meaning a musical sound or voice</note>, while we call them tones, although this seems inappropriate to Guido <note>Guido of Arezzo, the 11th-century monk who developed the staff and solfège</note>. Johannes <note>likely Johannes Afflighemensis, a music theorist</note> explains this beautifully (a). Long ago, however, while ancient musicians called only a musical harmony a "tone," grammarians began to call speech accents "tones" as well, usurping the word. And because it is established that there is no small similarity between the accents of prose speech and the ways of singing, we have decreed that this should be a general name for both. For just as the accent of a tone is tripartite—namely, low, high, and circumflex—so it is with prose. But where prose has its pauses—the *colon*, *comma*, and *period*, which mean the limb, the incision, and the closure (for the *period* is the end of all things)—musicians have chosen to call these the <term>diastema</term> <gloss>an interval or space between sounds</gloss>, the <term>systema</term> <gloss>the scale system or structure</gloss>, and the <term>teleusis</term> <gloss>the final ending or conclusion</gloss>. Whoever wishes to know more about these should look at Johannes.

## SECOND PART OF MUSIC

Ovid <note>original: "Naso"</note> suggests this:
->*I sang of joyful things to the joyful; now, being sad, I sing of sad things.*<-
-> <-

<margin>(a) Vol. I, page 258.</margin>
We are bound, however, by a regular range, as Berno <note>Berno of Reichenau, an 11th-century music theorist</note> prefers. The range <term>ambitus|the compass or total span of notes in a melody</term> of the tones, as Odo reports in his *Handbook* (a) <note>Referring to the *Enchiridion Musicae*, historically attributed to Odo of Cluny</note>, is a fixed law for the ascending and descending of any regular song. Therefore, every authentic mode <note>The "primary" or odd-numbered modes (1, 3, 5, 7)</note> has to ascend an octave <term>diapason|an interval of an eighth</term> from its final seat, and by license a ninth or tenth; they descend, however, only to the next note below the final. But the plagal modes <note>The "derived" or even-numbered modes (2, 4, 6, 8)</note> ascend as far as a fifth <term>diapente|an interval of a fifth</term>, and by license to a sixth or seventh; they descend a fourth <term>diatessaron|an interval of a fourth</term>, as is the will of all musicians, and as the present discourse on modern opinions agrees.

In ancient times, the ancients discovered four musical pitches <note>original: "phthongos"</note> which they used in likeness to the four seasons: just as the ages of the world are varied by the four seasons, so is every song varied by four modes. The Psalmist seems to note this, as it is written: *Sing praises to our God, sing praises: sing praises unto our King, sing praises.* <note>Psalm 47:6. The author uses the four repetitions of "sing praises" (psallite) to justify the four original modes.</note> Hence only four final notes are held. But even we moderns, who use measured song <note>original: "figurato cantu"; polyphonic or rhythmically defined music as opposed to plainchant</note>, continuously use these tones—that is, in pairs, or as one of the ancient ones.

There are four tones of the ancients: *protus* (or *argous*), *deuterus*, *tritus*, and *tetrardus* <note>Greek terms for First, Second, Third, and Fourth</note>, each of which contains two others within itself: the first and second; the third and fourth; the fifth and sixth; the seventh and eighth. However, I do not say that we cannot be content with a single tone, but because

<column-break/>

variety pleases modern ears, and since the authentic modes must ascend while the plagal modes must descend (as in this verse:
->*The odd mode tends upward, but the even tends to*<-
->*the lowest depths*<-),
one of these alone is not sufficient for variety, so we use them in pairs, or as one of the ancient modes.

### CHAPTER XVI.

We grant the semitone <term>hemitonium|a half-step</term> at the pitch *b-flat* or *b-natural* <note>original: "b. fa. ♮ . mi."</note> to two modes if it is necessary—specifically to the *protus* and the *tritus*—but we deny it to the other two. There are, however, some who deny it entirely to the "regal" <note>authentic</note> *tritus*, especially in the formal cadences <note>original: "actibus tonatis"</note>, while they attribute it totally to the "plagal" *tritus* (that is, the sixth mode). I marvel that this is denied to the master <note>the authentic mode</note> which is granted to the servant <note>the plagal mode</note>; for it seems inconsistent with reason, because the semitone is the ornament of the whole tone. Certainly, he who takes the ornament away from the master and gives it to the servant should repent. Since it is the task of all tones to conclude a song beautifully at the end, who would not understand that the fourth mode becomes discordant if a semitone is introduced, since it would begin softly but conclude harshly in the formal cadences? But the ancients granted this to the *tritus* mode, which contains both the authentic and the plagal. Our moderns make this void and reject the opinion of the ancients when they make the plagal more than the regal, admitting for themselves what they deny to the authentic. Furthermore, since its final seat is at the *hypate meson* <note>The Greek name for the note E</note>, they make it faulty by introducing a tritone <term>tritonus|an interval of three whole tones, famously known as the "Devil in Music" for its dissonance</term>, which is held by all musicians to be avoided as an irregular and most inconsistent sound. But I wish to withdraw my hand from the pen <note>original: "calamo manum subtrahere," a classical idiom for stopping writing</note>, lest I seem to suppress everyone with injustice, as they say; nevertheless, I leave everything to be corrected by the judgment of skilled musicians.

### Chapter XVII.

Lastly, they add a tone which they call the wandering tone <term>tonus peregrinus|A special melodic formula used in psalmody that differs from the standard eight modes because it uses two different reciting notes</term>; but some affirm it to be a variation of the eighth mode. I, however, would rather say it is a variation of the first mode, since it ends on the <term>lichano hypaton|The 'index finger' note of the lowest Greek tetrachord, corresponding to the note D</term> (a). Yet I do not wish to approve or reject anyone's opinion, for this tone is not counted among the [standard eight] tones, and in <term>figurative music|musica figurata; polyphonic or "ornamented" music</term> we have no concern for these variations. Therefore, I did not wish to include the variations of the tones, for they are all contained under the royal <note>authentic</note> and subjugal <note>plagal</note> <term>proto|first mode</term>, <term>deutero|second mode</term>, <term>trito|third mode</term>, and <term>tetrardo|fourth mode</term>. Thus it was not necessary, because among us there is a continual transposition of tones due to the inequality of voices in relation to the instruments. I too am forced to end every song of the first mode on the <term>lichanos meson|The 'index finger' note of the middle Greek tetrachord, corresponding to the note G</term> because of the organ: for a low-voiced singer <note>original: "baryphonizans"</note> was not able to reach the octave of the <term>lichanos hypaton|D</term> in the low register <note>original: "hypothesi"</note> with a true voice, and in the high register <note>original: "hyperboleothesi"</note> barely reached middle *a*; and so, when the cause is lacking, the effect also tends to be lacking; for a song is transposed sometimes not by whim, but out of necessity.

You have here what I think <note>original: "sentio"</note> regarding the tones, and Gregorian or <term>plain music|musica plana; unmeasured monophonic chant</term>, and plainchant,

<column-break/>

as well as the beginning of <term>figurative music|musica figurata</term>, which depends upon this, and the end of the second part. Since we believe there are few who understand these foundations with a healthy intellect, as necessity itself demands, I wished to set these things forth first, and finally to take up the journey into <term>measured music|musica mensuralis; music where the rhythm is strictly defined by the shape of the notes</term>. I have therefore completed the second part on plain music in order, as was touched upon before, with a brief rule for beginners; here the one who is rising may find a place to stand, according to my ability, where if they fix their foot, they will undoubtedly not look back while holding the plow.

->A Narration for the Present.<-

> We have seen the mass of the immense art of sounds,
> Which has moved my mind too much until now.
> Now it departs, and after a short time it is seen to have returned,
> To which both number and measure will give a beginning.
> Castalian Muses <note>The Muses of Mount Parnassus</note>, bring protection to the one calling,
> So that simple music may cease, and measured music may grow.
> And Musa, having always pitied my labors,
> Now also bring help in our endeavor.
> Join together, Pierides, Liberthides, Aganippides <note>Various names for the Muses derived from their sacred springs and mountains</note>,
> They now offer their service together with their art.
> Let Euterpe <note>The Muse of music</note> give the flutes, let Poland join
> The lute <note>original: "Barbiton"</note>, and the Thespiades <note>The Muses</note> both dances and instruments,
> Lest my name and work remain obscure.

# PROLOGUE TO PART III.

->BY ADAM OF FULDA, MUSICIAN,<-
->ON MENSURAL OR<-
->FIGURATIVE MUSIC.<-

*The short preface begins happily, as does Part Three.*

Poets recount that Mercury—believed to be a god by the blind <note>original: "cæca gente," likely referring to the pagans of antiquity</note>—is said to have first gifted the cithara <note>a plucked string instrument similar to a lyre</note> to the Dircean Amphion, the son of Antiope (daughter of Nycteus, king of Thebes and wife of Lycus) and of Epaphus (the son of Jove and Juno). Having received it, Amphion became so skilled in the art that the fables say stones placed themselves into walls of their own accord. Mercury himself, when he found a lyre made from a tortoise shell on Mount Cyllene, decorated it with seven strings and was the first to hand it to Orpheus, who is said to have called Eurydice back from the underworld with his song. Behold these men, who, though they lacked true knowledge of this art, possessed its spirit; if faith is to be placed in fictions, nearly all the books of the poets are full of what they achieved. But what might we do, we who are shaped by rules and precepts? All of us can understand for ourselves how much our beginning differs from theirs.

But listen to what honor or benefit we shall receive. Stones will not place themselves in walls of their own accord, nor shall we call anyone back from the underworld—for that is fiction and unfitting. But if we sing the praises of the most holy God, we shall obtain an unfading crown and receive eternal life. We can receive praise not only from the books of the poets, but our names shall also be written in golden characters in the Book of Life. Nor shall our art be from Mercury, who remains in the underworld, but from Christ

<column-break/>

Jesus, the God of all, who reigns in the heavens. Behold! How different is the merit, and how different are the teachers of the art we have. Therefore, receive the third part with a joyful face; understand the mode and form of <term>mensural music|musica mensuralis; a system of notation where the length of a note is determined by its shape and the surrounding context, rather than just the text</term>, contained here in a brief style through figures, and consider what follows.

### CHAPTER I.

This is the description of mensural music: its figures <note>notes</note> can be increased or decreased in value within the established signs according to the primary degrees of music: <term>mode|modus; the relationship between the Long and the Breve</term>, <term>time|tempus; the relationship between the Breve and the Semibreve</term>, and <term>prolation|prolatio; the relationship between the Semibreve and the Minim</term>, as has been said before. Indeed, all those who are zealous for this music must first consider twelve articles, in which they will easily find the whole art to be learned with ease. For a studious disciple commits the art he desires to memory point by point <note>original: "articulariter," literally 'by the joints' or 'by the fingers'</note>, as Ovid says in *Letters from the Black Sea*:
> *Behold, each one keeps the laws of his own study,*
> *And now each loves his own rewards, and*
> &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;*calculates*
> *what is useful with anxious fingers.* <note>original: "sollicitis computat articulis." Adam uses this to emphasize the technical, "hand-on" nature of learning the twelve articles of music.</note>

Now, these are the articles of the art: figure, mode, time, prolation, sign, <term>tactus|the beat or pulse</term>, <term>punctus|the dot used for addition or division</term>, <term>tractus|a line or stroke</term>, <term>ligature|notes joined together into a single symbol</term>, <term>alteration|the doubling of a note's value</term>, <term>imperfection|the shortening of a note's value</term>, and proportion. Number and measure rule over all these articles. Once these are considered in their proper place, believe me, you will quickly become skilled from even a small amount of talent; but it is necessary to repeat often that which is to be held in the mind forever.

### CHAPTER II.

A <term>figure|figura</term> is a visual form that makes the recognition of notes possible, through which every proportion is expressed harmoniously. Of these, we have eight...

We establish eight <note>referring to note shapes or values</note>, although the ancients established only five, dividing them into four species and believing the <term>duple proportion</term> <note>a 2:1 ratio</note> to be the smallest, as do Boethius and Johannes de Muris. They were not in error, however, because in these five, the proportion is formed through the first degrees of music—namely <term>mode</term>, <term>time</term>, and <term>prolation</term>—as will appear later. For the <term>maxima</term> <note>the longest note value</note> has the nature of the most general category; the <term>minima</term> <note>the "least" or smallest note value in the older system</note> indeed has the nature of the most specific species, which is divided only into two others, and another into another two, and so on into infinity. Therefore, it is said that there is no formal science regarding those notes that follow, but only a certain practical skill; thus the first authors of the art did not include them, but we do not omit them for the sake of that skill. These are the figures of the notes, as follows, of which one always arises from another. Naso <note>The Roman poet Ovid</note> agrees with this when he says:

> Nature restores some shapes from others. <note>original: "Ex aliis alias reparat natura figuras." — Ovid, Metamorphoses XV, 252</note>

The eight figures of the notes are:
**maxima** <note>a large rectangular note with a stem on the right</note> **long** <note>a square note with a stem on the right</note> **breve** <note>a simple square note</note> **semibreve** <note>a hollow diamond-shaped note</note> **minim** <note>a hollow diamond-shaped note with a vertical stem</note> **semiminim** <note>a filled diamond-shaped note with a stem</note> **fusa** <note>a filled diamond-shaped note with a stem and one flag</note> **semifusa** <note>a filled diamond-shaped note with a stem and two flags</note>

### CHAPTER III.

<term>Mode</term> <note>in this context, 'modus' refers to the relationship between the longest notes (maximas, longs, and breves)</note> is the coordination or arrangement of figures indicating various affects of the soul in singing. Regarding mode, there are various opinions among musicians, but I wish to reveal what seems more correct to me. For just as in <term>plainchant</term> <note>unmeasured Gregorian chant</note> "mode" shows the types of melodic leaps and consonances, so in the present study it also informs the number and values of notes through <term>time</term> and <term>prolation</term>. Ovid also seems to speak of this

<column-break/>

in the book *Metamorphoses*, where he says:

> There is a measure in things, there are, finally, certain limits. <note>original: "Est modus in rebus, sunt certi denique fines." Adam misattributes this quote; it is actually from Horace, Satires I.i.106. In Latin, 'modus' means both a musical mode and a 'limit' or 'measure.'</note>

This, however, must be understood musically; for where there is mode, there is also time and prolation, but not the other way around. This is because mode acts upon <term>longs</term> and <term>maximas</term>, and the "greater" mode acts upon <term>breves</term> regarding their increase. Mode is understood in two ways, or is double: namely, **major** and **minor**. **Major** consists of maximas and longs; **minor** indeed consists of longs and breves, but it triples nothing in the breves. This is divided into **perfect** and **imperfect**, as follows. But to tell the truth, these things are established by the will of musicians with little underlying reason; otherwise, mode would be involved in all musical signs. Mode is twofold: **Major** is when the maxima contains three longs, the long contains three breves, the breve contains three semibreves, and the semibreve contains three minims; and thus Major Mode is <term>Perfect Time</term> and <term>Major Prolation</term>. **Perfect Minor Mode** is when the maxima contains two longs, and the long contains three breves, but the breve contains two semibreves. **Imperfect** is when the maxima contains two longs and the long contains two breves, as occurs in <term>diminution</term> <note>the proportional shortening of note values</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

<term>Time</term> <note>Latin: 'tempus'</note> is a measure, sounded or omitted, under one continuous motion; or put another way: <term>Time</term> is the placement of two or three semibreves (or their equivalent value) against one breve. Time is twofold: namely, **perfect** and **imperfect**, and it acts only upon breves and semibreves, as follows. But the "time" of plainchant is the time of its own duration; for the time of measurement...

music has to be moved by the beat <note>The "tactus" was the physical movement of the hand used to keep time in the Renaissance.</note>. About this, Naso says:
> The seasons themselves also roll on in constant motion. <note>original: "Ipsa quoque assiduo volvuntur tempora motu." — Ovid (Naso), Metamorphoses XV, 179. The author punningly uses Ovid’s word for "seasons/times" to refer to musical "Time."</note>

**Time** is twofold. It is **perfect** when a <term>breve</term> <note>a square-shaped note</note> is worth three <term>semibreves</term> <note>diamond-shaped notes</note>; it is **imperfect** when a breve is worth two semibreves.

### CHAPTER V.

**Prolation** is the joining of a sound measured by semibreve and <term>minim</term> <note>the smallest standard note value at the time</note> figures; or put another way: prolation is the positioning of two or three minims (or their equivalent value) against a semibreve. Moreover, prolation is divided into two parts; it is either three against one, which is called **major**; or it is two against one, which is called **minor**; but it acts only upon semibreves and minims. In **plain music** <note>Gregorian chant, which lacks a fixed rhythmic beat</note>, however, prolation is simply the song itself.

Prolation is twofold. It is **major** when a semibreve is worth three minims; it is **minor** when a semibreve is worth two minims. Indeed, **mode**, **time**, and **prolation** are called the first and special degrees of the musical art, through which a student ascends as if by the most principal steps. If these are counted by the number three, they are **perfect** according to Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher whose works were the foundation of medieval music theory</note>, who says: "In music, every triple grouping shall be perfect." <note>The number three was considered perfect because it represented the Holy Trinity.</note> Virgil also seems to note this when he says: *God delights in an odd number.* <note>original: "numero deus impare gaudet." — Virgil, Eclogues VIII, 75.</note> Yet they differ: for **mode** regards <term>maximas</term>, <term>longs</term>, and <term>breves</term>; **time** regards <term>breves</term> and <term>semibreves</term>; and **prolation** regards <term>semibreves</term> and <term>minims</term>.

### CHAPTER VI.

A **sign** is that which provides the first knowledge of a song regarding its mode, time,

<column-break/>

and prolation. Regarding signs, the ancients felt most wisely; for in vain are mode, time, and prolation recognized without the signs that give prior knowledge of them, as one of the poets says: *A song is shown by many signs of order, so that all things created may sing of their author.* But the ancients established various signs, involving prolation, time, and mode within just one single sign. For instance, the sign for major prolation, major mode, and perfect time was this: <term>ʘ</term> <note>A circle with a dot in the center</note>; but the sign for major prolation, major mode, and imperfect time they placed thus, as seen here: <term>Є</term>. Likewise, in shorter prolation, they wished to include prolation, mode, and time together in one sign, as here: <term>O</term> <term>C</term>. We, however, omit these because of the slowness of the measurement; for where there is mode, there is also time and prolation, but not vice versa. Therefore, we establish a different division of signs, because in all signs there is time and prolation, but mode is not in all of them, as follows. In plain music, the signs are the "local letters" <note>alphabetical note names like A, B, C</note> and the positioned <term>clefs</term>. Signs are primarily fourfold: for some are signs of major prolation, some of minor, some of <term>diminution</term> <note>indicating a faster tempo</note>, and some of mode. Secondary signs, however, are threefold: namely, of restarting, of indication, and general pauses, as appears in the following figures. Signs are varied:

<term>ʘ</term> of major prolation and perfect time.

### CHAPTER VII.

The **beat** <term>tactus</term> is a continuous motion contained within a rational measure. This beat must be performed through the figures and signs in each of the degrees of music; for it is nothing other than the due and proper measurement of mode, time, and prolation. According to the diminution or augmentation of these, the shapes of the notes are "touched" <note>meaning "measured by the hand"</note>, the prior recognition of which is indicated by the signs. Prosper once noted this when he said:

> Behold, all movements are born from a twin source,
> And the shoots respond to their own beginnings.
<note>original: "En cuncti gemino nascuntur fomite motus, / Respondentque suis germina principiis." From the Epigrams of Prosper of Aquitaine. The "twin source" refers to the up-and-down motion of the hand in conducting.</note>

### CHAPTER VIII.

The **dot** <term>punctus</term> is a certain small mark which, when placed between two notes, either adds half the value to the first, or divides the time, or makes a note "perfect." Thus we set down only three types of dots, whereas the ancients used six: namely, the dots of addition, division, perfection, alteration, imperfection, and transposition. However, following modern practice, we consider these last three to be included under the dot of division. The dot is most useful among the notes. Regarding this, Horace says:

> *He has won every point who has mixed the useful with the sweet.*
<note>original: "Omne tulit punctum, qui miscuit utile dulci." From Horace's Ars Poetica. Adam is punning on the word "punctus," which in Latin means both a "vote" or "point" and a musical "dot."</note>

The dot is threefold: The **Dot of Division** is the separation of two "times" from one another. This is not sung, nor is it placed directly against a note, but a little higher or lower; it serves perfect time when prolation is removed, because imperfection exists there. The **Dot of Addition** is the simulation of a note to the side. This same dot is sung <note>meaning its value is heard</note>, and it always holds half the value of the preceding note by which it is placed; it serves all prolations, times, and modes. The **Dot of Perfection** is that which adds value to the preceding note and divides the following one; for it removes doubt and renders the preceding note "perfect" <note>tripartite</note>. This serves only perfect time. Finally, some have categorized this same dot as a dot of addition. We have no concern for the remaining three, because they are understood within these three, though in different respects.

### Chapter IX.

The **arrangement** <note>original: *tractus*; here referring to the physical drawing and layout of musical symbols</note> is the organization and effect of the entire song—namely of the figures, rests, notes, signs, ligatures, and so on. Now, this arrangement is twofold: that of rests and that of notes. First is the arrangement of rests, which indicates the types of pauses, half-pauses, breaths, and half-breaths. 

Rests were invented by singers because of the frailty of the human voice, for three reasons. First, for the restoration of breath; because just as we place the shapes of notes while singing, so we place rests during silence. Second, because of notes that are difficult to place, since not all notes serve the tone of the melody. Third, for the sake of variety; for to sing at one moment and rest at another is to create variety, and the more varied a song is, the more delightful it seems to the listeners. Nature, after all, delights in variety; and for those who have observed rests well, the fates will grant long times for quiet.

One type of rest is the **general rest**; it is a single or double vertical stroke <note>original: *virgula*</note> drawn through all the lines of the staff; it marks the end of a vocal part.

Another is the **rest of the mode**; it is a stroke reaching to the fourth line, occupying three spaces, and it is worth as many "breves" <note>the *brevis* or "short" note, which was a standard unit of time</note> according to the rhythmic mode.

Another is the **long rest**; it fills two spaces and crosses over one line, reaching up to the third, and it is worth a "long" note everywhere, except in certain rhythmic modes.

<column-break/>

A **rest** <note>the *pausa* proper</note> is a stroke from line to line; it fills one space and is worth a "breve" in all musical signs.

A **half-rest** <term>semipausa</term> is a small stroke descending from the upper part of a line to the middle of the same space; it is worth a "semibreve" in every sign.

A **breath** <term>suspirium</term> <note>a short pause, equivalent to a modern quarter-rest</note> is a stroke rising from the lower part of a line to the middle of the same space; it is worth a "minim" note everywhere.

A **half-breath** <term>semisuspirium</term> is a stroke equal to a breath, but hooked <note>original: *falcata*, meaning sickle-shaped</note> at the top; it is worth a "semiminim" in all signs.

->Example.<-

->General. Of the Mode. Long. Rest.<-

<image-desc>A musical staff displaying four types of musical rests: a Generalis (a vertical line spanning the whole staff), a Modi (a vertical line spanning three spaces), a Longa (a vertical line spanning two spaces and extending slightly above the staff), and a Pausa (a vertical line spanning exactly one space).</image-desc>

->Half-rest. Breath. Half-breath.<-

<image-desc>A musical staff displaying three types of smaller rests: a Semipausa (a short vertical line hanging from a staff line into the space below), a Suspirium (a short vertical line rising from a staff line into the space above), and a Semisuspirium (a short vertical line with a hooked flag at the top).</image-desc>

For these are the seven types of rests which we use in every song; their value is recognized through the figures in the signs and degrees.

### Chapter X.

The **arrangement of notes** is that which demonstrates the values and positions of notes, ligatures, and their properties through degrees and signs, as the following figures clearly show through their multiplication.

<image-desc>A horizontal diagram showing seven types of musical notes with their names and variants. From left to right:
1. Long (threefold): shows a rectangular note with a long stem.
2. Breve (threefold): shows a square note.
3. Semibreve (threefold): shows a diamond-shaped note.
4. Minim (threefold): shows a diamond note with a vertical stem.
5. Semiminim (twice): shows a black-filled diamond note with a stem.
6. Fusa (twice): shows a black-filled diamond note with a flagged stem.
7. Semifusa (twice): shows a black-filled diamond note with a double-flagged stem.</image-desc>

This application of figures could extend toward infinity, if only the human or material voice could be made to move with such swift agility—which is scarcely believed possible.

81. 27. 9. 3. 1. (a) <note>original: "a". This footnote refers to the printed musical examples. Since, therefore, the value of the notes consists in the **beat** <term>tactus: the steady down-and-up motion of the hand used to keep time</term>, the beat in the shapes of the notes, and the shapes in the signs, it seemed necessary to me to first set forth the multiplication of these shapes. Finally, I have added the values of the notes by means of the beat, and demonstrated them through the indication of the signs, the **mode** <note>the relationship between the Long and the Breve</note>, the **time** <note>the relationship between the Breve and the Semibreve</note>, and the **prolation** <note>the relationship between the Semibreve and the Minim</note>; for these are highly necessary in song. Through these things, the power of all shapes and **ligatures** <note>notes joined together in a single physical stroke</note> may be known at once. For just as the value of notes exists in the beat, the beat in the shapes, and the shapes in the signs, so it is also in ligatures, but in a different manner. It must be noted, however, that **coloration** <note>original: *color*; the practice of coloring notes red or filling them in to change their value</note> always takes away a third part—that is, it diminishes the value—but only in the **greater perfect time** <note>triple meter at the highest level</note>, with prolation excluded. But in the remaining imperfect <note>duple</note> signs, coloration represents the **hemiola** proportion <note>a ratio of 3:2, where three notes are played in the time usually taken by two</note>; although coloration there also takes away a third part of the beat, it does not do so perfectly in terms of the musical motion. In perfect time, however, coloration sometimes takes nothing away, but this is done for the sake of **perfection, alteration, or imperfection** <note>technical rules in mensural notation where the context of surrounding notes changes a note's duration</note>, but only in the mode (regarding Breves and Semibreves), in the time (regarding Semibreves and Minims), and in the prolation (regarding Minims and Semiminims).

### CHAPTER XI.

A **ligature** is a grouping of notes bound together

<column-break/>

according to a square or oblique form. Every ligature either ascends or descends, and it is "tailed" on either the left or the right side—having a tail that goes up or down—or it lacks a tail entirely, or it is tailed everywhere, as appears in the following figures. Indeed, in all the signs, however many shapes the beat represents, the present indication informs just as many. Furthermore, a ligature is divided into two parts in its primary division: namely, **ascending** and **descending**.

->*The Ascending Ligature.*<-

A ligature that is *tailed on the left* and ascending receives an "increase" in value: the first two notes are **Semibreves**, and the others are **Breves**. If it is descending, it receives no increase; all the notes are Breves.
<image-desc>Two musical staves showing ligatures with left-side tails. The first staff shows ascending notes, and the second shows descending notes.</image-desc>

A ligature *tailed on the right*, whether ascending or descending, is increased in value:
<image-desc>Two musical staves showing ligatures with tails on the right side, both in ascending and descending patterns.</image-desc>
all are Breves, except the final notes, which are **Longs**.

A ligature *tailed on both sides*: if ascending, it receives an increase; the first two are Semibreves, the others are Breves, and the last is a Long. If descending, it receives an increase; all are Breves, and the last is a Long.
<image-desc>Musical staves depicting ligatures with tails on both the left and right sides, covering various pitch movements.</image-desc>

A ligature *without a tail at the beginning*: if ascending, it is not increased; all are Breves. If it is descending from the beginning, it is also not increased.
<image-desc>Musical staff showing ligatures without initial tails.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

ways represents a long; and wherever a long is placed, a maxima could be substituted at the will of the composer. Every **ligature** <note>notes tied together</note> is therefore subject to the primary degrees—**mode, time, and prolation** <note>the various levels of triple or duple meter</note>—but it also respects individual accidents: namely the sign, the beat, the dot, the stroke, **alteration**, and **imperfection** <note>rules where a note's value is slightly shortened or lengthened based on its neighbors</note>, because all of these can be contained within a ligature.

### CHAPTER XII.

**Alteration** is the doubling of a note's own value according to its shape; or put another way: alteration is the doubling of a certain smaller note in relation to a larger one. It occurs in three ways within the primary degrees, though always in "perfect major" time <note>triple meter</note>, with prolation excepted.

**Alteration** <note>original: "Altera"</note> occurs in three ways:

1. In **mode** <note>the relationship between Longs and Breves</note>, whenever two breves are placed between two "perfect" longs (or before or after longs that have been made "imperfect"), the second breve becomes "altered." It will be worth two beats, as seen here: <image-desc>Musical staff showing two long notes with two breves between them.</image-desc>, or like this: <image-desc>Musical staff with a variation of the previous example.</image-desc>

2. In **time** <note>the relationship between Breves and Semibreves</note>, whenever two semibreves are placed between two "perfect" breves (or breves to be made imperfect by other means), the second semibreve is altered. It will be worth two beats, as seen here: <image-desc>Musical staff showing two breves with two semibreves between them.</image-desc> <image-desc>Musical staff with a variation of the previous example.</image-desc>

3. In **prolation** <note>the relationship between Semibreves and Minims</note>, whenever two **minims** <term>minima: a short note value</term> are placed between two semibreves in a complete measure (or one otherwise made imperfect), the second minim is altered and counts for two beats, <image-desc>Musical staff showing two semibreves with two minims between them.</image-desc> or as seen here: <image-desc>Musical staff with a variation of the previous example.</image-desc>

<meta>This page continues Adam of Fulda’s technical explanation of mensural music—the system of notation used in the late Middle Ages where the shape of a note determined its rhythm. On the previous page, he discussed ligatures; here, he explains the rules of "alteration" (doubling a note's value) and "imperfection" (shortening a note's value), which allow musicians to fit notes into groups of three (perfection).</meta>

<page-num>366</page-num>
<header>ADAM OF FULDA</header>

In these, however, **alteration** <note>original: "alteratio"; the doubling of a note’s value to fill out a triple meter.</note> has no place: specifically in the **maxima**, **long**, **semi-minim**, **fusa**, and **semi-fusa**, on account of the ternary number; nor even in **rests**, because alteration exists in the voice, namely in the singing itself. But among all rules, this is the most general: whenever in **major prolation** <term>prolatio maior: a rhythmic setting where a semibreve is divided into three minims</term> two minims are left over, or in **perfect time** <term>tempus perfectum: where a breve is divided into three semibreves</term> two semibreves are left, or in **major mode** <term>modus maior: where a maxima is divided into three longs</term> two breves remain, the second of the two must always be **altered** <note>Meaning the second note's duration is doubled.</note>. The reason why the breve in mode, the semibreve in time, and the minim in prolation are altered is this: just as the minim relates to the semibreve in prolation, so the semibreve relates to the breve in time, the breve to the long in mode, and the long to the maxima in the major mode. The **maxima**, however, is not altered, because it has no value greater than itself, nor can alteration occur in the **minim** among these figures, because it lacks a triple division below it.

### CHAPTER XIII.

**Imperfection** is the "theft" of a portion of a note's value within a ternary <note>triple</note> number; or put another way: imperfection, or "to make imperfect," is to render a **perfect** <note>triple-valued</note> note **imperfect** <note>double-valued</note>. Imperfection occurs in two ways: from the front and from the back, as was said regarding alteration. This happens in three levels: 1. In **mode**, a **maxima** is made imperfect by a **long** or by two **breves**; but a **long** is made imperfect by a **breve** or by two **semibreves**, either from the front or the back. 2. In **time**, a **long** is made imperfect by one **breve** or by two **semibreves**, but a **breve** is made imperfect by one **breve** from the front or back, and the same for the **maxima**. 3. In **prolation**, the **maxima**, **long**, and **breve** can be made imperfect by a **breve** or two **semibreves**, but a **breve** is made imperfect only by a **semibreve** from the front or back, as before.
A **rest**, however, is never made imperfect,

<column-break/>

nor can a note be made imperfect when it stands before another note of the same kind <note>original: "similis ante similem"; a rule stating that a note followed by an identical note must remain "perfect" (triple-valued).</note>, as **Rageno** <note>Rageno of Lisieux, an early music theorist.</note> testifies. There are, however, some who do not omit this, out of ignorance.

### Conclusion.

Therefore, these things already said concerning the individual levels of music—though arranged simply—are sufficient when understood with enough intellect and collected briefly. And behold! While I was completing these things, certain **learned scholars** <note>original: "gymnosophistae"; literally "naked philosophers," here referring to insistent academics.</note> came to me, urging that this little book be presented to princes. They tried to persuade me of this very thing with many words and examples, saying that the ancient musicians dedicated their short works either to princes or to high-ranking clergy: such as **Boethius** to the patrician **Symmachus**, **John** to **Fulgentius** the English bishop, **Guido** to Bishop **Theobald**, **Berno** to Archbishop **Pilgrim**, and so on. To those who ordered me to answer, I said: "Did not **Guido** also write to the monk **Michael** regarding an unknown song? Who forbade **Bernard** and **Odo** from writing in the form of a dialogue? To whom was the music of the priest **Rageno** dedicated? Why indeed did **Hermann** <note>Hermannus Contractus (Hermann the Lame).</note>, though he was a prince himself, not dedicate his little work to a prince or prelate—and many others, who led by their own will, wrote for the common good?" I have written these things not, as you believe, for the sake of profit or fame, but compelled by the love of the one to whom I write; I write under obligation, but not under compulsion.

<header>THE FOURTH PART OF MUSIC.</header>

# PART FOUR.
## THE LITTLE PREFACE OF THE MUSICIAN ADAM OF FULDA REGARDING PROPORTIONS, CONSONANCES, AND THE FOURTH PART BEGINS AUSPICIOUSLY.

*The prologue follows.*

There is no one who denies that Jubal <note>A biblical figure from the Book of Genesis, traditionally credited as the inventor of musical instruments.</note>, the son of Lamech, was the first to discover the proportions of sounds. He had a brother named Tubalcain, the first blacksmith; while spending time with him in the forge, Jubal is said to have first weighed the harmonies through the sound of the hammers and the bronze. As Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> says, he left this art inscribed upon two columns, which remained buried for a long time after the Great Flood.

Later, however, Pythagoras <note>The Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) famously associated with the mathematical laws of music.</note> discovered numbers, and throughout his life, numbers obeyed him in such a way that he strove to know all things through their power. He withdrew into a grove to debate this matter with himself, considering that harmonic sweetness consists in the sense of hearing; for if there were no hearing, any reasoning regarding voices would be entirely doubtful. Yet, he did not trust fully in the sense of the ears, but concluded that hearing would be a false judge in the functioning of harmonies, and that the true, commanding judge is the intellect. For the hearing perceives first through the experience of sensory cognition, but the intellect organizes that science and doctrine within itself.

Thus Pythagoras—moved, I believe, by experience (for before him, Orpheus was most skilled with the kithara, and Amphion of Dirce <note>In Greek mythology, Amphion's music was so powerful it moved the stones to build the walls of Thebes.</note> was most expert with the lyre, whom some among the disciples of Pythagoras imitated with great effort, though by his own command,

<column-break/>

so that you would have believed Amphion himself was present; Pythagoras was greatly delighted by their singing)—remained in a state of anxiety for a long time, wondering how he might fully discover the art. When he understood that the first inventor had weighed harmonies from the sound of hammers, he also ventured to seek out the workshops of blacksmiths. While passing a bronze forge one day, turning this thought over in his mind, he heard certain hammers emitting a wonderful sound and harmony upon the anvil. Overcome with intense wonder, he approached more closely so that he might hear and inspect what he had long sought. After greeting the men in the usual manner, he began to doubt: could such harmony arise from the strength of the person striking? He ordered them to swap hammers among themselves, but after they were exchanged, the original symphony remained. From this, he noticed that the concordances were contained not in the muscles of the men, but in the nature of the hammers, by the logic of number as well as measure and weight. 

The number of hammers was five, but the fifth was cast out as if useless because it sounded dissonant against the others. Yet, through its very dissonance, this hammer gave him a great opportunity for discovering the consonances and proportions. Thus, having considered the weights of the remaining hammers, he found the weights to be in the proportions of the **double** <note>original: "dupla"; the 2:1 ratio, forming an octave.</note>, the **one-and-a-half** <note>original: "sesquialtera"; the 3:2 ratio, forming a perfect fifth.</note>, the **one-and-a-third** <note>original: "sesquitertia"; the 4:3 ratio, forming a perfect fourth.</note>, and the **tone** <note>The 9:8 ratio, the whole step between notes.</note>. Therefore, with a calmed mind and a joyful spirit, Pythagoras returned home, and there, through the unequal tension of strings and the unequal length of reeds, he fully discovered the consonances and wrote them in a book.

<page-num>368</page-num>
<header>ADAM OF FULDA</header>

Now, consonance, as Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 480–524 AD), whose "De institutione musica" was the standard music theory textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> says, is the concord of different voices reduced into one. Indeed, the author of nature <note>A reference to God as the creator of the natural order.</note> made these wondrous consonances innate in the very fabric of things, and not man; for consonances existed before they ever appeared to men. Therefore, we also strive greatly to investigate these consonances; but we also embrace with a grateful mind the proportions in which consonances appear, as will be clear to anyone who looks closely.

### CHAPTER I.
#### On proportions.

Proportion is the inequality of two numbers, as Boethius testifies. From this definition, some conclude that the double <term>dupla: a 2:1 ratio</term> and quadruple <term>quadrupla: a 4:1 ratio</term> would not be proportions, which the following description denies: for proportion is a certain relationship of two quantities of the same kind, one to the other, in inequality or excess.

Some proportions are arithmetic, others are geometric, others are harmonic. Arithmetic ones are where the differences between the numerical terms are the same, but not the same properties; for an arithmetic arrangement divides quantities into equal parts only through their differences. <note>For example, in the sequence 2, 4, 6, the difference between each number is 2.</note>

Geometric ones are when the proportions between the terms are the same, but not the same differences; for Geometry joins terms by an equal proportion. <note>For example, in the sequence 2, 4, 8, the ratio between each number is "double," but the differences are 2 and 4.</note>

Harmonic ones are when neither the same differences nor the same proportions are found between the terms, but just as the greatest is related to the least, so is the difference between the greatest and middle term related to the diffe-

<column-break/>

-rence between the middle and the least term; for harmony does not only involve the contemplation of proportion in its terms, nor solely in its differences, but in both together. <note>For example, in the sequence 6, 8, 12, the ratio of the outer numbers (12:6) is 2:1. The difference between 12 and 8 is 4, and the difference between 8 and 6 is 2. The ratio of those differences (4:2) is also 2:1.</note>

All proportions, however, are contained within number, which we believe Pythagoras was the first among the Greeks to discover, and through whose power he presumed to find all things. Then, they say it was more extensively arranged by Nicomachus. <note>Nicomachus of Gerasa (c. 60–120 AD), an ancient mathematician whose work on arithmetic influenced Boethius.</note> Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius, a 2nd-century Roman writer; though famous for "The Golden Ass," he also translated scientific works into Latin.</note> first, and then Boethius, took care to translate this for the Latins. Therefore, I wished to attach his description with its associated divisions, so that all who desire to recognize proportions may be able to investigate them more easily and understand them more briefly from number, along with their foundations.

### CHAPTER II.

Number is a multitude made up of units, and if it is taken away, all things perish. Number is divided into even and odd, each of which is comprised of three species.

An even number is that which admits a division into two [equal] parts, but in such a way that in neither division is evenness mixed with oddness, or oddness with evenness—excepting the principal even number, the number two, which does not admit an unequal section. <note>original: "in duo inæqualia partitionem recipit." Adam uses "unequal" here perhaps to refer to the species of even numbers, but his examples show the division of even numbers into odd parts.</note> 10 is even; [it divides into] 5 and 5, which are odd; [as do] 7 and 3.

An odd number is that which, at any such division, is divided into unequal parts, as both species of number always show, so that one is never without the other; but one part is assigned to evenness and the other to oddness. [For example] 7 is odd; [it divides into] 3 (odd) and 4 (even).

<summary>Adam of Fulda defines the mathematical basis of music, explaining the three types of proportions—arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic—and providing a foundational definition of even and odd numbers.</summary>
<keywords>Boethius, Pythagoras, Nicomachus, Apuleius, proportions, arithmetic proportion, geometric proportion, harmonic proportion, even and odd numbers, music theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical mathematical foundation of Adam of Fulda’s musical treatise. Following the previous page’s introduction to arithmetic, geometric, and harmonic arrangements, he now defines the specific categories of even and odd numbers and introduces the five classes of musical proportions, maintaining his reliance on Boethian number theory.</meta>

<page-num>369</page-num>
<header>THE FOURTH PART OF MUSIC</header>
<sig>A a a</sig>

There are three species of even numbers. The **evenly even** <note>original: "Pariter par"</note> is that which can be divided into two equal parts, and each part into another two, and the parts of the parts into another two, until the division of parts naturally reaches the indivisible unit, as in the double <term>dupla: a 2:1 ratio</term> and the quadruple <term>quadrupla: a 4:1 ratio</term>.

The **evenly odd** <note>original: "Pariter impar"</note> is that which has been assigned the nature and substance of evenness, but is opposed to the evenly even number in its division; for while it is even and accepts a cut into equal parts, its resulting parts are immediately indivisible, such as 6, 10, 14, and 18. <note>In these cases, 6 divided by 2 is 3, an odd number that cannot be halved again into whole numbers.</note>

The **oddly even** <note>original: "Impariter par"</note> is that which is divided into equal parts, and whose parts can be divided into other equal parts: and sometimes even the parts of those parts are divided, but that equal distinction does not progress all the way to unity, such as 24 and 28.

There are also three species of odd numbers. The **first and uncomposed** <note>original: "Primus incompositus"; essentially prime numbers.</note> is that which has no other part except that which is named from the total quantity of the number, so that the part itself is nothing but unity, such as 3, 5, 7, 13, 17, 19, 23, 29, and 31. It is called the first and uncomposed because no number measures it except the units joined together.

The **second and composed** <note>original: "Secundus compositus"</note> is that which retains no primary substance in itself, but is composed of other numbers; it has parts named after itself and parts with a foreign name, but in the part named from itself, it will always be unity: 9, 15, 21, 25, 27. It is called secondary by itself because it is measured not only by unity but also by another number from which it is joined. <note>For example, 9 is composed of 3 x 3.</note>

->ANCIENT WRITERS ON MUSIC. PART III.<-

<column-break/>

The **relatively prime or composite** <note>original: "Per se primus vel secundus"</note> is that which accepts the measurement of another, but when compared to another number of the same kind, it is joined by no common measure, nor will they have equivalent parts. For instance, 9 and 25 compared to each other are "first and uncomposed" in relation to unity, but not in their parts; they are "secondary and composite" because 9 is three times three, and that three is not in 25, and vice versa.

### CHAPTER III.

Every number or proportion is thus organized into five genera: either in the **multiple** genus, the **superparticular**, the **superpartient**, the **multiple superparticular**, or the **multiple superpartient**. In a common harmonic sense, the middle term exceeds the first by a part of the first, and the middle term is exceeded by the last term by that same part of the last, as for example 6 and 8: [the 8] exceeds by two parts, which two parts are a third part of six; [similarly] the middle part [8] is exceeded by the last part, which is 12, by four, and a third part of twelve is four. <note>This describes the Harmonic Mean: the ratio of the differences is equal to the ratio of the terms. Here, (8-6)/(12-8) = 2/4, which is the same ratio as 6/12.</note>

Proportion is firstly of two kinds: **rational**, which creates consonance, such as the double, the sesquialtera <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio, the musical fifth</term>, and the quadruple; and **irrational** proportion, which is without melody, and there the half-tone is excluded.

Proportion is secondly of two kinds: **Equality** is the relationship of two equal quantities to one another, and it is not divided. **Inequality** is the relationship of two unequal quantities to one another: **greater inequality** is the relationship of a larger quantity to a smaller; **lesser inequality** is the relationship of a shorter quantity to a larger.

<meta>This page continues the technical classification of mathematical ratios begun on the previous page. Having defined the types of even and odd numbers, Adam now applies these categories to the five classes of proportions, which form the mathematical foundation for musical intervals. This section draws heavily on the Pythagorean tradition transmitted by Boethius.</meta>

<page-num>370</page-num>
<header>ADAM OF FULDA</header>

There are five types of proportions.
1. The **Multiple** <note>original: "Multiplex"</note> is the relationship of a larger quantity or number to a smaller one, containing it many times over; it creates the double, triple, and quadruple ratios <term>dupla, tripla, quadrupla: the ratios 2:1, 3:1, and 4:1</term>.
2. The **Superparticular** <note>original: "Superparticularis"</note> is the relationship of one number compared to another when it contains within itself the whole smaller number plus some part of it. If it contains a half of the smaller number, it is called **one-and-a-half** <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio</term>; if a third part, **one-and-a-third** <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio</term>. Following these names into infinity, it creates the one-and-a-half, one-and-a-third, one-and-a-fourth, and one-and-an-eighth <term>sesquioctava: a 9:8 ratio</term>.
3. The **Superpartient** <note>original: "Superpartiens"</note> is the relationship of one number compared to another when it contains the whole smaller number within itself and, additionally, several of its parts—either two, or three, or however many the comparison requires. If it contains two parts, it is called **super-two-part** <term>superbipartiens: e.g., 5:3</term>; if three, **super-three-part** <term>supertripartiens</term>; and so on

<column-break/>

infinitely, creating the super-two-part, super-three-part, and super-four-part.
4. The **Multiple Superparticular** <note>original: "Multiplex superparticularis"</note> is the relationship of a larger quantity or number to a smaller one, containing it many times over plus one aliquot part <note>A part that divides the whole exactly</note> of it; it creates the double superparticular proportion. (a)
5. The **Multiple Superpartient** <note>original: "Multiplex superpartiens"</note> is the relationship of a larger quantity or number to a smaller one, containing it many times over plus several of its parts, which do not combine to form a single aliquot part; it creates the double super-two-part proportion.

### CHAPTER V.

We did not say without reason that **superparticular** <term>superparticularis: a ratio where the top number is one more than the bottom (e.g., 3:2, 4:3)</term> ratios can sometimes lack concord. For every superparticular proportion is smaller than a **multiple** <note>original: "multiplici"</note> proportion. A multiple proportion contains the smaller number exactly twice, or three times, or four times, and so on; but a superparticular never contains the shorter number <margin>Add: twice or thrice <note>original: "bis vel ter"</note></margin>, but only once plus some part of it, whether one-half or

<meta>This page continues the mathematical exploration of musical ratios. Having defined the primary superparticular ratios like the fifth and fourth on the previous page, the author now explains the inverse relationship between numerical growth and interval size, leading into a discussion on why these ratios cannot be divided by a geometric mean.</meta>

# ADAM OF FULDA

2, or 3, or 4, etc.; for just as the types of multiple numbers <note>Ratios like 2:1, 3:1, 4:1</note> always grow in their natural order, so the types of **superparticular** <term>superparticularis: a ratio where the larger number contains the smaller number plus one extra part, such as 3:2 or 4:3</term> ratios decrease in that reversed order. For multiples grow without limit according to natural addition, but superparticulars naturally decrease.

One thing also tends to happen in these proportions: the larger the name of a numerical part is, the smaller that part actually is, and vice versa. For example, in the numbers 3 and 2, the name "three" is larger than "two," yet a third part is smaller than a half part. Thus, it follows that in superparticular ratios, a **one-and-a-third** <term>sesquitertia: a 4:3 ratio</term> part is shorter than a **one-and-a-half** <term>sesquialtera: a 3:2 ratio</term> part, for the latter contains the **fifth** <term>diapente: the musical interval of a fifth</term> and the former the **fourth** <term>diatessaron: the musical interval of a fourth</term>, and so on for similar cases. But because they naturally decrease, they eventually stop forming a **consonance** <note>original: "symphoniam"</note>. For the **one-and-seventeenth** <term>sesquiseptima decima: an 18:17 ratio</term> is actually smaller than a true semitone, because between the 17:16 and 18:17 ratios, no superparticular relationship has a proportional middle, and so on; and this is what most authorities maintain.

However, there are some who say that in superparticular proportions there is no "mean" <note>A middle value that divides the ratio into two equal parts</note>, such as **Archytas of Tarentum** <note>A Greek mathematician and Pythagorean philosopher (c. 428–347 BCE)</note> and many others, though they are rebuked by **Anicius** <margin>(a) Book 3 of *On Music*, chapter 11. <note>Refers to Boethius</note></margin>. Nevertheless, their opinion seems more probable than the rebuke of Anicius himself, which is proven thus: Let A and B be a superparticular proportion, such that A is 6 and B is 4. Let C and D be the "first numbers" <note>The lowest terms or roots of the ratio</note> of that proportion. Because they are the smallest, they are measured only by

<column-break/>

unity <note>The number 1</note>, just as at the beginning. For in every case, C exceeds D by only a single unit, and there is no middle between them. Indeed, there is a general rule: when the middle is not proportional, then no geometric mean can be found between the roots. Since, therefore, C and D have no middle, A and B also have no proportional mean, for C and D are the roots of A and B, as is clear in the figure.

| A. | 6. | 5. | 4. | B. |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| C. | 3. | no middle. | 2. | D. |

However, roots can be immediate while their products are mediated and of a different "middle-ness." For two and three are immediate numbers <note>Consecutive integers</note>, but 4 and 6 are mediated numbers, because five is their middle. But **Boethius** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), the primary musical authority of the Middle Ages</note> insists that a proportion is not obtained from this, for the smallest terms are immediate. In terms of **harmony** <note>original: "harmonicaliter"</note>, the smallest doubles <note>ratios like 2:1</note> can be immediate, but in terms of **geometry**, they are divided into great intervals.

### CHAPTER VI.

Now we must speak of **superpartient** <term>superpartientibus: ratios where the larger number contains the smaller plus more than one part, such as 5:3</term> ratios, where the smaller number is contained once along with some "part-quantity" and "part-count" of it. A **part-quantity** <term>aliquanta: a part that does not divide the whole evenly, like 4 is to 6</term> is said to be that which, no matter how many times it is multiplied or taken, does not return its whole perfectly, but always results in more or less—as in the **one-and-two-thirds** <term>superbipartiente: a 5:3 ratio</term>, the **one-and-three-fourths** <term>supertripartiente: a 7:4 ratio</term>, and so on into infinity.

### FOURTH PART OF MUSIC

| 3. | 4. | 5. | 6. | 7. |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 5. | 7. | 9. | 11. | 13. |

The **double super-two-part** <term>dupla superbipartiens: A ratio of 8:3, representing an octave plus a fourth</term> ratio is composed of the **double** <note>2:1 ratio, the octave</note> and the **one-and-a-third** <note>4:3 ratio, the fourth</note> proportions; that is, it forms the **octave-plus-fourth** <note>original: "diapason & diatessaron"</note> consonance. This interval is rejected by all the followers of Pythagoras as an **irregular sound** <note>original: "sonus irregularis"</note>. However, Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and music theorist</note> claims that this consonance is actually good, offering this proof: every simple, perfect consonance is contained within the **octave** <note>diapason</note>, and whatever is placed outside the octave is merely a repetition of those things contained within it, sounding as if it were a single number. Therefore, if a **fourth** <note>diatessaron</note> can be stretched within an octave, it can also be stretched above it. Yet neither Boethius, nor Johannes, nor Guido, nor any musician I have seen, settles this dispute. I have, however, read someone arguing with himself regarding a similar opinion of Jehan des Murs <note>Johannes de Muris, a prominent 14th-century mathematician and music theorist</note> as to whether the fourth—or, *more accurately*, the **fifth** <note>diapente</note>—is a consonance, or falls under the fifth. It is no wonder, then, that it might be considered excellent above the octave; yet he says it is not, for the **one-and-a-half** <note>sesquialtera: the 3:2 ratio of a fifth</note> is a larger proportion than the **one-and-a-third** <note>sesquitertia: the 4:3 ratio of a fourth</note>. Therefore, the fifth comes before the fourth. Just as in the nature of consonances and proportions, a greater thing is created through **stretching** <note>intensio: raising the pitch</note> than through **loosening** <note>remissio: lowering the pitch</note>, so too stretching has greater power; the fourth has a greater quality of consonance when it follows a fifth than when it precedes it.

But in my judgment, let experience be the deciding factor, and let each person’s ear be the judge for themselves. You will find that the fourth is not a consonance, as some

<column-break/>

claim, but rather a *part* of a consonance, because it is imperfect. Unless a perfect consonance precedes it, it will be a **semi-dissonance**; nor does it sound right before the fifth, which is larger than it. The reason is that the comparison of the **octave** <note>12:6</note> to the **fifth** <note>12:8</note> comes before the comparison to the **fourth** <note>12:9</note>. For example, 12 is compared to 8 before it is compared to 9, because 8 comes before 9. Therefore, the fourth comes after the fifth; indeed, if there were no fifth, there would be no fourth. But the fifth can be called—and is—a consonance in its own right, whereas the fourth seems to become a consonance not by its own action, but from the two together, as the fifth and fourth combined constitute an octave. Therefore, if it is not a consonance *below* the octave, it will not be one *above* it either, but rather an **irregular sound**. Some have said this is a fifth type of consonance, but it is not, unless the fourth is considered a consonance on its own and not just a part of one. This is how it seems to me, as experience teaches—and experience is the mistress of all things—as shown in this figure:
