#### CHAPTER VII.

Now, the whole tone, which exists in the **one-and-one-eighth** <term>sesquioctava: The 9:8 ratio, the mathematical basis of a whole tone</term> proportion, cannot be divided into two equal parts. As a certain singular musician puts it: anyone seeking to divide a tone into two equal parts is like one seeking to measure the diagonal of a square against its side, which is impossible <note>This is a famous mathematical analogy. In geometry, the ratio of a square's diagonal to its side is an irrational number (the square root of 2). Adam is explaining that because there is no whole number between 8 and 9, the 9:8 tone cannot be split into two equal whole-number ratios.</note>. For just as the diagonal is larger than one side and shorter than two, yet shares no common proportion that can perfectly measure the difference, so too one part of the tone is larger than a **one-and-one-sixteenth** <term>sesquisedecima: The 17:16 ratio</term> and shorter than two, and the other part is smaller than a **one-and-one-seventeenth** <term>sesquiseptimadecima: The 18:17 ratio</term> and larger than two, with no common proportion measuring the excess.

Therefore, the tone is divided into two unequal semitones, namely the **major** and the **minor**. The major is called the **apotome** <term>apotome: In Pythagorean tuning, the "larger" semitone (approx. 114 cents)</term>, and it is divided into a **diesis** and a **comma**, which is itself divided into two **diaschismata**. The major semitone exceeds the shorter one by the value of a comma, which is the smallest interval perceptible to the sense of hearing. Neither the apotome nor the comma are used to create **consonances** <note>original: "symphoniam"</note>, but only the diesis is used; for one diesis is larger than three commas and shorter than four, while one apotome is larger than

<column-break/>

four commas and shorter than five. Therefore, a whole tone is larger than eight commas and shorter than nine. Thus, a tone is divided into a major and a minor semitone, or into two minor semitones and one comma, or into four diaschismata and one comma, because it cannot be divided into equal parts. Let anyone wishing to understand the division of the tone hear Philolaus the Pythagorean <note>Philolaus (c. 470–385 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who was the first to document the Pythagorean mathematical system of music.</note> speaking on the subject:

> A **tone** is the sharp sounding of a voice according to the direct harmony and quantity that consists in the pitch of the voice.
>
> A **diesis** <term>diesis: Here used to mean the "limma" or minor semitone (approx. 90 cents)</term> is the space by which a **fourth** <term>sesquitertia: The 4:3 ratio</term> is greater than two whole tones.
>
> A **comma** is the space by which a **whole tone** <term>sesquioctava: The 9:8 ratio</term> is greater than two dieses.
>
> A **schisma** is half of a comma.
>
> A **diaschisma** is half of a diesis—that is, half of a minor semitone.
>
> An **apotome** is a space larger than four commas and smaller than five.

Anyone wishing to know the tone, the apotome, and the diesis through musical harmonies should proceed as follows. Their interval can be taken in the bass or the treble by either tightening or loosening—

### CHAPTER VIII.

Therefore, through these raised and lowered species, as well as by raising or lowering the intervals of the tone, the property and concord of all harmonic proportions can be evaluated. But the stubborn minds of many musicians often strive to confuse and corrupt these proportions. Thus, against the arrangement of the masters and a position well-founded in every respect, some build poorly, some pervert the signs, and some are accustomed to mix a **triple proportion** <term>tripla: A 3:1 ratio where three notes are played in the time of one</term> with a **sesquialtera** <term>sesquialtera: A 3:2 ratio where three notes are played in the time of two</term>, or substitute one for another, saying: "Lest perhaps they be found out." Furthermore, they even boast that they have done something new, known to no one but themselves; they refuse to consider

<column-break/>

that even a fool or a madman can conceive of something in his mind that no one else knows—just like an uneducated innkeeper who writes debts on a wall with signs readable only to himself. For this reason, I wanted to attach the proportions along with their signs, so that they might be more easily understood by those unlearned persons who wish to study.

Therefore, a **duple proportion** <term>dupla proportio: A 2:1 ratio; in rhythm, it means the music moves twice as fast</term> occurs when a larger number contains a smaller one twice, such as 4 to 2, 6 to 3, or 8 to 4, etc. Musically, this is when two **minims** <term>minima: A rhythmic unit; the "short" note of the period</term> are placed against one, four against two, or eight against four. Its sign is the binary algorithmic digit <note>The author is referring to using the Arabic numeral "2" rather than Roman numerals</note> associated with each individual sign, as in this example of "2."

### THE FOURTH PART OF MUSIC.

<note>original: "MUSICÆ PARS QUARTA."</note>

**Triple proportion** <term>tripla: A ratio where the larger value is three times the smaller (3:1)</term> exists when the larger number contains the shorter number three times, such as 3 to 1, or 6 to 2, or 9 to 3. In a musical sense, it occurs when three **minims** <term>minim: A standard unit of musical duration in this period, similar to a half-note or quarter-note depending on the context</term> are performed against one, or six against two, or nine against three. Its sign is the triple **algoristic figure** <term>algoristic figure: An Arabic numeral, which was becoming the standard for indicating proportions in the 15th century</term> added to any [mensuration] sign, as shown here in the example of 3.

**Quadruple proportion** <term>quadrupla: A ratio where the larger value is four times the smaller (4:1)</term> exists when the larger number contains the smaller four times, such as 4 to 1, or 8 to 2, or 12 to 3. **Sesquialtera proportion** <term>sesquialtera: A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2, where three notes are played in the time of two</term> exists when the larger number contains the shorter number once plus half of it, such as when three minims are performed against two, or six against four, and so on. It is also called **sextupla** <note>original: "sextupla"</note> or **hemiolia** <term>hemiolia: A rhythmic shift where three beats are grouped into the time of two, often indicated by "coloration" (filling in the note heads)</term>. **Sesquitertia proportion** <term>sesquitertia: A ratio of 1.33 to 1, or 4:3, where four notes are played in the time of three</term> exists when the larger number contains the smaller once plus its third part, such as 4 to 3, or 8 to 6. ->*Conclusion.*<-

**These** are therefore, most illustrious Joachim! <note>Likely referring to Joachim von Watt, also known as Vadianus, or another scholarly contemporary.</note> the excerpts of musicians that seemed more useful to me. From reading these, not only the learned, but even an experienced person with an unlearned mind can perceive that nothing has been omitted from those things which were necessary to be set down. For though I have not placed the authorities of individual teachers, nor agreed with the ancients in every process, nor situated the divisions of all properties, the promised brevity has made it so, as well as the clear, compendious, and sufficient instruction of the ancients themselves. From their writings, just like bees from flowers, I have collected all the more worthy things, so that to one looking closely, nothing seems to be missing. For if you seek the utility of the art, you will find almost the whole of it here; if you desire to know the names of the authors and the origin of the art, look at the first part and you will find it at your pleasure; if you wish to see the types of **monochords and tetrachords** <term>monochord/tetrachord: Ancient tools and groupings of four notes used to define musical scales.</term>, here the **enharmonic and chromatic** <term>enharmonic/chromatic: Ancient Greek musical "genera" or styles of tuning that utilized smaller intervals than the standard diatonic scale.</term> genres are situated under the **diatonic**; if indeed you wish to know plain and **mensural** <term>mensural music: Polyphonic music where each note has a specific, defined duration, as opposed to the unmeasured rhythm of plainchant.</term> music with each kind of proportion, here you will behold the entire force of it captured under musical figures; if fi-

<column-break/>

nally you venture to track down the whole art and its subtlety, so to speak, here the kernel is hidden entirely as if under a shell.

Receive therefore, most excellent man, with a favorable countenance, this little book dedicated to you by a man most devoted to you; for to whom rather than you should I send this to be corrected and amended? You, if you wish, can also defend it from the lips of detractors, you who are accustomed to counter those with ill-intent through arguments. And so, when you are about to read these things, you will be mindful—as I persuade myself—sometimes of your Adam, who did not fear to give himself to danger for love of you, and to expose himself to insults. Farewell.

->*Conclusion of the little book.*<-

# CONSTITUTIONS
## OF THE PAPAL CHAPEL.

->Giuseppe Santarelli, who today leads the Papal Chapel, shared this with me.<-

In the eleventh year of the Supreme Pontiff Paul III, 1545. The Constitutions of the singers of the papal system in the Greater Sacristy <note>The "Greater Sacristy" refers to what is now known as the Sistine Chapel.</note>.

When Rome was captured and given over to pillage by the impious during the time of our predecessor Clement VII <note>The Sack of Rome in 1527, where Imperial troops under Charles V devastated the city.</note>, even the writings—which were of no use as plunder—were consumed by fire. Among these, the laws of the musicians of the Greater Sacristy also perished. Therefore, those which were either retained in memory or seen as needing renewal, were restored, established, and published for perpetual memory by the command of the Supreme Pontiff Paul III and the care of the Right Reverend Lord Ludovico, Bishop of Assisi <note>Ludovico Magnasco di Santa Fiora, Bishop of Assisi and Master of the Chapel.</note>, Master of the singers of the said chapel, as follows:

### CHAPTER I.

In the Chapel of Our Most Holy Lord the Pope, there is an ancient custom that whenever the Reverend Lord Master of the said Chapel is requested to admit any singer into the services of the said Chapel, the aforementioned Master is bound to act with diligence and investigate whether the said candidate is a good man, of honest reputation, honest life, and well-mannered. And if he should find any defect of notable infamy in his life or morals, he must not propose him to the college of singers of the said Chapel.

### CHAPTER II.

*The Manner of Proposing New Singers.*

From ancient times it has also been the custom that

<column-break/>

when a new singer is to be received into the said Chapel, the Reverend Lord Master of the Chapel itself is bound to have all the singers of the said Chapel gather as a college. To those so assembled, he must propose the candidate in question and advise those same singers that they must examine him; and if he is found sufficient, they should be willing to receive him into the service of God and the Supreme Pontiff. The manner of the examination follows.

### CHAPTER III.

*The Manner of the Examination.*

After the Reverend Lord Master of the said Chapel has proposed the candidate to the college of singers to be examined by the said college, the following must first be considered: first, whether the singer to be examined has a good and perfect voice; second, whether he sings **figured song** <term>cantum figuratum: Elaborate, polyphonic music (multiple independent melodies) as opposed to simple chant.</term> well; third, whether he sings **counterpoint** <term>contrapunctum: The technique of composing or improvising a second melody to play against a given tune.</term> sufficiently; fourth, whether he sings **plainchant** <term>cantum planum: Also known as Gregorian chant; the traditional, monophonic ritual music of the Church.</term> well; fifth, whether he knows how to read well.

### CHAPTER IV.

*The Scrutiny Regarding the Admission of a New Singer.*

Once the examination of the aforementioned singer has been conducted by the said college, the Reverend Lord Master of the aforementioned Chapel, in a place to be designated by him, shall call the senior singer secretly. Having administered an oath to him, he shall ask him what he thinks of the examined singer, and whether he is sufficient for the service of the said...

### Chapter V.
->*The manner of giving the surplice and the oath to a new singer.*<-

For a new singer who has been sufficiently approved, the Master of the said Chapel is bound to hand over a surplice <note>term: cotta; a white liturgical vestment worn over a cassock, signifying the singer's official status.</note> to the approved singer as a sign of true reception and life-long admission, in the following manner: while the Master of the Chapel is seated and the other singers are standing before him in order, the candidate shall kneel before the Master. The Master shall then dress him in the surplice and cause him to take an oath upon the Holy Gospels of God, touching the sacred scriptures, that he will be faithful to Our Most Holy Lord the Pope <note>original: "S. D. N. Papæ" — Sanctissimus Dominus Noster Papæ</note>, etc., as was noted at the beginning.

<column-break/>

### Chapter VI.
->*The manner of admission for a new singer.*<-

Once the oath has been taken, the new singer—clothed in the surplice as described—shall kiss the hands of the Master of the Chapel. Then, approaching the most senior singer, he shall embrace him and kiss all the singers in turn. The singers must receive the new singer with this "kiss of peace" as a sign of true reception and life-long admission.

### Chapter VII.
->*Concerning the salary to be assigned to a new singer.*<-

If a new singer is admitted before the twentieth day of the month, he shall receive the full salary payment for that month.

### Chapter VIII.
->*The new singer is bound to pay two ducats for his surplice.*<-

A singer received or admitted into the said Chapel is bound to pay two gold ducats <note>original: "ducatos auri in auro de camera" — gold ducats of the Apostolic Chamber, the papal treasury.</note> to the college of singers for his surplice or the privileges of the chapel within the two months immediately following the day of his reception. If he has not paid these two ducats to the college within two months, the Abbot <note>The "Abbas" was the administrative head of the college of singers, distinct from the Master of the Chapel.</note> for the time being is bound to withhold the amount from the new singer's salary in the third month and deliver it to the college without any hope of excuse; these two ducats shall be spent on chapel business. In a similar way, the newly received singer must pay three gold scudi within three months of his reception for the right to litigate in the Rota <note>The Roman Rota is the highest ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church; this fee secured the singer's legal standing within the Roman Curia.</note> according to the form of the agreement made between the colleges...

### Chapter IX.
*A new singer is bound to pay ten ducats for the sharing of the regalia.*

If a new singer wishes to share in the regalia <note>original: "regalibus"; these were supplemental fees, tips, or "perks" collected from ceremonies and distributed among the chapel members</note> accruing to the said chapel, he is bound to pay ten gold ducats of the chamber <note>term: ducat; a high-purity gold coin used throughout Europe; the "ducat of the chamber" was the standard currency of the Papal Treasury</note> to the college of singers. If the aforementioned singer pays the said ten ducats at least thirty days before his admission, he shall share in all regalia accruing to the chapel after thirty days have passed from the date of payment. If, however, he does not pay the ten ducats within two months of his reception or admission, but pays them at any other time, he shall not share in any regalia accruing to the chapel for the six months immediately following the date of such payment.

### Chapter X.
*How the regalia are to be divided among the singers.*

When a new singer pays his regalia into the hands of the serving abbot of the said Chapel, the said regalia are to be divided among the participating singers, including those who were *absent or residing in Rome* during the admission of the new singer, even if they were sick. If, however, the new singer did not pay his regalia within the time established in the 

<column-break/>

preceding chapter, but paid them at any other time, then only those singers who were present in Rome and participating at the time of that new singer’s admission shall share in those specific fees paid by the new singer.

### Chapter XI.
*On observing silence while the divine office is underway.*

When the divine office <note>The "Divine Office" refers to the daily cycle of prayers and psalms sung by the clergy and choir.</note> is being celebrated, the singers assisting in the choir must observe silence and wear their surplices <note>original: "cottas"; a white liturgical vestment</note>, unless a legitimate reason interferes. This reason must be reported to the senior singer present in the choir, who serves as the "punctuator" <note>term: punctator; an official responsible for "marking" or "puncturing" the register to record attendance, lateness, or fines for misconduct</note>. They must not presume to speak to one another, read any letters, or show new musical compositions while the divine office is underway. Otherwise, whoever fails to observe these rules shall be "punched" <note>original: "punctabitur"; marked for a fine</note> double at the discretion of the aforementioned senior singer or punctuator. If the said office is held in the presence of Our Most Holy Lord the Pope, or the Sacred College of Cardinals of the Holy Roman Church, or on a day of public consistory <note>A formal meeting of the Pope and his Cardinals.</note>, any singer who does not have his surplice shall sit with the others, but regarding the regalia coming to the singers from that office, he shall be treated as if he were not present.

### CHAPTER XIII.
*On permission to go outside the choir for some particular business.*

No singer, for any private business, shall presume to neglect the service of the Chapel while the divine office is being held, without the permission of the senior singer present in the choir or of the said marker of the college. Anyone who violates this shall be fined according to the order of the divine office and the chapters written below.

### CHAPTER XIV.
*They must not sing Mass outside the Chapel.*

It is not permitted for singers to serve in divine offices outside the said Chapel. Therefore, if one, two, three, or more singers, out of regard for some friend or another singer or any other person, shall sing Mass or Vespers or any other divine office outside the said Chapel without permission from the said college of singers, each of the said singers shall be fined ten julios <term>iuliis; a silver coin used in the Papal States, originally minted by Pope Julius II</term>. If they should receive any salary or benefit from the office sung outside the Chapel, as mentioned above, they must be fined double the salary, prize, or benefit received by said singers, in addition to the aforementioned ten julios. This,

<column-break/>

however, is declared: in the event that some singers, having obtained permission from the aforementioned college of singers, should sing an office outside the said Chapel and receive a prize or salary from singing such an office, the said salary shall be distributed among the participating singers residing in Rome.

### CHAPTER XV.
*On the duty of the last and second-to-last singers.*

It pertains to the last singer <note>Meaning the most recently hired member of the choir.</note> to move the books, and to the second-to-last to place them on the lectern <note>original: "facistorio," a folding music stand or reading desk.</note> or reading desk, according to the arrangement of the singers—namely, the weekly counter-tenor <note>original: "contralti hebdomadarii"; the "hebdomadary" was the person assigned to a specific liturgical duty for that week.</note> or the Dean of the said Chapel. Likewise, the last and second-to-last singers are required to carry the necessary books of the Chapel during processions.

### CHAPTER XVI.
*On a singer who deserts the service of the Chapel.*

No singer admitted into the college of singers of the said Chapel shall presume to receive a provision or salary from another patron in the capacity of a singer. In the event that any of the singers enters the service of another patron and receives a salary from them, he must not be admitted further to his place, nor can it be said that he is any longer part of the college of singers. If he is to be readmitted, he must be received by the Master of the Chapel and the college of singers, if it pleases them; otherwise, he is not to be received into the aforementioned college, because he is considered a new singer. If he is readmitted, he is bound to pay his entry fees <note>original: "regalia"; see the note on the previous page regarding these administrative fees.</note> just as a newly received singer and must sit in the last place.

### Chapter XVII.
->*Concerning a singer causing a scandal.*<-

Because it is best to avoid scandals so that peace may be maintained among the singers—especially in the said Chapel where the divine offices are celebrated daily by the said singers—it is therefore ordained by our ancient predecessors and remains in observance that any singer currently in the said Chapel who, whether during the divine office or in the meetings <note>original: "congregationibus"; these were the formal administrative meetings of the choir members</note> of the aforementioned singers held for conducting the business of the Chapel, or at any other time, in any way, or under any sought-after pretext, speaks injurious words against or toward another singer that even result in a scandal, shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur," literally "marked," referring to the system where a 'punctator' marked a dot next to a name to denote a fine</note> at the discretion of the society of singers. And if a notable scandal of this kind arises in the presence of the Pope, the Right Reverend Cardinals, or the Master of the Chapel, he shall be fined at the discretion of the same Master of the Chapel along with the college of singers. Furthermore, if any singer, whether inside or outside the said Chapel, through persuasion or provoked by the words of another singer, strikes another singer with a fist, a kick, a staff, or weapons, or in any other way lays violent hands upon him, he shall be condemned at the sole discretion of the Master of the Chapel. The singer who provoked another singer to cause such a scandal shall similarly be condemned at the discretion of the Master together with the college. If, however, a scandal occurs between singers outside the said Chapel, it shall be condemned at the discretion of the college of singers, with the Master of the Chapel always intervening.

<column-break/>

### Chapter XVIII.
->*Concerning a condemned singer and the revealing of the college's decrees.*<-

A singer who, having been condemned for an error by the college of singers or who otherwise feels himself aggrieved for some other reason, must not appeal or complain outside the college, nor seek any intercessors, except to Our Holy Lord the Pope or the Master of the Chapel. And if such a singer, being condemned or otherwise aggrieved as stated above, complains outside the said college to anyone other than Our Holy Lord or the Master of the Chapel, or in any way reveals the secrets of the college, he shall be punished with a heavy penalty as a perjurer <note>The singers took a formal oath of secrecy regarding their administrative and disciplinary meetings</note> by the Master of the Chapel together with the college.

### Chapter XIX.
->*On the wearing of honorable dress.*<-

Because the singers of the said Chapel are the Pope’s Chaplains, they must therefore walk in decent and honorable dress. Therefore, any singer who walks publicly through the city for leisure, or to conduct any business in honorable places or courts, while dressed in scholarly attire <note>original: "habitu scholari"; referring to the short academic or student robes rather than the long, formal clerical cassocks expected of Papal Chaplains</note>, shall be fined one julio <term>iuliis; a silver coin used in the Papal States</term> for each instance, without hope of remission.

### Chapter XX.
->*The procedure to be observed in the meeting of the singers.*<-

When the singers gather as a college regarding any business of the said Chapel, before the case is proposed, the senior singers shall approach the Master of the Chapel on either side, if he is present; if not, they shall approach the Dean of the said Chapel, each one successively in order in his place...

### CHAPTER XXI.
->*When there is a dispute among the singers.*<-

If there is a dispute within the college of singers regarding a proposal to be decided, such that all the singers do not agree on the conclusion of the proposal—regardless of the matter or at whose request it was brought—a vote must be held. With white and black balls <note>original: "pallis," small tokens used for secret voting; white for 'yes' and black for 'no'</note>, each singer shall cast his vote secretly. And if the proposal concerns the imposing or relaxing of a penalty, or any other business of the said college, and two-thirds plus one vote of the singers agree, the proposal shall be enacted; otherwise, it shall not. However, in matters of clear personal finances, each man shall be the master of his own share. The Dean of the Chapel must admonish all singers so that each gives his vote without favor, fear, or hatred, or any other corruption, and so that no singer shows his vote—whether a white or black ball—to another singer, nor makes it public.

### CHAPTER XXII.
->*Concerning permission to go outside the city.*<-

A singer absent without permission may be marked with the ordinary fine for up to four days (exclusive); thereafter, he shall be fined at the discretion of the singer <note>original: "arbitrio cantoris," likely referring to the singer serving as the official 'punctator' or marker</note>. If he is away for more than ten days, he shall be fined at the discretion of the Master of the Chapel.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER XXIII.
->*Concerning permission to go to distant regions.*<-

Whenever a singer needs to travel to distant regions <note>original: "ad partes"; usually referring to the singer's home country or province</note> for highly important business, he should present his case to a convened assembly of the singers. After the assembly has heard the proposal, if the singer is of a Northern European nation <note>original: "nationis Ultramontes," literally "from beyond the mountains," referring to those from outside Italy, such as France, Flanders, or Germany</note>, they may grant a leave of ten months; if he is Italian, they may grant only five months. During these months, his usual provision or salary shall be granted. Once this permission has been obtained from the aforementioned assembly, the licensed singer shall similarly obtain permission from the Right Reverend Master of the said Chapel, whose hand he shall kiss upon his departure. In the event that a singer, licensed as stated, falls ill while away, the matter of his status shall remain at the discretion of the Master of the Chapel. Such leaves are not to be granted except to singers who have served the said Chapel for a period of five years.

### CHAPTER XXIV.
->*Concerning a singer returning from distant regions.*<-

If a licensed singer staying in distant regions is occupied with his own business for the whole of the said time, or should reside at his own benefices <note>church appointments that provided income</note> for one, two, three, or more years, and then returns to Rome, he is to be readmitted to his place, provided he did not receive a salary from anyone else as mentioned above. In the month in which he returns, he should not be fined, nor shall he receive a share of the fines collected that month; however, he shall share in other occurring royal distributions <note>original: "regalibus," special bonuses or fees distributed on feast days</note>. In the meantime, he is always understood to be a member of the college and shall always be recorded on the roll <note>original: "rotulo," the official membership list of the Papal Chapel</note>.

### CHAPTER XXV.
#### *Regarding a singer who has been in the service of the Chapel for 25 years.*

A singer who has served in the said Chapel for twenty-five years is rightfully to be rewarded; therefore, he ought to be exempt from the ordinary divine office of the said Chapel. However, he is required to appear for the first *Kyrie eleison* <note>original: "Kyrieeleison"; the opening prayer of the Mass</note>, or whenever the office is sung in the presence of Our Holy Lord the Pope or the Sacred College of the Reverend Lord Cardinals. He must also attend on Sundays, on days when a consistory <note>a formal meeting of the Pope and Cardinals</note> is held, and on the feasts of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Apostles, and the Evangelists, or for the consecration and the feast of the invocation of the Chapel for the entire office. He is also required to be present whenever the office is performed outside the Chapel. If he is not present for such services, he shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur," literally "marked"; refers to a dot placed by the name to indicate a financial penalty</note> just like the other singers who are not exempt, and he shall not share in any "points" <note>distributions of income based on attendance</note> occurring in the said Chapel. This is, however, declared: if it should happen that two, three, or more singers of one and the same voice part—namely two sopranos, or altos, tenors, or basses—exceed the said time of twenty-five years at the same time, no one shall enjoy such an exemption except for the singer who is more senior in that voice part.

### CHAPTER XXVI.
#### *Regarding a sick singer.*

If any of the singers is unwell—which God forbid—he is bound to excuse himself to the college of singers; namely, to the Proctor <term>Procurator; the administrative official of the choir</term> of the said college for the time being, while the divine office is standing. If he does not make such an excuse under oath, he shall be fined according to the regulation

<column-break/>

of the said Chapel. And if a sick singer, excused as previously mentioned, should be found after such an excuse has been admitted to be walking through the city for leisure or conducting some business, and he is found by any singer so walking about, it must be reported to the college of the aforementioned singers. The said sick person, having been so excused or reported, shall be fined double the amount of the ordinary office.

### CHAPTER XXVII.
#### *Regarding a sick singer returning to the service of the Chapel.*

Likewise, if the said singer, excused as a sick person as previously mentioned, should delay for ten days so that he does not go to the Chapel, and after the said ten days he should come to the said Chapel with the intention of serving, if he is not present for the ordinary daily office, he must be fined, and he shall not be a participant in the points made both for himself and for other singers in that month. And if the aforementioned singer, excused as sick, should present himself at a Papal Mass or a public consistory, but fails in the services of the said Chapel on the following days, he ought not to participate in the "regalia" <note>original: "regalibus"; special distributions or bonuses granted for high-ranking services</note> from that Papal Mass or public consistory.

### CHAPTER XXVIII.
#### *Regarding a singer sick for more than a year.*

Likewise, if a singer excused as sick should grow more burdened by illness day by day, such that for one entire year he does not come to the service of the said Chapel, he shall not participate in any "regalia" arising in the said Chapel during the said illness, but only and at most...

In any given month, a singer shall receive his salary or ordinary provision, as well as the ordinary gratuities <note>original: "mancias"; small tips or bonuses</note> granted by the Supreme Pontiff. ## CHAPTER XXIX.
### *Regarding a deceased singer.*

When a singer dies, the Reverend Lord Master Sacristan, all the singers, chaplains, clerks, scribes, and the keeper of the books must go to the place where the singer died. Preceded by the Master with the Sacristan (if he is present), the singers and others must walk two by two after the body according to their seniority. At the place where he is buried, they must sing in polyphony <note>original: "cantu figurato"; multi-part musical composition as opposed to simple plainchant</note> the following:
> ℟. *Deliver me, O Lord* <note>original: "libera me Domine"; the responsory from the Office of the Dead</note>,

The heirs, if there are any, shall have the salary for the month in which he dies; otherwise, it should be given to the poor for the benefit of his soul. If he should die intestate <note>without a will</note> and without heirs, or if the heirs are absent, then administrators of the deceased's goods are to be appointed by the Reverend Father Lord Master together with the college, until something has been ordained by Our Lord the Pope. The Abbot <note>the elected head of the college of singers</note> at that time shall take the salary of the following month, and when it pleases the heirs or the singers,

<column-break/>

the funeral services <note>original: "exequiæ"</note> shall be celebrated. From that salary, the same Abbot shall buy two large torches to be placed upon the grave, four torches for the altar, and one candle to be burned for each singer throughout the entire Mass. The remainder shall be distributed, as is customary, among the participating singers. The same is to be said regarding the Master, sacristan, chaplains, and clerks; and whoever is not present or has not been excused shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur"; literally "marked," referring to a dot placed in the ledger to indicate a financial penalty</note> two carlines <note>original: "carolenis"; a silver coin used in the Papal States</note>.

## CHAPTER XXX.
### *How the boxes of sweets are to be divided among the singers.*

At whatever Papal Masses or Vespers the Roman Pontiff happens to celebrate, there must be delivered and granted to the singers in the Great Hall <note>original: "tinello maiori"; the dining area or household hall of the papal palace</note> of the Pontiff himself . . . and one box of sweets <note>original: "scaptulam confectionum"</note>. This box is to be divided among the participating singers who have paid their royal dues <note>original: "regalia"</note> and are present in the Roman Court, even if they should be sick. This is done in their order, starting from the most senior through to the end. If any participating singer returns from abroad, he should receive such a box in his place in the rotation. If the rotation for these boxes has already passed, he must wait for the new rotation and enter his place like a new singer.

## CHAPTER XXXI.
### *Regarding the election of a new Pope.*

When the conclave <note>the locked assembly of Cardinals for the election of a Pope</note> is opened at the election <note>original: "creatione"; creation</note> of a new Pontiff, all singers are required to be present for the procession that goes to St. Peter’s, dressed in their surplices <note>original: "cottis"; short, white liturgical vestments</note>, and to sing according to the form of the ceremonial:
> *Behold the great priest* <note>original: "Ecce sacerdos magnus"; a traditional antiphon used to greet a high-ranking prelate</note>, etc.

## CHAPTER XXXII.
### *Regarding the dues to be paid by new Cardinals to the singers.*

When the Pontiff, after the creation of Cardinals, intends to hand over or gift the gold rings to those newly created Cardinals in a public consistory <note>a formal meeting of the Sacred College of Cardinals</note> following the performance of the customary ceremonies, then all the singers, dressed in surplices, are required to sing the *Te Deum* <note>original: "Te Deum Laudamus"; a traditional hymn of praise and thanksgiving</note> at the appropriate time according to the ceremonial protocol. Any singer absent from the aforementioned proceedings shall lose the dues <note>original: "regalia"; customary fees or perks</note> arising from the hats or from the creation of these Cardinals. These dues consist of thirty gold ducats of the chamber <note>original: "ducati aurei auri de camera"; a high-value currency used by the papal treasury</note> to be paid by each newly created Cardinal to the aforementioned singers. In the event that the payment of the said dues was not made by the Cardinals at that time, but was paid later at any other time, the singers who were absent during the singing of the *Te Deum* do not share in them; rather, only those who were present at the proceedings, sang the *Te Deum*, and were among the active participants shall share. And if it happens that a newly created Cardinal is absent from the Roman Curia <note>the administrative apparatus of the Holy See</note>, and before the *Te Deum* is sung, he pays

<column-break/>

such dues to the singers themselves, all singers who were present and participating in the Roman Curia at the time of that new Cardinal's creation—even if they were sick—must share in these dues.

## CHAPTER XXXIII.
### *Regarding the funeral rites of Supreme Pontiffs.*

When the funeral rites <note>original: "exequiae"</note> of a Supreme Pontiff are to be celebrated, all singers must assemble at St. Peter's dressed in their surplices. Before the rites begin, the Chamberlain must pay for four *cannas* of highest-quality black cloth for each Master, sacristan, singer, chaplain, altar clerk, scribe, and the keeper of the books. For nine days, the Mass for the Dead <note>original: "Missa pro defunctis"; the Requiem Mass</note> is sung, and every day forty pounds of wax tapers are owed to the singers, as well as two torches from the funeral itself. These torches are to be distributed to the two most senior singers first, and then sequentially in order to each of the other singers present until the end of the funeral rites; singers who are not present will not share in this distribution of torches. A singer who is absent from any funeral Mass shall not share in the dues of that Mass from which he was missing; however, he shall share in the tapers of that day as if he were sick. He shall be fined five julios for every Mass in which he was missing.

## CHAPTER XXXIV.
### *When the conclave is entered.*

After the funeral rites of the Supreme Pontiff are finished, on the day appointed by the Reverend Lord Cardinals for entering the conclave <note>the locked assembly for electing a new Pope</note>, all singers are required to be present dressed in surplices and to sing the Mass...

...already concerning the Holy Spirit, which being finished, the procession to the conclave <note>the secured assembly of Cardinals gathered to elect a new Pope</note> takes place, singing the hymn *Come, Creator Spirit* <note>original: "Veni Creator Spiritus"</note> etc. according to the form of the ceremonial; and any singer who is not present shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur"; literally 'marked,' referring to a mark in the ledger resulting in a deduction from pay</note> just as is done for Papal Masses.

### CHAPTER XXXV.
*The manner to be observed by the Cardinals remaining in the conclave.*

Once the conclave is closed, the Mass of the Holy Spirit is sung every day until the election of a new Pontiff, at the place and hour to be designated by the Master of the House of the Holy Palace. Anyone who does not attend the daily Mass shall be fined in the same manner as is customary for the ordinary office of the said Chapel. For this office, no excuses are accepted, except for illness alone. Furthermore, the aforementioned Master of the House of the Holy Palace is required to provide the singers with a midday meal in the greater dining hall <note>original: "tinello maiori"; the dining room for the papal household staff</note> every day until the election of the new Pontiff, by reason of their close association <note>original: "familiaritatis"</note>. In a similar way, the same Reverend Lord Master of the House, from the day the vacancy is declared until the day legal cases are resumed in the Rota <note>the supreme ecclesiastical court of the Catholic Church</note>, is bound every day in the morning to effectively provide the same singers with one flask of six measures <note>original: "pocalium"; roughly equivalent to cups or glasses</note> of good and pure Greek wine <note>a high-quality, sweet wine favored in Renaissance Rome</note>, and two loaves <note>original: "cacchiatas"</note> of fresh bread for their mid-morning meal, according to the custom of the greater dining hall.

### CHAPTER XXXVI.
*Regarding the funeral rites of the Reverend Lords Cardinals.*

At the funeral rites of the Reverend Lords Cardinals, all singers are required to attend without surplices <note>original: "cottis"; short white vestments</note> for the purpose of singing the Mass of the funeral itself. For the singing of such funerals, fifteen gold ducats of the chamber <note>original: "ducati auri de camera"; high-value currency issued by the papal treasury</note> are owed to the aforementioned singers, and

<column-break/>

forty pounds of wax tapers; and for the two sopranos who began the singing of the funeral office, two wax torches are owed, which are to be burned during the said funeral. Any singer who is absent at the conclusion of the Epistle of the funeral Mass shall receive only one taper and shall be fined two *carolinos* <note>a silver coin, often called a *carlino*</note>.

### CHAPTER XXXVII.
*Regarding the business of the Chapel to be handled by the Deputies.*

It is found in practice that the singers currently in the said Chapel, regardless of their place of origin, are grouped and divided into three nations: namely, the Italian, the French, and the Spanish, according to which one each person can most conveniently be assigned, and in which he is experienced in the mother tongue of that country or nation. Whenever any business must be sought or conducted on behalf of the said Chapel, the singers, gathered as a college, must elect or nominate three singers—namely, one from each nation. Once they have received their commission from the aforementioned college, they shall diligently pursue or conduct the business entrusted to them, without exceeding the limits of their commission. If any other singer involves himself in the business of the Chapel without the license or commission of the said college, he shall be punished with a penalty to be imposed upon him by the college.

### CHAPTER XXXVIII.
*Regarding the Abbey.*

In the said Chapel, there is an elective dignity, removable at the will of the aforementioned college, commonly called the Abbey <note>original: "Abbatia"</note>. Every year, for the purpose of governing this abbey, there is ap— <note>The text ends mid-word on the catchword "cre-", likely meaning "appointed" or "created" (creatur)</note>

# CONSTITUTIONS
<page-num>392</page-num>

...one is appointed from the college of singers, into whose hands all ordinary or extraordinary provisions, salaries, stipends, royal gifts, emoluments, and revenues coming to the aforementioned college of singers in any way or manner are placed. The singer elected in this way shall receive a double gratuity <note>original: "manciam"; a customary cash distribution or tip given to members of the papal household</note> and, on the Feast of the Purification, two wax torches bestowed by Our Most Holy Lord [the Pope], just as the Dean of the Chapel is accustomed to receive.

## CHAPTER XXXIX.
### *How the new Abbot is to be elected.*

In the creation of a new Abbot <note>the 'Abbot' of the college was an administrative leader chosen from among the singers, rather than a monastic superior</note>, between the first and sixth day of the month of January, all singers must be gathered as a college by the Dean of the same Chapel. If the singer previously elected as Abbot is found to be capable and sufficient for the rule or administration of such an Abbey, he may be confirmed anew for the following year. However, if he has committed any serious offense, or has behaved fraudulently in the administration of said Abbey, or should be found incapable, or if it otherwise seems right to the said college, he must be removed. They must then elect another suitable and sufficient singer as Abbot from another nation—namely the Italian, French, or Spanish, according to whose turn it is—to rule and govern such an Abbey. He must swear an oath in the hands of the Dean to behave well and faithfully in the administration of the said Abbey. It is, however, declared that every Abbot is bound to give an account of the administration performed by him for the said Abbey.

<column-break/>

## CHAPTER XL.
### *Of the Marker.*

There is also in the said Chapel an elective official, removable at the will of the said college, commonly called the <term>Marker</term> <note>original: "Punctator"; the official responsible for 'marking' or noting absences and tardiness to calculate fines</note>. This office must be exercised by one of the more senior singers who is capable, fit, and expert in the constitutions and observances of the said Chapel. All singers are required to be present as a college for his election. Once the election is held, the Dean of the said Chapel administers the oath to the same elected singer, which the elected singer shall swear in the hands of the Dean: that he will behave well and faithfully in the said office entrusted to him. Once the oath is taken, he shall be given the faculty to choose one junior <note>original: "modernum"</note> singer from another nation to be enrolled to assist in marking whenever there is need. If any singer should quarrel with the said Marker regarding the execution of this office, or refuse to pay the fines <note>original: "puncta"; literally 'points' or marks against one's record</note> affecting him, he must be punished by the said college of singers, for by quarreling with the said official, he has brought shame upon the whole college. Furthermore, if the said elected Marker should maliciously and falsely mark any singer, he must be punished as a perjurer, as was stated above concerning a singer who reveals the secrets of the Chapel. This Marker shall receive double gratuities, just like the Dean and the Abbot.

...on the second or third day after the said new singer has paid his royal dues <note>original: "regalia"; customary fees paid by new members of the college upon entry</note> to the same new singer, the Dean is bound to read all the constitutions of the college of the said Chapel individually. ### CHAPTER XLII.
->*Regarding the royal fees to be paid specifically to the Dean.*<-

A newly received singer is bound to pay individually to the Dean of the said Chapel one gold ducat of the chamber for a biretta <note>a square cap worn by clergy and members of the choir</note>. The Dean is bound to record or have written down the day of admission, the name and surname, and the diocese of the newly received singer in the books where such admissions and the names and surnames of other singers are described. He is also to teach the same new singer the manner or style of singing the lessons, prophecies, and anthems <note>original: "antiphonas"</note> in the said Chapel; and this is to be done after he has fulfilled his duty to the Dean, as mentioned above.

### CHAPTER XLIII.
->*Regarding the celebration of the Divine Office in the said Chapel by the singers and the college.*<-

First, the bell-ringing clerics are bound to ring the small bells <note>original: "campanellas"</note> in the morning, one hour after the final bell of St. Peter's has sounded. At the sound of the 

<column-break/>

aforementioned [bells], all singers are obliged to enter the Chapel of St. Paul and first pray before God. Having prayed, they are to put on their surplices <note>original: "cottis"; short white liturgical vestments</note>. One of the weekly soprano singers <note>original: "sopranorum hebdomadariorum"; a singer assigned to lead the services for that specific week</note> shall begin secretly with the *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>, and then in a loud voice: "O Lord, open my lips, etc." <note>original: "Domine labia mea aperies"; the traditional opening of the Roman Catholic Divine Office</note>. If any singer is not present at the start of the office in the chapel—namely, by the end of the "Glory be to the Father, etc." <note>original: "Gloria Patri"; the doxology ending the first psalm</note> of the first psalm—he shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur"; literally "marked" or "pricked" on a list for a deduction from his pay</note> three bajocchi <note>a copper coin of the Papal States</note>.

### CHAPTER XLIV.
->*How Prime is to be celebrated on Sunday.*<-

On Sunday, the office of Prime <note>the first of the "Little Hours" of the daily prayer cycle</note> must be celebrated by reading in a loud voice. Whoever among the singers is not present in the chapel by the end of the "Glory be to the Father, etc." of the first psalm, shall be fined three bajocchi.

### CHAPTER XLV.
->*How Prime is to be celebrated on other days of the entire year.*<-

On other days, both feast days and weekdays, Sunday excepted, the office of Prime is to be celebrated by singing. Whoever among the singers was not present in the chapel by the time the "Glory be to the Father, etc." of the first psalm is finished, shall be fined two quattrini <note>a small copper coin of lower value than a bajocco</note>.

### CHAPTER XLVI.
->*Regarding Terce.*<-

The office of Terce <note>the mid-morning hour of prayer</note> is to be sung every day of the entire year. If any singer is absent at the end of the "Glory be to the Father, etc." of the first psalm, he must be fined two quattrini.

# CONSTITUTIONS
<page-num>394</page-num>

### CHAPTER XLVII.
*Concerning the Mass.*

The Mass is to be celebrated with singing, as is customary; and any singer who is found to be absent at the conclusion of the epistle of the Mass itself shall be marked for a fine <note>original: "puncto notabitur"; literally "noted with a point," referring to the record-keeper marking a penalty against their name</note> of three baiocchi <note>a small copper coin used in the Papal States</note>.

### CHAPTER XLVIII.
*Concerning Sext during the season of Lent.*

The office of Sext <note>the midday prayer service of the Divine Office</note> shall be sung at the end of Mass every day of the year, except for vigils. Any singer who is absent, as mentioned above, at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* <note>original: "Gloria Patri &c."</note> of the first psalm shall be fined two quattrini <note>a low-value copper coin; four quattrini made one baiocco</note>.

### CHAPTER XLIX.
*Concerning None, Vespers, and Compline.*

When the bells of St. Peter's have rung at the usual hour, the bell-ringing clerics shall ring the bell of the Palace. At that time, all singers are required to be present in the chapel and to be dressed in their surplices <note>original: "cottis"</note>. The weekly ministers <note>original: "hebdomadarii"; those assigned to lead the services for that week</note> shall begin None <note>the mid-afternoon prayer service</note>, and they shall proceed together to complete Vespers <note>the evening prayer</note> and Compline <note>the final prayer of the day</note> through singing. Any singer who is absent from the chapel at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the first psalm of the said office of None shall be fined six quattrini.

Once the office of None is finished, the weekly minister shall begin to sing Vespers; any singer who was not present at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the first psalm of the said Vespers shall be fined twenty-two and a half quattrini.

After Vespers are finished, one soprano singer shall begin to sing *Grant, Lord, a blessing* <note>original: "Iube Domine benedicere"</note> in the accustomed place, and the weekly minister shall continue his office. If any singer is absent at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the first psalm of the said Compline, he is to be fined six quattrini.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER L.
*Concerning the verses to be sung in the chapel.*

All the verses of the individual hours, both in the daily chapel service and in Papal Vespers and Matins <note>the night or early morning prayer service</note>, must be sung by the soprano singers—specifically by the last and second-to-last singers admitted to the college, when they are required to be sung. It is not required that they be priests, provided they are among those most recently admitted to the chapel. On weekdays, one of these sopranos—specifically the most recently admitted—is required to sing alone.

### CHAPTER LI.
*Concerning Papal Masses celebrated by the Supreme Pontiff.*

When the Supreme Pontiff <note>the Pope</note> intends to celebrate Mass in St. Peter’s or elsewhere, the singers must sing Terce <note>the mid-morning prayer service</note> in the choir while the Pope recites the same Terce to himself. Any singer not found present at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the first psalm of the said Terce shall be fined two giulii <note>a silver coin worth ten baiocchi</note>. Anyone not found in the choir for the whole Introit <note>the opening chant of the Mass</note>, namely from the *Lord, have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie eleison"</note> of the Mass, shall be similarly fined another two giulii. Anyone absent for the entire Mass is to be fined for the whole duration, namely ten giulii.

Furthermore, the singers should always be attentive in responding to the Supreme Pontiff, especially on Easter Sunday <note>original: "diebus paschatis Resurrectionis"</note> when His Holiness says *World without end* <note>original: "per omnia secula seculorum"</note> and when he begins the *Our Father* <note>original: "Pater noster"</note>. The singers must not respond *Amen* because on that specific day, while a certain Supreme Pontiff was once celebrating and sang *World without end*, the Angels themselves were heard to respond *Amen*.

## CHAPTER LII.
### *Concerning Papal Vespers.*

In Papal Vespers <note>The evening prayer of the Divine Office when the Pope is presiding</note> to be celebrated in the Sistine Chapel, in the Basilica of St. Peter, or elsewhere, all singers are bound to be present. Specifically, they must be in the choir dressed in their surplices <note>original: "cottis"</note> awaiting the Supreme Pontiff or the College of the Reverend Lord Cardinals who wish to attend or celebrate the Vespers. And whichever singer is absent at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* <note>original: "Gloria Patri &c."</note> of the first psalm of the said Vespers shall be fined <note>original: "punctabitur"; literally "punctuated," meaning a mark was placed against their name in the attendance book</note> five giulii <note>original: "iuliis"; a silver coin of the Papal States</note>; and if he is absent for the entirety of the said Vespers, he shall be fined the full amount, namely ten giulii.

## CHAPTER LIII.
### *Concerning Papal Masses.*

Similarly, in Papal Masses to be celebrated in the Sistine Chapel, in St. Peter’s, or elsewhere in the presence of the Supreme Pontiff or the College of the Reverend Lord Cardinals—provided it is a Papal Mass—all singers are bound to be present in the choir dressed in their surplices, awaiting the arrival of the Supreme Pontiff or the College of Cardinals to celebrate the Mass. Any singer who is absent from the choir through the entire Introit <note>the opening chant of the Mass</note>, specifically before the *Lord have mercy* <note>original: "Kyrie eleison"</note>, shall be fined two giulii. If he remains absent even at the end of the Epistle, he shall be fined five giulii and shall lose the *regalia* <note>a special bonus or supplemental payment given for participating in high-ranking ceremonies</note> of that Mass. If, however, he is absent for the entire Mass, he shall be fined the full amount, namely ten giulii, and shall lose the *regalia* of that Mass.

## CHAPTER LIV.
### *Concerning the Matins of the night of the Nativity of the Lord.*

For the Matins <note>the night-time prayer service</note> of the Nativity of Our Lord Jesus Christ <note>Christmas</note>, all singers are bound to come

<column-break/>

to the chapel and, dressed in their surplices at the hour designated by the Supreme Pontiff, once the Matins have been started by the Supreme Pontiff or one of the Reverend Lord Cardinals, the Invitatory <note>the opening chant of Matins</note> of the said Matins must be sung—namely, *Christ is born to us, etc.* <note>original: "Christus natus est nobis &c."</note>—by two soprano singers. The choir must repeat the same in the "greater plainchant" <note>original: "cantu plano maiore"; a solemn or elaborated form of chant</note> for the first and last repetitions; the choir shall similarly continue the *Come let us adore, etc.* <note>original: "Venite adoremus &c."</note> in the greater plainchant, as is customary. The first three antiphons <note>short chants before a psalm</note> of the first nocturn <note>a division of the Matins service</note> and likewise the first Responsory <note>a chant following a scripture reading</note> are to be sung by the choir in counterpoint <note>original: "contrapuncto"; polyphonic music where different voices sing different melodies simultaneously</note> with repetitions, as is customary. The other antiphons of the other two nocturns are not sung in counterpoint, nor are the other responsories, except for the eighth responsory, which is sung in counterpoint. Whichever of the singers is absent at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the first psalm of the said Matins shall be fined four giulii; he who is similarly absent at the end of the *Glory be to the Father, etc.* of the second nocturn shall be fined three giulii. If he is absent from the entire office and from the music of the said Mass, he shall be fined the full amount, namely ten giulii, and shall lose the *regalia* of that Mass. Let it be noted that the Pontiff intones the *We praise thee, O God, etc.* <note>original: "Te Deum laudamus &c."</note> when he is present.

## CHAPTER LV.
### *Concerning the Matins of Tenebrae.*

The office of the Matins of Tenebrae <note>original: "matutinis tenebrarum"; the solemn services held during the last three days of Holy Week characterized by the gradual extinguishing of candles</note> is usually sung in plainchant <note>original: "cantu firmo"; literally "fixed song," referring to traditional Gregorian chant</note> and with devotion, and not in counterpoint. ...the Supreme Pontiff or the Reverend Lord Cardinals coming to the customary chapel; and any singer who is not present in the choir at the end of the first psalm is to be fined <note>original: "punctandus est"; literally "to be pointed," referring to a mark made against a name in the attendance ledger to docked pay</note> five giulii <note>original: "iuliis"; a silver coin used in the Papal States</note>, and if he is not present for the entire office, he shall be fined ten giulii.

### CHAPTER LVI.

*Concerning Vespers and Matins for the Dead.*

Vespers for the dead are to be said at the customary hour, and if any singer is not present by the end of the first psalm of the said Vespers, he shall be fined five giulii; similarly, if he is not present at the end of the first psalm of the first nocturn <note>one of the three major divisions of the night office of Matins</note> of Matins, he is to be fined ten giulii in total.

### CHAPTER LVII.

*Concerning the recitation of readings and prophecies.*

In Papal Matins, the singers are required to sing the readings when they are not sung by the Cardinals. The last-appointed singer <note>original: "ultimus cantor"; referring to the most junior member in terms of service</note> shall begin by singing the first reading, the second-to-last the second reading, and the rest of the singers must follow in succession according to their seniority. The same procedure is to be followed for the prophecies <note>biblical readings of a prophetic nature, common in the older Roman liturgy</note>. New singers must be instructed by the more senior members on the proper manner of singing these readings and prophecies. If any singer is unable to sing the reading or prophecy assigned to him for any reason, he must arrange for another singer to sing it in his place. Any singer who is not found present at the end of the first prophecy of Holy Saturday <note>original: "Sabathi sancti"</note> shall be fined two giulii.

<column-break/>

### CHAPTER LVIII.

*Concerning the Procession and Mass of the Body of Christ.*

At the hour designated by the Supreme Pontiff on the Feast of the Body of Christ <note>Corpus Christi</note>, all singers shall go to the Chapel of St. Paul, where, dressed in their surplices <note>original: "cottis"</note>, they shall await the arrival of the Supreme Pontiff and the Reverend Lord Cardinals in the said Chapel. Whichever singer has not arrived at the said Chapel by the appointed hour, or is not present with the other singers in his surplice for the procession before the Cross leaves the palace gate, shall be fined five giulii. Similarly, if he is not present by the end of the Epistle <note>the reading from the letters of the Apostles in the Mass</note> of the Mass to be celebrated in St. Peter's, he shall be fined ten giulii.

### CHAPTER LIX.

*Concerning the singing of Mass outside the Chapel.*

Whenever a Mass is sung outside the Chapel—whether before one or several Cardinals at the request of the Reverend Lord Master of the Chapel or the college of singers—as long as it is chanted outside the Chapel, any singer who is not present by the end of the Epistle shall be fined two carlini <note>original: "Carolenis"; another type of silver currency</note> and shall lose any royalties <note>original: "regalia"; special distributions or fees paid to participants</note> from that Mass, if there be any.

We, the undersigned Masters and singers, have unanimously accepted, provided for, and sworn to all the aforementioned rules, and therefore we have signed our names.

It is so. Ludovico, Bishop of Assisi, Master of the Chapel.

The other names and signatures of the said singers follow.

# THE ART OF CHANTING
## OR
## THE ART OF PSALMODIZING OR SINGING OF THE GREEKS.
### *From the St. Blaise Tables.* <note>original Latin: "Ex Tabulis San-Blasianis." These refer to musical tables found in the library of the Abbey of Saint Blaise in the Black Forest, published by Martin Gerbert in the 18th century.</note> (a)

Table N. 1.
**A** beginning, with the help of Holy God, of the signs <note>original: "σημαδίων" (sēmadia); the neumes or notation marks used in Byzantine music</note> of the art of chanting, both of the ascending and descending "bodies" and "spirits," and of every hand-gesture <term>cheironomia; the ancient practice of directing a choir through rhythmic and melodic hand movements</term> of the sequence, as composed for it by the poets of various times, both ancient and new.

The Beginning, Middle, End, and the system of all the signs. The **Equal sign** <note>original: "ἴσον" (ison); the fundamental note or drone that maintains a steady pitch</note> exists because without it the voice cannot stay straight; it is called "voiceless," not because it has no sound—for it is indeed sounded—but because it is not measured, due to its total equality. (**Table N. II.**) The "Equal" is chanted through all equality; the **Little sign** <note>original: "ὀλίγον" (oligon); indicates an ascending step of one tone</note> through all ascent, and the **Apostrophe** <note>original: "ἀπόστροφος" (apostrophos); indicates a descending step</note> through all descent. The signs are: Equal, Little, Acute, Apostrophe, Fluttering, Lightening, Pelason, Prick, Double Prick, the High, Apostrophe, two linked Apostrophes, Light, Low, Outflow, and the Under-flowing Prick. Of these, some are **bodies** and some are **spirits**.

The **bodies** <note>original: "σώματα" (sōmata); in Byzantine theory, these are neumes that represent a single step in the scale</note> are the Little, the Acute, the Fluttering, the Lightening, the Elastron, and the Double Prick; and among the descending signs, the Apostrophe and the two linked Apostrophes. There are also four **spirits** <note>original: "πνεύματα" (pneumata); neumes that represent intervals larger than a single step, which must be "carried" by a body sign</note>, (**Table N. III.**) and the descending spirits are the Light and the Low; the Outflow is neither a body nor a spirit, but a brief movement of the throat.

<column-break/>

Those that possess "voice" <note>referring to signs that have a specific pitch value or interval</note> are the Little, the Acute, the Fluttering, the Lightening, the Pelason, the Prick, the Double Prick, the High, the Apostrophe, the two Apostrophes, the Light, the Low, and the Under-flowing Sustainer. Within these signs, the entire melody of the art of chanting rises and falls.

The "voiceless" Great Signs, which are called the **Great Hypostases** <note>original: "μεγάλαι ὑποστάσεις"; these are auxiliary signs that do not have their own pitch but indicate ornaments, dynamics, or phrasing</note>, are these: (**Table N. IV.**) the Equal <note>here referring to a specific sustaining mark</note>, the Double Interceder, the Sustainer, the Roll, the Anti-empty-roll, the Tremolo, the Diverter, the Trembling Gathering, the Reckoner, the Reckoner-Gatherer, the Fast, the Slow, the Syrma, the Anti-emptier, the Level, the Inner Positioning, the Outer Positioning, the Awakening, the Supplication, the Second Supplication, the Dry-break, the Slow-compound, and the Fast-compound. Others pertaining to the chanter: the Contribution, the Flaying, the Place-and-Release, the Simple Position, the Dance-step, the Shaking, (**Table N. V.**) the Gathering, the Beginning, the Grasp, the Heavy sign, and the Bend. There are also these **Phthoreis** <note>original: "Φθορέων" (phthoreis); "corrupters" or modulating signs that change the scale/mode of a piece</note> for the modes: for the First, the Second, the Third, the Fourth, the Grave Plagal, the Nenano, the Half-voice, and the Half-corrupter for the Grave Plagal and the Plagal Fourth. There are also the "half-slows": the Sustainer, the Double, and the two linked Apostrophes, while the "Snap" <note>original: "τζάκισμα" (tzakisma); a rhythmic ornament</note> holds a half-duration.

### LETTER OF METROPHANES CRITOPULUS.

<note>Metrophanes Critopulus was a significant 17th-century theologian who traveled extensively in Europe, seeking to bridge the gap between the Greek Orthodox and Protestant traditions.</note>

O man, by proposing such difficulties to me—which another might have passed by heedlessly, not understanding at all what these names signify—you show that you have achieved great power in extensive learning. For it is impossible for someone who reads each word closely and attentively not to step, within a short time, upon the threshold of great erudition. If I had more leisure, I would have made a longer response. But now, since I am occupied by so many matters that I cannot even "tweak my ear" <note>A Greek idiom meaning to have a moment of rest or to pay attention to something else</note> to devote time to writing (for you see me preparing for a journey), I am forced to make my answer briefly. I ask you to be content with what is here and to receive it as kindly as possible.

Your difficulty, or rather your question, concerns what the names contained in this book mean: **Heirmos**, **Troparion**, **Kontakion**, **Hypakoe**, **Exaposteilarion**, **Photagogikon**, and **Canon**. An **Heirmos** <note>original: "εἱρμὸς" (heirmos), meaning a 'link' or 'connection'</note> is a melody which, according to its sound, is referred to one of the **eight modes** <note>original: "ὀκτὼ ἤχων" (oktō ēchōn); the system of eight musical scales used in Byzantine chant</note> (for there are eight modes among us in music, or rather in the art of chanting). Regarding the "bending" and "turning" <note>Refers to the melodic contour and cadence</note> of the melody, it preserves a certain specific style that differs from other *Heirmoi*. There are many *Heirmoi* referred to one mode or another, and it is possible for many *Troparia* to be referred back to one *Heirmos*.

A **Troparion** <note>original: "Τροπάριον" (troparion)</note> is strictly speaking a melody that does not have its own unique tune, but is chanted according to a certain *Heirmos*. It is called a *Troparion* because it "turns" <note>original: "τρεπόμενον" (trepomenon), from the verb 'trepo'</note> toward that *Heirmos* to which it is chanted... For the sake of an example, look in this book on page 333. You will find the *Heirmos* "In the depth he once laid low" <note>original: "ἐν βυθῷ κατέστρωσέ ποτε" (en bythō katestrōse pote); a famous hymn celebrating the crossing of the Red Sea</note> (though it is not written out in full because it is customary and known to all), and the *Troparia* follow after it.

<column-break/>

Most honored Sir! Your skill seems to me to acquire great strength in the abundance of learning, since it has proposed to me those doubts which another person, not much concerned with the meaning of these words, would have passed over inconsiderately. For it cannot be otherwise than that he will shortly obtain a high degree of manifold erudition who contemplates individual words with a fixed and attentive mind. Indeed, I would respond at greater length if I had more leisure; but now, since I am distracted by such business that I cannot even "pluck my ear" <note>A Latin variation of the Greek idiom, meaning he is too busy to even notice a distraction</note> to find time for discourse (for you see me preparing my departure), I am forced to respond briefly. I ask you to be satisfied with these things and to kindly accept what I was able to give.

Your doubt or question pertains to the understanding of the names contained in this booklet: **Heirmos**, **Troparion**, **Kontakion**, **Hypakoe**, **Exaposteilarion**, **Photagogikon**, and **Canon**. And so, an **Heirmos** <note>original: "εἱρμὸς", translated here as "tractus"</note> is a musical measure which, as far as the singing voice is concerned, is related to one of the **eight sounds** (for we have eight sounds of the musical or chanting art). As for the "flexing" and "turning" of the modulation, it preserves a certain proper mode, differing from other *Heirmoi*. There are many *Heirmoi* brought into different sounds, to which many *Troparia* can be "inflected" <note>Meaning the verses are molded to fit the melody of the model strophe</note>.

A **Troparion** <note>original: "τροπάριον"</note> is properly a musical measure which is deprived of its own singing rationale; it can, however, be chanted to a certain *Heirmos*, and for that reason it is called a *Troparion*, as if "turned" toward that *Heirmos* to which it harmonizes. If you look for the sake of an example in this booklet on page 333, you will find the *Heirmos* which begins: "In the depth he once laid low," (although it is not written in its entirety, because it is common and [known]...

<meta>The Latin text cuts off at "and," with the catchword "omnibus" (to all) indicating the start of the next page.</meta>

# OF METROPHANES CRITOPULUS

...four, until the phrase: *On the rock of faith* <note>original Greek: "Ἐν πέτρα μετῆς πίστεως" (En petra metēs pisteōs)</note>, which is the **Heirmos** <note>The model stanza that provides the melody and rhythm for a hymn</note> of the third ode. It is called a **Troparion** <note>A short hymn of one stanza</note> only in a loose sense, because it is not sung according to a model melody (as proper troparia are), nor does it have other verses that follow its pattern (as heirmoi usually do). You will find such hymns in the **Menologion** <note>A service book containing hymns and lives of saints arranged by the days of the month</note> on page 166 for every day of the entire year. These are also called **Apolytikia** <note>original Greek: "Ἀπολυτίκια" (Apolytikia)</note>, because they are the last of all the hymns sung, performed at the dismissal <note>original: "apolysis," meaning the end of the service</note> of the church assembly.

**Kontakion** <note>original: "Κοντάκιον" (Kontakion)</note> is a Palestinian word meaning a small, rolled-up and folded piece of paper. Certain hymns received this name from the following history. They say there was a certain monk named Romanus—later surnamed **the Melodist**—who originally had an unpleasant and very harsh voice. Because he was despondent that he was unable to sing along with his brothers, he was overcome by sleep in the church due to his distress around the feast of the Nativity of Christ. It is said that the ever-virgin Mother of God and Lady, Mary, appeared to him and offered him a rolled and folded paper (which they call a *kontakion*). In his dream, he seemed to eat it, and when he woke up, he immediately began to sing by divine inspiration a certain hymn that begins: *The Virgin today gives birth to the Supersubstantial One* <note>original: "Ἡ παρθένος σήμερον τὸν ὑπερούσιον τίκτει." This refers to Christ being "beyond essence" or "divine."</note>. This hymn is found on the 25th of December. He named the hymn a *kontakion* after the shape of the paper he believed he had eaten. From that time on, they say he wrote over a thousand *kontakia*, of which about four hundred survive among us today. From that moment, his voice was so beautiful that he was deemed worthy of the title "the Melodist."

<column-break/>

...known to all), which is followed by four troparia until the melody: *On the rock of faith*, which refers to the third song. In a loose sense, however, it is a troparion, because it is neither sung to a specific model melody (as troparia properly so called are), nor does it have other musical measures shaped according to its own pattern, in the way that model melodies have their own troparia. You will find hymns of this kind in the Menologion on page 166 for each day of the whole year, which are also called *Apolytikia*, because they are sung as the last of all hymns when the holy assembly is dissolved.

*Kontakion* is a Palestinian word, signifying a rolled-up and folded little scroll, and the hymns took this name from the following story. They say a certain monk named Romanus, later nicknamed the Melodist, at first had a voice that was unlovely and quite harsh. When he despaired of equaling his companions in voice, his body being weighed down by sadness around the feast of the birth of Christ, sleep overcame him in the temple. Then the Virgin Mary, always incorrupt, the Mother of God and our Lady, appeared to him and held out a rolled and folded scroll, which is called a *kontakion* among them. When he seemed to eat it and was released from sleep, he immediately sang a certain hymn from divine inspiration, which goes like this: *The Virgin today gives birth to the Supersubstantial*, which stands on the 25th day of December. He named it a *kontakion* from the form of the scroll which he thought he had eaten. From then on, they say he composed more than a thousand *kontakia*, of which nearly four hundred remain among us, and from this time he sang so sweetly that he was even held worthy of the nickname "the Melodist."
