<meta>This page continues the letter of Metrophanes Critopulus, a 17th-century Greek theologian and later Patriarch of Alexandria. The previous page concluded the story of St. Romanos the Melodist and began defining specific types of liturgical hymns used in the Eastern Orthodox tradition.</meta>

# LETTER OF METROPHANES CRITOPULUS

**Hypakoe** <note>original Greek: Ὑπακοὴ (Hypakoē); literally "obedience" or "listening"</note> is a hymn and a short poem, having as its subject the Resurrection of the Lord, which He Himself brought about by becoming (as a man) obedient to the Father unto death. Because it encompasses the great deed of valor achieved by Christ through obedience—I mean, of course, the Resurrection—it was named "Obedience."

**Exaposteilarion** <note>original Greek: Ἐξαποσελάριον (Exaposelarion); a variant of Exaposteilarion, meaning "sent out"</note>. This is a hymn having as its subject the mission of the apostles, when Christ Himself, after the Resurrection, sent them out into the world to preach the Gospel. Such *exaposteilaria* are not found here, but in the book called the **Octoechus** <note>original: ὀκτωήχω (oktōēchō); the "Book of Eight Tones," the primary liturgical book for Sunday services</note>. Those found here are called *exaposteilaria* by the same name but in a loose sense, not because they contain the subject matter I mentioned, but because they are sung daily at the same time as the proper *exaposteilaria* are sung on Sundays.

**Photagogikon** <note>original: Φωταγωγικόν (Phōtagōgikon); literally "leading to light"</note>. This is a morning hymn, containing a petition for the spiritual and true light, and for this reason it is called "Light-bringer."

**Canon** <note>original: Κανών (Kanōn); meaning "rule" or "standard"</note>. These are many hymns organized under a single "rule." A "Canon," according to the present study, signifies a hymnody; not a song that can be chanted in just any way, but one composed according to the style and the melody which the preceding **heirmoi** <note>original: εἱρμοὶ (heirmoi); lead stanzas that set the meter and melody</note> require. Canons consist of nine, eight, four, three, or at the very least, two odes. In each ode, the *heirmos* is placed first, having a subject from the Old Testament. Then come the **troparia** <note>original: τροπάρια (troparia); short stanzas</note> having subjects from the New Testament, or whatever the poet desires. You will find such canons in this book on Folios 321, 333, 340, 346, 355, and 410.

<column-break/>

**Hypakoe** <note>original Latin: Ὑπακοὴ</note> is also a concise hymn, having as its theme the resurrection of the Lord, which He performed when He showed Himself obedient to the Father (insofar as He was a man) even unto death. Since it therefore encompasses that great virtue—I mean the resurrection—which resulted favorably for Christ through obedience, it is called *hypakoe*.

**Exaposteilarion** <note>original Latin: Ἐξαποσελάριον</note> is a hymn concerning the mission of the apostles, when Christ, after the resurrection, sent them out into the world to announce the Gospel. However, these *exaposteilaria* are not found in this book, but in another, which is called the **Octoechus**. Those which are indeed in this book are called *exaposteilaria* homonymously and in a loose sense, not because they contain the theme I described, but because they are sung daily at the same time that the properly-named *exaposteilaria* are sung on Sundays.

**Photagogikon** <note>original Latin: Φωταγωγικόν</note> is a morning hymn, encompassing a prayer for the spiritual and true light, and for that reason it is named the *Photagogikon*.

**Canon** <note>original Latin: Κανών</note>. There are many hymns bound to a single "rule." A "Canon" in the present work signifies a song, not to be performed in various ways, but according to the method and measure which the preceding lead melodies <note>original Latin: "tractus," here translating the Greek "heirmos"</note> require. Canons consist of odes numbering nine, eight, four, three, or at minimum two. In any given ode, the lead melody occupies the first place, having a theme from the Old Testament; the second place is held by the *troparia*, which encompass themes of the New Testament, or whatever the author wishes. You will find such canons in this book on pages 321, 333, 340, 346, 355, and 410.

# LETTER OF METROPHANES CRITOPULUS.

<note>The following text appears first in Greek and then in Latin; both versions are translated here into a single English flow, as they are identical in content.</note>

This, then, is the explanation of the names <note>referring to the liturgical terms defined on the previous page</note> about which you previously asked; I earnestly pray that you receive it with kindness. If these things have been stated by me too briefly, do not be surprised. For first, I employed brevity because I was writing to a man capable of understanding great things from small ones, and much from a little. Second, it is because time would not grant me further leisure. Farewell to you, most honored man, in both the inner and outer person, in the Lord Jesus Christ, the one of the most Holy Trinity—the <term>God-man</term> <note>original Greek: Θεανθρώπῳ (Theanthrōpō); Latin: Theantropo. A theological term for Christ being both fully God and fully human.</note> and our only Savior.

In Nuremberg. In the year of our reconciliation with God, 1626, on the 18th of the month of <term>Skirophorion</term> <note>An ancient Athenian month roughly corresponding to June; the Latin text provides the date as May 14.</note>.

Metrophanes Critopulus, <term>hieromonk</term> <note>original Greek: ἱερομόναχος (hieromonachos); a monk who is also an ordained priest.</note>, a devoted admirer of your renown.

<column-break/>

This is therefore the explanation of the names, about which you asked before, which I ask you again and again to receive benevolently. But if these things have been said too concisely, do not wonder. First, I used brevity, since I was writing to a man who can attain great things from small, and many from few; second, because the time did not wish to grant me more leisure. Farewell, most honored man, according to both the inner and outer man, in the Lord Christ Jesus, the one of the most holy Trinity—the God-man, and our only Savior.

At Nuremberg, in the year of our reconciliation with God 1626, on the 14th of May.

Metrophanes Critopulus, hieromonk, a cultivator of your fame.
